Headline: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
Body: Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say. A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill. Milburn has said the government spends Â£22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics. He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support . Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits. Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them. The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from Â£5,000 to Â£10,000. But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow". Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost Â£5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage. She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around Â£60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". Salon-owner Collette Osborne says she is "inundated" with CVs from young people She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups. Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds. But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from Â£10.85 to Â£11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from Â£12.71 to Â£13.21. "I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government". "I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said. Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029". But Whately said it is "just absurd that they are taxing businesses here and they're going to subsidise things that look like jobs over here. Just stop doing the taxing". She said the Tories want to halve employer NI costs "because I talk to businesses who say they really want to employ young people but they just can't afford to anymore and the regulation that the Labour Party has put in place has made it harder". Milburn will say that if the government does go ahead with a gradual reduction in NI over five years, it should start with businesses such as shops, bars and restaurants. Headline: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
Body: The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC. Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker. Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers. The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them". Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power. Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food. "This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said. He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all. Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. "The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said. "If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union." The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional Â£5bn. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading. Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included. Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said. But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules. He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found. UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D. Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations. Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area. He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal". Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK. "I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said. Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said. Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations. "The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market. "Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said. Headline: Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
Body: The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years. Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week. Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five Â£1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges. "The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals. "She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come." The meeting with Modi was a late addition to the royal schedule after the Indian prime minister confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals. They will fly from Mumbai to Delhi for the meeting on Wednesday. "For the Prince, it represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage," a Kensington Palace spokesperson said. "We've seen him increasingly support the UK's diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level." The couple last met Modi on their official visit to India in 2016. The royal couple met Modi 10 years ago during a seven-day tour of India and Bhutan Arriving in Mumbai earlier on Monday Prince William posted a message about the trip on social media: "India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country." The royals will carry out a number of engagements in Mumbai related to the environment, cricket, young families and the Bollywood film industry. At an Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony, five innovations will be announced as winners of the million-pound prizes. Nominees range from projects to increase the number of electric rickshaws in India to a scheme able to detect wildfires faster than Nasa. The event will be hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers. Take That will perform and guests will include actor Rami Malek and Australian conservationist and TV presenter Robert Irwin, who joined Prince William when he was a surprise guest on The Graham Norton show last month . "There is a lot of environmental potential here in Mumbai," said Irwin. "There is also a huge amount of young people who have a passion for environmentalism and I think Earthshot is mobilising that here in India." Headline: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
Body: Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said. The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks. Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment. US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace. The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump. Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back". It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented. The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher. On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there". "Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design. On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine. "It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying. Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets. Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said. It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions. Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions. Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said. Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram. Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk. "On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram. "Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack." Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said. In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said. Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company. Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems. The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented. "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said. Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap? Headline: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
Body: Crew members stood atop HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch A Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol. The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest undersea deployment at sea for a British vessel. The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels. Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats. The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing. HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed , external when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault. The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet. Streeting said it "doesn't sit lightly" with him that crews were being asked to serve longer than intended. He said: "It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they've given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise. "I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent." Since 1969 the UK has always had at least one ballistic missile-armed submarine patrolling at sea in order to provide a "nuclear deterrent". The logic is that if Britain were under nuclear attack, it could launch a retaliatory strike on the aggressor, a concept known as mutually-assured destruction. The four 492ft (150m) long Vanguard-class submarines can carry up to 16 Trident missiles, each capable of delivering multiple warheads which are several times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome the crew home on Sunday In order to avoid detection the submarines remain submerged and in radio silence throughout the patrol because a transmission could give away their position. But they can ascend to shallower depths and receive encoded messages via a floating wire antenna or communications buoy. Crews have little contact with the loved ones apart from the "Familygram" - a 120-word message that arrives weekly, and they are not permitted to reply. Messages are vetted and bad news from home can be withheld if it might jeopardise the operational effectiveness of a crew member. Depending on the sea state they may be able to listen to radio bulletins. Most of the crew work in shifts of six hours on, six hours off and sleep in narrow bunks, sometimes nine to a cabin. Submariners returning from long patrols are said to find the outside world smells strange or even overwhelming because they have become so used to filtered air. Their distance perception could also be affected by living in such a confined space for so long and they are advised not to drive for a few days while they adjust. HMS Vanguard, seen here at Faslane, is thought to have set the previous Navy record for the longest patrol when it returned in April after 205 days at sea The Vanguard-class boats were commissioned in the 1990s with an expected service life of 25 years but are now expected to serve for up to 40 years before the first Dreadnought-class submarines start replacing them in the early 2030s. Streeting said that program was "on track" and that it was important to get those vessels out "as soon as possible". Patrols used to typically last three months but in recent years this has stretched to six or more because at least one of the boats has been out of action for refit or repairs. A major overhaul of HMS Vanguard at Devonport Dockyard in Plymouth dragged on for seven years before it returned to service in 2022. HMS Victorious is currently in dry dock undergoing a Â£560m "deep maintenance" that began in 2023, leaving only Vengeance, Vigilant and Vanguard operational. The previous record for a Royal Navy continuous undersea patrol is reported to have been set by Vanguard in April when it returned to Faslane after 205 days away. The patrol lengths of Russian or Chinese submarines are not known, but most navies are believed to send their vessels out for far shorter durations.

Headline: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
Body: A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed. Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse. City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon. Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

Headline: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
Body: Prince Harry made an emotional visit to meet injured war veterans inside Ukraine The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games. There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war." Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia. Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation. Prince Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted by a drone from the front "Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment. A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles. At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment. International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others. Mykhailo Damaskin, pictured with his dog Stitch, has received experimental treatment to walk That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again. In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes. He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla". "My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally. "I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo. At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind. He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet. In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine. And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you." Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties. Injured veterans took part in a game of wheelchair rugby Blast damage from missiles on an historic building in Lviv At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players. He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes. He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces. And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball. Ivan Voinov, who lost a leg, has learned to dance again with his wife Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again. He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity. At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome. A Banksy-style piece of street art in Lviv shows the missiles falling "Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime. He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games". There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham. The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges. Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect. "These people have so much to offer," he said. "Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation. Headline: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
Body: Russell Brand was accompanied by his wife, Laura, during his trial at Southwark Crown Court Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed. On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences. Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US. HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences. It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board. Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing. A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes. Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates. In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her. The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion. On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to." During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed. It featured the couple singing to the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together. Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty for the offences he had been jailed for. He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family". The Russell Brand I saw in court was not the flamboyant character most people will know Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says Male prisons are organised into four categories ranging from A, the highest security, to D, the lowest security open prisons. The HM Inspectorate of Prisons says Category C prisons, like HMP Littlehey, are for prisoners who "cannot be trusted in open conditions" but are not deemed as much of an escape risk. According to the Ministry of Justice, most prisoners are housed in Category C prisons, which provide training to help them resettle into the community upon release. Headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left Megaspeed in 2025, company says
Body: The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm. Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company. On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology. Headline: Cancer 'sponge' tests could be offered to more people with bad indigestion
Body: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend. The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body. They tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England. Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term. It's thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind. For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. This collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it's gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor. Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment. Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country. "Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage." However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds. The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease. Final recommendations by NICE will be made in the new year. The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid. Over time, this can damage the lining of the oesophagus. A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way. Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux. 'I'm happy to be a guinea pig in cancer screening trial'

Headline: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
Body: Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital after an alleged attack last month Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee. The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas. In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery. "This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said. "I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour. Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns. The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate. Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family. "All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement. "We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation." Headline: Black Friday and tax return scams - don't fall for these
Body: This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you. That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year. Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information. Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out. If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January. Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC. Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , external , text message , external or phone call , external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer. New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October. There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information. it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: Pause and check , rather than being blinded by a countdown timer Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

Headline: 'I'd throw up in the car park': How school anxiety is harming children's futures
Body: 'It felt like I was dyingâ: Why some teenagers donât go to school Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September. She describes how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door. "It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she recalls. "If I was able to get in the car, we'd drive to school," she continues. "I'd probably normally either faint or throw up while we were sat in the car park." Eva's one of the thousands of school pupils in England who misses more than half the academic year. Experts say that children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training. A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday. Eva is autistic and stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education. Every morning, one of Eva's parents would call her teachers to tell them she wouldn't be going in that day, and she says she would stay at home watching YouTube videos and episodes of Horrible Histories "just to try and keep up". Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school This year, she has started at an alternative provision school which has smaller class sizes, therapy animals and more freedom to take breaks. But she still worries about her future and whether her record of school avoidance might turn off future employers. Eva recognises that many older people will assume "tough love" is the answer, and that they might even call pupils like her lazy - but she believes the situation is more complex. "We're not lazy, we want to go, we want to do something, we want to live our lives, but we can't," she says. Eva now attends an alternative provision school with smaller class sizes Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels. In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%. The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000. Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people. New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24. "Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice. "That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day." Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days â the threshold for persistent absence. In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs". Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school. "The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains. Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education. "We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in." Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education. She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy." Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them. Paul Browne is an assistant principal at Cheshire College South & West "We're seeing [most of] our students now are more like they were before Covid, where doing exams and coming to college is the norm. But there's still that small cohort [who struggle] and it's about getting them ready and helping them back into education." Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago in year 10. "We didn't do our Sats because that's when the first lockdown hit," she recalls. "It was so isolating and so strange, but I loved it. I was able to sit in my own room and do schoolwork. "Going back into school, it was difficult. I started struggling with panic attacks a lot, to the point where I was being pulled out of classes." Mali was diagnosed with autism when she was 15.â¯ After she stopped attending school, her mental health deteriorated to the point where she didn't leave her bedroom. "It was like the second I got past my doorframe, my whole body would stop. My legs would go numb, my head would tense. It felt like I was dying. I can't explain it any other way." "I do get quite emotional about it. I feel like I've tried so hard and I went to school for so long and I went through so much and I have nothing to show for it. I don't have my GCSEs, I didn't even do my Sats." Headline: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
Body: Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall. More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. "I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs." In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word. That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges. The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves. But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root. The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country. The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".â¯ They had money, which back then meant power. This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent. But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger. Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there. "I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC. Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). â¯Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (Â£525bn). But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless. Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence. "They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round." And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion. "They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic. And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons. There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health." One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum. In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios. Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst. Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources. And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests. This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people. Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence. Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take". Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says. Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name. Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians. But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says. An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man. Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him. In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty. But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world. Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says. The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin. Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country. No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen. Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge. Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia toâ¦ [an] absence of the future". But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems. Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man." Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen." Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them? Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them? Body: The Daily Telegraph reports that former Prime Minister Boris Johnson believes "Britain would back Brexit" a second time if Andy Burnham forces anther vote on the issue. On Friday Andy Burnham will travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to seal an agreement on closer ties with the bloc. The Daily Express also leads on a potential bid for a Brexit reversal. It writes that campaigners are warning the prime minister that the UK would need to take in around 4,400 asylum seekers every year or pay Â£76m under the EU's asylum solidarity scheme. It also quotes Burnham as having recently said: "Britain has 'lost more than we gained' in the decade since the referendum". The Times leads with NHS leaders warning the government that new laws banning zero-hours contracts could make it harder to hire health workers and provide emergency cover for fire services in emergencies. Public sector bodies are urging a re-think of the plans before they come into force next year. A government spokesperson said: "We are committed to tackling the one-sided flexibility that can result from zero-hours and similar contracts". The Guardian says the prime minister has vowed early intervention to tackle the UK's youth joblessness crisis ahead of Alan Milburn's long-awaited report into the issue, to be released on Monday. Burnham's pledge includes more opportunities for vocational training in schools in a plan to help under-25s into employment and cut benefits bill. The Metro headlines on the government considering "a rethink on the age of consent" in the UK to prevent adults having relationships with 16- and 17-year-olds. It comes as a woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Russell Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed. Mia Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial, in which he was convicted of rape and sexual assault. The i-Paper says there is "mounting pressure" from campaigners to change the law, adding that ministers are considering a new "staggered" age of consent. Currently, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds under UK law. The Sun covers Brand's wife, Laura Brand, reading a statement from her husband as she returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday. Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US. The Financial Times writes that both democratic and republican lawmakers in the US have thrown support behind bills to crack down on advanced AI chips reaching China in the wake of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's resignation, after revelations he allegedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also called for an assessment of the chipmaker complying with export restrictions. The Daily Mail reports that Home Office data indicates the government has spent nearly Â£80,000 a day on transporting asylum seekers. A Home Office spokesman told the paper: "We have ended the unrestricted use of taxis and rooting out waste in the asylum system is a priority." The Daily Mirror says soaring energy bills are taking a toll on terminally ill people and their families following a call for help on energy bills from charity Marie Curie. The Daily Star's front teases a new study into gangland killings, including an interactive map of 1,000 cold-case crimes. It is also one of several papers to use a photo of Ezri Konsa celebrating after scoring the second goal for England in the Nations League. The team went on to win 3-2 against Spain. The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson has told the Daily Telegraph , external that "Britain would back Brexit again" if the country was forced into another vote on the issue - and he has urged Andy Burnham not to waste his premiership on Europe. But writing in the Daily Mirror, , external the prime minister says Johnson went for a much harder Brexit than the one promised at the referendum. Citing figures from the campaign group Stay Out, the Daily Express , external says a Brexit U-turn would mean Britain could have to take in around 4,400 asylum seekers every year - or pay an annual bill of Â£76m. The Times says , external NHS and fire service leaders have warned the government that banning zero-hours contracts will put the public at risk. They say it would be impossible to employ people as emergency cover, without guaranteeing them a certain number of hours or compensating them for late shift changes. A government spokesperson tells the paper it is considering responses to its consultation and working to get the detail right. Writing in the Guardian , external , the prime minister pledges to intervene early in children's lives to tackle youth unemployment, promising "a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood". Burnham promises to intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fall behind, and "long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state". The Sun , external quotes Reform UK, which argues that Labour's own tax rises have made it harder for businesses to hire young people. Writing in the Times , external , the Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy says she's convening senior members of the entertainment and sports industries to discuss systems to identify abusers early - and she warns them if they don't act, she'll step in. She says she believes abuse is still happening now, and cases such as Russell Brand's should be a wake-up call for us as a country. Sir David Beckham has "kicked up a stink" because his luxury perfumes are being distributed through the budget retailer Poundland, according to the Daily Mail , external . The paper says his lawyers are demanding more than Â£30m for associating his brand with cheap, discount products. The company that produces his fragrances, Coty, has denied selling them in Poundland - but says it has the right to decide where to sell the range. England's football victory over Spain dominates the back pages. The Daily Mirror , external calls it a nerve-jangling classic. The Telegraph says , external it was a magical night in Madrid.
