Headline: 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages
Body: Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday. In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions. Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular." To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular. It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final. If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment. The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist? Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina? How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently? Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings England hold on to stun world champions Spain in thriller The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half. This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession. Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted. But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win. Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters? "We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up. "Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory." Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach. Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football. What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them. England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented. It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them. England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right. From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain. When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be. In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge. Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level". There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup. Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them. If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions. Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest. The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here. But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything. And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure. "This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together. "The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room. "We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup." England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table. The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession. After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice. England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative. "I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent. "I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase." Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer. "Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance." Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

Headline: How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?
Body: James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group. But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina . So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look. First of all the context of the two games was entirely different. England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players. Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on. But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White. Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano. Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford. "Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners." 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages England cling on to stun world champions Spain in thriller Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it. In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off. Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward. But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend. However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward. The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute. And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance. However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs. Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute. "Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel. "So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game. "I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs." Dan Burn usually comes on when England are trying to hang on - but he was only introduced for the last few minutes England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm. In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53. Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41. In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%. In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia , as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%. "For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave." England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain . But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy. So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity? After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle. "I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live. "I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side. "There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side." Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game. "Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said. Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2. He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time. Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers." Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings England win in Spain - have they set a new standard?

Headline: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
Body: Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America. Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory". On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire. There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love." The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope. He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities. Headline: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
Body: Brand was jailed this week after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand. Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week. A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights." Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law. Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered. Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial. At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]. "I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. "But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence." Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper she was "devastated" by the decision and that police had said they didn't want the trial "to become 'the Alice show'", a reference to her pseudonym in the stories published in 2023. It is understood the Met Police has apologised for the language officers used in a meeting with Latter about her case. A Met spokesperson said: "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence." Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change. Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults". Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20. Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted. ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl. Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room. Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women. The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting". Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light." Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC that questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" Helen Whately, the shadow work and pension secretary, told Kuenssberg that it was worth debating a change to age of consent laws. Whately said she has teenage daughters and would be concerned if they brought home a man many years older than them. "I think any parent would look twice," she said, adding: "Let's have the debate." Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC charity, said 16 and 17-year-olds can be particularly vulnerable to grooming by some adults and laws have been changed in recent years to prevent more people in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with children of such an age. She said "other laws are failing to prevent them from being sexually exploited", adding: "Even though they are over the age of consent, young people are still entitled to be protected from harm." Headline: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
Body: Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo) Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement. Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden. The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee. Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented. Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior. Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority". The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area". It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats". The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure. The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Headline: Man and woman die and four arrested after police pursuit crash in Leeds
Body: Four arrested after two killed in Leeds crash Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds. West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco. The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York. The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed. The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening. A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation. Officers are appealing for anyone who witnessed the crash to get in touch The crash happened in the early hours of Sunday morning A spokesperson for the IOPC said it had launched an independent investigation at about 02:30 and sent investigators to the crash scene to "begin gathering evidence". The spokesperson said that inquiries were "at a very early stage". A police scene and road closure remain in place in Gelderd Road, and drivers are advised to avoid the area and seek alternative routes. A steady stream of cars is being directed by officers to turn around at the cordon. The area is made up of business units and car dealerships and was very quiet on this cold Sunday morning, with very few people about. A dark car can be seen a short distance away from a very badly damaged white Volkswagen just outside a used car dealership. Anyone who saw the vehicles before or during the crash and may have information or footage is urged to contact police. Headline: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
Body: The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power. The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms". Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards". The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools. The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year , external on the introduction of on-screen exams. But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future". In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day. The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms". Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons. Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England Ministers to issue guidance on children's screen use The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" . An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools". Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum." Figures from the most recent government survey , external show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all. The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children. Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing." As part of its proposal, the Tories said Â£900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a Â£250m fund for new textbooks. A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets. "It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said. They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need." A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day. Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems. The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March. A smartphone ban in English schools is coming into force. Headline: Workers should get paid time off to train for crises, say peers
Body: Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended. In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income. It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters. It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies. In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step". But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks. It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters. The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic. It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later. Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance. Army reservists can claim up to Â£400 a day , external from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so. In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles. They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers. Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark. In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption. The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies. It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added. The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience. It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war. The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies. Headline: Tearful McIlroy dedicates record-equalling win to ill dad
Body: Rory McIlroy celebrated defending his Masters title with dad Gerry watching on at Augusta National DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard -15 Hatton (Eng); -10 McIlroy (NI); -8 Chacarra (Spa), Lindell (Fin); -7 Olesen (Den), Reitan (Nor), Laporta (Ita), Lindberg (Swe), Perez (Fra) Selected others: -4 Wallace (Eng); -3 Rahm (Spa), Schaper (SA); Level Fleetwwod (Eng), Reed (US), Fox (NZ); +1 Rai (Eng) Rory McIlroy wiped away tears as he dedicated his eighth Race to Dubai victory to his ill father, Gerry. Moments after matching Colin Montgomerie's record of season-long European tour titles on Sunday, the Northern Irishman was asked about the health of his father. An emotional McIlroy revealed Gerry has been in hospital for two months after "a huge operation" - a double lung transplant - at the end of September. "He's recovering well, thankfully," McIlroy told the DP World Tour. "But before I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him. He said to me: 'Go win The Race to Dubai'. It came after a thrilling climax at the traditional season-ending DP World Tour Championship with Tyrrell Hatton securing a commanding victory, while McIlroy pipped Spaniard Eugenio Chacarra to the overall crown. Hatton's closing six-under-par 66 helped him romp to a five-shot victory on 15 under par but most eyes were on the thrilling battle that went down to the final hole. It is the fifth successive year that McIlroy has won the award and it has drawn him level with Montgomerie, the Scot who set a mark 21 years ago that few thought would ever be matched. "Yeah, double digits," smiled McIlroy when asked what would be his final target of Race to Dubai victories. "I'd love to surpass Monty next year and we'll go from there." McIlroy's confidence in going along with a target shouted out by the fans surrounding the 18th green at the Earth Course in Dubai on Sunday was refreshing to hear. But he appears to be playing and talking with a little more freedom in recent years - the sort of freedom that comes as a result of finally completing the career Grand Slam and winning successive Masters titles - and leads to declarations of winning 10, or more. "Winning eight Order of Merits (Race to Dubai titles) was never in my list of goals growing up," said McIlroy, who closed with a bogey-free 67 to finish on 10 under and must surely now be considered Europe's greatest golfer. "I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European tour and playing with him at the London Club in 2008, so to pull up alongside him and win eight of these means the world to me." Highlights: McIlroy wins the Race to Dubai After Jon Rahm's victory in Abu Dhabi last week, fellow former LIV Golf member Hatton showed his class with a five-shot success at the Earth Course at Jumeirah Golf Estates. Hatton showed his combustible side earlier in the week but, despite later admitting to being "weirdly nervous" he appeared serene on Sunday. In the final group and knowing he couldn't win the overall Race to Dubai title, he was detached enough to block out the scramble as he strolled to his ninth DP World Tour victory - even asking an on-course reporter who was going to win as he walked from the 17th green to 18th tee. It was that head-to-head battle between Chacarra and McIlroy that dominated the tournament, a battle that, after a long hard season, came right down to the wire. Both players knew victory would win them the title. There were permutations galore for finishing second, third, or below that. Chacarra and McIlroy went toe-to-toe in and the overall lead in the rankings chopped and changed down an absorbing back nine as neither man backed down. At one juncture just one-tenth of a point separated the pair. But a late surge from Northern Ireland's McIlroy allowed him to finish runner-up behind England's Hatton in the tournament and collect enough points to edge out the gutsy Spaniard. Chacarra, who earned around $15-20m during three years as a LIV player, is in just his second season on the DP World Tour. He is the only three-time winner of this year's campaign and was desperate to add his name to compatriots Rahm and Seve Ballesteros as the third Spanish order of merit winner. After four early birdies he looked in fine shape. The pressure began to tell as he posted three bogeys in four holes around the turn. But he responded brilliantly with two more birdies to push McIlroy all the way. Chacarra, the 26-year-old world number 39, finished in a tie for third to end up second in the overall standings and earn a PGA Tour card for next season. 'This one's for him' - McIlroy dedicates Race to Dubai win to his dad As tough as it was this year for McIlroy to win, mainly due to playing on the PGA Tour for the first half of the season, 2027 will be even harder because there will be some big names flooding in after the collapse of LIV Golf. Rahm and Hatton are just two high-profile LIV players who are suspended from the PGA Tour for a year following their involvement with the breakaway tour. They will both have a full season on the European circuit that will give them a big advantage over McIlroy. Along with many other big names such as Sergio Garcia, Joaquin Niemann and Tom McKibbin, there's even the possibility of Bryson DeChambeau, the biggest LIV name of all, applying to join the DP World Tour for next season. The American is eligible thanks to his 2024 US Open triumph, at McIlroy's painful expense, and had to apply by the end of the Sunday of the DP World Tour Championship. Tyrrell Hatton won his first DP World Tour Championship as Rory McIlroy claimed an eighth Race To Dubai After this latest addition to McIlroy's glowing CV it's hard to make a case against him being Europe's greatest ever golfer â and as he continues to find new targets to stay motivated one of them is very much to unequivocally nail down that title. Motivation was a problem in the immediate aftermath of finally ending his long wait to win the Masters in 2025 as he became just the sixth man to win the career Grand Slam. But a year later he had re-found it as he became just the fourth back-to-back Green Jacket winner with his brilliant defence at Augusta National back in April. That put him on six major titles, level with England's Sir Nick Faldo and just one behind the great Harry Vardon, whose name adorns the trophy McIlroy has just hoisted for the eighth time. Still only 37, McIlroy still has plenty of time to overhaul Montgomerie and hold the outright record for the most European number one titles â despite playing on two tours throughout the majority of his career. Targets have changed â McIlroy is not chasing the world number one spot or winning any old trophy. He's voiced his desire to focus on majors, play more in Europe and around the globe and keep stacking up these order of merit titles. An Olympic title is perhaps the only honour missing from his trophy cabinet, and he will have the chance to change that in 2028 on a familiar Riviera Country Club Course, which is a regular stop-off on the PGA Tour and where he finished second a this year's Genesis Invitational. He will be attempting to become the first man to win three Masters in a row next April, before the US Open at Pebble Beach and Open Championship at St Andrews offer great chances at venues McIlroy knows he can thrive on. McIlroy has won six Ryder Cups as a stalwart for Europe and is just seven points behind all-time leader Sergio Garcia. But even if the Northern Irishman quit the game right now he's already built a more than compelling argument that he's the greatest player the continent has ever seen. Headline: Townsend hails Scotland's defence in Australia 'arm wrestle'
Body: Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend hailed his team's defensive efforts after they edged past Australia in a Nations Championship "arm wrestle" at Murrayfield. Off the back of being dismantled by New Zealand last weekend, in which they failed to score a second half point, the spotlight fell on Scotland's leaky defence. But on a chilly and damp Edinburgh day where physicality was king, they delivered a much-needed win and showed they are capable of winning ugly. Even so, Townsend's side didn't make it easy. Max Jorgensen's late converted try gave the Wallabies hope, and with the clock in the red, the visitors broke from their own half. Murrayfield held its breath, but Darcy Graham hauled Australia full-back Tom Wright into touch with a superb tackle. "When we saw the rain half an hour before kick-off, you still hope you'll be able to move the ball," Townsend said. "You could tell defences were coming off the line a bit quicker, knowing they could pressure the ball carrier. "Both teams had to adjust and I thought we did that well. Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years. Set after set we were putting them under pressure. "We were on that edge of physicality but disciplined, hitting hard in the tackle, putting pressure on, listening to the referee, getting back onside. That makes it hard for the opposition to get into our 22m, which was a learning from last week. "It was just constant effort. Today, we showed we can play another game, too." Final whistle a blessing as Scotland edge dull Test against Australia Nations Championship: Scotland hang on for scrappy win over Australia - as it happened Leading 12-5 at half-time, there was one eye on whether Scotland could clinch a bonus-point victory that would have both boosted their points difference and helped their chances of climbing the northern hemisphere table with Japan to come on Saturday. However, it soon became apparent that would not be forthcoming in a match that will not live long in the memory. "It was about winning at all costs today," former Scotland prop Peter Wright said. "We hoped we might get something quite end-to-end, 50 points to 48, loads of tries, but to come out on the right end of a war of attrition like that, it's a good feeling. "When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style at any sport. We just want to get victories under our belt. "It was a bad game last week so getting some momentum going into the Japan game next week was really important. In the absence of Sione Tuipulotu, who was ruled out of playing against the country of his birth with a knee injury, Rory Darge captained Scotland and led from the front with a player-of-the-match display. The Glasgow Warriors flanker was immense in contact and at the breakdown, and also had the presence of mind to tell Finn Russell to kick at goal instead of going to the corner in the closing stages. The resulting three points put Scotland 10 points in front and proved to be the winning score. Townsend praised the performance his stand-in skipper, while also pointing to a wider effort defensively. "You know the opposition will get phases of attack and we'll have to defend. Rory with his tackling, with his effort and his post-tackle presence really helps us. "There were a lot of other players that stood up physically. The shots that were going in, the effort going in was outstanding." And Darge himself was heartened by how Scotland responded to the All Blacks loss. "We were disappointed after last week's performance," he said. "A lot of that disappointment was with the physical side of the game and we did that really well. "It was a bit of an arm wrestle, the conditions played their part. We know they want to throw the ball around, we like to play an attacking style but today was a battle of the defences." Headline: Teenager Andreeva caps stunning week with WTA Finals title
Body: Mirra Andreeva is the third teenager to win the WTA Finals singles trophy on debut at the tournament For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament. The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week. The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years. The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina. Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches. She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez. "I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said. "Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!" As well as Â£2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test. Mirra Andreeva is the youngest WTA Finals champion since a 17-year-old Maria Sharapova in 2004 One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity. In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions , external on court in the past. However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament. Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent. After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front. While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10. "This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports. "This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed. "I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing." Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament. She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday. She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed. Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg. "I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said. "For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself." 'I want to thank myself' - Andreeva's journey to Grand Slam glory Ukraine's Svitolina was tearful after the defeat, but reaching this stage capped a fine turnaround after she lost 6-4 6-0 to Andreeva on the first day of the tournament. She pushed Andreeva throughout, drawing her into lengthy baseline rallies before fatigue set in. She will finish the year at six in the world rankings, having made it back into the top 10 for the first time since 2021. Svitolina returned from maternity leave in 2022, and joked that daughter Skai would have some questions for her after the match. "She's probably still awake and is going to ask me why I didn't win today," the 32-year-old said. "I'm really happy to be in great form and coming back after pregnancy. Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it's possible. "I also want to say thank you to people in Ukraine for supporting me and being on this journey with me." Headline: Ronaldinho, 46, makes comeback for Ravenna
Body: Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby. The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense. He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal. The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box. He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved. At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch. Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0. A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli. The game was streamed in several countries around the world. Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut. A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally. In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill. He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005. He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro. Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one. "It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia. And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back." Headline: Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion
Body: The winning captains: Australia's Isabelle Kelly, her men's counterpart Isaah Yeo and England wheelchair skipper Lewis King Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not? It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are. The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear, , external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement. But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers. For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final. Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world. England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early. And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit. "This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo. "Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding. "I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow." That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (Â£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments. Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though. The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022. That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons. For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant. While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (Â£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (Â£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams. , external Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America. With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed. England become world champions for third time Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership. That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago. Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident. France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58. Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out. "I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport. "Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup. "I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10. "It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play." A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits , external before a ball was kicked. The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other. In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird". And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12. And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men. Highlights: Australia beat New Zealand to win world cup for a fourth time in a row 'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup Tonga fans streamed to stadiums in their numbers to support their team An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer. Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased. That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago. In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts. This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby. Highlights: Australia beat New Zealand to win Women's Rugby League World Cup Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure. Instead of adults paying more than Â£20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to Â£9.74 per ticket. But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game. The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters. Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October. That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full. "Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that. "Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt." Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached. Australia's women cantered to a record fourth World Cup title against New Zealand Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures. Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza. This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments. In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games. Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either. Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC. "There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be." In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible." And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition. The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (Â£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July. Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around Â£21.5m per year. Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled. And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

Headline: Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
Body: Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships. Canada said it would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine. "Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement. It said that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer." The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC). "The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it said in a statement. "The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments." Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the ban. It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in its events. The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine and along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships. Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo. On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating. It is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport. This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes. Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March. The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland. In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted. In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable". However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria. While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics. Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

Headline: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
Body: Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation. Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021. Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence. Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity. Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday. Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently." A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy. Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021 , allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida. She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year. The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease. Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination. Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise. At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

Headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
Body: Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube channel of his lawyer A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools. Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated. The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation. Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance. "I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday. "I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating." When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam. He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly. "It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested. The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating. The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end". Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said. The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students. Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped? A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology. Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again. Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case. "We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement. It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators. Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated. Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities. Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months. Exams watchdog warns of rise in high-tech cheating

Headline: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
Body: The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision. It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday. The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for. The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them". New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder. Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders. "We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference. The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added. A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days. Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident. There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority. Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side. Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort. The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway. Headline: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
Body: Organisers said around 400,000 people took part on Sunday Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media. Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom. The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs. Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests. Czech households currently pay â 205 crowns ($9.44; Â£7.06) a month for public TV and radio. Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended. "I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency. "If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore." The protesters say the planned changes could allow politicians to stifle media freedom Prime Minister Andrej Babis has insisted the government does not want to control public media. "The funding system is changing, no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do, no one wants to nationalise them," Babis told the Czech News Agency. "We are doing this because the system is already outdated and most of Europe is going the same way today and others are joining in," he added. Some European countries, including France and Norway, have moved away from the public licence fee model in the last few years. France removed it in 2022 and its public media, which also carries advertising, is now funded by a portion of the income from VAT. Norway abolished its license fee in 2020 and moved its public broadcaster's funding into the national budget. Reuters said the proposal would amount to a 15% cut in funding for the public broadcasters Czech TV and Czech Radio. These protesters held a sign depicting the animated character Vecernicek and saying "We stand with Czech TV" Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Vecernicek, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades. Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power. Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media. "Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June. Headline: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
Body: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time. "Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower. But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea. The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.
