Headline: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
Body: Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletes Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business. More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him. Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram alone Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia â George Weah â was formerly a professional footballer. So why not a judoka in the ÃlysÃ©e Palace? "Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the ÃlysÃ©e would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro. "But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes." For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously â or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly. But it is also because the state of French politics â outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right â is one of total disarray. The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May. So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" â politicians have to take note. Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next president It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling. Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!" In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks. All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices. "People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said. "Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the streetâ¦ if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool." It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election? France's Marine Le Pen, fighting court conviction and running for presidency But if he is serious â and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion â then the hard work begins now. What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine? In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate? Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen. In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes. The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off. Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed RaphaÃ«l Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right. The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February. President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to run The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for MÃ©lenchon more likely. So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," MÃ©lenchon told reporters on Friday. The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals". That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss. Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist". Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way". If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt. Headline: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
Body: When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified. They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. "Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive. This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded. Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry. Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community. After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience. "As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works. The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate. Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team. After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve. Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north. This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance. After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea. This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre. "She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says. Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance. He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids. Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. "The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea. In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding. Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified. "I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains. Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok. The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him. However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely "We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC. For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region. He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance. Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns. "We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC. They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation. After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust. "I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real. But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding. Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says. "Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate". He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion. But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone. Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community. He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly." He agrees too with the recent report by MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing . "The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says. The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment. Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease. "Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited." Headline: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
Body: Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks. Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday. US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers. Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe. On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network. According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper. This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted. As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned". He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper." Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag. In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. "You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said "You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added. A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel". He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware. The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations. Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport. Have you been affected by the flight disruption? Get in touch 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended. There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco. Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning. A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport. Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned. Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada. Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations." But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened. FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys. Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys. By Sunday morning, the situation had improved, but the impacts of the stoppage were still being felt with more than 2,400 flights delayed and 1,400 cancelled. Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness. As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems. But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund. In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason. a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers) a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls) free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later. The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary. It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001. "This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify. Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system. "That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said. The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored. Have you been affected by the US flight disruption? Headline: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
Body: In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass. Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him. More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends. Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward. "He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma. Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes' Jojo was less than a year old â an infant clinging to his mother â when he was captured and sold. Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him. Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction". "He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat â to interact with us," he says. Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Ãric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary. When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised. "If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes â the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas." King â who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes â remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin. "They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive." Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla. But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester. In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose. It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate â a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover. "Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him. "I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma." Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers. The bonds between gorillas â what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group. And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space". But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla. No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility. Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully â perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other. These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen â when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress. The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations". Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes. "They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester. And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas. "Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him. Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own." Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females." But while those phases â of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant. Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely. "[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group." That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male. "It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison. "Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him." Headline: Investors sue chip giant Intel after 29% stock plunge
Body: Shareholders have sued US chip giant Intel, accusing it of hiding the severity of a slump in personal computer (PC) sales, which they say led to a nearly 29% one-day collapse in the firm's stock. A proposed class action lawsuit in San Jose, California said Intel was too late to alert shareholders about how slowing sales could impact its earnings, allegedly artificially inflating its stock price. Intel shares plunged on 30 October, erasing tens of billions of dollars off its market value the day after it forecasted disappointing revenue in its coming earnings report. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has been accused of making "materially false and/or misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, the complaint said. In October, the firm announced that its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from Intel that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit said the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings â a drop of 9%, or about $800m, to $8.1bn. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though the stock is still up by 51% overall this year. Headline: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
Body: Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment. Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague". McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed. But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work. His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade. However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year. Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job. He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness. How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted. Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service. Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense' Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this." He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to." He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today". Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added. Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending. But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs". She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing. Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said: a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage. From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently. It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year . Headline: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds but are they value for money?
Body: It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (Â£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use. "I spent Â£160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid." Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of Â£100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated. High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out. But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier. "I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist. She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product. "For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales." Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products" Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy." Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items" Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing". So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to? "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them. "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent Â£99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it. In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says. Headline: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
Body: A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets. With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns. But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips. It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. The city-state has had some success in policing this. It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places. They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties. In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore. The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere. Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed. But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department. Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months. Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case. Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing. In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times. Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses. Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness. In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively. For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law. But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities. Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case. BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road. In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed. Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS. Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences. Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government. Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023 All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore. "For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said. Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore". But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips. With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts. Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China. Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said. "Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said. But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China". "This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour." Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit. Headline: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
Body: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem. "Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said . "In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur." Headline: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
Body: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world. Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries. From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues". In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday. Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery". In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away. Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up". The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email. When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent. Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed. Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected. From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed. In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected. The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted. Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage. Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report. Headline: Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
Body: How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security? US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC , external . "The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. Headline: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
Body: How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security? Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December. Nvidia has lost $550bn (Â£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X. "The American people deserve answers," he added. Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony. Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China. A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee. Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO. Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires. Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia. Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago. Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector. Headline: Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
Body: Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016. The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November. Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire". The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset". While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election. Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this. The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU. Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes. Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc. Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion? Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit. Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line. "But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line." Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too". He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016." Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see Â£5.1bn worth of annual benefits. Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration". Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards". On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill." The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU". Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy. The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".
