Headline: Thrift shop ask donors to nominate a charity
Body: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. Headline: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
Body: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about Â£20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our Â£4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments. Headline: Football kit giveaway aims to boost participation
Body: Millie Bright said she wanted girls to feel "comfortable and confident" in their kit Former England captain Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds as part of an initiative aimed at keeping girls in sport for longer. Thirty teams based in communities facing social or economic challenges were chosen by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out for the donation. Bright, who began her career at Doncaster Belles, said it was "vital" to keep girls playing sport. "Every young girl deserves a kit, no matter what level they play at, and, whilst the top of the game is doing really well, real life still exists. People can't afford to give their children kits, but that doesn't mean they should go without." Craig Gilmore set up Champions CIC, in Beeston, six years ago, to provide free Saturday morning training for children in the local area, as well as breakfast and lunch. "With the cost of living, football's expensive [and] bills come first," he said. "We work with a lot of families that can't afford the direct debits and the ongoing costs of grassroots sport nowadays. "The new kit is amazing. It gives them that sense of belonging, that team pride, it's a massive boost for them." Bright spoke with young footballers during the event in Leeds The new kit was provided by Kick it Out, in partnership with the Morrisons Foundation. They hope it will inspire these girls to continue sport as young women and adults. "Girls' participation struggles with drop-out rates," said Gemma Clark, from Kick it Out. "One of the barriers is kit. We want to remove that barrier so that more local girls can keep playing." Bright told the BBC she was fully behind the campaign. "As a girl or a woman, it's about feeling wanted and equal," she said. "We deserve to have kits. I don't want to see any girl dropping out of the game because they don't feel valued or comfortable. "These are the days that really make a difference. Hopefully this shows the girls that the people at the top care. The power of having a kit is a small gesture, but has a massive impact." Headline: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
Body: Nils Borstel said his business was making less money despite more than doubling the price of a sausage Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices â from Â£8 bratwursts, Â£11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even Â£5 for a few marshmallow sticks. But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed? Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more. One trader said it costs at least Â£4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back. Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999. He said a sausage that previously cost Â£3.50 now sold for Â£8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years. Manchester Christmas market traders explain prices Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices. About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK. He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years. For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said. Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost. He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses. Poppy (left) and Neve questioned whether the portions they bought justified the prices Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18. Neve, a student, said she had spent about Â£15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid Â£11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap. "I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said. Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty. Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices. Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls. She said each stall cost at least Â£1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least Â£4,000. Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved. Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas. CT Catering director Charlotte Whittle says her business employs 57 people across four Manchester market sites She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees. Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost Â£100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods. "They think that you're just selling cookies," she said. Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years. Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off. "We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said. She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants. But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices. Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls. He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by Â£2. Clark Murphy (left), pictured with his nephew Davis, said his business had reduced the price of its largest crumble Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas. "We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said. A notice at one food stall offered customers Â£1 off each drink or dish if they paid in cash He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs. At another food stall, a notice offered customers Â£1 off each drink or dish when paying cash. "Card fees are crazy â help us keep it simple," it said. Ernie the Elf said visitors can enjoy the Christmas markets without having to spend money Meanwhile, a gift trader calling himself Ernie the Elf, who sells handmade Christmas decorations in Albert Square, said visitors could still find affordable products. His decorations cost Â£4 each or three for Â£10, while metal signs were priced at Â£9. Ernie, who is in his second year at the Manchester markets, said traders faced substantial expenses, including accommodation and parking. But he believed the markets offered good value, pointing out that people could enjoy the festive atmosphere without having to spend money. Tyler, from Australia, and Rebecca, from Hong Kong, were enjoying their first Christmas in England with their daughter. Rebecca bought four brownies for Â£10, while Tyler paid Â£6 for a meat pie, which he said was not unreasonable compared with some other prices. However, he described another stall charging Â£5 for three marshmallow sticks as "outrageous". Tourists Rebecca and Tyler said they enjoyed the festive atmosphere, although they questioned the value of some products The couple said the markets were part of enjoying their first Christmas in England with their daughter. Despite questioning the cost of some products, Tyler said the experience was worthwhile. "I think if you don't buy anything, it's still great to come," he said. Headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
Body: Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent. Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app. It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately. The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech company. A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal. The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts. Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator. The regulator said it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system". It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision. Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine. "This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings." Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices. A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

Headline: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
Body: GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D games After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks , the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching. The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation. And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment. "We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow. Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch? Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says. Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft Auto The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards. Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase. Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table. "At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?" Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car". He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together". The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D After two expansion packs set in London, GTA 2 was released in 1999 and introduced rival crime syndicates GTA 3 showed a big step up in graphics when it came out in 2001, following protagonist Claude's missions around the 3D open-world of Liberty City. GTA Vice City, released in 2002, captured the feeling of 1980s Miami as it traced lead character's Tommy Vercetti's rise to power. In 2004, GTA San Andreas saw players follow Carl "CJ" Johnson's story, set in the 1990s, and based in the California-inspired Los Santos Rockstar released GTA IV in 2008 - a gritty, modern reimagining of Liberty City following Eastern European veteran Niko Bellic In 2013, players returned to modern-day Los Santos again in GTA V, a sprawling heist thriller featuring three playable protagonists The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer. But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book". "At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds. Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it". "For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow. "And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?" Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt. "We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way." GTA 6 - all you need to know about Rockstar's blockbuster game Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today. Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald. "It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US." Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem. Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA. "It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says. "Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole." The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's map When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (Â£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time. The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming. "I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones. MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round. She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself. As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life". "It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving." "It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, left GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue. Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history. This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it. The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game. "Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald. "It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time. "It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in." Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it? "I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says. "But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well." Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful". "It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic." Headline: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
Body: Are we too reliant on big tech companies? A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms. The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic. The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society. Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running". "For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said. The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world. Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries. The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect , knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India. Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack. There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT). Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight". "Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said. Microsoft says email queues 'approaching normal levels' after global outage hits Outlook and Teams users Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies, said while these kinds of outages weren't unheard of, what was unusual was the time it took for Microsoft to recover from it. A spokesperson for the US tech company said "given the scale of demand" it restored services gradually. "While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," a spokesperson said. Orosz said the resulting upset showed "our reliance on a few large US corporations". He said a solution for the future could be to split services per region to reduce the impact, something which already happens with Amazon's cloud computing service, AWS. For now, Microsoft said it was reviewing what went wrong, with the findings expected to inform steps to prevent a similar disruption from happening again. Headline: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
Body: What happened overnight with the Microsoft global outage? At least 74 countries were affected by the Microsoft outage which was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday. Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, all experienced "connectivity problems", the company said. As of early Friday afternoon (GMT), Microsoft was reporting improvements, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption was widespread. Here is what happened around the world. In the US , staff with the House of Representatives told Politico , external their work had been halted by the outage. "We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge â¦ with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work." Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage. Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email. The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time. "City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted." In Canada , a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure. The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected. Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails. Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers might not be able to receive emails about their trips because of the outage. Disruptions were also reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue What we know about the global Microsoft outage In Japan , some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications. "Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times , external . The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted. "We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters. Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational". Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters. In the Philippines , the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed". In India , the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly. People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day. "Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity. Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too. Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world. China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC. Australia's spy and federal police agencies were affected by the outage, though officials suggested the impact was minimal. "The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system," the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters. Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services. European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported. Speaking to the same news agency, the head of Germany 's BSI cybersecurity agency, Claudia Plattner, said the country's authorities had not been affected because they did not rely on Microsoft 365 services. However, Reuters reported that Germany's national rail operator, Deutsche Bahn, was having difficulties sending out timetables for diverted trains due to the outage. Plattner added the disruption was "affecting the whole world". "It is a global disruption that spans a vast number of data centres â stretching from Asia right across to the US, via Europe," she said. In Antalya, Turkey , advisers and officials attending the UN Climate Change Conference, Cop31, were left frustrated by the outage. James Young, a climate change adviser at the Inuit Circumpolar Council, the organisation which represents around 180,000 Inuit people living in the Arctic, told Reuters the council relied on emails and Microsoft Teams to communicate across several countries. "It's just been really frustrating and challenging to maintain contact with our colleagues and to be able to effectively participate here," he said. "I think our dependence on technology leaves us vulnerable to situations like this." In the UK , GPs, police and pharmacies were among services affected. Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report. Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down. A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible. "Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue." Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa were unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives. However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship. One winemaker in South Africa said almost his entire business had been brought to a "standstill" by the Microsoft outage. "It's incredibly frustrating," Peter Pentz added. "We export a lot, so communication with exporters in Europe has come to a standstill." Order processing, dispatch, communications and even "critical production work" were halted, he said, as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Headline: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
Body: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage. Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down. NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime. Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption. The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected. The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues. Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide. The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails. NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said. Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy. Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need. Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting Outlook and Teams but says fixes not going 'as expected' What we know about the global Microsoft outage A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions". The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts. There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed. The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts. "Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected". Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters. Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services. In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need". Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected. That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers. One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports. Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments. Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties. Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp. Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage. The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain. "Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained. "Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here." He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others". "Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge." His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption. Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over. But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools. Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices. Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed. "We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said. Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match. Headline: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
Body: Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky. Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich. From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky. Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade. As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare. It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon. Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east. Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus. Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter. It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too. It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise. Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily. Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November. Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter. "They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich. The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star. If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month. At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky. Pre-dawn on Monday could bring better viewing conditions for more of the UK Sunday night is forecast to be drier, as the day's rain and hill snow clear. However, wintry showers will pester northern Scotland with plenty of cloud. Also the odd shower will pop up around north-west facing coasts. Otherwise, the night looks mostly clear and dry, apart from the odd mist of fog patch. To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes. The best time to view the planetary lineup is approximately 45-60 minutes before sunrise. Headline: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time
Body: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket for the first time, after a flight lasting 22-and-a-half hours. The rocket returned to Earth and hovered near its launch tower, whose mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - then secured it. The company had hoped to catch the bottom part of the rocket as well, but this was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. SpaceX needs to reliably recover both parts of Starship so that it can fly repeatedly and drastically reduce costs. The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday There were loud cheers from SpaceX staff who were watching the flight as the rocket returned to the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas. This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable. The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time (19:47 GMT) on Friday. The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half-minutes later when it returned. But the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding. Elon Musk later posted on X that the booster had been "slightly low on fuel". The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet. The Ship completed 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower. SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. But this was the first time the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has been grabbed by the "chopsticks". Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space. Any problems would have resulted in the ship being brought down in the ocean in the same way as the booster. A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX. In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster. Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch. Landing an entire Starship rocket would take spaceflight to the next level, said Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society - but it didn't happen this time. "Not recovering the first stage is a setback. But they have recovered Super Heavy before and so successfully returning and recovering the Ship is a substantial step forward," he added. "They have demonstrated the two halves of the recovery challenge, just not yet on the same flight. "The next milestone would be stitching those achievements together and then proving they can do it reliably, repeatedly and economically." After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa. The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline. What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next? Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface. But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown. Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule. Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage. Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended. But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida. Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027. Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

Headline: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
Body: Spread by midges, bluetongue poses no threat to the public or food safety The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down. Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep. There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025. The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland. The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock. The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months. Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed. There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland. The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season. Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera. "It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety â milk and meat are safe to consume." Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera. "Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries. "I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals." The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025. A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected. Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals. The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

Headline: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
Body: Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El NiÃ±o. The developing El NiÃ±o - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter. The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards. This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns. Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south. There is also some evidence that El NiÃ±o can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter. No two El NiÃ±os are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes. UN warns of 'supersized' El NiÃ±o as countries prepare for impact The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El NiÃ±o can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA. This typically leads to wetter winters during El NiÃ±o years. The likely impacts of El NiÃ±o on winter weather vary across different parts of North America. The latest three month forecast , external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027. South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall. The El NiÃ±o winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida. Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024. California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely. Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency , external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides. Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks. Many past El NiÃ±os have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El NiÃ±o of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall. Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves. This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El NiÃ±o reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further. It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more. The shift of the Pacific jet stream generally leads to warmer and milder winters in the north-west USA, Northern Plains and Ohio Valley - as well as western and central Canada. This lessens the risk of flooding, but reduced rainfall can leave groundwater and river levels low, fuelling drought and wildfires in spring and summer. Ski resorts can also suffer from a lack of snow. Long-range predictions suggest a dry, warm winter is more likely than usual this year. However, El NiÃ±o does not guarantee this. For instance, the winters of 1982-1983 and 2015-2016 were wetter than normal in the north-west USA. In much of the northern USA, and large swathes of Canada, a greater chance of dry and warm weather makes snow less likely. Further south, however, above-average precipitation typically leads to big snowfalls in the Californian mountains and southern Rockies - good news for water stocks. It can also increase the probability of snow at lower levels in the southern and eastern USA - but only if enough cold air is in the mix. The area around Washington DC often receives more snowfall than usual in an El NiÃ±o winter - but not always. Snowfall caused chaos in Washington DC in February 2010. The winter of 2009-2010 delivered record-breaking snowfall that brought the city to a standstill, while widespread blizzards affected much of the US east coast in 2016. However, some of Washington DC's least snowy winters have also occurred during El NiÃ±o events, including 1972-1973 and 1997-1998 which brought just 0.1in (0.25cm) of snow. Higher winter temperatures in eastern Canada and the north-east USA can mean precipitation that might normally fall as snow gives rain instead. This can increase the chance of freezing rain events, with the so-called Great Ice Storm of 1998 , external being blamed partly on the effects of El NiÃ±o. It is worth saying that snowfall amounts are decreasing overall in most places due to human-induced climate change, meaning predicting the impact of El NiÃ±o is even more complex. An added complication is the possible impact of El NiÃ±o on the polar vortex, a ring of strong winds that circles the North Pole in winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) up in the stratosphere. It holds cold, dense air in place above the Arctic but sometimes it can weaken and disrupt, and there is some evidence that the energy released into the atmosphere by El NiÃ±o makes this more likely. Disruptions to the polar vortex sometimes ripple down through the atmosphere, weakening the polar jet stream and opening the door for cold air to spill across Canada and the USA. However this does not always occur and the links are far from clear. Super El NiÃ±o sets another record as it strengthens to 'unprecedented levels'

Headline: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
Body: Some bin collections were missed partly because of the heatwave Some bin collections were missed over the summer in a county partly because the heatwave became so serious it posed a risk to the lives of workers, a council worker has said. Flintshire County Council's Chris Goddard said crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking hot weather , causing a spate of widespread missed collections. During the summer, drought was declared in all of Wales and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country . Goddard said: "We do have to make some difficult decisions but ultimately if there is a fatality in the workplace because of a decision I've made, that's something that I would have to live with - and probably defend." Despite the missed collections the council remained on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target this year, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. Flintshire County Council is on track to hit its waste recycling target despite the disruption Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer. "Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else. "My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors. "That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too." Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate. "Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd. "It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside." Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption. The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer. Headline: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
Body: More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests. The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%. Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond. Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network. BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted. Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways. They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged. These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets. The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours. Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024. More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year â an average of about 274 a day. It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage. The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa). Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need. However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa. Scottish Water figures , external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day. When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day. The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours. Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500. The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not. There were 1,270 spills, totalling almost 1,500 hours, last year into West Lothian's River Almond, which is nearly 28 miles in length. Local campaigner Ruth Plevin said swimming in the river was part of her childhood and that she now wants to protect it for her own grandchildren. She said any investment in improving the infrastructure of the water system was welcome. "It's what's not visible that is our concern - the microplastics, the pharmaceuticals, the agrichemicals, stuff that you can't see," she said. Ruth Plevin wants the River Almond clean for her grandchildren Plevin, a member of the River Almond Action Group, said she wants the group's legacy to be clean, safe water. "It's precious and I think we need to regard it as precious. Value it, look after it and make it safe. "I want it to be clean - it's not a lot to ask for, really," she said. Further along the east coast at Belhaven in East Lothian, surfer Brian Allen has been testing the local water for pollution. Each week he sends samples to an accredited laboratory to be tested for E.coli and intestinal enterococci. He says this is the same sampling as done by Sepa, except he tests all year round and not just during the bathing season. Sepa monitors bathing water quality at about 80 sites across Scotland between May and September. It also looks out for algae, seaweed and waste. Brian Allen said most of Belhaven's water testing has been positive Allen, the regional representative for Surfers Against Sewage, said the results had been providing "really good news" for Belhaven. He said 86% of the samples were rated as excellent, good or sufficient water quality, which was fine for recreational water users. "In fact 77% of the results are coming back as excellent. What we don't know is whether that picture is being replicated across the rest of Scotland," he said. Allen welcomed Scottish Water's increase in data publishing and said working collaboratively would help build up a bigger picture of water quality. He said the figures had showed there were almost daily discharges from the two overflows in the area â but it was not known if there was a link between discharges and water quality. One of them, at West Barns at Dunbar, recorded 3,300 spills last year - the second highest number in Scotland last year and a newly-monitored site. Simon Parsons, director for wastewater at Scottish Water, said most of the time overflows were doing the job they were designed for - draining rainwater out of the sewer system. "The vast majority of those spills aren't harmful to the environment because they're nearly always about rainwater," he explained. Scottish Water said 99% of spills were rainwater, surface water, road run-off, "grey" water from households (not human waste), infiltration of groundwater, and trade effluent. The overflow monitors identified more than 100,000 spills last year Parsons said the increase in monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network and helped identify locations requiring improvement. "We didn't necessarily know how and when our overflows were operating so we've got a much better picture now than we've ever had before. "We can actually identify those areas where we need to think about investment. "We've got a number of locations across Scotland where actually we've identified links between how our pumps work and how our treatment works work, which have told us where we do get some spills when we shouldn't have them - and we'll make the improvements." Scottish Water's Simon Parsons said the monitors help identify problems in the system Monitoring in Scotland remains far lower than in England, which has 100% coverage . Differences in recording means Scotland's figures are not directly comparable with the rest of the UK. Scottish Water said its monitoring had now grown to about 50% and that it was aiming to reach 100% over the next five to six years. Parsons said the cost was relatively small but represented good value in terms of the intelligence they provided. Headline: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons until she died after her home was destroyed
Body: Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home. Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 . But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded. "Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that." The BBC report from last year when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours. It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town. Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her. "She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms. "The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her." Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth, and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end "We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly." Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home. Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface. "Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn. This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia "But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather." The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events . Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter, with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable" . Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months. "As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70. "When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad." Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its Â£1m refurbishment in the next few weeks. Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year. The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surged towards her end-of-terrace cottage. "Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC. "They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it." What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare. This was what Emily Frost saw of her house, on the left of this picture, as she looked back while their family were evacuated on a life raft during Monmouth's flooding in November 2025 Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home. "There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled. "We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed. "It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most." The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again. Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal. This was Emily Frost's kitchen the day after her family home was flooded for the second time in five years "They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things," said Emily. "Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with." Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas. An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued. Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again. Alan and Jennifer Morgan said they spent their life savings renovating the house Alan grew up in and has been in his family for three generations so "it means a lot to us" "I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70. "The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer. "People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof." The River Monnow burst its banks and the official report into the flood said floodwater reached depths 1.5m high, almost 2.5m in some extreme cases The official Section 19 report , external into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit. Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening. The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached, and after shops and homes had been flooded. Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service , external but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated. Prince William was in the Monmouth area in October, visiting communities affected by the 2025 flooding caused by extreme weather conditions and met with Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council "When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said. "Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change." The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively". It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow. NRW said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons". Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up. This is how the River Monnow usually looks at Monmouth but it swelled to 18-times its normal depth in November 2025, after torrential downpours during Storm Claudia NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys. The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences were fit for purpose. "We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW. "We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact." The Welsh government said it was spending almost Â£1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including Â£700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith. "We have made Â£85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement. NRW said they had done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they have more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains. Storm Claudia devastated the residents of Monmouth in November 2025 when the historic market town was hit by the worst floods in living memory "We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council. "If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains." Insurance companies in the UK paid out Â£565m to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary , external . "I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not. "But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."
