Headline: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
Body: PM Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to go to COP31 Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone". Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue. But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions. In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion. Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer. He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office . Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic. As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri. Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates." As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added. This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year. The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement. Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words. "The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said. Homes in the West Midlands were destroyed after record wildfires this summer in the UK On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down. He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity. The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels. Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth. But Burnham has been accused of having double standards. "The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam. Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security. And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps. Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made. Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target , external . The BBC's climate editor, Justin Rowlatt, investigates the impact of the changing climate on our weather. Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 9 November. Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech. "As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet â and future generations â so urgently need. "Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do." Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech. In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees." Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands. For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years. Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate. The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot. As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began. Headline: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
Body: Lydia Dibben wants more small farms around Wales growing produce Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned. The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales. It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this. Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets. Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture , external , only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture , external . Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain. "We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher. Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency. Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets". He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways. "That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks. "If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away." Duncan Fisher said he has hope that Wales will be able to increase its fruit and veg growing Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets. They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers. As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things. "If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there." But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland. However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land. Lydia Dibben, one of the growers, said even though it was a difficult year they were able to grow a lot of food One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers. She said if her home was not provided she would have to get another job to be able to afford rent, and then would end up without enough time to farm. "I'm only growing on about just over an acre this year, and we're now doing 50 veg boxes a week," she said. "We've been doing four farmers' markets a month up until the beginning of October. We're also supplying into regional and national wholesale as well. "I don't know how many people we're feeding, but it's got to be hundreds of people on just a couple of acres." She believes there are lots of people who want to do similar work, and they should be given access to land and affordable housing to do so. Lydia Dibben said she got into growing vegetables in lockdown and decided this was what she wanted to do as a job Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different. "We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said. This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates. Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing. "The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said. "I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier." She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat. When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00". She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered. Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different. "Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added. "We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think. "We've just not had the crops to make it worth it." Lydia Dibben said every day is different on the farm She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding. Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep. "But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added. The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system". "There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson. The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing Â£200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology. "The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient." Headline: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
Body: Old landfill and industrial sites have been major sources of the chemicals in rivers like the Mersey Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment. One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue. Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated. PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties. They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally. The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer. , external As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last 10 years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively. Levels in freshwater fish have fallen 49%. "It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University. There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used. The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one. The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment. The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced that it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies. The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels had fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea. "There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson. One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are currently just two such suitable sites in the country. Headline: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
Body: Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image) Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia. Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola. The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack. All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday. Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada "Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added. The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare". He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather". Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC. "When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said. Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area. The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found. "Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement. "We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

Headline: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
Body: Plans to sell land and farms in Devon had already caused upset among tenants on the Duchy estate Plans by the Prince of Wales to sell off up to 20% of the Duchy of Cornwall could see more tenant farmers across England asked to buy their farms or move out. Up to 40 farm holdings across Devon, Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands could be affected by the sale, according to the Tenant Farmers Association (TFA). Locals say talks over the future of nine farms on the Bradninch estate in Devon have already caused "distress" for some tenants who fear they cannot afford to buy. A spokeswoman said the Duchy could not confirm the total number of tenants affected by the ten-year sale plan , external but told the BBC the estate was "supporting them through the process with care and respect". The Duchy's rural director Matthew Morris said he was listening to feedback from farmers The Duchy, which covers around 51,800 hectares (128,000 acres) in 19 counties, plans to use the Â£500m raised from the property and land sale over the next decade to invest in local communities, affordable housing and environmental projects. Former GP Mary Ryan, a local Lib Dem councillor who has lived near the Bradninch estate for around 35 years and is supporting the farmers, said some of those affected were "experiencing enormous mental and emotional distress" as a result of the planned sell-off. She added that while the Duchy had reportedly apologised to tenants last month, the handling of the process had been "pretty dire". The sales programme has now been extended from Bradninch, near Cullompton, to the Duloe Estate in Cornwall and to individual holdings elsewhere in Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands, according to the TFA. The Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, told the BBC he was listening to feedback over how the sales were being handled and offering support and mental health advice to tenants. Morris added that the Duchy was "still committed to agriculture" but that there "may well be other disposals in the future". In terms of immediate evictions, he said, there were "no cliff edges here" and that the Duchy was working closely with every tenant to find a suitable outcome. "In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained. "For many of our farmers, it's a generational aspiration to own their farm. A few people have said it to me: 'My grandfather wanted to buy his farm. My father wanted to buy the farm. And now I've got the opportunity and it's an amazing outcome'. "That's kind of what's driving me through what, at times, has been a little bit of turbulence." The Duchy - which was established in 1337 - currently has around 700 agricultural lettings, with around 300 whole farm holdings made up of a farmhouse, land and buildings. Farmers are on a mix of contracts ranging from time-limited to lifelong, with an option to pass the tenancy down through a family. George Dunn, TFA chief executive, said the organisation was in "deep discussions" with the Duchy and that poor communication had led to tenants "facing prolonged uncertainty over valuations, timing and the options available to them". "Once a family is told that its long-term relationship with the Duchy may change permanently, that uncertainty lives with them 24/7," he told the BBC. He added that while he welcomed the Duchy's assurance that "nobody will be made homeless" not every tenant "will be able or want to buy the farms that they operate and fair alternatives must be explored for those for whom ownership is unaffordable". A spokeswoman for the Duchy said: "We are engaging with people directly and supporting them through the process with care and respect. "We recognise that each of our tenant's circumstances are different, and we are taking a careful, case-by-case approach." Prince William selling 20% of duchy property for housing and nature projects

Headline: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
Body: Agnes Shikoli says she fears either drowning, or being crushed by her house "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya. Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi. The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water. Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives. "Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it." With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding. "I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us." Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the front line of preparations for the potential impact of El NiÃ±o. Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world. In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual. Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water. This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El NiÃ±o . Rubbish clogging Nairobi's drains and sewers was seen as a major factor in the deadly floods earlier this year Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers. But the workers have a huge task on their hands. Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape. The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives. Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare. In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants. Nairobi's drainage system has not been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades "The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about seven million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says. He adds that investment of up to $192m (Â£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely. But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money. The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary. However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers. "Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk." Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says. Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come - or how much rain there will be. But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December. A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El NiÃ±o during October-December 2026". So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned. In East Africa, this El NiÃ±o is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya. Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that is because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El NiÃ±o and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall. "For this season we have a very strong El NiÃ±o already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian NiÃ±o" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean . "We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country." The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods. Dozens of people died in floods in Kenya earlier this year Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El NiÃ±o. In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather - including the risk of both floods and drought. The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country. The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El NiÃ±o. Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El NiÃ±o could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain. It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high. There are fears El NiÃ±o's impact will worsen existing issues. Communities like Kibera are already grappling with poor housing and rampant poverty, while parts of Somalia are in the middle of a devastating drought. National governments in many countries are doing what they can to prepare but the extent of El NiÃ±o's impact is impossible to predict. Back in Kibera, Shikoli and her family are preparing for the worst. Council officials have told them they should leave their home on the riverbank until the rainy season has passed but Shikoli makes just $2 a day selling groundnuts and fruit from a small stall next to the river. "I want to move," she says. "But I don't have the means. "We just have to persevere and leave it to God." Headline: Extreme weather leaves gardeners hedging their bets
Body: Plants and trees from hotter parts of the world are being brought into Sussex Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather. West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought. The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely. Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there. Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year. "That's probably going to continue," he said. "We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things. "That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers." This year's heat and lack of rainfall were unprecedented Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees. The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future. Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things". Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future. It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued. Headline: Climate action discussed at youth COP meeting
Body: Dorset was hit by widespread flooding earlier this year School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey. Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers. Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change. A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit. The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors. Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues." "The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future." The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester. The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders. The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges. The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts. Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas. "We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added. Headline: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
Body: The National Trust hopes to create new wildlife habitats to attract wildlife including water vole and turtle doves A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years. The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey. The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space. Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate." The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows. Northfield is a rich natural site with a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the tenants. The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge". There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period. The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit. Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge". Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like." The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come. Community drop-in sessions about the vision , external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November. Headline: Pupils fascinated by space get astronomy lesson
Body: Dr Robin Catchpole shared his knowledge with pupils at First Tower School Jersey primary school children have enjoyed learning about space in a lesson delivered by an astronomer. Dr Robin Catchpole of the Cambridge Institute of Astronomy was invited to the island by the Jersey Astronomy Club and shared his extensive knowledge with pupils aged 10 and 11 at First Tower School. Year 6 pupil Lola, 11, said her favourite part was learning about how the planets were created while Vihaan, 10, said he was fascinated by black holes and how they were formed. Catchpole, who has written and co-written more than 100 research papers and articles on astronomy, said his trick for making space accessible to children was to show them planets they would be familiar with. Catchpole said he first became interested in astronomy when his grandfather gave him a book about the subject and his mother showed him the Moon through a telescope on the beachfront in Torquay, Devon. "I saw craters and shadows of mountains and I thought that was very exciting," he said. Year 6 teacher Lee Bradshaw said it was a great opportunity to have an expert like Catchpole answering questions and children proved inquisitive about the subject. Headline: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
Body: Swans and ducks have enjoyed the wetland reserve at Slimbridge for 80 years Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important. Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT). Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world. Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands." Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK. Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change. So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change? The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes. Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl. He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them. Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl. Sir Peter Scott with the first nine NÄnÄ geese he hand-reared at Slimbridge in 1952 "He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation. As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature. He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund. In 1973 Sir Peter Scott became the first person to be knighted for conservation work. Moore explained: "Scott was talking about the impact that man was having on the natural world, long before we started talking about climate change and global warming. "David Attenborough called him the Patron Saint of Conservation, and I think that is more than deserved," Moore added. Electrical items caused fatal fire, inquest hears Residents protest against plans for greenbelt homes One of Scott's typically ambitious projects was to save the Hawaiian Goose, or NÄnÄ. Unique to the Pacific islands, the NÄnÄ was hit hard by road building and development. By 1949 barely 24 birds remained. Scott heard of its plight, and asked Hawaiian authorities to send a few geese to Slimbridge where he hand-reared them. "Unfortunately they sent us two females," chuckled Enid Cole, a WWT volunteer at Slimbridge. "Peter asked them for a gander - 'It would help', he said." Nine chicks were later born, and hand-raised successfully to adulthood at Slimbridge. Dave Harvey helped to feed the NÄnÄ geese at Slimbridge Today there are more than 3,000 NÄnÄ geese, most of them living peacefully on Hawaiian golf courses. But a handful still live at Slimbridge, where Enid Cole and her friends hand feed them lettuce every day. "It's a marvelous project, and typical of Sir Peter," Enid smiled. Over the last 80 years, the teams at Slimbridge have hand-reared several other species, including the Common Crane and the world's rarest diving duck, the Madagascan Pochard. It was while they were working to save the Madagascan Pochard that they realised how vital the wetland habitats were. "We realised that to save that species, we had to bring the wetland back," explained Sarah Fowler, WWT's chief executive. "And to bring the wetland back, we had to work with the whole community in Madagascar." Ian Hollister, a volunteer warden at Slimbridge, said: "The wetlands are great at absorbing carbon, they're like a soggy secret weapon." Scientists calculate that 85% of the world's wetland habitats have been lost as marshes drained for agriculture, and swamps cleared for construction as cities expand. And yet, as Fowler explained, "40% of the world's species rely on wetland habitats for survival". What started at Slimbridge has spread to 10 wetland reserves across the UK with the charity now working with local councils to restore wetlands, even in small city areas. Wetlands are 'mood-boosting, flood buffering habitats' said Sarah Fowler, Chief Executive of WWT The Wetlands Charity A scheme in Bristol has seen small floating islands of wetland plants moored in the city's harbour. Across the world, they are campaigning to restore one million hectares of lost wetland, partly to provide safe habitats for endangered species but also because wetlands help absorb carbon far quicker than even forests. "Every time the big tides go over them, the plants that have grown up in the salt marsh get buried. Those plants are full of carbon, so they are a massive carbon sink. "And the brilliant thing about salt marshes is they do this four times faster than trees. Wetlands are vital in our fight against climate change, and we must restore them." What started 80 years ago as a bird reserve on the banks of a river in Gloucestershire has grown into a global campaign to restore wetlands, which they call the "soggy secret weapon" against climate change. Headline: BBC Inside Science
Body: The Conference of the Parties (COP 31) has kicked off in Antalya, Turkey, with a focus on implementation and acceleration. But as countries work towards their climate targets, a familiar question remains: what about those not moving fast enough? China has long been singled out as a major climate culprit. Yet its carbon emissions appear to be plateauing, while investment in renewables is surging. Is China turning a corner, and is it enough? Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder and lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, and Michael Grubb, Professor of Energy and Climate Change at University College London, join Tom Whipple to discuss what the latest figures mean for the global fight against climate change. And Sarah Griffin is in love with her AI companion. She discusses the relationship, the stigma surrounding human-AI companionship, and how it has brought greater fulfilment to her life. Plus, Lizzie Gibney, senior reporter at the science journal Nature, brings us the latest science news you may have missed. BBC Inside Science is produced in partnership with The Open University. Headline: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
Body: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON. For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared. Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011. And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard â and not just for the UK. As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between. America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels. Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet. The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills? On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil. Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a Â£1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security. Panorama, Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas. Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra Â£63bn â around Â£2,200 each â according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations. Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable. At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama. But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt." "We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy." There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it. Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!" Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field. Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks. Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills". "If we use our own gasâ¦ that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice. Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets." Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had." Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year â even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead. Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption. The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another. With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination. Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel. The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables. The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ãrsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs. Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power. And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills. All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills. And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars. And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember. The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on. I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market". Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said. Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering. "There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was. Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs. Foreign investment, then - just not from China. Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says â a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C. Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest â and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early. And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo. If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices â and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin. Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis? The NHS is relying more on charities - and that might be creating problems for patients Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. Headline: UK ethics watchdog chief steps back from role over sexual misconduct claims
Body: Stuart Sterling was appointed chief executive of the Ethics and Integrity Commission last year The head of the government's main ethics watchdog has stepped back after it emerged he was investigated in a previous job over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues, and had, in one case, been sanctioned. Stuart Sterling was appointed as the first chief executive of the newly formed Ethics and Integrity Commission in October 2025. The existence of the allegations against Sterling, and the investigations into them, were first reported by the Sunday Times. Following the report, a government spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role while we swiftly establish the facts." The Labour Party promised in its 2024 manifesto to create the commission to "ensure probity in government" in response to scandals during the Covid pandemic. As its head, Sterling's role included advising the prime minister on tackling misconduct in public life. The Sunday Times reported that, in 2003, Sterling had been subject to a "full misconduct hearing" when he was a junior officer with Northamptonshire Police in what was treated as a case "of sexual harassment". The paper said he had been accused of inappropriately touching the breasts of a female colleague in a police station, and a male colleague who allegedly witnessed the event had reported him to his superiors. It reported that he had been suspended on full pay. A representative for Mr Sterling said: "Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002. He complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction." The Sunday Times reported that he was given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay. It said that, at the time, that was the maximum sanction possible short of forced resignation. He then received two police commendations and was promoted to be a detective sergeant. The Sunday Times said that by 2008 Mr Sterling had been reported to the force again after another allegation of sexual misconduct against a female colleague, this time at a social gathering outside work. Mr Sterling's representative said: "He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards". The representative added: "He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily". Northamptonshire Police has confirmed that it holds a digital record of a misconduct process from 2002. It did not comment on the later allegation. In 2009, Sterling joined the Cabinet Office. It is not clear what vetting process he underwent. He has since served in a variety of senior roles and in 2019 was seconded to the National Police Chiefs' Council. In 2023 he received an OBE for helping to plan the funeral of Queen Elizabeth. It is understood the Cabinet Office will now examine whether appropriate and correct disclosures of information were made.

Headline: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
Body: Watch: Philp and Yusuf have public clash over immigration Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans. The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers. The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration. Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed. Asylum centre on military base near Piddington approved A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation. The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken. There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council. In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire. Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners. Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it were opened by Labour. Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives. He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government. "So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?" Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power. He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring". Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room." Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government. Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics." Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power. As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging." Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people". McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent." While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters. Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives , and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power. Up to 1,256 men could be housed at the site near Bicester under the plans Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels. Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community". Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers. Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission. Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application". He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre". Headline: Firm offers to fake artworks for wealthy migrants seeking UK 'talent' visas - BBC investigation
Body: Watch: BBC undercover reporter is offered fake art and awards for 'talent' visa Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found. The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists. Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception. Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years. We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee. A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation. No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than Â£100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said. In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work. A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists. "There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood. Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected. The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the Â£100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation. A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system". They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused". The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based. Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English. Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us: At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application For an extra Â£28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address. We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims , when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum. The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching. A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu. In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artistâ¦ Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approvalâ¦ We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well." An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement". Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said. While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud". The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained. Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration. About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025. Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year. The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories. Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent". We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said. "We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK. Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (Â£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London. Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained. To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time. During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes. Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (Â£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win. The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor. It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges. Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experienceâ¦ online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English. This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf. Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter. The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029. The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about Â£98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling. The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application. The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass. "There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result." He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer. Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law". When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made. "We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us. iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever". "The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him." The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate. It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships". Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight. Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address. Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through. We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence. Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them. The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors. The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation". It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it. Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks. "It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment." Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says. Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work. The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK. While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found. Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.
