Headline: Welsh Labour leader says party has focused too much on powers for Senedd
Body: Ken Skates became Welsh Labour leader in July Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party's past stance on devolution, telling members the party had treated standing up for Wales as wanting more powers for the Senedd. In his first speech at his party's Welsh conference since becoming leader , Skates apologised to voters that "needed a Welsh Labour government". He said in the past the party had prioritised things that had led to a "lively debate in constituency party meetings". Skates spoke after Andy Burnham suggested the party may not have devolved enough powers to communities when it ran the Cardiff administration. It is the first conference since Labour lost control of the Welsh government . A review also criticised the former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy , dubbed the Red Welsh Way , saying that demands for more powers had fallen flat with voters. The party lost to the pro-independence party Plaid Cymru in May's Senedd election . Ken Skates says Welsh Labour didn't focus on improving people's lives He told the Venue Cymru conference in Llandudno: "Sometimes we've treated standing up for Wales as though it simply means seeking more powers for politicians. "I reject that test. Standing up for Wales means standing up for the people of Wales, people's jobs and wages, the NHS." He said "to the people of Wales, on behalf of my party, I am sorry. I'm sorry we fell short on what matters to you most." Skates said: "Speaking frankly, we sometimes didn't prioritise the things the people truly cared about. "We didn't make enough impact for those who needed us." He said Labour "sometimes angered the electorate, making it easier for people to look for something different". Labour sometimes prioritised "things that sounded good on paper or things that would lead, obviously, to a lively debate and constituency party meetings", but didn't necessarily answer "the fundamental question of how is this going to improve people's lives", Skates said. "What is the Labour Party for, if not to alleviate poverty and lift people's living standards, to create jobs, to improve our communities and deliver for people." Endorsing Burnham's push for more devolution to communities , Skates said: "This won't be easy for some to hear, but too much power has been retained in the centre and not devolved onward, where it can make the greatest difference to people's lives. "The first great chapter of devolution was about moving power from Westminster to Wales. The next chapter must be about moving power closer to people." He added that Welsh Labour "must be confident in its identity, but judged by what that identity means for jobs, wages and public services". Skates said he would hold the Plaid Cymru government to account "not by the constitutional arguments they start" but "by what happens to waiting lists, school standards, household bills and jobs". He said Plaid's actions in government were not as progressive as it had portrayed itself at the election, criticising the party on NHS waiting lists, payments to struggling households and the decision not to revalue council tax. Both Ken Skates and Stephen Kinnock spoke at Welsh Labour conference on Saturday At a conference fringe event, former First Minister Mark Drakeford reiterated the calls he made in government for the devolution of justice. Burnham has indicated he is open to the devolution of policing - the UK government is yet to endorse concrete proposals. Sat alongside his former counsel general Mick Antoniw, Drakeford said the status quo is "indefensible". "We lock up more people as a percentage of our population than are locked up in England," he said. Drakeford said prisons were "bulging at the seams". "The case is absolutely evident that the status quo is not working, is doing immense harm and where there are no solutions on offer that give you any confidence that things could be done better and differently." Asked by BBC Wales what Antoniw and Drakeford made of Skates' comments, Antoniw complained of "confusion" on the topic. "Everything Andy Burnham is talking about is reform and devolution, which is what the constitution is. "Of course you don't go knocking on doors and saying, you know, what do you think about the constitution today? "When people want things done, you have to look about what the powers to enable you to do that." Skates made no mention of justice devolution in his speech, but Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock did. He promised to deliver on previous promises to "enhance the Welsh government's role on youth justice and probation services, to improve the way in which youth justice and probation work by better integrating them with the wrap-around services that are already devolved". Kinnock said: "Devolution was never meant to be an end of itself. It was always the means, the vehicle for changing lives. "Wales is in danger of becoming the most centralised nation in the UK. "The destination should not be Cardiff Bay, it should be the people." He accused the Plaid Welsh government of failing to match-fund a defence technical college. "Time wasted means investment stalled and careers delayed. We're honouring our side of the bargain; it's time for Plaid to step up and honour theirs." Headline: Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
Body: A review by Alan Milburn (left) could create political headaches for Andy Burnham Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are. He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street. Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms. To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out. Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government. Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks. Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets). In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit. Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorus to water. But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected. Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one. Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip. And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind". There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform. First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings. Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade â gradualism, not a short, sharp shock. Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants. Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns â at least privately â about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall. This time, they are on board. One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts. But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off. Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs. Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time. There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms. One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging â from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health. Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place. York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress". She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work. She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on. Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year. He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution". But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail". So much of politics - like comedy â depends on timing. For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn. But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line. Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts. Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work". And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis". So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations. But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government. Headline: Smart glasses banned from Welsh Parliament after ruling they could be used for speeches
Body: Jason O'Connell has used smart glasses to deliver speeches in the Senedd The Senedd's presiding officer has in effect banned the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament, days after it emerged he would allow them to be used as a teleprompter. Huw Irranca-Davies had ruled that using them in such a way was OK - provided he was alerted first - but Members of the Senedd (MS) have now been told he "will not be considering any other requests" to use the devices. He said that will remain the case until a review into the use of the devices on the Senedd estate ends. Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech . O'Connell, whose glasses do not include a camera, said he had voluntarily agreed not to use his device until the review is complete. The MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr previously said he had started using glasses as a teleprompter to improve his speaking skills and to avoid looking down at his notes. A letter from Irranca-Davies from 20 October, published in committee papers last week, said he had "determined that members may use smart glasses as a teleprompter in the chamber, provided that they give me advance notice". Unlike other types of smart glasses that have caused controversy, like the ones above, O'Connell's do not have a camera built into them On Tuesday, an official working for the presiding officer told MSs that "he will not be considering any other requests to use AI-equipped glasses in the Siambr until the review has reported". They said: "Following further helpful discussions, no members will be using the technology until the review has been completed." The official said the next stage of the Senedd Commission's review would include a consultation with MSs and staff, and would be completed by the end of 2026 with recommendations "brought forward in the new year". O'Connell told BBC Wales after the decision: "I've voluntarily agreed to stop using the ones I'm using as a teleprompter until the review completes." Asked how he felt about the matter, he said: "I'm ambivalent. They were a useful tool to be used on occasions. "I was no way reliant on their use. But I look forward to using them again once the Senedd approves them." The Senedd declined to elaborate on the statement to MSs after being asked why the presiding officer's stance had changed. Reform is currently holding an unrelated boycott of Senedd proceedings , after its member Joe Martin was barred from speaking by Irranca-Davies, after Martin claimed in parliament that white people were being "replaced" in the UK. The smart glasses decision was issued to MSs before the presiding officer's ruling on Martin was issued . Headline: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
Body: Young people should have a legal guarantee to a job or training, Milburn says Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC. Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work. He claims the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it spends on supporting them into employment , and believes the ratio should shift to two to one. That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support. Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - Â£25 to one, and we can take everything to Â£2 to one". He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits." The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare. Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion? Milburn said the government is already spending Â£22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive, and that money needs to be spent differently. He has already said that the under 25s should no longer be able to claim some health benefits â the personal independence payment and the health element of Universal Credit. In his other major announcement, Milburn spoke of the proposal he calls an "opportunity guarantee" for young people. This would put a legal duty on government to ensure young people have access to a route into employment. He said: "It should be a guarantee for a young person. Because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is a very simple thing. To get a benefit. What sort of life is that?" The "opportunity guarantee" might work similarly to the way that councils have a legal responsibility to offer homeless people accommodation or advice, or accommodate children in care. Milburn argues previous employment schemes have been temporary, and says a permanent legal entitlement is needed to tackle the long-running problem of young people not in education, employment or training. The government is expected broadly to welcome the proposals, which will be published in full on Tuesday, with a statement in Parliament and draft laws early next year. Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training - otherwise known as Neet - according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics . Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full. Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require. Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance". Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic. "It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said. The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning. Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future". Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available". Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail. Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence. Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away. "It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down." Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment. Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty." The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person. They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school. The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency". But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said. "A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive." Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences. Headline: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
Body: There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others. Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted forâ¦ no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country." It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc. And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which â for Burnham â Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility. Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off. Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether. But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party. Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022. The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines â not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement â but is open minded to changing those at the next election. Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain. "We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public." But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk". Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out. Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship. But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries. A voice from the past has a different set of concerns. Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful". The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal. "If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'." Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem". "How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy." For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate. The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing. Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister. Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide. Badenoch has pledged that a future Conservative government will withdraw the UK from the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react. The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards". But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters. In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing. "The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it." The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham. Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016. "If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a Â£40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said. The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party. Headline: Piddington to bring legal challenge over asylum base plans
Body: Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in September over the plans The government will face a legal challenge over plans to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers at a former military site near Piddington, the parish council chairman has said. Planning permission for the development at the MoD Bicester site near the Oxfordshire village was approved by the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner after the Home Office used a fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed and of national importance. Opponents have six weeks to challenge the decision. Parish council chairman Tim McNally said ministers should "absolutely" be ready for a legal challenge. Defence minister Luke Pollard said the government would continue to engage with the community. Piddington, a village of about 350 people, symbolically voted to leave the UK in September over the planned use for the site, and last month the group Wrong Plan Wrong Site appealed for a judicial review into the proposals. Up to 1,256 men could be housed at the site near Bicester under the plans McNally told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the village could also apply the new Hillsborough Law. Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour which compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place. McNally told the programme: "Last night, [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham was on a podium talking about the violence, sexual violence towards women, and bringing it upon the media industry as their responsibility to manage. "But the reality is, is that this is exactly what the government is doing to us here." Asked how the village would respond, he said: "There's going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward. "Today is a day of reflection, and we'll work out where we plan to go from this point. But I will say, the Hillsborough Law is there for a reason, and we're going to apply it." Asked if ministers should be braced for a legal challenge, he said: "Absolutely, absolutely." A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against and one in support. It also said Rayner had ruled permission via an Urgent Crown Development application should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high". The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the building of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities. Melise Witkin shared her concerns about the site with the BBC Melise Witkin, who has lived in Piddington for six years, told the BBC that she was "extremely disappointed but not surprised" to hear the plans had been approved. She said she moved to the village because she wanted "tranquility" and to live in a community, which she said "we have". "I think people are angry but scared," she said. "Where are they [the asylum seekers] going? We've got no pavements, we've got no street lights, we've got no pub, we've got no shop, so what are they going to do?" "It's wrong for them, and it's wrong for us." Jo Haw-Cook said the village will "carry on fighting" Jo Haw-Cook, who has lived in the village for 56 years, said she is "saddened" but "not surprised". Speaking to the BBC earlier, she said: "There's still a long way to go, and we're still going to fight on. "I think the mood is reasonably positive, obviously we are disappointed, but we're resilient, and we are a community, and we will come together to fight this as a community." Defence minister Luke Pollard told LBC: "It's pretty obvious that there's a strong sense of feeling from the community around Bicester, especially in Piddington. "The Home Office continues to engage with those. "There's still a few more stages to go here, so it's not yet fully locked in and delivered, so that we can understand where the concerns are, so they can be mitigated. "I recognise that any change for the people around MoD Bicester will be a concern, and that's why it's so important that the Home Office engages with the community." Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe for locals, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community". She continued: "As the prime minister himself has said, we do not want a situation where it's only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers who believe all parties to play their part." Asked what he would say to the women of Piddington, the spokeswoman said: "I think he would say we completely understand the strength of the feeling here and the safety of the public will always be our top priority, and that's why we will work with police and other partners to ensure security arrangements are in place." A Home Office spokesperson said on Thursday: "Planning permission allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester. However, a final decision to proceed is yet to be taken. "The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over Â£1bn saved in costs since the election. "This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. "These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community." Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch during her visit to Piddington in September In a statement posted on social media, Bicester Town Council said it is "deeply disappointed" by the government's decision to grant planning permission. "This decision was taken through the Urgent Crown Development process, bypassing normal local planning scrutiny, despite strong and well-founded objections... regarding the suitability of the site, infrastructure capacity, community safety, and the lack of meaningful consultation," it said. The council said it will now prepare a formal response to the government "setting out its continuing concerns and seeking clear assurances on the issues raised". Cherwell District Council, which formally objected to the proposals in September, said "important planning questions remained unanswered". Leader of the council Lesley McLean said: "This is disappointing news, and local residents will rightly be feeling extremely angry and let down by this development. "They have campaigned tirelessly and peacefully to have their voices heard, and this decision suggests their concerns have fallen on deaf ears. "We know that despite planning approval being granted a final decision on whether the site will be used has not been made." She has urged the Home Office to "engage urgently and constructively" with residents to "listen to their concerns and give them a voice in decisions that could have far reaching impacts on their lives". Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the plans were a "betrayal of the women of Piddington" and "emblematic of Labour and Angela Rayner's disregard for the law and women and girls' safety". She said on social media: "When I visited Piddington I met a village terrified of what was about to land on their doorstep. "The Government said it was listening, instead it's completely ignored this community's concerns. "The 1,000+ male migrants that Labour are about to deposit in Oxfordshire are in Britain illegally. They should be deported as soon as possible, not housed in areas completely unsuitable for the task." Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said Piddington has become "ground zero for the invasion of Britain". Speaking in Piddington, he told broadcasters: "Despite an enormous campaign from local residents demanding that the government doesn't dump 1,200 illegal migrant men into their village, Angela Rayner has approved it. It's absolutely shocking." On whether using the former military site to house asylum seekers is a better use of taxpayers' money than using hotels, Yusuf said: "The only thing that should be happening with these people is them being detained and deported back to the country from which they came." Headline: Tories pay artist for Burnham images after legal threat
Body: The Conservatives handed out bottles with Chow's illustration on them at their party conference The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minister. Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture - which Burnham has used on social media - without permission. He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. It is understood the Tories agreed to pay a Â£1,000 fee for use of the image - and contributed an unknown sum to Chow's legal fees. The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler". Chow posted on Facebook: "The Conservative Party have settled after their recent indiscretion of using my image without my permission." He added: "Maybe ask firstâ¦ admittedly I would have said no, but it would have been a damn sight cheaper for the Tory Party if they just hired any illustrator to do their take on a cartoon of Burnhamâ¦ hopefully this a lesson learned. Copyright matters." A Conservative spokesman said: "The Conservative Party values the importance of intellectual property in the creative industries. We consider this matter closed." The original image of Andy Burnham was created by Chow in 2021 Manchester United fan Chow, a Labour supporter, has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho. He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city. He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager. Headline: Reform could try to remove Senedd presiding officer over member's speaking ban
Body: Huw Irranca-Davies became the Senedd's presiding officer following the May election A senior Reform politician says a no-confidence vote in the Senedd's presiding officer is "not off the table", after a party member was banned for claiming white people were being "replaced". LlÅ·r Powell, Reform's chief whip in Cardiff Bay, said his colleague Joe Martin had the right to raise "legitimate concerns" that were being "infringed upon". Martin was told he would not be called to speak in the Welsh Parliament until he apologised for the remarks made on Tuesday, which Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive". Reform withdrew from most Senedd proceedings on Wednesday in response. Powell, who as chief whip enforces party discipline in the Senedd's Reform group, was asked on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast if his party would put forward a no confidence vote in Irranca-Davies. He said: "I'm not going to say that we're going to do that now, but what I would say is it's not off the table right now because freedom of speech and the right of members to raise legitimate concerns should be the main priority. "And for us, right now, we see that as being infringed upon." Powell denied Martin had made any connection to a far-right conspiracy theory that the white population was being deliberately replaced by the immigration of other ethnic groups. "Joe was asking a legitimate question based on demographic changes," Powell said. "The idea that he was framing some far-right theory is false. "He was talking about legitimate concerns that is out there for data for all to see." Reform's Joe Martin, party leader Helen Jenner and chief whip LlÅ·r Powell announced the boycott on the Senedd's steps on Wednesday During business questions on Tuesday, Martin had asked Welsh government minister Heledd Fychan for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place in the UK". "Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said. Fychan had asked the deputy presiding officer, who had been chairing the session, whether the question broke Senedd rules. Irranca-Davies later called Martin's statement "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive" and "clearly discriminatory" when he issued the speaking ban. He said that unless Martin apologised to the Senedd chamber "we will not be calling him to speak". Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, criticised Martin on Wednesday, saying "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat". Martin, a Member of the Senedd (MS) representing Caerdydd Penarth, was accused by Plaid Cymru of dangerous rhetoric in June when he claimed attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable . The next day MSs walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read, and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs . He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the crisis-hit Welsh Gender Service . Headline: Youth scheme branded 'failure' over success rate
Body: Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training (Neet), according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics Less than half of young people supported by two government-backed youth schemes in London went on to take up further education, employment or training (Neet) opportunities, according to new data. Only 1,100 of 2,600 young Londoners supported by the Â£20m Youth Guarantee Trailblazer scheme moved into further opportunities. Former youth worker and Conservative peer Shaun Bailey said the scheme was a "failure" and called for more support for employers but Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was helping young people furthest from the labour market and that it was still "early days". A major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out proposals for tackling the problem next week . Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics. London is one of eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazer areas in England already exploring ways to help young Neets. More than Â£20m in government funding is being spent on a variety of initiatives across London, from youth hubs to mental health support. The money is funding two trailblazer projects in London, one focused on care-experienced young people in 12 boroughs, and a broader scheme that works across the capital. The Greater London Authority (GLA), which leads the projects, has shared the initial results from year one of the two schemes with the BBC. By the end of June 2026, London's two trailblazer schemes had offered support to more than 2,600 young people. The programme offers a range of support, including access to mental health and wellbeing services at colleges and universities, help moving into further education, work experience, careers events, mentoring and practical help finding a job. The programme is funded for two years until the end of March 2027. Mattie Davies is a 19-year-old from London. He recently left college, and since then, has struggled to find work. "I applied to a good few thousand and it's constant rejections," Davies said. He has found work as a delivery driver but he says the wage is not enough to pay his bills. "Uber will take anyone and that's what I didn't want," he said. "I wanted a job I could go into and break down all of my barriers and build myself up as a person." He has not been receiving support from London's two Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes. Instead, he's been getting support from Millwall FC, where he plays football, and its youth programmes. Mattie Davies says applying for jobs has been a struggle Lord Bailey said the government should instead focus on helping businesses employ young people. "Sixty per cent of young people not moving into full-time employment or education show you it's actually a failure," Lord Bailey said. "That money would be better spent giving businesses some headroom so that they can actually afford to employ young people." The skills minister said London's Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes were helping young people who face several challenges, such as mental health difficulties or experience of the care system. "The fact that a lot of them are succeeding at the first opportunity is a good result," the minister said. "It's worked exactly in the terms we set for it, which is young people who were furthest away from the labour market able to get back into the labour market, and learning about how we engage with some of those young people." The eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazers in England have received a total of Â£90m in central government funding over the two years of the programme. The trailblazers were part of the Labour government's plan to help 16 to 24-year-olds classed as Neet, whose number has been rising in recent years. There were 125,949 Neets in London at the end of 2025, the highest number of any region in England, according to government data. Headline: Parliament date set for 'summer of sex' debate
Body: MP Samantha Niblett has launched a campaign calling for lifelong sex education An MP has been given a date for a House of Commons debate following her campaign calling for lifelong sex education. Dubbed the "summer of sex", the campaign was launched to push education about consent, respect and healthy relationships, with the aim of preventing abuse and violence, but has received a mixed response in Westminster. Samantha Niblett has previously said she also planned a separate event to display a number of sex toys and sex education aids in Parliament as part of the campaign. However, this is unlikely to take place until the new year. The backbench debate is due to take place in Parliament on 26 November, it has been confirmed. The South Derbyshire MP applied in March for the debate, but said she faced a "longer wait" for it to be granted because she wanted it to take place in the main chamber, rather than a lower-profile venue such as Westminster Hall. "I wanted it to be in the main chamber as the gravity of the topic warrants the surroundings that most people think of when they think of Parliament debates," she said in a Facebook post. Niblett (right), launched her campaign alongside sex educator Cindy Gallop (middle) and Lucy Litwack, the CEO of Coco De Mer in London this summer She also said she had been "astounded" by the support she had received for the campaign, which was initially met with reluctance. "Today, I was finally granted my debate, which will take place on Thursday 26 November, when I'll deliver my speech based on the huge journey I've been on these past seven to eight months, and making some initial recommendations to government," she said. "But what is clear is this is just the beginning, and in light of recent events this campaign has never been more important." In a session of Prime Minister's Questions in September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed to meet Niblett on the issue and praised her for "raising important issues that others won't talk about". He added: "It's very clear to me that her summer was more exciting than mine." MPs who are not in government can apply for backbench debates on a topic of their choice to a dedicated cross-party committee. The debate is opened by the MP who requested it, and other backbenchers from any party can contribute. A government minister and the opposition frontbench also respond with their views on the issue. Headline: MPs urge Labour ministers to get on with trophy hunting ban
Body: The government has been accused of dragging its feet on its manifesto promise to ban the import of hunting trophies. Labour pledged at the 2024 general election to outlaw bringing the parts of animals killed by hunters for sport, such as heads or horns, into the UK. But it has so far failed to bring a bill enacting the ban to Parliament, and in the two years since the election more than 40 import permits have been granted for hunting trophies. Speaking during a debate on the subject, Environment Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter insisted the government was still committed to a ban and a bill would be delivered "when parliamentary time allows". Labour MP Clive Efford, who had proposed Wednesday's Westminster Hall debate, said the minister's promise "really is not good enough". "Who is the government afraid of?" he asked, arguing that only a "tiny minority of people" opposed the ban. He continued: "This issue has been debated widely, over a great many years; there is not much more that we can learn from either side of the argument - this is the time that the government have to act and move forwards." A ban was first proposed by the Conservative government in 2019, and in 2022 a bill implementing a ban was passed by MPs but ran out of time in the House of Lords. Conservative MP Henry Smith, who sponsored that bill, accused peers of using "parliamentary devices" to block its passage into law. During Wednesday's debate, several MPs urged the government to restart the process by introducing a fresh bill to Parliament. Efford said: "Trophy hunting is not about conservation, it does not resolve issues of wildlife-human conflict, and it does not bring economic benefits to rural areas âcertainly not in the way that tourism can. "Local people have been attacked, their land stolen and their human rights abused. Private companies are stealing their homelands. Britain should not be accommodating this industry." Labour's Rachael Maskell also called for a ban, but said the government could, in the meantime, make it illegal to advertise safari hunting and make it a criminal offence for UK residents to "celebrate their kill" by posting images on social media. Labour MP Irene Campbell said she found it "upsetting" that hunting trophies could still be exported from the UK, pointing to an instance of a Scottish stag head being exported to Zimbabwe. DUP MP Jim Shannon said the flow of hunting trophies coming into the country was continuing at "nearly two dozen a year while the government drag their feet". Addressing the minister, he said: "I ask her to give us a timescale, give us a date and tell us when [the ban] will happen." Conservative Roger Gale criticised those who hunted the animals, saying: "A yellow streak runs right through those people and they are revolting." More than one MP suggested that the government was being pressured by the US not to introduce a ban. Earlier this year, The Telegraph reported , external that Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, wrote to the UK government arguing: "Legal, well-regulated hunting â particularly trophy hunting â plays a vital role in supporting healthy wildlife populations, restoring habitat and supporting local economies." Responding to MPs, Riddell-Carpenter said the government remained committed to banning "the import of hunting trophies from species of conservation concern". "Our aim is clear: to introduce the bill at the earliest opportunity and within this Parliament," she said, although she declined repeated invitations from MPs to set out a more specific timetable. Opponents of the ban argue that it would undermine local economies and reduce the amount of money that could be spent on conservation projects. The Community Leaders Network, a group of rural representatives from countries in southern Africa, argues that regulated hunting helps pay for rangers and wildlife management. "In practice, a ban could do the opposite of what it intends: less funding can mean fewer patrols, more poaching, poorer habitat management, and ultimately less wildlife," it says. An Oxford University report from 2024 concluded , external that a ban would not ease pressure on threatened species, and said around 79% of imports to the UK between 2015 and 2021 had came from countries where hunted species were "stable, increasing or abundant". Currently it is legal to bring hunting trophies into the UK, as long as there is a permit to do so. The government has said permits are only issued when "strict conditions" have been met, including demonstrating that their import "will not have a detrimental effect on the conservation status of the species". Between July 2024 and September 2026, the government issued permits for 41 imports including 21 African elephants, four hippos, five lions, a leopard and a giraffe. Headline: Some childhood offenders may no longer have to reveal convictions to employers
Body: Some job applicants in England and Wales would no longer need to declare criminal convictions they received as children under government proposals designed to improve the employment prospects of rehabilitated young people. The changes would mean criminal records for people detained when they were under 18 years old would no longer show up for life during checks carried out by employers. The Ministry of Justice has also launched a consultation on relaxing disclosure requirements for some specific drug-related and violent crimes committed by children. Young people who have not re-offended as adults struggle to find work because of their past behaviour, the government says. Many employers require applicants to undergo a background check, which in their most basic form require people to self-declare if they have a criminal record. For more sensitive roles, such as working with children or joining the police, an employer can carry out a standard or enhanced check, which allows them to request information from the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS). How long a criminal record must be volunteered for or will show up in those checks differs depending on the severity of the offence, the punishment received and how long ago the crime was committed - sometimes referred to as whether a conviction is 'spent'. For example, a young person who was convicted and fined for an offence when they were under-18 will have that information show up in checks for five-and-a-half years. If they were given a custodial sentence, that will be disclosed for the rest of their lives. The government wants to reduce the number of young people those disclosure rules apply to if an applicant has not continued to offend as an adult. Five offences would be removed from a list of crimes which will show up in background for checks for life if committed by an adult. They are: affray, violent disorder, supplying a controlled drug to a child, robbery and assaults occasioning actual bodily harm. Between March 2022 and March 2026, around 8,500 under-18s were convicted of those offences, according to Ministry of Justice data. The government says that type of crime is often a result of peer pressure, exploitation and "adolescent impulsivity" by individuals who are still developing, as opposed to a broader propensity for crime and violence. Under the new rules, they would cease to show up in checks after five-and-a-half years. Lifelong disclosure would also be removed for offences which led to a detention period of less than two years, the maximum which can be handed out by a youth court, and replaced by a new 11-year disclosure period. In cases where a child was given a sentence longer than two years - which can only happen if the severity of the crime meant they were dealt with by an adult crown court - the rules would stay the same. The most serious offences - including severe violence, terrorism-related crimes and sexual offences - would be exempted from the reforms. Cutting or removing altogether the disclosure period for offences which led to a fine, the majority of which are for driving-related crimes Ending disclosure of offences which were dealt with via an out of court resolution, which have primarily been used to tackle knife possession and assault Reforming how long earlier offences appear in checks for young people who committed more than one crime as a child Announcing a consultation on proposals, justice minister Jake Richards said: "Many young people who offend do not go on to lead lives of crime. "They take responsibility, turn their lives around and want to make something of themselves. "When they do, we should recognise that progress and support them â not put unnecessary barriers in their way." The proposals come as the government prepares to publish a long-awaited report authored by former Labour minister Alan Milburn on tackling the number of young people not in work or education . In May, he warned the UK was at risk of a raising a "lost generation" as almost one in eight young people are not working or studying. Richards pointed to that intervention as he announced the disclosure reforms, saying barriers to employment can be "particularly difficult to overcome" for people who committed crimes as children. Headline: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
Body: Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested him A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map". Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister. The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official. Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role. The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved. Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence. In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security. But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China. Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party. Chris Cash, left, and Chris Berry met in 2018 when they were teaching in China With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others. Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media". He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources. Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with". He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster. Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government. The espionage row that rocked Westminster Watch: Inside the China Spy Case on the BBC News YouTube channel , external UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state. England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time. This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government. China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander". The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation". In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China. In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anywayâ¦ not really intending to do anything." Listen: Berry tells Cash about his invitation to meet a senior Chinese official Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound. The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says. He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea." Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing". At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win. Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question. "And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash. After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now". In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state. But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party". The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweetâ¦ We may have a use for you yet". "I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friendâ¦ I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact." So who was the mystery official Berry had met? "I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought." Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff. Berry identified Cai Qi (left) as the man he had met - a trusted aide of Chinese President Xi Jinping Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi. What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system. For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really." We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us. Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says. Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked. Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together". The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said. At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary. He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026. Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy? Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK. He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster. The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch. It was to be their final face-to-face conversation. Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh. "They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says. "I was in complete shockâ¦ quivering... My mum was hysterical." Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London. Chris Berry was also arrested the same day. It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends. But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport. His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded. Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China." As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK". The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine. They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients. According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents. Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily. The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy. Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someoneâ¦ in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function. Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it. But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on. Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work". One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities. Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues. Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says. Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life. But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament. Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up." Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage. In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor. "Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges." His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story. Cash's life has changed almost beyond recognition, he says, but he is positive about the future At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing. Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life." Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated." There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up." "I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible." Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university. "We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited. He is also no longer in contact with Berry. "I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says. "I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down." But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government? "He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends." Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain". Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed. Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited. "It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive personâ¦ I'm positive about what the future holds." Get in touch â politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk , external

Headline: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
Body: If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through a large ship 80 miles north west of Shetland Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments. There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective". But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits. Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval. Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support. One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate". "The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said. Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer. Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test. "It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices." Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise." The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period. The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh . She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh will formally announce the Rosebank decision, expected in the coming weeks Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields". Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively. But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday. During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails." Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future". She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency." Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake. "Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added. Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it. Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either". "This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.
