Headline: Young, Welsh and into politics - but with different views on independence
Body: Cerys and Patrick have different opinions on whether Wales should remain within the United Kingdom in the future Cerys and Patrick have a lot in common. They're both young, Welsh, and very interested in politics. The one thing they don't agree on is Wales' future within the United Kingdom. A leading academic said the conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" amongst young people. This week, the Plaid Cymru Welsh government set up a new body to consider the case for Welsh independence, as well as more devolution for Cardiff Bay. For Patrick, he thinks his country is better off in the UK with more devolved powers, while Cerys believes an independent nation could offer more opportunities to people. Nationalist party Plaid formed a government in Wales for the first after winning 46 seats during the May 2026 Senedd election . While it hasn't called for a referendum on independence, the second line of its constitution says: "As the National Party of Wales, the party's aims shall be: to secure independence for Wales in Europe." Pro-union party Reform UK is the second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election. Its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said voters "do not want to see Wales ripped out of the United Kingdom" and said the commission was "ridiculous". A recent poll by Survation for the pro-independence group YesCymru suggested people under 35 in Wales were more in favour of independence than their older peers. "People feel left behind, especially my age," said Patrick, a 20-year-old student from Newport. He added that he could understand why people were "energised and enthusiastic" about independence because of issues such as "student loans, the cost of living, the geopolitical scene". But he said: "As of right now, I just do not think there is a case for it." However, Patrick, said he would support further devolved powers for Wales within the union. He said that "practical elements" such as whether there would be a border between Wales and England remain unanswered questions for him. In Case You Misssed It - Young, political and torn on the future of the UK Are younger Welsh voters driving a shift towards independence? We examine why support is rising among under-35s, hear arguments from both sides and ask what the political future of Wales looks like. For Cerys, learning to speak Welsh as an adult and broadening her understanding of history led to a "realisation" that Wales "in reality deserved a lot better than we had been given in the past and in the present". "I think if we were independent, we could offer people more opportunity here," said the 35-year-old from Bridgend. She added she'd like Wales to have further powers over policing and justice - a policy area currently controlled by Westminster. "People seem to be kind of dangling the carrot of more devolution and never actually giving it to us," she said. "More powers would be great but I will believe in those powers when I see them and until then, I think our best option is independence." Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he was open to the idea of giving the Welsh government control of policing in Wales. Cerys recently spoke at an independence rally in Aberystwyth alongside Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth A leading academic from Cardiff University said "it's staggeringly important" that "young people are a majority in favour of independence". "They see nothing strange or impossible about Wales becoming independent in the future," said Prof Laura McAllister, from the Welsh Governance Centre. She said that there was "great scepticism" around the topic when you look at the opinions of people aged over 65, adding there was a "real demographic schism". "There's going to need to be something much closer to support at least half the population supporting independence before there is any chance of a referendum being won," McAllister believes. She added nobody "can afford to be complacent about the future of the union" because "the concept of the United Kingdom has no God-given right to survive in its current form". "What we've seen in politics in recent times is that the potential for change is intrinsic to everything that happened," she said. In 2024, McAllister co-chaired a commission which concluded Wales leaving the United Kingdom is a "viable" option . Independence is one of the options being considered With polling suggesting between 20% to 30% of people in Wales would be in favour of independence , external , academics have compared the current situation to Scotland in the years leading up to the independence referendum in 2014 . "In some ways the situation here looks similar to Scotland in 2007," said Dr Jac Larner, a pollster and political analyst from Cardiff University, reflecting on when the Scottish National Party [SNP] took power. "You might think now we have a party like Plaid Cymru, there's this inevitable march to this endless 50-50 that you see in Scotland, right? "What's different here [in Wales] is that we still have a lot more hostility to the idea of devolution. "You have about a third who want to get rid of the devolution altogether, maybe just less than a third who want independence." Dr Jac Larner said attitudes towards independence and devolution are often driven by national identity First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "I have a vision for Wales, I support an independent Wales." He said it was about "improving a lot of the people of Wales, tackling injustices, tackling unfairness, tackling inequalities, creating prosperity". He added: "In the here and now, I deal with those issues dealing with the UK prime minister." In October, the first ministers of Wales and Scotland met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Glasgow for the National Economic Council , where devolution and funding were discussed. Ap Iorwerth said there was "a new understanding of the injustice of rail expenditure in Wales" from Burnham, as well as "a realisation that this hasn't been given enough attention politically by UK governments in the past". Following the 2026 Autumn Budget , ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales there were " paltry sums of money coming on rail , when they've said there's Â£14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services". A UK government spokesman said: "The prime minister passionately believes in our union and is optimistic about the future of the United Kingdom. "Our position on referendums is clear - the prime minister is focused on practical solutions to help people with the cost of living and make a positive difference in people's everyday lives, not constitutional questions. "Through the convening power of No10 North , the prime minister will build a constructive working relationship with each devolved government to explore how we can together contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode." Headline: The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds
Body: Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened. Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England. This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education. Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education." But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says. Hetton's principal, Vicky Pinkney, says low incomes shouldn't mean poor results The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English. In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely. What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results? From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift. In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs. Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome. Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils. Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says. "It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim. Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says. Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education. The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry , external found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success. So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control. But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors. So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.) After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy. But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English. It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney. The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos. For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard. While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings. There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject. Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together. It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff. Pupils who feel they "belong" at school tend to perform better in their GCSEs, a government-commissioned study has found And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs. Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil. Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves. It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons". But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success. Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children. The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education. The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance. Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.) That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work. The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades. The likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing GCSEs has barely changed in many years, says John Jerrim, an education professor at University College London But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks. "Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says. She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive. Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term. Does the principal think other places could replicate its success? Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically. "I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve." Wales has an education crisis. Can it be fixed? Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis? Headline: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
Body: Kashim Chowdhury fraudulently earned more than Â£284,000 of taxpayers' money Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023. He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work. At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked. She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial. She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court. Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer. That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week â more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than Â£284,000 of taxpayers' money. In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid Â£350,000. Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain. But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs for several more months. It was the government's National Fraud Initiative that flagged suspected fraud to Defra. As a result, the Defra Investigations Team launched an investigation and Chowdhury was arrested and interviewed under caution in July 2023. He was dismissed by the civil service in September 2023. On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence". Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him. He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head. He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box. Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013. He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time". But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system. Chowdhury sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long? Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication. Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said. "That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs." There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country. Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her. But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP. In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency. While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period. His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job â this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere. Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs. Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems. But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years. In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than Â£40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including Â£45,000 in premium bonds. A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers. An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management. "Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said. "But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement." A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost Â£285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions. "This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account." The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers". Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue. He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark. Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home. The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered Â£500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months. Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her Â£2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it. At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer. Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence. Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud

Headline: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
Body: It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation. The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade. It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis. When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation. A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making. How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments. The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming. Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed, , external he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented." But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted. On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work. He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one. He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts. But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other. And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee". He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people. Millburn has already said under-25s should no longer be able to claim the personal independence payment and the health element of universal credit Westminster jargon often describes earnest sets of recommendations published in reports like this as "wide-ranging". This review genuinely is, arguing for changes not just in welfare, but in the health and education systems. It's a real expansion of the state's involvement in the next generation, from one of the Blairites still standing, with the expensive Paul Smith knitwear to match. He is not the first government veteran nor is Burnham the first PM, to try to sort out this problem. But what Milburn and his allies say is different this time round is they're pushing for a whole new system that's permanent, not just another scheme that gets introduced by one secretary of state, then is dropped or scrapped by the next one that turns up. And the notion of a legal guarantee is designed to make the state, likely through local councils or mayors, take responsibility for making sure young people have something useful to do when they emerge from school â for good. The recommendations apply to the whole UK, but the precise way the powers might be used in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will be worked out when it gets to the finer details of draft laws. The scale of the practical challenge can be seen from space. New research from the Lib Dems this weekend suggests that if nothing was done, the number of Neets would hit 1.26 million by 2031. And Milburn himself cites figures that puts the cost of the issue at Â£22bn a year. No politician would argue for the status quo. But agreement that something must be done doesn't automatically translate into consensus over what that something is. For all Milburn's talk of grand ambition â his plans will not, any time soon, make much difference to the ballooning costs to welfare. His plan will take as long as a decade before making a real dent in the benefits bill. And it will require taxpayers' cash at the start, although not the Â£6bn guesstimates that have done the rounds. He's still coy about the upfront cost, but it will be billions over the years. And he says plainly there are many young people who are capable of working but don't, although tiptoes carefully around any accusations that some take advantage of the system, saying he's convinced the vast majority of young people do want to work. Milburn's forthcoming report has been described as a "watershed moment" by PM Burnham The Conservatives and Reform have both put saving tens of billions from the welfare bill, and fast, at the top of their list. The Tories said Milburn was right that benefits must be cut - but that "unlike Labour, our plan goes to the root of the problem" including by halving employer National Insurance for young people and creating 100,000 new apprenticeships. Reform said the review "is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away" and it cannot be "another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down." Milburn and the government can expect sustained criticism that it's not acceptable the plans would take so long to start cutting the enormous bill for the taxpayer. There is no question the expected increases in benefit payments are absolutely eye-watering. The opposition from that quarter, and indeed from the Greens on the left arguing already that what they have seen so far is "cruel", is entirely predictable to Downing Street. What's harder to read, and therefore more difficult to contend with, is how Labour MPs will respond. Sir Keir Starmer tried, and painfully failed to make changes to welfare, sabotaging his own authority when he backed down in the face of backbenchers. That's why Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, has spent hours and hours talking to Labour MPs in the last year, trying to patiently make the case for this plan. And why Milburn, as he was keen to point out, has continually been in touch with No 10 and 11, trying to get Burnham on board even before he made it to Downing Street. A government source said hopefully, this time "we've done the ground work â it's not a rushed Treasury process driven by numbers". As my colleague Iain Watson has written, the signs are healthier for Milburn, with a few key critics from last time showing more than an open mind to the new plans. The political climate is completely different with Labour, for now, cheerier about the polls, and backbenchers reluctant to make trouble. Burnham still is in possession of course, of the enormous majority that Starmer won. Pat McFadden - pictured here with Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham - has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms There will, without doubt, be voices on the left of the party, concerned perhaps about opposition from the Greens or the SNP in their constituency who will never sign up to anything that would mean a cut to payments for anyone on benefits now. "Look at the chaos Starmer got into," one source on the left warned, saying Burnham wouldn't be so "boneheaded" to do the same as "he wants to be everyone's friend". So a possible fault line may become whether the reduced benefits apply to those already claiming, as Milburn believes, or only those in future. A No 10 source is plain the plans would have to apply to those on benefits now, warning they must act as soon as they can, although new laws will take time. They told me "an argument on welfare is an argument we are happy to have". Let's see if that sentiment stands the test of time. The Milburn review was set on its path by Starmer. But it will emerge blinking into the light under a different leader, and in a very different political moment. Perhaps, some in Labour wonder, Milburn's ideas are arriving at a time when a newish prime minister has big rhetoric but perhaps is short of big concrete ideas, mocked by his opponents for reportedly bringing in private consultants to fill out his much-vaunted 10-year plan. Burnham is widely expected to adopt most of Milburn's genuinely radical ideas. Months of arguments lie ahead, however settled the political picture appears right now. But Milburn's ideas just might have come around at the right time for a relatively new government . As one senior Labour figure believes: "You need some meat on the bones that isn't just, 'nationalise everything' â this could be it." Headline: Doctor burnout putting maternity patients at risk, says regulator
Body: Trainees in obstetrics and gynaecology are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning. The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns. Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture. The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority. The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people. Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients. "Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential." He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership." Adam Kay says he wasn't well supported while working as a doctor Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor. He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby. "I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it." He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago. "The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read." Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing. "There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry. "It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment." Dr Miriam Broughton is training to become a consultant Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant. While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world. "Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless." The main challenge, she says, are the sheer number of demands placed on a doctor in her field. "It could be that there's two or three ladies whose babies need delivering, and then somebody else coming in on maternity triage whose baby isn't moving, and you might also be getting calls from A&E about a lady having a miscarriage who's bleeding really heavily. "There's just one of you to manage all those jobs." Broughton says while she has largely had positive experiences, it is important to step back and look at the wider culture. "You do hear things from other hospitals about people feeling nervous about calling the consultant...which isn't great." Kat Barton says doctors need to be supported so patients receive the best care Dr Kat Barton, chair of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) National Trainee Committee, says workplace issues end up affecting patients. "Many of us feel overstretched and close to burnout. This reflects staff shortages, working beyond our hours, and knowing that despite our best efforts, the care women receive is being affected. "We know the safest care comes from teams that are well-supported, well-resourced, and listen to each other and to women and families. "We need the government to invest in safe staffing at every level, protect our time for training, and support our wellbeing and careers, so we can give women the safe, compassionate care they deserve." Recent high profile maternity reviews into maternity failings, which looked at outcomes for mothers and babies, also highlighted concerns about workplace culture, leadership and the ability of staff to raise concerns. Obstetrics and gynaecology trainees were more positive than average about some aspects of patient safety reporting, the GMC survey indicated, including how to report patient safety incidents and near misses. A DHSC spokesperson said: "In all the investigations carried out in recent years into failings in maternity services, one of the key lessons has been that members of staff must feel empowered to speak up if they have concerns about workload, or patient safety, and their concerns must be acted upon. "All NHS trusts are now required to have a dedicated Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and internal pathways for staff to raise concerns about the working environment, patient safety, or their own wellbeing. "Alongside this, we are continuing to grow and strengthen the workforce to help relieve the pressures on busy maternity units, and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year. "Since coming into the role in July, the Secretary of State has made maternity services a personal priority, and the Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing is working to respond to the concerns raised by staff and families alike, and ensure that every maternity unit meets the highest standards of patient safety and care." Headline: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog
Body: Cancer charities and doctors say sunbeds are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions. The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use". Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems. The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly. The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice. "Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett. "Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health." Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers. Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey. Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules. "We want young people to be properly informed about the risk of sunbed use and we recommend using trusted, regulated sources to find out information such as the NHS , external or cancer charities , external ," she added. The wider health and beauty sector in the UK is estimated to generate sales of Â£6.1bn a year, according to market researchers Whito The CAP said it had identified a series of misleading health claims in sunbed advertising, including suggestions that tanning beds can ease eczema symptoms, improve brain function, reduce inflammation and boost circulation. Earlier this year, the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), which enforces the CAP code, banned five adverts that claimed sunbeds could help manage conditions including osteoporosis and depression. The new enforcement notice warns businesses not to make medical claims, promote sunbeds as a source of vitamin D or suggest sunbeds are safe. Sunbed use is legal and regulated in all parts of the UK, with limits on the strength of the UV light the beds can emit and a ban on under-18s using the devices. According to the Sunbed Association, its members train staff to screen out high-risk customers with very fair skin and, under its guidelines, no individual should be allowed to buy more than 60 sessions a year. The organisation's chairman, Gary Lipman, said he would never encourage members to use health claims to promote their products. He said he has worked with the CAP to ensure the code would not stop members explaining how they comply with regulations. "We fully support action against misleading advertising. But there is a world of difference between claiming something is risk free and explaining that a business operates responsibly," he said. The CAP said that advertisers have been given until 7 December 2026 to make sure any marketing claims are compliant. It said it would be using an AI-based monitoring system to identify ads that continue to break the rules and would "take further action where needed". Headline: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month
Body: Consultant doctors in England have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government. The walkout was due begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only. This is known as Christmas Day cover and was likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services. But the British Medical Association, the trade union for doctors, said it was pausing the action to discuss pay and working conditions with the government. Consultants â the most senior doctors in hospitals â were given a 3.5% pay increase this year. But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account â although this is using a measure of inflation that tends to be higher than the one favoured by economists. The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken. Meetings have been taking place over recent months, but the BMA is now entering formal talks with the government's negotiating team. They could start as soon as this week. In a statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta said: "We welcome the opportunity to enter formal negotiations with the government and hope this marks a turning point in a dispute that has gone on for far too long. "We've always said strikes do not need to go ahead as long as the government is willing to genuinely negotiate and now is their chance to do so. "We have received assurances that there are no constraints on what we discuss in these negotiations, and we look forward to hearing their proposals on both pay and working conditions." But government sources said giving them a bigger pay rise this year was not on the table because of the state of the public finances and current level of their pay. Average earnings for consultants top Â£150,000 a year. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the cancellation of the strike was "welcome news for patients and the wider NHS". "I had a constructive discussion with the BMA on reforms that could give consultants a stronger voice, greater flexibility and more freedom to innovate, while improving services for patients." In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part. The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.

Headline: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
Body: Successive governments have been "asleep at the wheel" on adult social care, says the head of the independent commission looking into the sector in England. Baroness Louise Casey said care services for older people and adults with disabilities had been developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way, unlike the deliberate design of the NHS in 1948. As a result, she suggested a postcode lottery had developed with different levels of services available depending on where people live. And she also highlighted the fees that self-funders pay, saying they were much higher than councils were charged for people entitled to state support. Baroness Casey said care services, such as home adaptations and personal care like helping people out of bed and with washing, were simply not valued enough. Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care". And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that. Last month the inquiry published a report which said the care sector appeared to be " something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic, allowing Covid to spread like "wildfire" . Baroness Casey, who will address a conference of social care leaders later on Wednesday, said the findings were "so awful" and "a national shame". "Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. We've got our heads in the sand." Her final recommendations for services for older people and adults with disabilities, including care homes, will be published next summer. It comes as her commission publishes research showing England is an international outlier for having no "clear system of stewardship" for social care, unlike countries such as France and Germany. She said the market was dominated by private providers and said the regulator â the Care Quality Commission â as being a "spectator at the site of a car crash". Two people with the same condition having different experiences depending on where they live â different assessment processes, waits and levels of support Those who paid for their own care â social care is means-tested â are charged on average 40% more than the councils pay for care they arrange When Andy Burnham became prime minister, he said social care was one of his key priorities although the Casey commission was set up by the Starmer government. "Together, we can build a new settlement for care," Baroness Casey said. "One based on values I still believe this country shares â decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves." Headline: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
Body: One drug comes out top in a large analysis , external of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression. Escitalopram performed best at preventing patients from relapsing in a study involving nearly 10,000 people prescribed different medications for up to a year. Two other pills - agomelatine and duloxetine - came next, while Prozac (also known as fluoxetine) ranked just below them. Experts stress the findings don't mean that everyone with severe depression should switch to escitalopram, or that other antidepressants aren't any good, because all the drugs can work and each has its pros and cons. Depression is common, affecting around one in six people in the UK. With the right treatment and support, people can make a good recovery although for some their depression can return. To prevent relapse, doctors already recommend people stay on antidepressants for at least six months after depression ends, and then taper off gradually. The new analysis, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, looked at previous studies comparing the effectiveness of more than a dozen common antidepressants in total. The differences found were modest and experts say longer studies are still needed to find out more. There are many contributing causes to depression and a variety of ways to treat it, including drugs and talking therapies. Experts say patients should discuss what treatment options are best with their doctor. Many medical guidelines recommend SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) antidepressants, like escitalopram, sertraline and fluoxetine or Prozac, as the first drug of choice. These drugs increase serotonin, which is linked to mood. According to the new analysis, compared to Prozac (fluoxetine): people on escitalopram were more likely to see their symptoms improve and stay that way, and less likely to stop taking their medication agomelatine (an atypical antidepressant) and duloxetine (an SNRI or selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) also performed well other medicines, including sertraline, were no better One of the researchers, Prof Eric RuhÃ© at Radboud University medical center in The Netherlands, said the choice of medication can vary for each individual. "Nevertheless, our study can help inform the decisions that prescribers and patients make together: if you start an antidepressant, choose one that not only helps you to get well, but also keeps you well." Dr Sameer Jauhar, an expert at Imperial College London, said while the research provided useful information, "it cannot tell us which antidepressant will work best for an individual patient." "I would not interpret these findings as a reason for someone who is responding well to their current antidepressant to change treatment," he added. Prof Allan Young from the Royal College of Psychiatrists said: "While some medicines appear to have a small advantage over others for longer-term outcomes, the differences are modest and are unlikely to outweigh individual factors such as side effects, previous response and patient preference when deciding on treatment." Like all medicines, escitalopram can cause side effects, including sleep problems, constipation and weight gain, although not everyone experiences them. The NHS says , external if escitalopram or a similar SSRI is ineffective or not suitable, doctors may suggest a different type of antidepressant, such as an SNRI. Older tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, are now less commonly prescribed. The mental health charity Mind says people need access to clear information about the potential benefits and side effects of antidepressants as well as other forms of support, including talking therapies and mindfulness. "It's common for people to need to try more than one medication before they find the right treatment that works for them. And what works may change over time," the charity said. Headline: I had to explain to my teacher what a young carer was - we need more support
Body: As an ambassador for young carers, raising awareness is important to Neraya Neraya is only 15 but cannot remember a time when she was not a carer for her two sisters. She is among the young carers crying out for what they have called crucial support, with Neraya saying she has even had to explain what she does to her teachers. On Monday, the Welsh government will publish a national strategy for unpaid carers, which will have seven priorities including earlier recognition and mental health support. Neraya, from Bridgend, said people in her position wanted the chance of "a childhood of our own". Carers Wales said the strategy looked positive in parts, but it was "disappointed" manifesto promises would be excluded and raised questions over how it will be funded. There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK , external , 170,000 of whom are young. The 2021 Census said this included about 120,000 carers, aged five to 17 in England and 8,200 in Wales. Scottish government recognised there were 42,050 unpaid carers identified in the 2021-22 Carers Census. Neraya's sisters have varying needs and she helps with practical things such as helping them get ready for school, as well as emotional support, and said there was a lack of understanding about the sacrifices young carers make. "There's not the understanding that you might not have been able to go somewhere because we had some sort of problem within the household because my sister was ill and I'm worrying about my sister, that kind of thing," she said. Neraya said she used to get "picked on" because people did not know what was happening with her siblings and others tended to assume they were just "naughty". Once, in primary school, she said she was called to stand in front of her class and explain what she did because "teachers themselves didn't understand what it was". Being a carer does not take away from her life, she said, but having support and being made to feel "valid" would give people like her "the chance to have a... childhood of our own at the same time". The Welsh government said its strategy would focus on seven priority areas, shaped by conversations with carers with the aim of improving early recognition, access to support and respite, and better information on their rights. It also indicated more support for mental health and wellbeing. Reece says support with helping build CVs and fun trips help young carers Reece Peachy, 17, from Ebbw Vale, Blaenau Gwent, helps care for his youngest brother while his parents support his other siblings with additional needs. He said being a carer was "difficult but easy at the same time", but has to be home more than the average teenager. He said: "If I have plans me and my mam will talk about it and I'll watch him. You naturally just help them out and I've been doing it for so long its just an instinct." Reece said it could be "tough sometimes" as he balances his responsibilities with seeing friends and going to college as he puts his brother "before anything else". "It can feel very frustrating and lonely because I wont spend much time with other people and sometimes I have to push aside things I want to do." He said his local young carers group helped a lot by providing trips around Wales and helping him get his Duke of Edinburgh award to add to his CV. He plans to finish his college course in carpentry before doing an apprenticeship, all while continuing to help his parents. "I know if I move away too far they will struggle. My parents always say they are so grateful for what I do." Cerys Morgan wants to see more support for carers under 10 who might not understand what their role is Cerys Morgan, 19, has helped support her 16-year-old brother, who is non-verbal and autistic, as well as being physically disabled, since she was eight. She helps with mostly physical tasks - such as getting him ready for school and taking his medication - but also provides emotional support. "I've developed an understanding more than I think other people would as a sister," she said. "I understand how he's feeling, what his needs are and how I can support him if he's having a hard day or a happy day and know what's best for him, in that way as being a sister, to support him." She called emotional support for young carers "really important" in order to help them develop skills and resilience in their roles, especially those who find themselves in the role at a young age. "When I was eight I didn't understand what a young carer meant," she said. She suggested the Welsh government could look at mentor schemes to link young people up - something she wished she had "when I was little to support me and for me to communicate with as well". Deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, described unpaid carers as the "backbone of care" across Wales. But Carers Wales said the strategy does not go far enough. Head of external affairs Rob Simkins said: "There are some welcome parts of the new strategy, particularly around access to respite care and a desire to see more carers receiving support. "However, it is not clear how the government intends to make the step-change needed without additional investment to provide the extra support that unpaid carers desperately need. "It is also disappointing that the manifesto commitment to ensuring carers' needs assessments , external are completed within 28 days is missing from the strategy." He said the organisation wanted to make sure unpaid carers lives are better and was not sure that this strategy "will go as far as we want it to". The Welsh government said: "We have engaged extensively with a wide range of social care groups and our national strategy for unpaid carers will help ensure they get the recognition and support they deserve. "We are considering whether changes are needed to strengthen support for carers, including imposing a timescale on the completion of carers' needs assessments." Headline: Mental health is no joke - but I've turned it into a stand-up routine
Body: Michael says he did "a lot of practising" for his stand-up debut Stepping onto the stage for the first time, Michael Hart is "flying" with adrenaline. He didn't think he had it in him, but he's about to tell his own jokes to a room full of strangers. He stutters at first but soon gets his first laugh from the crowd and the nerves he's feeling are washed away by a wave of elation. Michael is part of a group of people who have struggled with mental ill-health and are now giving stand-up a go to build up their self-belief and connect with others. Through the Finding Our Funny workshops run by the charity Inspire, they're turning their experiences into comedy material - and then taking it on the road for three gigs across Northern Ireland this month. The comics have performed gigs in Enniskillen, Londonderry and Belfast Michael has sought help for his mental health over the past few years and has struggled with his confidence. Given those circumstances, throwing himself into stand-up is a daunting prospect - but he's embraced the challenge. "The first thing I said was: 'What's the worst that can go wrong? "I did stutter at the start, I sort of froze - but I came back in again. Just a joy to get up there. I think I kept it together well. "My wee trick was I done a lot of practising." He's now performed three gigs, using all his own material. "It's all true, I didn't make any of this stuff up." Carla Sloan says she's had mental health issues for most of her adult life and had never imagined trying her hand at stand-up until now. "I've done lots of mental health courses on emotional resilience and stuff but this was something completely different. "The first day I drove into the car park and then I was like: 'No.' "I turned the car around and I drove back down the road and then I thought: 'Ah, I'm here, I might as well go in and see what it's about'." Carla says her stand-up experience has boosted her self-esteem As a mum of teenagers, Carla's jokes are about her real-life experiences of parenting. "All my material is based on teenage girls and the fun you have raising them but also when they do something that they aren't meant to do," she smiles. Tim McGarry is a veteran of the Northern Ireland comedy scene, best known for playing Da in the long-running BBC sitcom Give My Head Peace. For decades he's given audiences the giggles with his own stand-up shows, so who better to mentor this bunch of budding comics? For McGarry, the approach to comedy should be a simple one. Tim McGarry shared some of his tricks of the trade, such as comic timing and dealing with a crowd "I just sat down with them and said, well, what makes you laugh? What's something funny in your life? "Most of them went off and wrote stuff themselves and I tweaked a bit and helped a wee bit - but it's coming from entirely the participants themselves." While some comic techniques can be taught, McGarry says, much of his work as a mentor involved building their self-belief. Getting "out of their comfort zone" and taking that first step onto the stage is the hard part, says McGarry - but the payoff is worth it. "There is no better feeling than coming off stage and going: 'You know what? I made people laugh'." Michael is keen to keep his stand-up career going "When I looked back at my videos I couldn't believe how well I'd done. My family is very proud of me," he says. "My goal is to get back into work - and this has raised my confidence even more." The experience has given Carla a fresh belief in herself too. "I've learnt not to underestimate myself - and that was a big one for me as I do tend to underestimate what I'm capable of. "Maybe I need to look at myself a bit more and be aware of just how much I can do. "I might have to take things slower than other people - but I can still do it." Kerry Anthony says the workshops helped the group to build resilience and confidence Inspire chief executive Kerry Anthony says the project is something very different to what the charity would normally do. Much of its work involves helping people who are dealing with mental ill-health, homelessness or addiction - but Kerry says that talking about those "heavy" topics through humour has been "wonderful" for those in the stand-up workshops. "People who use our services... have worked with us over the years to use their voice around very serious issues to do with mental ill-health. "This was a time that they could use their voice in a totally different way. "Comedy isn't a treatment for mental ill health - but comedy is important for everybody." Headline: Woman with terminal cancer gets dream wedding on hospital ward
Body: Maggie Heginbothom was married in her hospital room at Ysbyty Gwynedd A woman with a terminal cancer diagnosis married her partner of 15 years in the hospital where she is receiving palliative care - and her horses even made the ceremony. Maggie Heginbothom, 68, who has advanced liver cancer, thanked staff at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor for organising a wedding ceremony on Monday, just two days after her partner Mark proposed. The horse lover and former clinical scientist with Public Health Wales, described hospital staff as being "like family to me". "It was so beautiful and I honestly never thought it was going to be possible, especially seeing both my horses there as well," she said. Heginbothom, originally from the Vale of Glamorgan, was admitted to hospital nearly three weeks ago after becoming unwell while riding one of her horses. After her partner proposed from her hospital bedside, staff on the Tegid Ward volunteered to pull together a celebration that included flowers, decorations, a harpist, food, cake and Heginbothom's beloved horses Ozzy and Quiosque. Horse lover Heginbothom says the "little touches" made her wedding special The horses were brought to the hospital by Pen LlÅ·n Stud and Riding School, where Heginbothom rode and competed for many years. "From the beautiful decorations to all the little touches that made our wedding so special, I cannot thank them enough," she said. Ward manager Rachel Parry said her team were determined to get things right. "On the morning of the wedding, we transformed Maggie's room with white sheets and fairy lights to create a beautiful space for the ceremony, while the relatives' room became a reception area," she said. Staff at the hospital joined the "special and emotional" celebrations "Everything ran like clockwork, and some of our colleagues even came in on their days off to help make it happen. "It was such a special and emotional occasion. "There wasn't a dry eye in the room, and it was particularly lovely that some of the other patients Maggie has got to know during her time on the ward were able to join the celebrations." Matron Ceri Newell said it was an example of the compassion and dedication shown by NHS staff. "Nursing is about so much more than treating illness," she said. "It is about compassion, kindness, humanity and recognising that sometimes the most important thing we can do is help make someone's wishes come true. "What the team achieved for Maggie and Mark in such a short space of time was truly remarkable, and I could not be prouder of every single person involved. "Everyone went above and beyond, working together to create something incredibly special for a couple going through such a difficult time. "Moments like these remind us why we do what we do, and I am so proud of what the team achieved." Headline: 'I cycled across America in memory of my wife - I know she's proud of me'
Body: Declan spent almost seven weeks cycling from the west coast of America to the east coast Declan Faulkner and his wife Patrina always intended to return to the United States, a place they visited shortly after getting married almost 30 years ago, and maybe make a cross-country trip. But, as is sometimes the case, life had other plans. They moved close to Patrina's home village of Ballygawley, County Tyrone, developed their careers, raised three children â and then Patrina was diagnosed with breast cancer. Four years later, in 2017, she died. But Declan never forgot the journey they were meant to take together â which is why the 55-year-old just spent seven weeks cycling coast-to-coast across the US, from Portland, Oregon on the west coast to Portland, Maine. "When things got tough throughout the journey, I just had Patrina's voice in my head and I dug deep thinking about what she and other cancer patients go through," he said, reflecting on one of the hardest but more rewarding challenges of his life. It was during Patrina's illness that Declan found an outlet in the form of endurance sports, setting him on a path to his 3,800-mile (6,115km) epic cycle across the US. "I've always been a keen runner and love to cycle, and even when she was sick Patrina would give me the green light to go off to the Mourne mountains for the day," he said. "I just loved the serenity of running and cycling there and I suppose mentally it really helped me hold things together at the time. "I'd remembered talking to Patrina about this idea I had in my head of going back to America and cycling coast to coast. "Ten years had passed since she died and the kids have grown up, and I just thought wouldn't it be great to see America on two wheels with the memory of Patrina on my shoulder along the way." Declan said he loved the serenity of running and cycling So at 55 years old, Declan, who is a financial adviser by day, decided to take a short career break to fulfil a lifelong dream, while raising cancer awareness along the way. He was joined on the road by his friend from Cork, Donncha O'Brien, another keen cyclist. Declan said: "We had met a few years back on cycling trip in Kerry and had become great friends and thank God he was there because he kept pushing me. "There were days when you felt like your body was just shutting down and you were sore all over, because we were spending sometimes 10 hours a day on the bikes without a break." The men spent 43 days on their bike and averaged 85 miles (137km) a day, but on some days cycled up to 120 miles (193km). They cycled 45,000m of elevation, the equivalent of five-and-a-half Mount Everests. The journey took them through some of the most spectacular landscapes in North America - over the Big Horn Mountains in Wyoming and along the Great Lakes. Among the spectacular places Declan passed through was Yellowstone National Park Declan said he had several pinch-me moments throughout the trip. He said: "Cycling into Devil's Tower, Wyoming, which I think was one of the first national parks inaugurated in 1906 and it's just this big volcanic plug - we cycled there on a beautiful day. "Seeing that for the first time was special. "Then coming into Vermont in the autumn and some of the colours of the trees were just stunning. "And we cycled through this amazing lightning storm in upstate New York in the dark, with the lightning strikes just lighting up the whole place." There were also many hard days along the way too. "Cycling through the strongest winds I've ever experienced in South Dakota was probably the toughest. "Leaving South Dakota Badlands National Park we actually ran out of water and my sugar levels just dropped and I nearly fell of my bike a number of times, I was just exhausted." The gruelling journey involved storms, strong winds and much-needed breaks by the roadside Declan's journey started at the Pacific Ocean and ended at the Atlantic Ocean. He says seeing the Atlantic coast is something he will never forget. "Our final destination was this beach right on the Atlantic Ocean, and the last 20 miles to it just went in a flash, and taking the bikes down to the water on that last day was totally surreal. "I wasn't overly emotional until that evening when a friend sent me a picture of Patrina and I from 30 years ago when we were at a party at college. "That just brought the tears because I was looking at that picture and felt like she was with me the entire way." As part of the cycle, Declan raised almost Â£20,000 for Charis Cancer Care, which runs a specialist care centre on the banks of Lough Fea in County Tyrone where Patrina spent many days after her diagnosis. Arlene McAvoy from Charis Cancer Care praised Declan for his achievement The centre in the foothills of the Sperrin Mountains, just outside Cookstown, provides a free-of-charge service offering emotional, physical and practical support to people with cancer. Arlene McAvoy from the charity said: "With Declan doing this cycle in Patrina's memory and raising awareness, it's just amazing what he has achieved. "Each year we have about 1,400 people who come to our centre. "It's not just for the person who is going through cancer, but it's also for their families and carers as well, and I know this was a special place for Declan also." Reaching the Atlantic coast was an unforgettable moment for Declan Now that Declan is back home, he says it is taking a bit of getting used to. He added: "You wake up thinking: Have I pumped the tyres? Have I greased the pedals? Are the lights charged?' "It's mad because you've been in that cycling bubble for so long. "But now that I'm looking back on it, I am very proud, and I do think about what Patrina would think. "She'd probably laugh and say: 'You're not wise' - but I know she'd be proud too."
