Headline: Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?
Body: Are branded cold and flu tablets really worth the extra money? Your throat's painful, your head throbs and your blocked nose has kept you awake all night. It's that time of year again - flu season - and you'll try anything to feel normal. But is that pricey max strength flu remedy really any better than a basic box of painkillers? "The big brands have been around for a while, they've been tested, and there are adverts on the TV saying they're really good," says Prof Jayne Lawrence, head of the pharmacy division at the University of Manchester. "But in reality, there's very little difference. Personally, I'd always go for the cheaper ones - and theyâve also been tested." The trade association representing over-the-counter medicine makers says familiar brands can reassure shoppers and help them find the right product on crowded supermarket shelves. The medications we've highlighted all contain similar ingredients with marginal differences to their quantities. Cold and flu drugs fall into three broad camps: household names such as Lemsip and Sudafed, supermarket own-label alternatives and single-ingredient medicines containing paracetamol or ibuprofen. A packet of 16 Lemsip All-In-One Max Strength tablets retails at Â£7.30, more than 20 times the Â£0.35 cost of paracetamol pills in some supermarkets. Both contain 500mg of paracetamol, which doesn't treat the underlying infection but does relieve pain and can bring down a fever. The Lemsip version, along with many of its competitors, also contains the decongestant phenylephrine. It's meant to constrict leaky or swollen blood vessels in the nose which can cause congestion. But Lawrence says there is little evidence it works when taken as a tablet, rather than as a nasal spray, because much of the drug is broken down before it can reach the bloodstream. In 2024, the US drug regulator said it wanted phenylephrine removed from all cold and flu pills, saying it was simply not effective, although that proposal has yet to be finalised. Some cold and flu remedies contain a third active ingredient - guaifenesin - which is meant to loosen mucus in the airways. That sits in more of a grey area: some studies report improvements in chest congestion, while others find little or no benefit. A spokeswoman for Reckitt, which owns Lemsip and Nurofen, says the ingredients in its products are approved by regulators and formulated for multiple symptoms including fever, congestion and coughs. Many popular max strength remedies can also contain up to 65mg of caffeine per pill, about the same as a mug of instant coffee. As well as acting as a mild stimulant, research suggests caffeine may boost the effect of paracetamol , external and help it work slightly sooner, although any benefit is likely to be modest. Almost every brand can also be found as a flavoured powder to dissolve in hot water, typically costing slightly more per dose than pills or tablets. That warm drink can be soothing and a study funded by a drug company , external found it may be absorbed into the bloodstream more quickly, but whether patients notice any major difference in their symptoms is much less certain. The entire over-the-counter medicines market in the UK, including cold and flu remedies, is worth Â£3.3bn a year according to industry estimates Yet ingredients are only part of the story. Bigger brands have more money to spend on in-store adverts and displays, according to a former manager at a large chemist chain. Well-known names or premium own-label products are often positioned at eye level, while budget alternatives are tucked away on the bottom shelves. "You are always going to promote the ones which are more expensive," says the former manager, who doesn't want to be named as she still works in the industry. When it comes to medicines, some shoppers assume that paying extra means getting something more trusted or effective. "Nine times out of 10, people would come in and ask for a certain brand," she adds. "Even if I explained there was little difference, and I was only trying to save them money, they would still want the big name." The PAGB, which represents the consumer healthcare sector, argues that "trusted and recognisable" brands can simplify choice and build confidence at a time when "health misinformation is widespread". If you're suffering with cold and flu symptoms, doctors advise the following: Rest, plenty of fluids and painkillers like paracetamol to control temperature swings Remember not to double up by taking paracetamol alongside cold and flu remedies that also contain it, as this can easily lead to an accidental overdose The NHS recommends gargling with salt water , external to relieve a sore throat, while a homemade hot lemon and honey drink can soothe a nasty cough , external , adds Dr Jamie Hynes, vice president of the Royal College of GPs See a GP if a cough has lasted for more than 21 days, says Hynes, or if you've lost weight unintentionally or, in urgent cases, if experiencing chest pain or breathing difficulties And, note some cold medicines are not suitable for pregnant women so do check with a midwife, pharmacist or GP before taking Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Headline: Women in town hit poor health earlier than average
Body: The average age of onset of poor health for women living in Luton is five years below what it is nationally according to the report A study of female health in Luton has revealed that women in the town see the onset of poor health five years earlier than the national average. The Let Women Speak , external report, commissioned by the Borough Council, also found over 70% of women aged 45-64 had an at-risk Body Mass Index (BMI) level. Luton's director of public health Kelly O'Neill said: "Women are spinning a lot of plates as part of what the expectation of being a woman is, so many have put their own health and well-being secondary to the well-being of others. "That meant they weren't turning up for cervical screening, breast screening and many things that help them stay healthier for longer." Director of Public Health Kelly O'Neill said good public health needs to be part of everyday life More than 250 people from a range of ages and cultures were interviewed for the report that focuses on the wellbeing of the 112,400 women and girls who live in the town. The study found the average age of onset of poor health for women in Luton is 55.8 years compared to 60.9 nationally. In June the BBC reported that life expectancy for women and men is also lower than the national average at 82.6 for women and 78.6 years for men. 24% of school-age girls in Luton skip breakfast and 15% skip lunch, which is often linked to stress, time pressure and concerns about body image. Only 52.5% of women in Luton aged 25-49 take up cervical screening. Only 27.3% of women in Luton access long-acting reversible contraception. In 2025 only 63% of eligible women in Luton had a breast screening, compared to 71% nationally. Councillors have now agreed to champion women's health , external and support the delivery of actions to improve health and wellbeing. Luton-based GP Dr Eva Patel said language can be a barrier when people come and visit her at the surgery Dr Eva Patel is a GP at Luton Medical and Dental clinic. She said she often sees woman coming in who are managing multiple responsibilities. "Working, bringing up children, looking after elderly parents or supporting other family members often from large families means their own physical and mental health is often the last thing they prioritise," she said. Thirty-seven young South Asian women were also interviewed about their experience of social isolation. Patel said: "Language can be a barrier. If a woman comes in by herself and they don't feel comfortable speaking English then they might find it difficult to explain symptoms, even with a translator." Headline: Rare cancer discovered after mum underwent hysterectomy
Body: Donna Marklew from Finham, Coventry, was diagnosed after tests following a hysterectomy Donna Marklew had to undergo a hysterectomy to treat complications caused by childbirth. But the operation led the Coventry mum to receive a life-changing diagnosis when tests later revealed she had a rare form of cancer. She was diagnosed with neuroendocrine cancer , external , which was only discovered after tissue removed during a hysterectomy at Warwick Hospital was analysed following a uterine prolapse. "I was very shocked because I'd never heard of neuroendocrine cancer," she said. "[I] was left with not much information because it wasn't known to anybody, and then trying to explain to people [that] I've been diagnosed with neuroendocrine cancer, you're kind of met with blank faces." The rare cancer, which starts in the nerve and cell glands that make and release hormones, is estimated to affect 6,000 people in the UK every year, according to the charity, Neuroendocrine Cancer UK. Lisa Walker, the chief executive of Neuroendocrine Cancer UK, said that the average time between people experiencing a first symptom and getting a diagnosis is five years. "That is because the symptoms could be other conditions, and then people find themselves perhaps going down a different route and then needing to go back when the symptoms change or other symptoms are added in, which then start to look more like neuroendocrine cancer," she explained. Marklew is now trying to raise awareness of the disease, which coincides with World Neuroendocrine Cancer Day , external on Tuesday. She said that the disease is actually a group of cancers that develop in hormone-producing cells throughout the body. Diagnosis can be particularly difficult, especially for women, she added. Donna underwent a nine hour operation in 2025 to remove as many tumours as possible Marklew, an occupational therapist who works in Leicestershire, said that after she was diagnosed, scans revealed tumours were discovered in her appendix, Fallopian tubes and surrounding tissue. In March 2025, she underwent a nine hour surgery at Warwick Hospital to remove as many tumours as possible. However, surgery alone has not been enough, and Marklew has to have three injections every week to try and keep the cancer under control. She has also just started Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) , external which is administered four times a week, every two months. "The tumours are slow growing, which is one of the benefits of this type of cancer. "There's a different type of neuroendocrine as well, which can be more aggressive. but fortunately for me, mine are grade two, which means that they grow quite slowly, although mine are still growing." However, Marklew, 44, said while she is able to live a normal life during her treatment, the disease has had a huge mental impact. "'I've got four young children and my husband, my mum and my friends, and I think the reason why I've really wanted to get up and shout about it is because I just don't want anyone to have people feel so vulnerable when you find out that you have this diagnosis because nobody knows about it [the condition]." Boy saved by cannabis oil faces fresh fight as supplier collapses Medal gifted anonymously to Bradley Lowery charity Region honours the fallen on Remembrance Sunday Walker added: "It's a complex and diverse cancer and can develop in any part of the body, which is one of the things that makes detection difficult. "It develops in the neuroendocrine cells. They produce and release the hormones that essentially regulate our different body functions and are found throughout the body. "So it can affect any organ. Most commonly it does affect the lungs, the digestive tract, and the pancreas, but it can be found anywhere." Marklew said that prior to her hysterectomy, she had no identifiable symptoms, although looking back, she thinks a trip to Scotland may have been an indicator. "I was anxious and had palpitations during a trip to St Andrews for my first wedding anniversary, but my GP suggested that was down to me being perimenopausal." She said unlike other cancers, because neuroendocrine is not as obvious or as widely known as others, few people understand how she feels. "I could talk to my friends and family all day long, but no one will understand what it is like to live with this condition. "It's really really hard and because it's invisible everybody will say - oh you look great." She said she reached out to the charity Neuroendocrine UK , external for support and advice. "They're an absolutely invaluable resource for people that have been diagnosed and they have patient groups in other areas, so I said I'd really like to set one up. "We did one in September and one other person came along, which was nice because it was a nice opportunity for me and her to have a couple of hours conversation along with one of the nurses as well. "Then we [did] it bi-monthly, we had six people and it felt so good". Headline: Psychiatric intensive care unit for women to open
Body: Dr Afifa Qazi from Kent and Medway Mental Health NHS Trust said the opening was an important step forward The first NHS intensive care unit for women with serious mental health needs in Kent and Medway is due to open. Women in the region will have access to a dedicated NHS psychiatric intensive care unit for the first time, following a Â£4.63m investment by Kent and Medway Mental Health NHS Trust. The 10-bed facility at Littlestone Lodge in Dartford will provide short-term, intensive care for women experiencing serious mental health difficulties who need extra support. Dr Afifa Qazi, chief medical officer for the trust, said the opening was an important step forward and that until now women needing intensive care and support "have not been able to receive this specialist care from our team". The unit is expected to provide around 2,500 bed days of care for women each year, and is due to welcome its first patient towards the end of November. Qazi said: "This new service means we can now provide specialist, compassionate care at a particularly difficult time in their lives. "Our team will take the time to get to know each woman, understand what matters to her and recognise her as a person, not just her mental health needs." The trust said the unit would create a more joined-up pathway, helping women move smoothly between hospital wards and community services as their needs changed, with care planned around each woman's circumstances. Two of the 10 beds will also be available to women referred by other NHS trusts, depending on individual needs. The trust already provides intensive mental health care for men at Willow Suite, a 12-bed unit at Littlebrook Hospital. The new unit extends this specialist service to women. The unit is expected to provide around 2,500 bed days of care for women each year. People with personal experience of mental health services helped shape the unit, and its design also takes account of sensory needs, including those of women with autism and learning disabilities. Jim Dickson, MP for Dartford, said women experiencing serious mental health difficulties deserved "care that treats them with dignity, compassion and an understanding of their individual needs". "I'm pleased to see this new unit open in Dartford. It is an important investment in mental health services for women and their families across Kent and Medway," he said. Headline: 'My brother died, so I smashed up his TV'
Body: Ellie Goudie (L), who is pictured with her mother Kerry, turned to a rage room after her brother died When Ellie Goudie's brother Ryan died aged 23, she could not bear the thought of anyone else having his belongings. Instead, she paid to smash them to pieces. Armed with a baseball bat in a Swindon rage room, Ellie destroyed some of the possessions Ryan had left behind, including his beloved television, saying it helped her cope with the pain of losing him. "That was his. He can't have it any more, so no one should," she said. For Ellie, the experience was about far more than breaking objects. "I felt Ryan in here. He probably was doing it with me," she said. "I'm glad I've done it for him." Ellie is one of a growing number of women turning to rage rooms, where customers pay to destroy household items with baseball bats and crowbars in a controlled environment. Operators say many visitors are seeking an emotional release during some of the most difficult periods of their lives, including bereavement, trauma, relationship breakdowns and stress. At The Rabbit Hole Rage Room in Swindon, owner Paul Bunney said about 70% of customers are women. He said he sees a visible change in people after they come out of a session. "Some people are quite reserved when they come in, and then when I go and speak to them after they have a big smile on their face." he said. "They're hot, they're sweaty, and they've got rid of a lot of emotion." Paul Bunney says 70% of his customers are women Visitors travel from across the region to take out their rage on objects that were destined for landfill, like printers, crockery, hifi systems, kettles and old wine bottles. Paul said materials are often separated and recycled afterwards. For Ellie, the attraction was the sense of release she felt after months of grief. "You're taking out your anger and you don't have to talk," she said. "It takes away the emotion for the good hour or so you've got in here. And then you feel a relief when you come out Ryan Willis wrote rap music, which his sister played in the rage room A similar story has emerged at another rage room in Bath. Charlotte Bagnall, who runs Raging Bath, said what began as a fun attraction had developed into something much more meaningful. "I think everyone at the moment needs release," she said. She said many customers arrive carrying emotional burdens they have struggled to process elsewhere. "The people I've got to meet and the things they go through is fascinating, but also quite sad at times. "To lighten that load they're carrying is huge." Among them is Ceri Crannis, who booked sessions for her family after her daughter was stillborn. She said the experience provided something she had struggled to find elsewhere. "You don't get that release in therapy when you're talking," she said. "There are some things that are just so deeply hidden that it comes out here, where loud music, smashing, breaking really does just hit the spot where nothing else has managed to do that before." Ceri believes rage rooms can offer women a rare opportunity to express emotions that are often suppressed. "Social norms are geared up that women are well behaved, they don't swear, you don't break anything." Ceri Crannis used the facility after her daughter was stillborn Another rage room visitor, Sarah Bear, agreed. "You can't shout and scream at the people in the world because actually those people have done nothing wrong, but you can take it out on stuff here that isn't going to hurt anyone," she said. "So it's a really safe, controlled way to do it. And yeah, there might be some tears at the end of it, as, like, the relief washes over us, but it's worth it." It's no surprise that rage rooms can offer an immediate feeling of relief, according to associate professor of psychology and inclusion at the University of Bristol, Dr Nilu Ahmed. "You've got a set amount of time so you know what you can do. You know that it's going to come to an end. So you're not going to go on a rampage and riot out in the streets. You know that it's going to be contained." But Ahmed said it can't replace long term therapy. "For deep rooted issues, it's going to come up again and again. And the question that I always talk about is where are those feelings being discussed? "And if they are being taken into a rage room, what that is telling the individual or telling me as a professional, is that individual hasn't got a safe space to go and talk about that." For Ellie, smashing Ryan's possessions did not take away the loss. But she says it gave her an hour to channel her grief, remember her brother and leave feeling lighter than when she arrived. Headline: One of the most commonly injured parts of the body that many of us never train
Body: They are the body's primary shock absorber, vital for balance, standing, walking and running, but most of us rarely think about our ankles - until we hurt them. These painful incidents are very common, says Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist who has worked on shows like Strictly Come Dancing. Ankle injuries account for 5% of visits to A&E in the UK, according to NICE , external . But Tawiah tells What's Up Docs? they can be avoided "if you are strong and aware of your foot and ankle and the chain that affects it". Here are three ways to strengthen your ankles: This article contains content provided by Instagram. You may want to read Metaâs Instagram cookie policy , external and privacy policy , external before accepting. To view this content choose âaccept and continueâ . The foundation to building strong ankles and reducing the risk of injuries is being "brain to body aware", says Tawiah - meaning you can sense what movements your ankles are making without relying on looking down at them. "It's about sending information from the brain down to our foot and ankle to ground us and build a good foundation for any exercise training that follows," she says. To build brain body awareness Tawiah has some examples of exercises that require you to watch your foot while you do them. She suggests starting with smaller movements of the toes as this can affect how we "load [weight] through the ankles". Two examples are: Pressing the tip of your big toe into the floor, holding it and watching how the arch of your foot engages. "This will feel like something pulling through the arch of your foot," she says. Putting a pen on the floor next to, and parallel with, your big toe. Then try to move the big toe towards the pen, which is called toe "abduction". How can you better look after your ankles? Listen now. Tawiah says the function of the ankle is to help us balance, weight bear and transmit force. Heel raises - Stand next to a sturdy surface and lift your heels off the floor and roll onto your toes, making sure your ankles don't wobble or stick outwards. Balance - Walk with one foot in front of the other, like a gymnast along a beam, and maintain your foot control. Control - Moving from a sitting to a standing position on one or two legs and going up or down stairs are also examples of exercises used to improve ankle balance and control. "If you go up the stairs and you find that you lead with one leg, practice leading with the other side." Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist, says the foundation to building strong ankles is being "brain to body aware" Those recovering from ankle sprains might want to try balancing on one leg while throwing and catching a ball. Or work on their landing control by stepping to either side and balancing on the landing leg. And for those with tendinopathy, chronic pain in the tendon, a slow and heavy load is important. Try calf raises with weight - for instance on a leg press. Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles. "A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front. "It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over? "Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them." She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task. She says different activities require different shoes. "If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place. "Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate." For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree." Headline: Inside Health
Body: If you need an operation in the future, there's a good chance a robot could be involved. Around 70,000 robot-assisted surgeries are performed every year in England. But the plan is for that number to grow to half a million surgeries by the year 2035. In the recent budget, the UK government announced £100 million would be spent speeding up the rollout of robots across operating theatres in England. Those in favour say it is better for patients and surgeons – but why is that and how strong is the evidence? And with robotic systems costing millions of pounds, is this a good use of NHS funds? Laura Foster dons her scrubs and is invited into an operating theatre at Southmead Hospital in Bristol to witness a robotic surgery and speaks to surgeons and patients about how it works. Then a panel of experts, including Nuha Yassin from the Royal College of Surgeons England, Professor John McGrath from the NHS England Robotic Surgery steering committee and general practitioner and director of the Centre for Evidence and Values in Healthcare at St Andrews University, Dr Margaret McCartney, discuss the pros and cons of the technology. Headline: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'
Body: Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basis You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life. In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar. "We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London. "He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us." Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea. "OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute. "But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night." Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire , external and moved to Wales â taking her pets with them. One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges". "Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk." "We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic." Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too. Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success. Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property. "It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says. Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery. The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left). The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past. "I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says. So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year. "Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album." Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint. " To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey, " she sings on To Love Somebody , external , soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up. Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy , external , declaring: " Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless ." But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant , external . Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists. Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett "That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses. "Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself." The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham. "It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless." The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says. Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022 , Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop. "I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says. "It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn." Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades. "I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says. "Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music." "I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in. "I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters." The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona â more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty â with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn. The single Too Cute To Be Lonely , external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party. " Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress ," she teases the object of her affections. Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love. " Your stupid face is my sorry fate ," she harrumphs, cross at herself. " For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love ." Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie. "I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals. "We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us. "I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good." Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and Adele Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World. "It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting. "But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished. "So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more." That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her. And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits. Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head. "If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says. "Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist." Headline: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
Body: The mathematician was diagnosed with cervical cancer six years ago Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer. The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020. She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific". "As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky." In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said. "Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy. "I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic systemâ¦ that was when it really started to come down." The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point". "It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said. Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two â the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance". Fry attended a Cancer Research UK reception hosted by the King and Queen at St James's Palace in June While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged. She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me â it was horrific." Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there". She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital. "I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said. But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it. "I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it." The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London. She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics. Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life. She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor. At 36, Hannah was diagnosed with cervical cancer. She underwent a radical hysterectomy and later explored the decisions surrounding cancer treatment in a documentary. Having recently attended her five-year all-clear appointment, she reflects on how the experience changed her outlook on life. Headline: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
Body: Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 Warning - this story contains graphic content A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times. Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial. Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny". Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers. On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation. Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said. Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV. She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]." She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage. It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times. Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults. "I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But â¦ if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence." She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign. In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial". A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape. "Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made. "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence." Headline: Brand, Walliams and MAFS: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
Body: A jury at Southwark Crown Court found Russell Brand guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open. On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault. Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women. By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him. Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show. These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry. In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence. All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago. From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting. "The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me. In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court. Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry. It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him . The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations. What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave". When looking at whatâs driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement. It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed. In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one. Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued. "There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman. It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing. Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegations When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar. Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked . Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused". One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking. "I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me. But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up. Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs. She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained. "There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriouslyâ. For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult. Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention." Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm. Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up. And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate. Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change â although not always. Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted. Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past. But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judgeâs remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths. When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no." "I think attitudes have changed,â said Freeman. âIt doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.â Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards. Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny . Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era. However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past. "This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen. "There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK." David Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry. And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too. None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued". But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over". "It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more". "On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows." Channel 4's office in central London. Its bosses will be questioned by MPs next week following the cancellation of Married at First Sight UK Then thereâs the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out. Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named. "There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me. This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use. Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday. When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation. It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code. There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims. "People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark. "Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate". What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change. Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment. Headline: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
Body: Vincent van Gogh's ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh. ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), which carries an estimated value of $180m (Â£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday. But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis. Sotheby's says its own "extensive research" has not established this, but that it will work with the family to try and reach a solution. "Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs," the auction house told the BBC in a statement. "We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history. "While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognise the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution." The painting is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection. Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890. It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934. The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says. Four other owners have had it prior to it being put up for auction this year. Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , external , has written to Sotherby's on their behalf. He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

Headline: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
Body: Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title. Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section. She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points. There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner. Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the competition at 19 years old Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations. Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd. Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines. And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit. However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote. Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote. Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea. Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie. Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 points Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now. There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world. Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win. Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England. "It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie. "The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added. They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show. For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building. However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy. The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries. Headline: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
Body: Russell Brand (L) pictured with Noel Fielding in 2007 Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows. The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault. Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction. Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years". "I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said. "I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years. "Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them." Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward." Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper. "How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded. Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'" Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives. Fielding said he was "appalled" by some of the jokes he had made alongside Brand Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others. Further allegations against him have been made in recent days. More women have made allegations about him in interviews with the Times and a Netflix documentary. The Times said it could not publish the investigation until the criminal case ended. Brand has denied non-consensual sexual activity. Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women. The disgraced entertainer is being detained at HMP Wandsworth. BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations. If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Headline: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
Body: King Charles appears in special episode of Elton John's podcast King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday. Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together. The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts. "We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience". The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older." The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning. The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary. "I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said. "I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing." Sir Elton performed for the 10th anniversary of the King's Trust in 1986 at Wembley Arena The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others. Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano. The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful". Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee. "I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said. "It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message." The pair reunited in 2000, where Sir Elton performed alongside the Backstreet Boys at Party in the Park The show opened with Tina Turner's hit Proud Mary. The King described the late pop icon as an "electrifying character" and recalled that the guard at Buckingham Palace played her hit Simply the Best following her death in 2023. "It was, I hope, a small way of thanking her for the times she has performed for my charities and indeed for the joy she brought to millions of people," the King said. The pair also chose Sir Rod Stewart's Handbags And Gladrags, Elvis Presley's Hound Dog, Pete Townsend's Let My Love Open The Door and Raye's Joy. The programme will be rebroadcast on Apple Music One at 17:00 and 22:00 Saturday and again on Sunday at 02:00 and 06:00. It will also feature on Apple Music Hits on Sunday at 10:00 and 14:00. Headline: Star-studded MacGowan tribute album gave grieving wife purpose
Body: Shane MacGowan was best known as the frontman of The Pogues, a band that injected rural folk songs with the punk spirit of the 1970s On the day of Shane MacGowan's funeral , his heartbroken wife found comfort in the same thing that moved and captivated the rest of the world that afternoon - the music that filled a parish church in Nenagh, County Tipperary. Mundy and Camille O'Sullivan performed Haunted. Nick Cave sang A Rainy Night in Soho. And Glen Hansard and Lisa O'Neil led mourners in a send-off rendition of Fairytale of New York . "I thought, well, if we just got all the people who were at the funeral on a record, that'd be something pretty special," Victoria Mary Clarke told BBC News NI. On Friday, three years after her husband's death, that idea came to fruition with the release of 20th Century Paddy. "It must be wonderful for Shane... I think up in heaven, he's very aware of what's going on," said Clarke. There are 36 tracks on the new album - all penned by MacGowan - and 40 bands and soloists. Among those are contributions from two acclaimed Irish artists who have passed away since recording their covers for the album. Glen Hansard is featured performing Bottle of Smoke, while Moya Brennan provides her interpretation of Mother Mo Chroi. "I feel love and connection between the artists (on the album) and Shane. "And also, you know, for me personally, it feels like a lot of love because when somebody sends something nice to Shane, they're sending it to me." The Pogues frontman died aged 65 at his Dublin home in 2023, following a hospital stay after being diagnosed with encephalitis. Shane MacGowan and Victoria Mary married in 2018 after several decades as a couple Victoria was too fair to say who delivered her favourite cover on the album, but she was frank about how she personally benefited from the project. "It gave me so much pleasure and it gave me so much joy and hope for the future to work on it because it gave me something to do every single day for three years and it got me out of bed and it got me to make new friends." In the aftermath of her husband's death, that "social life and a sense of purpose" was invaluable to her. But while the album is certainly bound up with MacGowan's death, it's not overshadowed by it. "I think the artwork, if I had to pick, might be my favourite thing about the album," she chirped, an artist herself. Bruce Springsteen spent time with Shane MacGowan at his home before his death The term a 'who's who' doesn't quite capture the calibre and genre-defying diversity of the line-up featured on 20th Century Paddy. There are hall-of-famers like Bruce Springsteen and Tom Waits. Iconic, generation-crossing indie bands like The Jesus and Mary Chain and The Libertines. And for anyone who needs reminding of how far above its weight Ireland punches when it comes to music, have a look at the back of 20th Century Paddy. U2, Hozier and Bob Geldof - people with permanent residencies at top of the music industry. There are stalwarts and custodians of the Irish folk tradition, Damien Dempsey perhaps foremost among them. And lots of other artists, less established but very much in their ascendancy - Amble, Kingfishr and Madra Salach, to name but a few. David Keenan said Shane MacGowan serves as an example of the importance of authenticity in art David Keenan, a singer-songwriter from Dundalk, whose thoughtful lyrics and intense live performances invoke something of MacGowan himself, told BBC News NI he was honoured to be asked to add to the album. "Fairytale of New York is as old as Christmas for me," said David. But his epiphany moment came when an uncle gave him The Pogues' third album. At 11 years old, Keenan said If I Should Fall from Grace with God "lit a flame" inside him. "Up 'til that point it was just chart music. "That (album) was the first time I heard all these references to mythology and drink and rebellion and, you know, heartache. The Louth man described it like an awakening. "It gave me permission as a kid to get stuck into real lyric writing. And to do it in the traditional and folk form." On 20th Century Paddy, Keenan covered Sick Bed of CÃºchulainn - a celtic punk ballad from their 1985 album Rum Sodomy and the Lash, the central allusion of which is the mythical Irish warrior CÃºchulainn. This has real significance for Keenan, who as a child in Louth used to play near the standing stone (Clochafarmore) where Cuchulainn was said to have been killed. He did his recording of the song in Drumlish, County Longford, where he said "Shane used to record too". "It was just was surreal and at the same time perfect, you know." Before putting his version down on tape, Keenan did something few artists would have done: he recited a poem he had written in Irish asking permission from MacGowan to sing the song. "I felt connected to Shane's energy during the recording, you know." Keenan said the quality of the artists on 20th Century Paddy showed the "global respect that was there for Shane's abilities, you know, as a lyric writer, a poet". He added that, at a time when there is "a lot of pressure on young musicians now to go viral on TikTok and dumb themselves down... here's an artist who didn't do that". "In an age of ChatGPT and generative AI", said Keenan, MacGowan is a reminder for "human beings to be authentic". Keenan's top picks from the album included Summer in Siam covered by Tom Waits, Jimmy Artache's version of USA, Glenn Hansard's Bottle of Smoke and Steve Earle's If I Should Fall From Grace With God. Headline: Charlotte Church closes wellness retreat after five 'beautiful' years
Body: The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021 Charlotte Church will close her wellness retreat after five "beautiful years", the company has announced. The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality. The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series. Last month, the team at the retreat announced it would be "pausing" operations to "reassess" what it should offer. But it has now confirmed it is shutting down. In a statement on social media, the team said they had hoped it would be a "period of hibernation, rather than an ending," but have come to realise it is the "end of our journey with The Dreaming". "What a beautiful, wild and wonderful few years it has been," the post added. According to documents filed to Companies House , external in March 2025, there were five employees at The Dreaming. "We've shared stories, made friendships, held space for one another and found moments of stillness in a world that so rarely allows us to slow down. "Thousands of you have found your way to this little corner of the Welsh hills, each bringing something of yourselves, and each leaving a little something behind. You have made The Dreaming what it is." Last month the business said it was in the process of "germinating new dreams for the future" and was set to "hibernate". Rhydoldog House was the former proerty of fashion designer Laura Ashley Earlier this year, Church said that The Dreaming was a response to the pressures of contemporary life. She said: "I am really passionate about what we do, because I believe more than ever the world and the people of the world are in dire need of being held through some very difficult times. "There are some very difficult transitional times for us as human beings on this Earth. "This is also due to the excesses in which society is so much based around, capitalist values and ideologies, meaning there is then less around care, people, community, nature and belonging. We are crying out for these things, every single one of us." Church previously confessed she had blown "pretty much all my life savings" on the Â£1.5m, seven-bedroom property. The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Ashley and her husband Bernard and was owned by the family until his death in 2009. A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation. Since opening, The Dreaming hosted more than 3,000 guests and offered a "pay what you can" scheme starting at Â£1 per night, as well as free stays for NHS workers. Headline: 'Hardest challenge of my life' - Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need ride
Body: Owain Wyn Evans cycled almost 400 miles from Glasgow to Cardiff Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need. The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles , setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday. The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised Â£4,760,086 in the process. Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%. "I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown." In total, Children in Need raised Â£38.7 million in its 46th campaign . The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity. Headline: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
Body: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences". It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences". When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law". In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s". "Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added. Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened. "We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process." Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media. Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women. The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams. The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another. Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room. In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with. "I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. "And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did." He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me." Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books. Headline: Bonnie Tyler remembers loved ones in posthumous Christmas single
Body: Bonnie Tyler died aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday. The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year. Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace". The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight." The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death. Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts. The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977. Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded. Tyler had "no big ideas" about recording until she was spotted by a talent scout Tyler's husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan, previously said she would have wanted fans to hear the music she was working on, and gave his blessing for the song's release . Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club. After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years . In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for her at Swansea Minster.
