Headline: 'It's like you're in one of his paintings' Kyffin Williams' art brought to life
Body: An interactive reproduction of a self portrait by Kyffin Williams will allow visitors to feel the texture of the thick oil he used in his paintings For the first time, the paintings of Sir Kyffin Williams have been brought to life in a new immersive experience at the National Library of Wales. Technology similar to that used for exhibitions of Van Gogh, CÃ©zanne and LS Lowry will immerse visitors in the mountain landscapes, hillfarms and stormy seas created by the painter, who is considered the defining Welsh artist of the 20th Century. Images from Williams's oil paintings such as the hill farmer and sheepdog are animated in a 360-degree centrepiece and Sir Kyffin's life story is narrated by Sir Bryn Terfel in a bilingual presentation, with original paintings illuminated on the walls. The National Library, which received grants of Â£500,000 to fund the project, said it hoped it will introduce a new audience to Sir Kyffin's work. There are also interactive installations including a recreation of a self-portrait which can be touched, giving visitors a sense of the texture of Sir Kyffin's oil paintings. He painted using an impasto technique - where paint is applied so thickly on to a canvas that it stands out in three dimensions. Sir Kyffin, who was born on Anglesey in 1918, had a long relationship with the National Library, in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, which has about 2,000 pieces of his work in its collection. Moving images taken from Sir Kyffin's paintings are projected on to walls in what used to be an office in the national library In 1950 the library bought its first two pieces from the young artist soon after he left the Slade School of Fine Art in London. Morfudd Bevan, art curator at the National Library of Wales, said the library paid Â£15 for an oil painting of Cader Idris and Â£7.10 for an ink and wash drawing of Tre'r Ceiri on the LlÅ·n Peninsula. Today, original work by Sir Kyffin sells for tens of thousands of pounds. Bevan added: "The library saw the potential of this young artist. "It was really important that we were encouraging and supporting young artists at the beginning of their careers, when Kyffin was trying to establish himself as a professional artist." It was the start of a close bond with the artist. When he died in September 2006, he left a substantial part of his estate to the library, more than 1,200 works on paper, about 200 oil paintings, more than 300 original prints and his personal archive. The national library holds the largest collection of Sir Kyffin's work in the world. Morfudd Bevan said the national library has a long relationship with Sir Kyffin Williams - it bought two pieces from him for Â£22 at the start of his career The library hopes the new attraction will introduce more people to his work. Director of experience Carys Ifan said: "It's by no means a traditional exhibition. "You go on a journey, literally moving through three rooms that used to be old offices. They've been repurposed because we are so keen to open up more and more to the public." Profiad Kyffin Experience was made possible by technology invented by Focal Studios, an immersive experience company and the main designers of the exhibition. Chief executive Dennis Outten said working on the project had been a "labour of love" and an "incredible journey for everyone involved". In the first room Sir Bryn Terfel tells the story of Sir Kyffin's life in a biligual narration while images taken from his work are projected on to the walls Focal Studios worked with another company, leo&hyde, to animate Sir Kyffin's paintings in a 360-degree immersive experience so they come alive in projections on the walls and floor. "It's like you're in one of his paintings, I love it," Outten said. "It's not like virtual reality, because you can hold the hand of your child, you can sit there with your grandmother or your friend and you experience it together. I think that's incredibly powerful." Inside the "projection cave", visitors see scenes painted by Sir Kyffin come alive as the cattle, waterfalls, the farmer and his sheepdog move around them. Outten said high fidelity scans of Sir Kyffin's original work and creative techniques helped bring the paintings to life. "We actually created a 3D model of Kyffin's farmer and dog, and then using animation techniques, puppeteering them essentially to move." Rhodri Llwyd Morgan, the library's chief executive, said the new experience was part of a strategy "to be more popular, more appealing and that's our aim". Headline: Dept Q crew member dies after being injured at Edinburgh film studio
Body: Police Scotland said a man had died at FirstStage studios in Leith A member of the crew for the Netflix series Dept Q has died after being seriously injured at a film studio in Edinburgh. Emergency crews were called to FirstStage studio in Leith at about 15:00 on Thursday and the man was pronounced dead a short time later. Left Bank Pictures, which is involved in making Dept Q, later said it was "shocked and saddened" by the death of a crew member. Police Scotland said the death was not being treated as suspicious but inquiries into the circumstances were ongoing. The Health and Safety Executive said it was "aware" of the incident. A Left Bank Pictures spokesperson said: "We are deeply shocked and saddened by the tragic death of a member of our Dept Q crew. "Our thoughts are with their family, friends and colleagues at this incredibly difficult time, and we are offering support for those affected." A Netflix spokesperson said: "Our deepest condolences are with the family and loved ones of the crew member we have lost, and with everyone on Dept Q who knew and worked alongside them. "This is an incredibly sad time and we are working closely with our colleagues at Left Bank Pictures to support everyone affected." 'It's a big step up': Behind the scenes as Netflix hit Dept Q returns to Edinburgh FirstStage was started by Sean Connery's son, Jason, and took over an empty former warehouse unit in Leith in 2020. The "big blue shed" includes five sound stages and production office space. Screen Scotland invested Â£1m towards the initial set up of the facility. Aside from Dept Q, it has also been used for filming the supernatural thriller The Rig for Amazon, and for part of the production of Marvel's Avengers: Infinity War, which was partially set in Edinburgh.

Headline: Why so much love between Ireland and Garth Brooks?
Body: Country music superstar Garth Brooks will perform a multi-city tour of Ireland in 2027 Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027. The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998. The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing , and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added. So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years? Cathy O'Reilly previously saw Garth Brooks live at two of his Dublin concerts in 2022 Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields. She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles. "It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much." She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland. "He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here." Garth Brooks last performed in Ireland in 2022 Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÃ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot". "There could be a fourth show in Belfast," he said. Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold. In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them. Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled. Stephen Butler performs as a Garth Brooks tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls and described his job as "easy" due to the love of Garth Brooks' fans Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls. His love for the musician also goes back to his childhood. "My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs. "I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do." He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time. Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music" "I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go. "His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems." Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music". "I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm. "I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can. "My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me." Garth Brooks performing at the King's Hall in 1998 Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs. "Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge. "I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels. "And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said. "And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality. "It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart." Country legend Garth Brooks returns to Belfast with 2027 gigs

Headline: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
Body: Russell Brand has been in HMP Wandsworth for a week Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said. Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison. He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons. Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth". He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen. "He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly." How the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence. Wandsworth prison is by far the worst I've visited The Russell Brand I saw in court was not the flamboyant character most people will know A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison. A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival. "Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done. "We're very aware of that feeling," they said. Brand will have had his possessions confiscated when he arrived at HMP Wandsworth Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle, depending on where in the prison he is housed. On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who have been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size". The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. This is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop, according to the charity Prison Reform Trust. Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, former inmates said. "Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain if he wanted. Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC that there were a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries. They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault while mixing with other inmates. Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences of which he has been convicted could make him a target for other inmates. Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed. "This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates' own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved." The South London jail is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and these have to go through the system to be signed off. Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications. "There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." Atkins said it took five weeks to see his young son when he went inside. It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison. At this stage, nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities. The guidelines state that offenders jailed for four or more years for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years. Headline: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
Body: Newman will head to Australia with Harry Styles next month after more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Manchester Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021. It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland , external last month. Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly." Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20. The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014. The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John. During her opening night in Brixton, Newman debuted her new song Survival and was also joined by fellow London soul-pop singer Gabrielle for a duet of her 1993 hit Dreams. Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants. Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026 Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana. But after three more gigs this weekend and an extra date next weekend, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues. She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her. "Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me. "I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere." She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always." Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC. "The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted. "No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill. "But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time." After more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Manchester, she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles next month for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked". "'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request. "It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zayn were my favourites. "So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental." 'It's incredible, surreal': Skye Newman wins BBC Sound of 2026

Headline: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
Body: Some schools have removed David Walliams books from their libraries following the publication of allegations against the best-selling children's author and comedian. "Head teachers are already making difficult decisions about whether or not these books should remain on the bookshelves of libraries at the moment," said Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders. "I'm aware from several of our members that they've already taken the decision to take them off their shelves." Walliams sold more than 50 million copies of books including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy. He has denied allegations of sexual misconduct and abuses of power. Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one". Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications. The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said. Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams. "So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said. Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet". "I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live. "I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened." The Department for Education has been asked for comment. Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September. Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books. Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff". Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils. Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries. "The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said. "Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock." A Telford and Wrekin council spokesperson added that after the "recent media coverage and allegations published in the press" they had taken the decision to "remove all Walliams' books and audio books from their library catalogues". Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow". Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage. A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships. "Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display." On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law". Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Headline: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?
Body: Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all? Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found. More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage. Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK. Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art. Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley. Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council. Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds. As of April, just 26,899 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have? Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display. All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April. Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities. "If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said. "It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think." Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby" Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset. "We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people." The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection. Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years. Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24. The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of. For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools. When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection. Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the town Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April. At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept. "I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so." The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North. The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives". Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks , external . Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art. "We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place. "The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time. "From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it." He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances. Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits. But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums". Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26. Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work. Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display. One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum . Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works. Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public. That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events. It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation. Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been" Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme. "We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on." Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council. "A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said. Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time. "Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment." Headline: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-up
Body: Eleven celebrities will enter the Australian jungle camp on Monday Former England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew entering the jungle Down Under for this year's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here! They will be joined by Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson, Paralympian and presenter Ade Adepitan, actress Claire Sweeney and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup. TV presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Jack Skipper, Love Island contestant Chloe Burrows and model Leomie Anderson round out the team headed for Australia. Hosts Ant and Dec will return with the ITV show's opening episode on Monday, 16 November, with the series now in its 26th year. Wayne Rooney said he wants to go one better than wife Coleen, who was runner-up in 2024 Ade Adepitan - Paralympian and documentary maker, who will be the first wheelchair user in the show's history Leomie Anderson - Model and co-host of Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star Chloe Burrows - Love Island finalist, Kiss Radio breakfast presenter and host of Chloe vs The World podcast Mariella Frostrup - Broadcaster, author and journalist, including appearances on Loose Women and Times Radio AJ Odudu - Big Brother presenter and former Strictly Come Dancing contestant Joanna Page - Stacey from hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, and host of TV series including Shift the Thrift and Shop Well For Less Wayne Rooney - Former Everton, Manchester United and England striker turned football manager and pundit Sharky - one of YouTube's Beta Squad (alongside Celebrity Traitors star King Kenny among others), who have 12 million subscribers Jack Skipper - Stand-up comedian and social media star Claire Sweeney - Coronation Street and Brookside star and musical actress Ricky Wilson - Kaiser Chiefs singer, ex-Virgin Radio drivetime host and former The Voice UK coach Rooney is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen, who was runner-up on I'm A Celebrity in 2024. "If you're going in you want to win it," he said. "Coleen's already tried and obviously she finished second in the show so I'm here to bring that title back to the Rooney household." Rooney admitted that jumping out of a helicopter is his biggest fear. "I've been booked to jump out of a plane three times before and never made it on the plane," he said. "I don't like snakes or what is in the water either - I don't go in the sea." Ade Adepitan said he is "overwhelmed" to be the first wheelchair user on the show Producers are making adaptations to the Australian jungle camp so it is accessible for Adepitan. In a press statement, he said: "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first." Keith Lemon comedian Leigh Francis is not among the official line-up but is rumoured to become a late addition. The last I'm A Celebrity series was the all-star version in South Africa, which was marked by heated arguments and walk-outs among the cast during the live final in April. Headline: Hidden tongue movement found in 'strong R' study
Body: Dr Danielle Turton says the study was "so fascinating" as you could see the difference in tongue movements between generations "really clearly" Scientists have observed "hidden" tongue movements in one of the last places in England still using a distinctive pronunciation of the letter R and they also witnessed a decline in the historical sound. By using ultrasound technology, Lancaster University researchers have been able to watch how the tongue moves during speech. The rhoticity study focused on people in Blackburn, as its older residents still pronounce a "strong R" sound after vowels in words like star and heart. Dr Danielle Turton, who led the research, said the findings were "fascinating" as she witnessed the centuries-old sound "gradually disappearing" as the younger generations who took part had much weaker tongue movement. Dr Turton told BBC Radio Lancashire : "East Lancashire is one of the last places in England where people are [distinctively] pronouncing the 'R' sounds. "But that distinctive sound we found was gradually disappearing so we went to Blackburn with an ultrasound machine - the same technology we would use to look at babies in the womb - and we used it to monitor people's tongues moving as they spoke." Researchers say they found hidden tongue movements in the distinctive R sound (pictured right) She added: "What we found was so fascinating because we can see the difference between generations really clearly. "The younger people were making weaker tongue movements. They were still doing that traditional Lancashire 'R' but they didn't have the strong tongue movements the older people were making." She said it had been a fun study, adding it was the last sound acquired when learning to talk. "We think of language change as something that happened hundreds of years ago but this research we can see that change happening right before our eyes in people's mouths," she said. The study focused on Blackburn as Dr Danielle Turton said it was one of the last places in England still using a distinctive pronunciation of 'R' Dr Turton said English had changed beyond recognition over the past 1,000 years which was evident in "Shakespeare, Chaucer and particularly older texts such as Beowulf". "However, language isn't just something that changed in the past. It is changing all around us, all the time, in such small increments that we rarely notice it happening." "We can never observe language directly inside the brain, but we can get physically one step closer by observing the movements that create speech," she said. "Ultrasound allows us to see tongue movements that would otherwise be completely hidden. "What's exciting here is that we can actually monitor the physical movements involved in a sound change that's happening today." The work forms part of a growing body of research using articulatory imaging to understand how accents change over time and how speech is produced across different communities. The study Rhoticity in Decline? An Ultrasound Study of Lancashire /r/ , external was co-authored by Dr Robert Lennon and funded by the Leverhulme Trust - an independent charity providing scholarships for research and education. Headline: Eleven officers convicted of crimes still on Police Scotland payroll, chief confirms
Body: Jo Farrell confirmed the figure in a letter to the justice committee Eleven officers who have been convicted of crimes - including eight who have been violent towards women and girls - are still on the Police Scotland pay roll. In a letter , external to the Scottish Parliament's justice committee, Chief Constable Jo Farrell said there were other cases with "incontrovertible evidence" against officers, but they cannot be sacked quickly enough. Farrell also said the Â£4.5m annual cost of the 80 officers who are currently suspended was down to "sluggish" conduct arrangements, as well as the time necessary for cases to go through courts. She described the state of affairs as "intolerable" and called for a modernisation of the police conduct regime. The revelation follows a number of high-profile cases of police officers who have been exposed as rapists this year alone. Derek McNee , Campbell Petrie , Carmichael John Williamson and Cameron Ross have all been convicted and are no longer on the payroll. Meanwhile, Alan Greer , who was named as a violent serial rapist by a BBC investigation, took his own life in May after police raided his home. It also emerged last month that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls. (L-R) Campbell Petrie, Carmichael John Williamson, Derek McNee and Cameron Ross - all police officers who have been exposed as rapists Farrell wrote the letter to justice committee convener David Linden ahead of a meeting this week. She said: "There are cases of proven criminality where the existing process has taken too long because of sub-optimal regulations. "This can leave individuals who ultimately have no place in policing within the organisation for longer than they should be." She continued: "There are other cases where there is incontrovertible evidence against officers which cannot be fast-tracked for dismissal under current arrangements. "This is intolerable to me, as Chief Constable, and would rightly be intolerable to the public." That officers remain suspended for years, she said, has a "welfare impact, a cost to the public purse, and reduce policing's overall deployable resource". Last month, Farrell said that between 300 and 400 officers had now been re-vetted as part of new rules brought in following the murder of Sarah Everard by Met Police officer Wayne Couzens . Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women Misconduct probe after police officer admits abusing woman The committee will be discussing options that will allow Police Scotland to act quicker in cases where there are convictions. Farrell said the proposals under consideration would "modernise the police conduct regime, to accelerate hearings for the most serious cases and enhance transparency of outcomes". "I strongly support the focus on treating witnesses and complainers in a trauma-informed way," she said. Justice Secretary Neil Gray said: "The Chief Constable is right that cases involving officers convicted of serious offences should be dealt with more quickly. "This is why we have introduced regulations to Parliament that will allow Police Scotland to act quicker in cases where there are convictions." He added: "These are aimed at improving transparency and strengthening support for victims and witnesses, while retaining appropriate safeguards."

Headline: Sea of phones at Christmas event prompts backlash
Body: This Carnaby Street Christmas light switch on video prompted a strong reaction online When BBC London uploaded a video , external of the Carnaby Street Christmas lights being switched on last week, the comments section filled with thousands of people reacting to what they saw. But, it wasn't the bright lights or the pretty fireworks that they were reacting to, it was the sea of spectators filming on their phones. "Remember when we used to look at stuff directly with our eyes? Those were the good old days," said one comment. Another simply said: "It's such a sad sad sight." Former EastEnders actress Natalie Cassidy commented: "Why is this piece not mentioning the fact that no-one is looking through their eyes at this beautiful display? It's really scary and depressing." Many of the comments questioned why people would film the fireworks rather than watch them in real life, with one saying: "Nice to see everyone living in the moment, there's a 90% chance they will never watch the video again too." One comment on the Instagram post quipped: "Anyone manage to get a video of this?" Since camera phones became so universally owned, a number of studies have been conducted to understand the impact on our memories when recording events via photos or films. Many of these studies conclude that taking a photograph or film of something can actually prevent us from remembering something accurately, rather than helping us remember the moment. Scientists have termed this as "photo-taking-impairment" , external , a phrase first coined by cognitive psychologist, Dr Linda Henkel, during research on issue in 2014. Subsequent studies and experiments conducted on memory have repeatedly shown that humans subconsciously rely on the camera to do the work of remembering, rather than tasking the brain with memorising events as they happened. Dr Regehr says people are less likely to remember the textures, smells, sights, and sounds of an event when recording through a phone For Dr Kaitlyn Regehr, from University College London and the University of Toronto, the interesting bit here is not the people filming en masse, it's the people angry about it online. "This is not the first year that people have attended events and watched those events through screens," said the smartphone academic. "But what's significant is that this year there's a lot of critical public discourse happening. And that, I think, is really, really positive," she added. The professor said the comments, such as those on the Carnaby Street video, "say a lot about where we are as a society at the moment," and said it showed "our discomfort with the amount of influence that big tech is playing on our lives". Dr Regehr said this shift in attitudes towards phones, and recording events was down to a number of factors, including the social media ban for under 16s in the UK, due to begin in March 2027, as well as lawsuits against social media companies in the US. She said these more negative news stories were building "public understanding", and said it was encouraging people to "want to take greater control over these technologies". At another switch-on event, this time at Oxford Street, spectators were encouraged by the organisers to use their phone torches to add to the light display Dr Regehr said the "backlash" on the Carnaby Street video could be due to the fact it's Christmas, and people feel strongly that it shouldn't be experienced through a phone. "We, as millennial parents, have memory of Christmases prior to smartphones. "We have quite visceral ideas about what that meant to us and I think people are becoming increasingly uncomfortable with their children not having those same experiences or the way in which technology is mediating those experiences for their children. "Parents are now becoming really uncomfortable with the hold through which technology has on their families' lives." Headline: Schoolboy imposter subjected ex-professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'
Body: Brian MacKinnon lived a double life as teenage student Brandon Lee An imposter who made headlines around the world for posing as a school pupil in while in his 30s has appeared in court and admitted hiding in the home of his former university professor before subjecting him to a "terrifying ordeal". Brian MacKinnon targeted Prof Brian Whiting, 87, as he lay in bed with his wife, the day after a BBC docudrama on his ruse was broadcast. My Old School chronicled MacKinnon's return to Bearsden Academy, as Brandon Lee, a 16-year-old who had supposedly just moved to Scotland from Canada. MacKinnon hatched the plan so he could pursue his dream of becoming a doctor having been thrown out of Glasgow University, when Prof Whiting was dean of the medical school. The model pupil who was a 30-year-old imposter MacKinnon - who was formerly a pupil at the East Dunbartonshire school from 1974 to 1980 - returned in 1993 and secured five As in his Higher exams. As a result he earned a place at the University of Dundee to study medicine. But in 1995 an anonymous tip-off revealed he had previously spent two years as a medical student at the University of Glasgow and did not complete the course. MacKinnon was thrown out of the medical school in 1983 following a failed appeal. When his double life was exposed, Prof Whiting was interviewed by BBC Scotland News. The archive footage was used in the 2022 docudrama, which starred Alan Cumming as MacKinnon. Details of the case, which called before the High Court in Glasgow on Thursday, were first reported in the Mail on Sunday , external . The court heard MacKinnon, now 63, went to the retired academic's home on 28 September last year - the day after My Old School had been repeated on the BBC. Prof Brian Whiting speaks about Brian MacKinnon in a BBC interview from September, 1995 It is believed MacKinnon sneaked into the property, in the west end of the city, around 16:30 as the rear door and gate were unlocked. Prof Whiting was in his study and his 83-year-old wife, Marlene, was in the garden. They went to bed around 23:30, unaware MacKinnon was hiding in their home. About two hours later they were awoken when their room door suddenly opened. A figure wearing dark clothes, a grey cap and a mask over the lower part of his face walked up to the side of the bed and told Marlene: "No lights." Prosecutor Eilidh Robertson told the High Court in Glasgow: "She sat up and MacKinnon demanded that she lie back down or he would really hurt her. "Both the Whitings were very frightened by this point. "MacKinnon then pointed at her husband and asked: 'Is that Brian Whiting?'." MacKinnon then said he had brought "two statements" which he wanted the couple to "release". Robertson said MacKinnon threatened to kill the couple and hurt their families if they did not comply. Alan Cumming played MacKinnon in the 2022 film, My Old School Marlene did not know who the intruder was before he said his name was "Brian MacKinnon". Robertson added: "MacKinnon then spoke to Brian Whiting directly blaming him and two colleagues for ruining his life and having responsibility for the death of his parents." MacKinnon then briefly left the room and, on his return, suddenly asked to be let out of the house. Marlene got up and led him downstairs hoping he would go. She asked how he had initially got in, he boasted: "That was easy." Marlene got a good look at MacKinnon after he took off his mask. The advocate depute said: "She unlocked the front door. "As MacKinnon was leaving, he stated that he had people working for him that would check if the witnesses were complying with his demands. "If not, they would be dead. He then left the house and turned down a lane." MacKinnon returned to Bearsden Academy in 1993, having previously left in 1980 He went on to show her an online photo of MacKinnon and she identified him as the man who had invaded their home. The court heard how the two statements left by MacKinnon had been made to look as if they had been completed by Prof Whiting. Each alleged the retired dean had "succumbed to intolerable pressure to make a misleading statement about Brian Lachlan MacKinnon". They also said: "Via a BBC Scotland television broadcast, I stated falsely that MacKinnon had not met the required standard as a medical student after he had set out to study medicine at Glasgow in 1980. Nothing could have been further from the truth." The documents claimed there had been a "conspiracy" to exclude "incandescently bright" students like MacKinnon. Pupils at Bearsden Academy reading the revelations about the ex-pupil Brandon Lee They also included "defamatory" remarks about Glasgow University, BBC Scotland and Alan Cumming. MacKinnon was not initially traced but DNA recovered at the house helped link him to the crime. CCTV from a nearby property had also captured him walking near the Whitings property that afternoon. MacKinnon was eventually arrested as he returned to his home in Milngavie, East Dunbartonshire, hours after the incident. Police Scotland officers went on to recover a mobile phone and three notepads. In one, there was handwritten text which stated: "I will regain a place to study medicine at a reputable university". An envelope was also seized and a "statement" similar to those given to the Whitings was discovered inside. MacKinnon made no comment when quizzed by detectives. MacKinnon appeared in a stage production of South Pacific while at high school Last week he was brought into court in a wheelchair and pleaded guilty to a charge of attempted extortion. Sean Templeton, defending, told the hearing: "It is clear that he has had an extraordinary life, thrust into the public gaze in the 1990s by attending a school when he was over the age of 18." He added MacKinnon had always wanted to be involved in medicine to "assist the public", but his "ambitions to become a doctor came to an end". Templeton said after he was exposed, it had "characterised" his life in the many years since, including the docudrama which MacKinnon "did not agree to". The defence advocate said: "It is something that has dogged him since the 1990s." MacKinnon had been assessed by a psychiatrist after his initial appearance in court in late September last year, but it was eventually concluded that he was "fit to stand trial". Templeton told the court MacKinnon was "frail" and suffered from uncontrolled movements in one of his arms. Lady Anwar continued his remand in custody as sentencing was deferred for reports until a later date. MacKinnon is currently being held at HMP Barlinnie in Glasgow. She told him: "You subjected Mr and Mrs Whiting, both in their 80s, to a shocking and terrifying ordeal in their home. "It is likely you will face a significant custodial sentence."

Headline: Man dies after being hit by ambulance
Body: The stretch of the A19 where the accident happened is now open again A man has died after being struck by an ambulance transporting a patient near Sunderland, police have said. Northumbria Police said the crash occurred on the A19, between the junctions for the A1018 and A690, shortly after 02:00 GMT. The ambulance was travelling on the northbound carriageway and did not have its blue lights on when it hit the man, who was in his 30s and died at the scene. Neither the patient nor their partner who were travelling in the ambulance were injured in the collision, while the vehicle's driver, a man in his 40s, was also not hurt and remained at the scene to assist police with their inquiries. The North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said the patient in the ambulance and their partner were transferred to another ambulance. Officers from Northumbria Police's roads unit have launched an investigation into the collision. Sgt Ben Rutherford said: "Our thoughts are firmly with the family and loved ones of the man who has tragically died following this collision. "We will continue to support them in any way that we can at this incredibly difficult time." Anyone with CCTV or dashcam footage of the incident itself or the moments leading up to the collision has been urged to contact the force. Rutherford said anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, "could prove key to our investigation and help provide answers for the man's loved ones". A NEAS spokesperson said: "Around [02:00] one of our ambulance crews was involved in a road traffic incident with a pedestrian on the A19 northbound, while transporting a patient and their partner to a nearby hospital. "We dispatched a number of resources to the scene. "The patient on board and their partner were transferred to another ambulance and taken to hospital for further treatment. "Sadly, despite the best efforts of our crews attending, the patient injured as the result of the collision passed away at the scene. "This is a hugely tragic incident for all involved. "Our thoughts and condolences are with the patient's loved ones. "We will now, of course, be working closely with the police to support their investigation." Headline: Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados hotel room, BBC learns
Body: Watch: Abusive ex-Met detective filmed video of hotel room where wife died Warning: Contains graphic details of Rebekah Arter's death - and references to coercion and sexual abuse A former Metropolitan Police detective, investigated for sexually exploiting vulnerable crime victims it was his job to protect, later lied about the death of his wife in a Barbados hotel room, BBC Panorama has learned. Warren Arter first met his wife Rebekah after she reported domestic abuse to the Met. He then abused her for more than a decade. Her death two years ago has never been properly investigated. Panorama can reveal failures by Barbados authorities to preserve evidence and interview hotel staff about Arter's suspicious behaviour before and after Rebekah's death, aged 47. Despite a request from her family for assistance, the Met did not send detectives to the Caribbean island. Arter subjected Rebekah to sexual and domestic abuse, coercive control, and drugging The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made. Rebekah's family, speaking publicly for the first time, have told Panorama the Met failed her. The cause of her death is still not known with a coroner in the UK recording an open verdict. We have also spoken to hotel staff who were called to the room in June 2024 after Arter rang reception to say his wife had collapsed. Interviews with the staff, police sources - plus Arter's erratic communications following Rebekah's death - reveal: Arter gave conflicting accounts - telling staff and Rebekah's family she had choked, fallen and banged her head, or he had woken up and found her dead Evidence was not secured, vital forensic tests were not taken and Rebekah's organs were inexplicably "chopped up" by a pathologist in Barbados Four days after Rebekah's death, a senior Met boss from its Gold Command was briefed about the incident in light of Arter's alleged offending - but it did not lead to officers travelling to the Caribbean island Arter, 54, took his own life in HMP Wandsworth, days after he had returned from Barbados and been arrested for allegedly abusing another woman. Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship when Arter investigated her case in 2006. The detective then pursued a relationship with her and moved in not long after. Three years later, he was placed in charge of a unit in south-east London investigating rape cases. Arter was later suspended by the Met and investigated over his conduct towards eight alleged victims by its watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) - but was never convicted. Warren Arter took his own life in prison days after Rebekah died Over the seven years he was suspended, Arter continued to receive his full detective inspector salary, before being dismissed in 2023 for drug offences. All this time, he subjected Rebekah to sexual and domestic abuse, coercive control, and drugging, which the BBC has seen video evidence of. Panorama has now spoken to several members of staff who were working at the luxury O2 Beach Club in Barbados on the night of Rebekah's death. All say Arter behaved suspiciously. Two of them entered Arter's hotel room after he had called to say his wife was unwell. Both say it was immediately clear Rebekah was dead. Andrew, a security guard, says he had to prevent Arter from going to a nearby street party, before emergency services arrived. "So I'm asking him, why do you need to go when you have a bigger issue here?" Andrew says Arter responded: "Oh, I just need to clear my head." Watch Panorama: The Predator in the Police on BBC iPlayer from 0600 on Tuesday 17 November - or on BBC One at 21:00 that evening (not in Wales and Northern Ireland) Arter then began crying "crocodile tears" and conducting performative CPR despite Rebekah's lips being blue, according to Andrew, who says Arter's explanation of what happened kept changing. Initially, Arter told Andrew she had fallen near a chest of drawers - but her body was some distance away, near the kitchen. When police arrived, Andrew says he heard Arter tell them he had found her like that. There was no sign of Rebekah having a head injury, Andrew says, despite bloodstains on the bed, the wall and the living room area. Arter was trying to find "the right story that fits and none of them added up", says Andrew Arter recorded a video of the room and sent it to family and friends in the UK. "It looks like chocolate but it's blood," he can be heard saying. Andrew says he told Arter to phone family in the UK - and then heard him tell them that she had been unwell. "He was just trying to find the right story that fits and none of them added up," says Andrew. The security guard says he told Barbadian police officers what he saw and gave a statement but was never formally interviewed. Panorama has seen some of Arter's messages and spoken to Rebekah's friends and family who were contacted by him shortly after her death. They reveal that Arter provided other possible causes of death - that Rebekah had "choked" or that her drink had been spiked. Rebekah's son Elliot and his wife Lacey have told Panorama the Met failed her These accounts are contradicted by Rebekah's daughter-in-law, Lacey, who says he told her they had both been asleep for 18 hours and he had woken up and found her dead. "He was outright lying. He was forgetting what he was telling people," says Lacey. Arter was briefly detained by Barbadian police but released a short time later. One of the police officers who attended the room that night refused to share information with Panorama without payment. He still had a photograph of Rebekah's dead body on his phone. Police in Barbados did not respond to our request for comment. Arter appeared "controlling" and "didn't allow Rebekah to do anything on her own", says hotel security supervisor Kenneth Other hotel staff members have told the BBC they were concerned about Arter's treatment of Rebekah during their stay. Security supervisor Kenneth says Arter appeared "controlling" and "didn't allow Rebekah to do anything on her own". Rebekah also frequently appeared to be "intoxicated", he says. A third member of staff, who worked on the front desk, says staff suspected Arter was "drugging" Rebekah. Panorama has seen a video, filmed by Arter on his phone when she was still alive, which shows Rebekah clearly intoxicated. She is wearing the same clothes that she is pictured in after she died. If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line In the early hours of the morning after her death, during the staff member's night shift, Arter approached the hotel front desk to ask when Rebekah last had a massage in the hotel spa. She says his question struck her as bizarre and felt like he was trying to get his story straight. Meanwhile, back in the UK, Rebekah's son, Elliot, and his wife, Lacey, were becoming increasingly concerned after visiting the home she shared with Arter. Inside, they say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up in the house. They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent. "The moment I gave Warren's name, it was like chaos" - Lacey says Met officers were initially not interested in Rebekah's death Four days after Rebekah's death, they went to Bexleyheath Police Station, the same station where Arter once led rape investigations, to report her death to the Met and raise concerns about his possible involvement. "The front office staff said, 'Oh well it's happened in Barbados, it's a Barbados issue' - and tried to brush it off at first," says Elliot. "The moment I gave Warren's name, it was like chaos - we had sergeants coming down to the front desk," says Lacey. "But it really wasn't about Rebekah, it was more about Warren," she says. That evening, an officer briefed a Gold Commander within the Met, a senior boss who decides how to respond to incidents. The Met did not send detectives to Barbados. UK police forces can be asked to help investigate a death of a British national overseas - usually at the request of local police where the death occurred. Under Foreign Office guidance, the case for such involvement is strengthened when families request assistance and there are credible concerns about the circumstances of the death, as there were in Rebekah's case. The Met told the BBC it made immediate efforts to obtain information in order to assess whether to travel to Barbados but decided it would not be appropriate without an allegation of criminality. Rebekah's death in a Barbados hotel likely involved intoxication and unlawful killing could not be ruled out, concluded a UK coroner An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados. This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated. The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted. The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation". He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict. He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out. The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope. Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes. A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later. In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death. "We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out." Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother. "My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says. "For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away." Headline: What happened after a small town introduced a balaclava ban
Body: Face covering bans are being enforced in several places across the East Midlands National headlines were made this autumn when Nottingham became one of the UK's first cities to bring in a balaclava ban, with neighbouring towns and cities now looking to follow suit. Since September, authorities in the city have had the power to request face coverings are removed and to issue fines if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to cause trouble - although to date, no fines have been handed out in Nottingham. But 12 miles (19km) away, one small town in Derbyshire has been quietly pioneering a ban for more than two years. Heanor, a market town with a population of more than 24,000, took action after an increase in reports of anti-social behaviour. As in Nottingham, Heanor's balaclava ban is part of a modified public spaces protection order (PSPO), which was drawn up in the face of rising problems of anti-social behaviour in early 2024 . It allows police and community protection officers to ask people to remove face coverings if worn in an attempt to conceal their identity to cause harassment, alarm or distress. This includes scarves, masks, and balaclavas, but not coverings worn for religious or cultural purposes. Amber Valley Borough Council, the authority responsible for Heanor, said concerns had been raised at the time over "group-related anti-social behaviour", which included people wearing face coverings" in a way that was causing alarm among residents and visitors". Other incidents included reports of eggs being thrown at members of the public , along with "reckless" and intimidating behaviour on bikes and scooters. PSPOs are not uncommon. So much so, they largely follow a template when introduced - no begging, no drinking, no urinating and defecating in the street, among other measures. But in Heanor, Derbyshire Police's beat officers brought a wishlist of ways to amend the order. These included restrictions on cycling, skateboarding and scootering in the PSPO area, playing "unreasonably loud" music, gathering in groups, and face coverings. "We said these are what we would like to put forward as conditions, what do your legal team say about it?" PC Levi Tabbron said. "And to our disbelief, they actually got approved." The PSPO covers all of the town centre and surrounding streets So fast forward two and a half years, has the ban made a difference? The force said there were no exact figures for incidents dealt within the PSPO area under its terms. When it comes to fines, the borough council said police had issued two fixed penalty notices under the PSPO. Both were paid. According to police-recorded data published on Police.uk, in February 2024, the month the PSPO was being passed, across all of Heanor and Loscoe there were 46 reports of anti-social behaviour, including crimes which do not fall under the PSPO regulations. A year later, there were 25 reports of anti-social behaviour in the same area in February 2025, and in February this year 15 reports were logged. The council added the PSPO "is one part of the wider work taking place with partners to address anti-social behaviour" - and that it was "not aware of significant ongoing problems in the town centre". Tabbron said the balaclava ban, and other elements of the PSPO, were not just a stick to beat troublemakers with. She said: "We don't want to issue out fines willy-nilly, because that doesn't help in every situation. "The tickets that have been issued, it's made a clear difference when they have been because word gets round. But if we can engage, persuade and advise first off before the tickets even come into place, then brilliant. "We're not going to just see somebody on a scooter or an e-scooter, go up to them go 'oh we're seizing your e-scooter and you're having an Â£100 fine' all in one day. "If we've got a rapport with the community, they're more likely to work with us in the long run. "We want to remind the public that the PSPO is in place, we will be looking at using it if we need to, and also remind those that are potentially breaching the conditions that we will be looking out for it." Heanor was not the only place to dream up a ban on face coverings, although it was one of the first. Wolverhampton has had a ban for a few years already too, Stafford has one coming in to force in December, while cities like Derby, Stoke-on-Trent and towns like Mansfield and Loughborough are also considering following suit. Ward councillor for Heanor West at Heanor and Loscoe Town Council, Paul Jones, felt the ban was a good example to other towns and cities in the UK. Paul Jones said bans were sensible, but added enforcement was crucial He said: "I think any sensible person's got to welcome it, you have to have a really extreme, valid, reason to go around with balaclavas on. "The problem we have is there's lots of people on e-bikes with balaclavas, driving around intimidating people and it's very difficult to recognise them and take action. "But in principle I think it's a great idea and we should encourage more assertive action by the police in stopping the young people trying to be disruptive to the local community, because it puts people off coming." Speaking to a dozen or so visitors to the town centre, most agreed a balaclava ban was a sensible measure - although only one resident the BBC spoke to was aware that Heanor already had one. Carol Wilkinson, 72, said congregations of masked youths were "intimidating" in the town's Market Place, and added: "Come teatime, you do see groups on bikes. "I know children have got to go somewhere but they seem as though they're just bothering about - if you know what I mean." Heanor is "not a place you want to come to of an evening", Carol Wilkinson said Andrew Guest, 71, of Heanor, said: "Personally, I believe maybe they should be banned. You immediately think something's going on. "Older people like myself, and ladies, do get concerned. When they see a gang, quite often they'll take the opportunity to cross the road, stay out of the way, hope nobody takes anything up with them and pass by as soon as possible." Heanor "is not like how it used to be", fellow resident Karen Marsh felt, who said people might be avoiding the town centre. She said: "I think balaclava bans are absolutely right. I think it's a bit intimidating for people when somebody's got a balaclava on and you can't see the face." Heanor resident Tamsin Cox, 68, has noticed bad behaviour stretching out to other areas - not just the town centre. She said: "We're in a WhatsApp group and every day there's messages about anti-social behaviour, about people riding, people covering their faces, people speeding, doing wheelies. "They're not only asking for trouble, they're putting other people in danger." All face coverings ought to be banned, Martin Storer, 71, from Marlpool just outside the town, said. He said: "We don't really come into Heanor at night - well that would be one of the main reasons I suppose. "For two and a half years, you've been seeing people walking around with balaclavas on so obviously the police aren't doing their job." Claire Winfield, 67, was the only resident approached who knew there was a PSPO in place. Balaclava bans are "probably a good idea", Claire Winfield said She said: "I think there is an issue - I think it gets a lot of press that it's getting worse but I'm not sure that it is, it's always been kind of a low level of anti-social behaviour. "You do see kids going round with their faces covered in the summer where you think, that's not really a cold factor, it is so people aren't being identified. "It's probably a good idea. I guess the problem is enforcing it." Headline: Man in life-threatening state after shop robbery
Body: Police remained at the scene on Gladstone Street on Sunday A jewellery store employee is in a life-threatening condition after a robbery in broad daylight at a shop in Peterborough. Cambridgeshire Police said six men raided Lala Jewellers on Gladstone Street at about 11:50 GMT on Saturday. A senior councillor later said it was believed that the victim had been stabbed , external . The city's MP described it as a "horrific and violent act", while police have appealed for witnesses to come forward. They said shelves were emptied and two employees behind the counter were assaulted, before the thieves fled in separate vehicles. Two of the robbers were wearing white, traditional Pakistani clothing, officers added. One employee, a 50-year-old man, suffered serious injuries and was taken to hospital, where he remains in a life-threatening condition. Police have appealed for any witnesses to support their investigation Zameer Ali, Peterborough City Council cabinet member for communities, said he was "deeply concerned". "Nobody should have to fear being attacked while going about their daily life," the Labour councillor said. Police stated they were carrying out a substantial investigation to identify those responsible. They have appealed for people in Gladstone Street who may have seen something suspicious to come forward. Andrew Pakes, the Labour MP for Peterborough, said officers had agreed to carry out extra patrols in the area over the coming days. "This was a horrific and violent act. My thoughts are with the family and everyone affected by the attack," he wrote on Facebook , external . An air ambulance was pictured close to the scene of the robbery on Saturday Paul Bristow, the Conservative mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, added: "This is not who we are. "We stand together with those who just do their job, run their business and want to be free of the fear of the dreadful people who would do such a terrible thing."
