Headline: Banton hits century and bowlers sparkle for England to level ODI series against Australia
Body: Baker was making his first appearance against Australia England 355-6 (50 overs): Banton 121, Cox 67, Root 62 Australia 220 all out (44.3 overs): Green 64, Renshaw 63; Atkinson 4-28 England won by 135 runs; series level at 1-1 Tom Banton scored a century and Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson impressed with the ball as England's wildly inconsistent one-day team hammered Australia to set up a series decider. Banton scored a fine 121 â pushing his case for selection further with a second ODI hundred â in England's 355-6. After being knocked over for 131 two days ago in Perth, England's total was their highest in one-day internationals in Australia. And then their bowlers, who failed to defend 430 against Sri Lanka last month and were undone by an improbable last-wicket partnership against Pakistan, reduced Australia to 29-4 inside seven overs and easily closed out a 135-run victory. The win ends a seven-match losing run against Australia across formats in Adelaide - and a run of six consecutive defeats by Australia in 50-over cricket away from home. But, more significantly, it corrects their course after those damaging defeats against Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Australia and offers positives amid the frustrations going into the decider on Wednesday (03:30 GMT) in Hobart. 'England aren't ready to win World Cup now... but there's potential' Curran's best weapon? The moon ball strikes again TMS podcast: Banton blasts England to victory in Adelaide Will the real England please stand up? Before those defeats in Rawalpindi, Lahore and Perth, England had won three ODI series this year. This win only adds to the feeling they are extremely difficult to figure out. Banton was superb and, even more encouragingly, Atkinson and Baker were too. This England team has often struggled for new-ball wickets and Baker, brought in for Jamie Overton in an attempt to correct that fault, found significant swing. He took the key wicket of Australia captain Mitchell Marsh, taken high at slip by a diving Joe Root, for two. Atkinson used nip to nick off Travis Head for seven â the second match in a row he has dismissed the Australia left-hander â and also have both Cooper Connolly and Josh Inglis caught behind. Career-best figures of 4-28 are reward for good recent performance that have often gone unrewarded. England were not perfect. They dropped four catches â first Inglis and then Matt Renshaw and Cameron Green, who made 63 and 64 respectively to drag out Australia's score. But by the end, Sam Curran had taken two wickets in two balls, including bowling Jack Edwards with his moon ball, in a boost after his poor run. Green was also out stumped when the ball deflected off Jordan Cox's shin and onto the stumps and Liam Dawson took 2-41 as he was preferred again to Adil Rashid. These are the performances that suggest England can challenge at next year's World Cup, but plenty more are needed. Banton's hundred follows his first against Sri Lanka in September Banton's chance as opener has come courtesy of Jacob Bethell's knee injury. In nine innings, he has scored four fifties and two hundreds. The spot should now be his going forward. The 28-year-old right-hander was hit on the helmet on 10 by left-armer Spencer Johnson but afterwards attacked Adelaide's short square boundaries with his pull. A partnership of 137 with Joe Root was steady and important â given Ben Duckett had slashed to point for nine and the recent memory of Perth. It was Banton's hundred, 67 from 49 balls by Cox and 54 not out by Will Jacks that, with Australia's match-winner from the first ODI, Mahli Beardman, rested, took England to a dominant position, however. Banton scored around the ground but the majority of his boundaries were pulls into or over the leg side Cox came in after captain Harry Brook, on five, deflected the ball onto his stumps when trying a ramp to push on the scoring. Jacks joined him when Banton holed out at deep square-leg after one too many of those pulls. Cox and Jacks were scoring at a run a ball when taking England to 245-4 after 40 overs but together helped their side take 110 from the last. Cox, after a run of lower scores as he fills in for Jos Buttler, drove, cut, scooped and pulled. A reverse scoop for four off Xavier Bartlett was outrageous. He has one more chance in this series to push his case further - possibly more if Buttler does not recovery for the January series against South Africa. "Banton has really found his flow for batting," former England captain Michael Vaughan said. "I don't know who the person was to say 'you can open the batting in 50-over cricket, Tom' but it's been a tremendous move. He and Ben Duckett look a good combo. "Banton seems to have all the time, all the strokes. He's got the pull shot, he's got the drive down the ground and he plays spin great. Headline: Milder day in store before more cold health alerts take effect
Body: Another round of cold health alerts is set to come into force on Sunday following a brief break from the weekend's subzero temperatures. After readings dipped as low as minus 7C early on Saturday, most places on Sunday morning were milder and free of frost. Widespread rainfall will put a dampener on any outdoor plans, however, with hail and thunderstorms possible for parts of Wales and southern England. Into the new week, the wintry chill is set to return with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) cold-health alerts beginning for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber from 21:00 GMT on Sunday. Following the lowest temperature of the autumn so far on Saturday - minus 7.2C at South Newington in Oxfordshire - milder air will dominate on Sunday. As weather fronts move in from the west, areas of showery rain will drift eastwards across much of the UK through the day. Outbreaks of rain will be fairly widespread by midday on Sunday with the chance of mountain snow in Scotland and thunder and lightning in the south. The heaviest of the rain first thing is likely to be in Scotland and Northern Ireland as well as south-western parts of England and Wales. Outbreaks of rain will then become widespread by the middle of the day, with a chance of thundery downpours in the south. Some disruption is possible due to bursts of heavy rain. Trees will be shedding leaves readily due to the rain and the brisk winds, and these could block drains - leading to localised flooding. The slightly milder weather will not stick around long. Beginning at 21:00 GMT on Sunday, UKHSA cold health alerts will come into effect for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber lasting until 09:00 GMT on Thursday. As low pressure clears eastwards on Monday, rain and wind will ease, but colder air will again move in from the north bringing a return to frost and fog. Temperatures on Monday afternoon will be around 5 to 8C across most of the UK with a noticeable wind chill near eastern coasts. Monday will see temperatures fall back below average and the chilly northerly winds will make it feel colder still The exception will be the far southwest of England where highs may reach 12C ahead of the next Atlantic weather front bringing rain and wind. Monday night's wet and windy weather will sweep across many parts of the country with gales likely around western coasts. The rain may be preceded by a spell of sleet and snow across the high ground including Snowdonia, parts of the Pennines and in the Highlands. A Met Office yellow weather warning for ice will be in place across parts of Scotland and northern England from 18:00 GMT on Sunday until 10:00 GMT on Monday, with icy conditions possible on roads and pavements. Elsewhere, it will be too mild for any wintry weather. The remainder of the week will be a temperature rollercoaster with alternating spells of mild and cold weather. Headline: Call to review sentence for driver who killed boy and fled to Latvia
Body: Keaton's mother described her son as "funny, caring, loving and full of life" and said he "loved football more than anything" An MP says she has written to the attorney general seeking a review of the jail sentence given to a speeding driver who killed a 12-year-old boy and fled to Latvia. On Friday, Aleksanders Dolars, 23, was sentenced to nine years and four months in prison for causing the death of Keaton Slater by dangerous driving in Coventry in June 2024. Dolars evaded capture for Keaton's death for more than two years by fleeing to Latvia and he was finally brought to justice following a determined campaign by Keaton's parents. Their MP, Taiwo Owatemi, is supporting them and has written to the attorney general to suggest the sentence is reviewed and ask whether a life sentence might have been appropriate. Judges use guidelines set by the Sentencing Council , external to assess the seriousness of the offence based on culpability. Taiwo Owatemi asked the attorney general to consider referring the case to the Court of Appeal Warwick Crown Court heard Dolars had been driving at 75-76mph in a 30mph zone when he struck the schoolboy, killing him instantly. Judge Kristina Montgomery KC told him his speed had been "excessive" and added: "Your selfish and dangerous driving took his life." But speaking after they left court, the family said they were unhappy with the sentence. "They gave him the maximum they could, but it's not enough is it?," his father Clint said. His mother Louise said as Dolars would only serve two-thirds of his sentence in prison, he would be out in six years. "I know afterwards he can't drive," she added. "That's good to know - he's not going to be on the roads doing it to another family. "To be in prison for six years, I think he should've got longer. My baby only had 12 years on this planet." In her letter to Attorney General Ellie Reeves, Owatemi said she was asking if the legal threshold had been met for the case to be referred to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme , external . She sat with the family during the sentencing and said it had been "heartbreaking" to watch the footage of the crash. Owatemi said: "I make this request in light of the pain Keaton's family have endured, Dolars' decision to leave the scene and evade accountability for more than two years and the fact that his driving ban is substantially longer than his prison sentence." She said she shared the family's concern that just over six years in custody failed to "reflect the seriousness of what Dolars did or the injustice they have endured". In her letter she suggested the sentence should "make clear that dangerous driving carries serious consequences". She also asked whether sufficient weight was given to Dolars' decision to flee the country, Keaton's vulnerability as a child pedestrian, the speed which Dolars was driving at and his failure to stop or call for help. "I ask you to consider whether the court fully considered the sentencing powers available to it, including whether the statutory criteria for a life sentence were met," she said. Headline: I met the love of my life on Roblox, now we're getting married
Body: Kiara from Tasmania, Australia, met Jacob from Derbyshire on online gaming platform Roblox When Jacob Smith logged on to online gaming platform Roblox at 04:00, he had no idea he was about to meet the love of his life. In the small hours, the gaming fan, from Swadlincote in Derbyshire, joined a "random" Australian server on the platform and was approached by fellow player Kiara Williams. Jacob, who started playing Roblox to be "a bit more social", got more than he bargained for as the pair hit it off straight away. Despite the 11-hour time difference and disrupted sleep schedules, the pair bonded over their love of gaming and the couple finally met when Jacob took his first ever flight to see her in Tasmania in 2025. Kiara, 22, then swapped the dramatic wilderness and wildlife of the Apple Isle to join Jacob in Derbyshire after his parents bought her a plane ticket to live with them for six months in August. But Jacob, 20, had big plans. He organised a special proposal in secret at a gaming convention in London in October. Down on one knee with baited breath, she said yes, to rapturous applause from attendees. The pair are now planning a wedding in Kiara's home Down Under and are fundraising Â£6,000 for visa applications and legal fees so they can live together in the UK or Australia permanently. Roblox is an online platform where users can play games and socialise in virtual spaces created by other players Roblox attracts millions of players worldwide and allows users to interact, chat and collaborate in virtual worlds created by its community. The game mode Jacob joined is called Mic Up - a virtual social hub where users control avatars and chat to others using voice communication. Kiara, who first approached Jacob after admiring his avatar, said she "really liked" his accent. Jacob, in return added he "felt connected to her" straight away. The pair began communicating nonstop for hours and days on end, with video calls and sessions gaming together. Jacob told the BBC: "She saw my avatar in the game and thought it was very unique - she came up to me and we started talking and we just kept talking for hours that night. "The next day, we exchanged pictures of each other to see what we actually looked like, because we were both curious. "I was very scared to send one, because she loved my avatar, I was hopeful she would like me in real life as well. "When I saw her I was like, 'oh wow, she's beautiful'. The pair said they ruined their sleep schedules in order to keep in contact with each other Kiara said: "I liked him so much even though we just met and couldn't see each other. "We ended up talking about personal things and we just weren't afraid to talk about anything, we just knew that we were so comfortable with each other." The pair continued to communicate non-stop for months until they expressed their feelings for each other on a video call. Kiara said her parents were a little sceptical when she told them about Jacob, her boyfriend 11,000 miles away in the UK. "My parents at first didn't like him because they mentioned stuff about him being online and that he could be fake," she said. "But when they noticed just how much we would talk, I'd ruin my sleep and he'd ruin his, they realised it was real. They'd ask me 'how's your boyfriend?' before we were proper official. "But later when Jacob came to visit me, they really liked him." The avid gamers said they spoke to each other every day For that trip, Jacob flew over with his parents, his first ever plane journey. "As soon as I laid eyes on Australia coming in to land I was like, 'wow this is amazing'," he said. "When we landed it was just it's like a different kind of vibe, it's just so nice." A quick layover in Melbourne and it was another flight to Tasmania. A car journey to where Kiara was staying followed. "My heart was pounding in my chest, I was so nervous when I first got there," he said. "Kiara was as well because before I even got out the car to walk up to the door I saw her peek out the door and close it because she was too scared." "I thought I wouldn't be nervous, why would I be? We've been talking for ages on FaceTime and stuff but when he text me to say he was pulling up at the house, I said to my friend 'I can't do this, please help'," she said. "But it was fine, it was so good to actually see him in person." The pair spent their time together with but Jacob had to go home after just four days - their time together cut short by the conflict in the Middle East. Kiara is currently in the UK and the pair plan to head over to Australia for the wedding in February "I was very sad when we had to go home so early, I was crying a lot," he said. But Kiara would end up making it to the UK - Jacob's parents bought her a plane ticket and she arrived in August. "I was very happy, I just couldn't wait to see her. It felt like the time was going so slow," he said. Before the big proposal in October, Kiara, who had not left Australia before coming to Derbyshire, said she did not have the UK down as a place she would have visited. But she said the country had surprised her, including the heatwave summer weather. From the laidback day-to-day in Tasmania, Kiara touched down at Heathrow Airport and travelled up to South Derbyshire. "I was just standing there in shock that I was in the UK - I initially thought it might be a bit boring but the places I've been so far are super nice and it wasn't grey and cold at all," she said. "It just felt so weird going into a someone's bedroom that I've seen on a video call but in real life I was like, 'wow I'm actually here'." The pair got engaged on stage at a gaming convention in London Fast-forward to October, the couple attended TennoVIP, an official community event in London hosted by Digital Extremes, the developer of the action game Warframe. Kiara thought it was a day out, but Jacob had a different motive. He contacted the organisers in advance to arrange a marriage proposal. During a raffle, Jacob's number was called and the pair were invited on to the stage, where he got down on one knee and proposed in front of fellow members of the gaming community. "I thought this could be perfect, I sent the organisers an email and they thought it was really sweet," he said. "They organised a fake giveaway and they called me to the stage to collect a fake prize - they set it all up for me, I was so nervous but luckily, she said yes." Kiara said she had "some idea" something was amiss as they had been browsing rings in the past but added she was "shocked". "We got on the stage I remember thinking 'something might happen' and then he went on one knee and proposed - it was crazy, so many were cheering." Their romance comes as Roblox continues to face scrutiny over online safety. An independent developer told the BBC back in March the platform's age verification measures do not go far enough and argued children should be closely supervised while using it. Roblox has said safety is a top priority and points to measures including mandatory age checks and restrictions on communication between children and adults. Roblox is the most popular gaming platform for children aged eight to 12 in the UK Meanwhile Kiara and Jacob are busy planning their February 2027 wedding, due to be held in Tasmania with their closest family members and friends. The ceremony will take place at a "beautiful lodge, with a lake and mountains" providing a stunning natural backdrop. Kiara said the wedding was meant to embrace the area's natural beauty, vibrant colours, and scenic landscape. The couple have launched a crowdfunding campaign to help fund the visa applications needed to live together permanently. This includes a subclass 309/100 Australian Partner Visa for Jacob and a UK Family Visa for Kiara, giving them the flexibility to build their future together in either Australia or the UK. They estimate the total cost of the applications, including legal fees, will be at least Â£6,000. But in the long-term, Jacob told the BBC it will eventually be game over for his life in the UK as the couple make Australia their permanent home. Headline: Family's move to Portugal delayed by premature birth
Body: Mafalda wanted to thank the hospital staff for their amazing care A family whose move to Portugal had to be delayed after their baby was born 11 weeks early have thanked the hospital that cared for her during the most "incredibly challenging time". Baby Matilde was born at Watford General Hospital in August at 29 weeks and stayed in the care of its neonatal team for 61 days. Her mother Mafalda said: "They cared for Matilde when she needed them most and supported us as parents through an incredibly challenging and emotional time." The family has now raised Â£800 for the unit to show their appreciation. West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, which runs the hospital, said the family had been living in the UK for 13 years and had planned to move back to Portugal before Matilde was born. Instead, she was delivered via emergency caesarean section nearly three months prematurely. The family, which includes Matilde's father Duarte and her two siblings, have since moved back to Portugal. The move was only possible when Matilde was feeling better, a hospital spokesperson confirmed. Baby Matilde had to stay at the hospital for about two months In the moments Matilde's parents could not be with her due to other family commitments, they used the hospital app that shares overnight updates about sleep and feeding. Mafalda said: "It was really reassuring for us as parents to have those updates when we couldn't physically be with Matilde. "The team really save lives of babies but also support and heal parents too. "We wanted to give something back by raising funds to help the team to continue their amazing work." Due to family commitments parents Mafalda and Duarte could not always spend the whole day with baby Matilde Dr Sankara Narayanan, consultant neonatologist, said: "It was a pleasure to look after Matilde, Mafalda and her family. "It's been a privilege for us to get to know them, and to see baby Matilde get healthy enough to go home to her siblings and family." Mafalda said: "The neonatal team's care and support means more to us than we can put into words." Headline: Lucky escape for man after car crashes into house
Body: Mario Lleshi said when he was at home he would usually relax in a chair in the room which was hit A man fears he could have been killed had he been at home relaxing in his usual "chilling area" when a car crashed into his house. Mario Lleshi, 22, said he had been at work at the time of the crash but would normally have been relaxing in the back room of the house he rents on Upper Road in Shrewsbury. That room is now just rubble with only the supporting walls in place. Lleshi said: "Maybe I would be dead by now, or probably badly injured in the hospital." West Mercia Police said there had been no reported injuries and it was investigating. The force said it was called to the property at 13:38 GMT on Saturday. Nearby homes were evacuated as a precaution because of a reported gas leak. Lleshi said he returned from work at about 18:00 GMT, unaware of the incident. He said he saw the road was closed so parked his car and walked down to see what had happened. "I just see the car in my house," he said. He also discovered firefighters had knocked down his front door to get to the main gas line. The car crashed into the back of the house on Upper Road on Saturday afternoon Two streets were closed for several hours and residents reported a strong smell of gas following the crash. The police said a refuge area was established at Meole Brace Bowling Club for residents who had needed to leave their homes. They were able to return when the cordon was lifted just before 16:00 GMT. There is little left of the room at the back of the house Lleshi rented Lleshi has been living in the house for just six months, but said it was "lovely area". He said he had been told by the police that the driver was also unhurt and added: "Thank God I wasn't here or nobody was here and nobody got injured." He has been reassured his landlord will arrange for the damage to be fixed and said it was just "an unfortunate thing" that had happened. Headline: 'I was ashamed of my hoarding and couldn't move on with my life'
Body: Emma Beagley contacted The Good Sort decluttering service when her home became too unmanageable Many of us would admit to owning too many possessions and being surrounded by clutter, but what happens if our behaviour starts turning to hoarding? People who struggle to organise their belongings often report having mental health issues and an overwhelming sense of being out of control. The mess can lead to feelings of embarrassment and shame, according to decluttering and mental health professionals. Emma Beagley, from Bristol, started to struggle with clutter following a stroke, which caused permanent paralysis on her left side. Her psychologist recognised that she was "bordering on hoarder status" and would need to find a solution before moving on with her life, she said. 'Brunel spinning in grave' - Bristol's bridge crisis Volunteer charities 'honoured' by King's awards Breaking the link between booze and rugby Hoarding disorder was formally classified as a mental health condition by the World Health Organisation in 2018. It is estimated that up to four million people in the UK live with it. Anna Davies, co-founder of The Good Sort, an organising and decluttering service based in Shirehampton, Bristol, said there was often a deep reason why people held onto their possessions and it was "only with support that they could start to ask questions". Mental health professionals agree there are many reasons why people hoard. Gemma Mason, a psychotherapist from Trowbridge in Wiltshire, said it was important to address the underlying causes. "We have to be careful of removing the surface problem, but not the underlying psychological need, which is not met if you just take items away," she said. Anna Davies (L) and Sarah Sampson, who founded The Good Sort, say there can be many reasons why people hoard Beagley, who is in her 40s, said her mental ability to process things deteriorated after the stroke in 2018 and it had been difficult to adapt to needing carers. "My house was stacked with boxes and things that weren't adding to my daily life," she said. "I struggled to answer the carers' questions about where to put things, so stuff started to pile up." She got in touch with Davies and Sarah Sampson, who started The Good Sort together four years ago to offer practical and emotional support to people who were floundering. "They needed my input to tell them how they could help me to rearrange my living space so that I didn't have to spend so much of my energy and time explaining things to carers," said Beagley. Decluttering services to help people organise their belongings are becoming increasingly popular Davies says clients usually approach her because they are overwhelmed by their environment and do not know where to start. "Decluttering is about asking yourself why you're holding on to the things you're holding on to," she said. "It's understandable that there's a temptation to keep everything from your past, especially if it cost you a lot of money. Our belongings can connect us to old identities, lost capabilities, financial guilt and difficulty accepting change. "But the 'what ifs' keep you locked into living in the past," she added. Chloe Wright says clients can be "manipulated" by marketing into buying too much stuff Chloe Wright, who runs Goddess Organising in Frome, Somerset, said she had experienced many clients who had been "manipulated" by marketing into buying more items than they actually needed. "It could be somebody who spent loads of money on makeup and cosmetics and even though they're not using them any more, or they're not right, they still can't get rid of them because they feel guilt-tripped and don't want to be wasteful and add to landfill." Wright says people often feel "embarrassed and ashamed" when they meet her, but soon change once they started the process of decluttering. "Every decision can be quite slow and traumatic and it involves a lot of coaching and negotiating and then by the end of the day, they've realised that the world hasn't burnt down by removing this thing and their decisions get easier," she said. Mason, who has been in practice for 26 years, said often people who develop hoarding tendencies have had a traumatic event in their childhood. "They may have grown up in a poor environment or they may have lost someone at an early age, so the clutter becomes a manifestation of something they've not been able to psychologically process." She said it was important to understand what the symbolic meaning of possessions was to the client as the clutter often "represented something to them that they can't let go of". "One of the common themes that I've seen is that people become very ashamed of their home environments and so they don't invite people in and it becomes a kind of secret that they keep." Gemma Mason says hoarding tendencies can be linked to childhood trauma Gemma Nicoll founded The Home Edit Bristol in 2022 and specialises in helping clients with ADHD and neurodivergence. She says there is a growing interest in decluttering services as people are increasingly recognising how much their home environment can affect how they feel. "The particular struggles for people with neurodivergence can be task initiation, so they sit at home and know that they want to get things organised, but can't actually get the job done. "It helps for me just to work alongside them, so they've got somebody to keep them motivated," Nicoll added. Gemma Nicoll specialises in helping clients with ADHD and neurodivergence One of her clients, Ellys Binding, from Yate, who is neurodivergent, said making decisions was the hardest part of decluttering. "I just freeze up and it can be very overwhelming when you look at a space and it's really hectic," she said. "The storage spaces in my house are quite impressive, as I have very big cupboards. "But what's happened is that all those spaces have gotten full of the stuff I don't need, and all the stuff that I use on a daily basis is on the surfaces so that I can grab it quickly." She said it had got to the point where everywhere she looked was "always a complete mess". "To be able to have someone like Gemma come along and say, 'this time we're going to focus on this' and to do it with you, really helps me to stay on track," she added. Headline: Man charged with raping 15-year-old girl
Body: The rape was reported to police on 6 November A man has been charged with raping a 15-year-old girl as she walked near a recreation ground. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said the teenager was walking near Eccles Recreation Ground in Salford before she was attacked between 23:00 GMT on 23 October and 02:00 on 24 October. Aaron McColl, of Brindleheath Road in Salford, has been charged with rape and sexual assault. The 32-year-old is due to appear before Manchester and Salford Magistrates' Court on Monday. Headline: Guide dog made member of church clergy
Body: Lance the loveable Labrador cross is a guiding light for his owner A guide dog has been made a member of a church clergy in recognition of how he enhances the life of his blind owner during her service within the community. Lance the golden retriever and Labrador cross has become an honorary canon in celebration of how he supports the Reverend Canon Emerita Stephne van der Toorn. The three-year-old pooch, a familiar face within the Diocese of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich, will receive the accolade at St Edmundsbury Cathedral on Sunday. "I feel very blessed that the faithful service of my guide dog is being recognised," said Van der Toorn, who has 5% vision. "A long time ago, a parishioner pointed out to me that God is dog spelt backwards. I have found that very helpful in my faith journey with blindness." The Right Reverend Joanne Grenfell (left), the Bishop of St Edmundsbury & Ipswich, and Reverend Canon Emerita Stephne van der Toorn with Lance Van der Toorn has trained with Lance this year following the retirement of her previous guide dog Coco, who was also made a canon. Coco, who has become Van der Toorn's husband Joop's pet dog, assisted the 73-year-old from 2016 in the Benefice of East Bergholt and Brantham until her retirement in 2023. Van der Toorn, a mother of four daughters, is a spiritual director in the diocese and undertakes public speaking on behalf of the Guide Dogs charity. She also continues to assist at the Benefice of Great Barton and Thurston in West Suffolk and at the cathedral in Bury St Edmunds as a chaplain on duty. She said her pooch was a "very loving, gentle, playful soul" and "plants his paws and refuses to move" if she starts walking in the wrong direction. The three-year-old pooch ensures his owner can live her life to the full "I have found that when I am chaplain on duty people will tell my dog things that they wouldn't dream of telling me. They smile and become very chatty," she added. "He guides me up to the altar rail for communion. Once there, he places his front paws on the altar step and wags his tail until I have received the bread and the wine. "He then ushers me back to my seat, knowing he's been very clever. So far, we have not had a disaster as he has not tried to snaffle the wafers." As well as in the church, Lance helps Van der Toorn access the library, village shop and community centre, and safely cross roads. Grenfell said Lance was as deserving a dog as any to receive the canon title The decision to bless Lance with the title of canon was welcomed by The Right Reverend Dr Joanne Grenfell, the Bishop of St Edmundsbury & Ipswich. Grenfell said appointing an honorary canine canon was "almost unheard of for us" but Lance was Van der Toorn's "rock" and gave her "the confidence to live life fully". "Lance's appointment recognises the invaluable role not just in the life of Steph as one of the county's priests, but also our parishioners who benefit from his calming presence," she added. Headline: Teen tops 24-hour backflip world record
Body: Austin says he hopes the challenge will inspire other people A teenager from East Yorkshire claims he has exceeded the existing Guinness World Record for the most backflip somersaults in 24 hours. Austin Beasty, 18, from Market Weighton, completed 2,470 flips, double the record of 1,234 and is raising money for the Yorkshire Air Ambulance. Independent witnesses monitored the attempt in line with Guinness World Records' standards, but the organisation has yet to confirm the record officially. Austin set himself the challenge in memory of his brother, Jaygo, who died aged 17 in a road traffic collision in 2022. Austin, an engineering apprentice, said: "To actually go out and do it feels great." The attempt started at 06:00 GMT on Saturday and was due to finish at 06:00 on Sunday at Wolds Gymnastics Club in Driffield, where Austin competed as a junior. The club confirmed the total on their Facebook page in the early hours of Sunday morning. "Two thousand, four hundred and seventy of your finest flips," the post said. "What a thing to witness! Hopefully this amazing guy has inspired some of you today!" Volunteers witnessed the world record count Speaking after he had completed 1,426 flips, already surpassing the record, the teenager said: "I'm doing one every 20 seconds. I'm having regular breaks, keeping hydratedâ¦ I just keep chugging away." "You can't do them fast because you fatigue too fast, and then you get cramps," Austin explained. "It's something I could only dream of," he said. Tracey Beasty, Austin's mother, said she was very proud. "He's worked really hard for it," she said. Austin lost his older brother, who he was very close to, four and a half years ago. "We had a really, really good network of people, and the gymnastics club - that support network for Austin, was amazing," Tracey said. Austin has raised money for the Yorkshire Air Ambulance and the gymnastics club previously with a fundraising backflip attempt when he was 14. On Sunday his JustGiving page total for this challenge had passed Â£4,000. "It's really nice to give something back," Tracey said. Headline: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
Body: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing â known as a tie-back in industry terms â before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add Â£2.9bn to the economy. The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank. Jackdaw's operators said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989. The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit. Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production. But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully . The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process. The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them. An inside look at Jackdaw, the UKâs newest and most contested gas platform. When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter. However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills. In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined , external . "With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks. Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities. McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank. He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy. Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil. But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets. Headline: Former geography teacher becomes first female head gardener in site's 332-year history
Body: Gillian Boyle is the first female head gardener in a history spanning more than 300 years A former geography teacher has become the first woman to helm a garden in its 332-year history. Levens Hall, near Kendal, Cumbria, holds the Guinness World Record for the oldest topiary garden and has only employed 11 head gardeners since its creation in 1694. Gillian Boyle is now the 12th and said being the first woman to take on the role was not a big deal, but still good news. She said she returned to her "primary passion" of gardening and trained in horticulture because she wanted to spend more time outside, and has now moved into a cottage on the estate having taken on "the best job ever". Boyle said: "I first visited Levens Hall more than 10 years ago, and was very impressed by it, particularly the topiary which is wonderful. "When the job came up, I thought I'd go for it, give it a try. "The person before me was there for 40 years, so it's not one you get a chance to go for very often." Although she is the first woman to become head gardener in Levens Hall's history, she said it was "not a big deal". "I've been lucky to work with lots of incredible women in horticulture," she said. "Many of them have been head gardeners, so I'm not special in any way, but this is still a good thing." Levens Hall is home to the oldest topiary garden in the world Gardening was always her "primary passion", she said, but horticulture was not her first career choice. "I did spend a short stint as a secondary school geography teacher," Boyle said. "For a while I did really enjoy it, but I like getting outside and that wasn't happening enough, so I thought I'd better change. "I think a lot of people change to horticulture as a second career. "There are a lot of courses you can do, which is a very good way in as you can do it part time - and there are still some college courses, though unfortunately they're dwindling in number - but I also think volunteering is good because you can then find out if it's for you. Welcoming her to the post, a spokesperson for Levens Hall said: "We haven't exactly eased her in. "Her first big job has been leading our gardening team through the annual trim; over 100 topiary trees, including two 300-year-old Umbrella Trees more than 10m high, plus the towering beech hedge that runs half the length of the garden. "She calls the team an incredible group of gardeners, and we couldn't agree more." Headline: 'I didn't think I'd become a pub landlord aged 20'
Body: Will Avery has become the landlord of a pub in the Fens at just 20 years old At an age when most of his friends are just starting out in their careers, Will Avery is running his own village pub. The 20-year-old has become the landlord and head chef of the Cross Keys pub and restaurant in Upwood, Cambridgeshire, after working his way up from being in the kitchen. "It's fun, it's challenging, but it is really good," he said. He said his friends were "pretty jealous" of his new role, adding: "Absolutely no way at any point would I have thought I would have been where I am now." Since becoming a chef in the pub aged 16, he said being able to meet and serve people in his community had been rewarding. "Everyone's a bit jealous that I'm doing my own thing and getting to have fun with it." Most of the staff in the pub are young adults. "People hear about it's been taken over, and they ask who's the new person in charge, and I am like 'oh yeah, that's me'," he said. "They are like 'oh OK' and that's a bit of a setback, but then you get talking to them and they realise that it's not a bad thing that it's a young person behind the bar." Will became a chef in the pub before becoming its landlord in September He added that taking on the challenge of becoming a landlord at 20 was not straightforward. "It's not easy, nothing is just handed to you, so finding a way of being able to do it was difficult," he said. Data by the Office For National Statistics showed that an estimated 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 years , external in the UK were not in education, employment or training from April to June. Alan Milburn's year-long report , to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. "It's very generalised that young people have to just go [work in] retail or anything like that," said Will. "If you want to be able to do something that you actually want, if you put your mind to it and you're determined, I think you can definitely do it." Les Jones is a regular at the Cross Keys pub and restaurant Les Jones, a regular at the Fenland pub, said Will becoming its landlord was "a great opportunity" for him and that he would do a "smashing job" of running it. "He's a great young lad, he's going to go far, his food's beautiful you know and he's a good lad," said Jones. "He's quiet, but we're getting him out because he's always been behind the scenes now he's in front of the scene. "He's coming out of his shell and doing a great job." Em Avery is Will's sister and also works at the pub Will's sister, Em, is the front of house at the pub, looking after the bar and customers. "Hospitality can be a very demanding job, but with that it's also very rewarding," she said. "It's hard work, especially for Will, but I think being so young and doing what he's doing is incredible. She said her brother has created a "relaxed work environment" and is a "very good boss". "Everyone gets along with him and he cares about us, how we feel and how we are at work, so it's a great environment to be in," she added. Will said "the support from the community is very overwhelming", after taking it on in September. He has taken on a three-year lease for the pub and hopes to eventually buy it outright. Headline: 'I'm lucky to be alive': Woman's warning over black market weight-loss jabs
Body: Kay Roscoe was found unresponsive at her home in October A woman has described how she could not speak or stand before being rushed to hospital after taking an unlicensed weight-loss jab. Kay Roscoe, 38, from Birkenhead, said she had used a substance sold as retatrutide, or "reta", for two months before falling seriously ill. The experimental drug is not approved for general use and is available only through clinical trials. Products claiming to contain it are widely sold online, but it is not known whether Kay took genuine retatrutide. She is now warning others about the risks. "I am the luckiest person to be alive. Honestly I can't say it enough, get off the pens," she said. On the day of her collapse, Kay had been due to go out for a roast dinner with a friend. When she failed to answer her phone, her friend went to check on her at home and found her unable to speak or stand. "I was frothing at the mouth, not responsive at all," she said, recounting what her friend later told her. "My eyes were moving around, but I couldn't speak or move or do anything." Kay, who has no memory of the episode, said her friends rang an ambulance and told paramedics she had been taking "reta" before she was rushed to hospital. She said it took more than an hour for her to regain consciousness. Kay took this selfie the night before she became unwell and said she felt "absolutely fine" Hospital tests confirmed Kay had suffered severe hypoglycaemia, a condition where blood sugar falls to dangerously low levels. Medical records attributed the episode to an unlicensed weight-loss injection. Kay said doctors warned her she could have died if her friend had found her just half an hour later. In the weeks since, Kay said she has continued to suffer health problems, including extreme fatigue. She said further tests had shown she had signs of liver damage and high cholesterol, neither of which she had before the episode. . "I don't drink very much, I don't smoke," she said. "I've never had a problem with anything like this. I just feel run down and drained. My body feels all over the place." Kay said she lost a 'drastic' amount of weight while taking the jab, but was also hardly eating Kay had started injecting herself with the substance about two months earlier. A former regular gym-goer, she said she was attracted to the prospect of quicker weight loss after seeing posts on social media. "Going to the gym takes longer. I saw my friends on it and saw them losing weight. And I thought, everyone is taking it and they've all been fine, so I'll try it. I didn't really read into the licensing," she said. Kay bought the jab from a friend and said she believed it was legitimate after scanning a QR code on the pen, which took her to what appeared to be a pharmaceutical website. Initially, she was pleased with the results, saying she lost a "drastic amount" of weight within weeks. But the injections had also significantly reduced her appetite. "I was made up with the change, but I was never hungry," she said. In the days leading up to her hospital admission, Kay said she had eaten very little. Retatrutide is being developed by pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly as a potential treatment for obesity. Unlike existing weight-loss drugs, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, which target one or two hormone receptors, retatrutide acts on three, earning it the nickname "triple G". The drug is still undergoing clinical trials, with Eli Lilly planning to apply for approval in the US early next year. A previous BBC investigation found vials purporting to be "reta" were being sold in gyms, beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers. Eli Lilly said retatrutide had not been approved by any regulator and could not legally be sold for human use. A spokesperson said: "Counterfeit and black market medicines are unverified, unregulated and potentially dangerous - in some cases, deadly." The company said it was working with the UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, police and social media platforms to remove illegal products. "Stronger, coordinated law enforcement must be sustained to protect UK patients from unsafe fake medicines," the spokesperson added. Dr Nas Khattak is a research doctor who has worked on clinical trials of weight-loss drugs Dr Nas Khattak, a research doctor based in Chester who has worked on clinical trials of weight-loss drugs, warned of the dangers of injections obtained through unregulated sources. "You cannot verify the dose, purity, sterility, or even the contents," he said. "If something goes wrong there is no proper medical oversight." Dr Khattak said he had seen substances advertised through messaging apps, bodybuilding forums and private sellers, with users openly sharing dosing advice and supplier recommendations. He said he had also encountered serious complications during his NHS hospital work, including a young woman who required intensive care after taking a weight-loss injection obtained from a beautician. He said it was never established exactly what substance she had taken. "It really does feel like a roll of the dice," he said. The UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, has seized products claiming to contain retatrutide and says it is working to disrupt their illegal importation and distribution. Dr Khattak said common side effects of weight-loss injections included mild nausea, feeling full more quickly, constipation and tiredness. He said headaches, dizziness, a dry mouth and very dark urine could be signs of dehydration and should prompt medical advice. However, he warned people to seek urgent medical attention if they experienced more serious symptoms, including: Kay said she now plans to return to the gym and eat healthily Since sharing her story on Facebook, Kay said she had received messages from about 100 people describing their own experiences with weight-loss injections. "You never think anything's going to happen to you. But we all do things because we want to lose weight," she said. "You see a new thing on the market and want to try it. I just think it's very dangerous." Kay also revealed the impact her ordeal has had on her family. "They've gone mad at me and warned me not to take it. They said, 'There's nothing of you', but you don't see yourself like that, do you?" She now plans to return to the gym and eat healthily. "Please, everyone, stop taking a needle to be skinny. Imagine not waking up, like I nearly didn't. And then my poor family losing someone over taking something you didn't even know what it was." Headline: Could the status of Lancashire's two cities be at risk?
Body: Preston is one of only two cities in Lancashire As Lancashire waits to hear what the future of local government will look like, questions have been raised over whether the county's two cities could lose their status. Preston and Lancaster are Lancashire's only cities, having gained the designation at different points in their history. Lancaster was the first, and although it received its original charter in 1193, it was formally granted city status in 1937. Preston became a city much later, after being awarded the status by Queen Elizabeth II as part of her Golden Jubilee celebrations in 2002. The city won the Golden Jubilee city competition, beating 26 other contenders, including Blackburn. Queen Elizabeth visited Preston as part of a ceremony to unveil it's city status in 2002 The government is planning a major overhaul of local government in Lancashire. Under current proposals, the county's 15 councils would be abolished and replaced with a smaller number of unitary authorities. Both Preston and Lancaster are expected to become part of much larger council areas. It is understood that unless steps are taken to protect their city status, there is a risk they could lose it because the status is currently and intrinsicly linked to the councils themselves. There is precedent for this. Rochester, in Kent, lost its city status following local government reorganisation in 1998, when it became part of Medway Borough Council. This was down to an adminstrative oversight. Lancaster City Council will not exist under the current local government reorganisation plans According to council papers published in 2003: "A conscious decision was made by the former Rochester upon Medway City Council not to proceed to make the appointment of Charter Trustees." Charter trustees are a legal mechanism used to preserve city status in places that do not have their own district or town council. That arrangement could potentially apply to Preston and Lancaster once the existing councils are abolished. However, there are also examples of places regaining city status after losing it. St Davids in Pembrokeshire and Armagh in Northern Ireland both lost their statuses in the 1800s before they were restored by the Queen in 1994. However, if Preston and Lancaster suffered the same outcome, it would not affect local services or change things like council tax bills. It would mean they would simply lose the legal right to describe themselves as cities unless alternative arrangements were put in place. Lancaster Cathedral is also known as The Cathedral Church of St Peter According to the House of Commons library, city status can be associated with having a cathedral, university, a particular form of local government, or having a large population. Historically, cities were places that had a cathedral, although these days it is not a requirement for a town to have one in order to become a city. In the case of Preston and Lancaster, both do have a cathedral, but this was not part of the decision to grant them the status. For a place to become a city, something known as letters patent is usually used, this is a legal document issued by the monarch on the advice of ministers. There are no additional powers or government funding for becoming a city, but it is seen as an important part of a place's identity and heritage. While it could be said there is a risk that Preston and Lancaster could lose their city status during local government reorganisation, ministers have indicated they are keen to prevent that from happening. The issue has already been raised in Parliament by Lancaster and Wyre MP Cat Smith, who sought assurances from local government minister Jim McMahon. He said: "The government has heard concerns from places about retaining their city status and has committed to making it a priority to protect them and will consider all available options, including bringing in new legislation if necessary." Although the precise legal mechanism has yet to be confirmed, both Preston and Lancaster are likely to retain their city status, potentially through the same use of letters patent issued by the King on the advice of ministers. A final decision on Lancashire's new councils is expected in the new year, and so any arrangements to protect Preston and Lancaster's city status are also likely to be some way off. Headline: Fly-tipping, condemned buildings and anti-social behaviour: Life on troubled Baguley Crescent
Body: Patrick Connelly says he feels he has been constantly "let down" by his landlord Baguley Crescent has long been blighted by fly-tipping, a condemned building and anti-social behaviour. I have been reporting on life on this small Greater Manchester estate - located just off the M60 between Prestwich and Middleton - for years. But what I saw when speaking to some social housing tenants about a recent fire - in which a man in his 60s died - really shocked me. Residents here feel forgotten by the very authorities that are supposed to look out for them. Local MPs have claimed that police officers - fearing for their own safety - have been too afraid to patrol the road. And, despite years of complaints, they say the area has seen little improvement. The area has been blighted by persistent fly-tipping despite council clear-up efforts Patrick Connelly, an 80-year-old who lives in the apartment block where the fire took place, showed me round his flat. "Almost 10 years ago I told my social landlord that my cooker didn't work and there was no response, so my daughter bought me an air-fryer... but it means I can't have my grandchildren round for a Sunday lunch." Patrick, who has lived on Baguley Crescent for 17 years, added: "I've asked to move several times because of the anti-social behaviour on this road but the housing association keeps letting me down - all they've done is paint the walls a few years ago." The social landlord Great Places Housing said: "Customers are responsible for providing their own appliances but we may be able to offer assistance to replace a broken cooker via our tenancy sustainment and support services. "Upgrade works to the kitchen and bathroom were carried out in 2022/23 and a survey last year by an independent surveyor found both to be in good condition." Patrick said the cooker inside his flat had not worked for nearly a decade Greater Manchester Police said there were no suspicious circumstances surrounding the death of 67-year-old David Mills in the fire in his Baguley Crescent flat on 7 November. The fire service is still investigating the cause. Patrick, who moved to the UK in 1966 from Ireland, said: "I've known Dave for 17 years and when the fire alarm went off, we saw the smoke coming from his flat but we couldn't get inside the door and it was too late. "Meanwhile, the water from the firefighters came through the ceiling and left my bed with a soaking mattress." Great Places said: "We were deeply sorry to hear that the customer involved in this tragic fire lost his life and where there was damage to other properties as a result of the fire, repairs have been arranged." Two days after the fatal fire, a burnt mattress was left outside the block of flats The Great Places Housing Group owns or manages more than 28,000 affordable homes in more than 30 local authority areas across north-western England and South Yorkshire. Another tenant of Great Places, who lives in the same apartment block on Baguley Crescent, told me he had been living alone in his one-bedroom flat without a washing machine. David Gilifillian, 50, said: "A washing machine is one of the basics you need to get your clothes clean but I have to go to the launderette and that's expensive. "I'd like to move to a bigger flat because my girlfriend and my 11-year-old son often stay with me but there's no room for them both, so it's uncomfortable." Great Places said: "David's housing priority is set by the local authority and we will visit his home and identify possible solutions to the issue over his washing machine." David Gilifillian said there was no room in his one-bedroom flat for a washing machine I have spoken many times with residents on Baguley Crescent, including long-term owner-occupiers, who have witnessed the decline of the road over the last 10 years. They blame many of the area's problems on the large number of privately rented flats, which have a high turnover of tenants who have either recently arrived in the UK or have struggled to find accommodation elsewhere. When a new tenant moves into one of the flats, furniture is often dumped outside. Things did seem to improve in the summer, when a multi-agency "day of action" took place involving local people, the police, the fire service and Bury Council. A burnt-out caravan was cleared, an abandoned car was removed and tonnes of fly-tipped waste was cleaned-up. But when I visited the road last week, I saw more abandoned mattresses, refrigerators and sofas dumped by the side of the road. Much of the furniture was left next to an abandoned block of flats, beside empty land where - until recently - there were dozens of unsafe, derelict garages. Dozens of derelict garages on Baguley Crescent - pictured here two years ago - have now been demolished Three years ago, a large blaze led to a block of flats being abandoned and there was a fatal fire in a different apartment block in May 2025. For a long time, the abandoned block became a magnet for drug dealers and squatters - although recent attempts have been made to secure the building. Despite that, windows in the block remain smashed, the roof is damaged, each of the flats have been vandalised and the electricity supply has been disconnected. A spokesman for Bury Council said: "We are continuing to tackle fly-tipping in the area and there are live cameras linked directly to the council's CCTV control room. "We also empty general waste bins more frequently than is available to most households across the borough - in recognition of the challenges experienced in the area - and we regularly remove fly-tipped waste". Headline: Film aims to show 'Christmas isn't all tinsel and gingerbread'
Body: John Bradley, Nigel Planer, Richard E Grant and Celia Imrie (L-R) are among the stars of Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint "If this was an American film, they would have spent millions building a set," says actor John Bradley, "we've just got it on our doorstep." Speaking at a gala screening of new festive flick Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint, the Game of Thrones star spoke glowingly about York's "warm, timeless and cinematic" charm. Set in the city, the film opens with a snowy shot of York Minster, with the historic cobbled streets and famous festive markets also prominently featured. While for some York may be the real star of the show, the cast isn't short of a few stars itself, with director Jack Spring describing it as packed with "British legend after British legend". Richard E Grant, Celia Imrie, Jim Broadbent, Kiell Smith-Bynoe, Karl Pilkington and Adjoa Andoh - among others - were "amazing at their jobs and all lovely people as well", he added. Spring, Bradley and writer Chris Boyle-McQuarry returned to York on Monday, almost exactly a year after filming in the city, for a the screening and Q&A. Familiar sights like York Minster, the city's cobbled streets and the view from the Bar Walls all feature in the film Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint tells the story of model soldier enthusiast Aubrey Flint (played by Bradley) who hates Christmas - and people. But when a confrontation with a man on a mobility scooter lands him in community service, he is set to work helping to direct a production of A Christmas Carol at a struggling care home. Spring told the audience the inspiration came from a 2018 BBC News clip showing two drama teachers staging plays in care homes. Two years later he met Boyle-McQuarry, who came up with the idea of setting the story in York. "My sister and nephews live in York," Boyle-McQuarry said. "Jack came to me about coming up with a Christmas film and I remember thinking 'where's a great place to set something at Christmas?' and York popped into my head. "The little shop where [Aubrey] buys the model soldiers, I could see that in York. It just spiralled from there." Writer Chris Boyle-McQuarry (left) and director Jack Spring spoke at a gala screening in York Spring said Monday's screening was an opportunity to say "a little thank you to the people of York that made our life so easy when we were filming here". "I've shot films all over the place but York by far was the most seamless, amazing, hospitable city to make a movie in," he said. Boyle-McQuarry added that residents were "perfect" during filming. "They'd have a look, see that we were filming but they were great when we needed to clear something to do a take, everyone would just pause, hold their chat and let us film," he said. Bradley praised the city's "unique backdrop", which he said suited the festive theme perfectly. "There's something really warm and timeless and cinematic about it. It's unlike anywhere else in the world, and it's lovely to be back." In a message for residents, he told the BBC: "Sometimes when you see something every day you forget how beautiful it is. "Hopefully when you see your city on screen, what we've done to it and how we've shot it, you'll fall in love with it again, we hope." John Bradley plays reclusive model soldier enthusiast Aubrey Flint "One of the things I wanted to get across is that Christmas is lovely, but for some people Christmas isn't all tinsel and gingerbread men," Boyle-McQuarry explained. "It can be a reflective time, a tricky time. We wanted to try and get that balance." While the review's have been mixed, speaking shortly after the film's general release, Spring said its reception from the public had been "really good". "It's making people laugh, making people cry and hopefully they're coming out of the cinema feeling a lot more Christmassy than when they came in." Jo Patton, who watched the screening in York, said he "just had a smile on my face for the last half an hour". "They've captured something which is very human and very British." Filming took place last year outside his toy shop, Totally Awesome, with the shop-front featuring on screen. "The turquoise of the shop popped really well - they featured it really beautifully," he said. "You only ever see a tiny bit of that puzzle," he recalled. "I don't know how many takes we saw. I didn't know what was going on." The turquoise exterior of Jo Patton's toy shop "popped" in the film, he said Fellow audience members Tee and Ed Herwitz Gray thought York was "absolutely beautiful" on the big screen. "It is like a picture-postcard. If it was Disney, they'd have to build a set to make it look like that," said Tee. "York is becoming more popular for film and television, but it is still really rewarding." "York is made for Christmas and it just seemed so natural," said Ed, 62. Tee added: "I'm 63 and if I end up in one of those old folks' homes, I hope we do a Christmas play and that I'm in there with someone just as fabulous as Richard E Grant." Headline: Saracens leave it late to battle past Leicester
Body: Sione Va'enuku was one of three try-scorers for Saracens Tries: Stooke, Moli Cons: Bailey 2 Pen: Bailey Tries: Elliott, Va'enuku, Hadfield Cons: Davidson, Keylock Saracens left it late to secure a third-straight Prem Rugby Cup win with a hard-fought victory over winless Leicester Tigers in the driving wind and rain at Welford Road. The visitors had trailed since Elliot Stooke got the opening try for the Tigers shortly before the break, but James Hadfield's converted score with four minutes remaining put Saracens in front for the first time and they held on. Sarries move a point behind Group B leaders Harlequins, while a fourth defeat in a row for holders Leicester means their title defence is now all but over. Stooke's converted try for the hosts gave them a 7-0 lead at the break but the game opened up slightly after the interval. Saracens' Tobias Elliott and Tigers hooker Sam Moli traded tries before Sione Va'enuku crossed for the visitors to set up a tense finale, which Hadfield and the extra two points from Finn Keylock ultimately decided. Quins win again in cup as Gloucester also triumph Both teams struggled to hold on to the ball in sodden conditions, with passing, handling and kicking all affected. Leicester were the more threatening early on â only a brilliant last gasp tackle from Angus Hall stopped Ollie Myall from scoring on his first start. Saracens had scored 150 points in their two cup victories coming into this one but they had to feel their way into the game, taking 17 minutes to break into the Tigers 22. Hall had a chance of his own but lost control of the ball under pressure as he made for the line before the hosts eventually got the first points on the board. Stooke forced the ball over the line amid a mass of bodies with Orlando Bailey converting with a tricky kick. Noah Caluori thought he had put the visitors on the board just 60 seconds after the interval but a review ruled the try out after a knock-on at the maul. Saracens were not to be denied, however, and two minutes later Luke Davidson's outstanding cross-field kick picked out the leaping Elliott who gathered brilliantly before touching down. Orlando Bailey scored seven points for Leicester Max Malins was then shown a yellow card for a deliberate knock-on and Tigers immediately took advantage with Moli bulldozing his way over the line and Bailey again expertly providing the extras. Saracens rallied, however, forcing their way into the hosts' 22, with Va'enuku scoring his seventh try in as many matches before Davidson put his conversion between the posts. Conditions continued to hamper both sides but Bailey's penalty extended Leicester's lead to five points. They could not hold on in the face of increasing Saracens pressure, however, and finally went in front when Hadfield got the ball down following a powerful driving maul and Keylock's conversion secured the two-point win.

Headline: Families of the Disappeared to meet the Pope
Body: It is thought that the Pope will read the 'Prayer for the return of The Disappeared' which was written by Father Joe Gormley Some families of the Disappeared will meet Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday in what is hoped will be a "spiritual boost" for the relatives. The Disappeared are those who were abducted, murdered and secretly buried by republicans during Northern Ireland's Troubles. Despite extensive and painstaking searches, the bodies have never been found of four out of 17 people listed by the commission set up to locate victims' remains. The trip has been organised by the WAVE Trauma Centre which has supported the families since 1995. Speaking before the group departed from Dublin Airport on Monday morning, Sandra Peake CEO of WAVE said the trip was "many months in the making and we are all very grateful for those who have made it possible". Alongside the families travelling to Rome are the head of the Catholic Church in Ireland, Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin, and Fr Joe Gormley. It is thought that the Pope will read the 'Prayer for the return of The Disappeared' which was written by Gormley. Peake added that praying with the Pope would be hugely significant for members of the families as it will be an "immense spiritual boost". "For so many years the families of those abducted, murdered and secretly buried were cowed into silence. "But they are silent no longer and bringing the story of the Disappeared directly to the head of the Catholic Church in this way amplifies their calls for those with information to look into their hearts and end the torment of these families." Columba McVeigh, 19, was kidnapped in 1975 Columba McVeigh, 19, from Donaghmore, County Tyrone, was abducted and murdered by the IRA in 1975. His body has never been found. His family has strongly rejected an IRA claim that he was an informer. His sister Dympna Kerr said: "My faith is what enables me to get up in the morning to face the day. "Every day I pray for Columba and all those who have suffered and those of us who continue to suffer the terrible pain of not having our loved ones home with a grave to tend knowing that they have had a Christian burial." The Disappeared were people abducted and murdered by republican paramilitaries, and then buried at secret locations. As well as Columba McVeigh, the Independent Commission for the Location of Victims' Remains (ICLVR) is still leading the search for the remains of Joe Lynskey, Capt Robert Nairac and Seamus Maguire. Headline: Reported bird flu case being investigated
Body: The flock will be culled if avian influenza is confirmed A reported case of bird flu at a commercial poultry farm in County Tyrone is under investigation. "Significant" mortality and clinical signs consistent with the disease were observed at the site and movement restrictions have been imposed. Samples have been sent to the national reference laboratory in England for analysis, with results expected on Monday. The flock will be culled if avian influenza is confirmed. The Agriculture and Environment Minister Andrew Muir said the situation was being treated with "the utmost seriousness". The Chief Veterinary Officer Brian Dooher urged all flock keepers of any kind to be vigilant and observe strict biosecurity protocols. Bird flu presents little risk to human health but can be catastrophic for poultry flocks. The commercial poultry sector in Northern Ireland is an important economic player, so the disease is treated very seriously. The impact this would have on the flock keeper was recognised by the minister. "While the disease has not yet been confirmed, we are treating this situation with the utmost seriousness. "We have robust contingency plans in place and stand ready to implement the measures required to respond at the affected premises should Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza be confirmed," Muir said. A housing order was introduced in England and Scotland last week, due to the heightened risk at this time of year and a series of outbreaks across Great Britain. Wales has also brought in restrictions although no cases have yet been confirmed there. Muir said similar measures have not been ruled out for Northern Ireland. "In light of these findings, we are actively considering the need for further disease control measures across Northern Ireland, informed by the latest veterinary and epidemiological advice and assessment of risk." Dooher said officials stood ready to implement disease control arrangements if the disease was confirmed. If results came back positive, a cull would be carried out on the farm. And he encouraged all flock keepers of any nature to take precautions. "I urge all poultry keepers to remain vigilant, maintain good biosecurity and report any concerns about the health of their birds to DAERA without delay." While bird flu has already been detected in wild birds , external this season, this is the first outbreak in a commercial setting in Northern Ireland so far.
