Headline: How a child sports camp shows the changing face of grassroots hurling
Body: Each week more than 50 players (aged 9-12) from south Belfast to Strangford village have been attending a new camp at Saintfield's indoor 3g facility Dark, autumnal nights are not the traditional training time for young hurlers and camogs more used to summer days. But in Country Down more than 50 players, aged from nine to 12 and from south Belfast to Strangford village, have been coming to Saintfield for a camp that puts hurls in the hands of the younger generation. Amid the echoing thwack of stick on ball, many at the indoor 3G pitch are wearing club jerseys - Carryduff, Darragh Cross, St Kevin's, RGU, Kilclief and Saul - while others have come to try the sport for the first time. The brainchild of the Social Slashers - a group of former hurlers based in Saul, near Downpatrick - the camp points towards the changing face of the sport in the county and beyond. In most of Down, outside of hurling strongholds like Portaferry, Ballycran and Ballygalget, Gaelic football rules the roost when it comes to GAA. That is reflected throughout much of Ulster GAA. Out of 360 clubs, only about one in three offers hurling or camogie. That's compared to roughly to one in two in the rest of Ireland's 1,600 clubs. While Ulster counties and clubs have regularly tasted success in Gaelic football, no Ulster county has ever won an All-Ireland hurling title. Antrim, historically the county with the greatest level of hurling participation in Ulster, has six camogie All-Irelands and two All-Ireland club titles via Loughgiel Shamrocks. But in Down, there have been signs of a shift in recent years. More players from clubs like Liatroim, Carryduff and Bredagh have been breaking into the county hurling team. That team has also seen notable progress â including big victories over Ulster rivals Antrim. In both hurling and camogie there are now more clubs and schools competing than in years previous In camogie, Clonduff, a team based out of the Mournes village of Hilltown cemented its position as the county's best some time ago, whilst Mourne-based rivals Liatroim dominated underage competitions. In both hurling and camogie there are now more clubs and schools competing than in previous years. The camp, which received funding from the Noah Donohoe Foundation, is the brainchild of the Social Slashers, a group of former hurlers based in Saul near Downpatrick There's a lot at play here. A new research report for the GAA , external has recommended revamping youth competitions, with the aim of better retaining underage players through their teenage years. Meanwhile the GAA's own demographic report , external highlighted the impacts of urbanisation and falling birth rates on clubs and communities. Eastern counties such as Down are expected to suffer less than others, with some urban clubs struggling to keep pace with the surge in youngsters looking to play. But in rural areas, there are many clubs experiencing declining numbers with coaches frantically monitoring weekly WhatsApp polls to ensure there are enough players available to compete. Perhaps that is where initiatives like the one in Saintfield, where children from multiple clubs come together, fit in. Social Slashers founder Shay Deegan said he's hoping the camp, which received funding from the Noah Donohoe Foundation, could be a blueprint for "four or five" more next winter all across Down. Social Slashers founder Shay Deegan said he would like to see four or five of these camps running next winter all across Down That might sound ambitious, but Deegan said he is seeing growing demand first hand. He has also been involved with introducing hurling into Saul â a club better known for its football offering. "In Saul we've 10-15 coaches in the three age groups we have at present â nursery, under 8.5 and under 10.5 and there's 100 kids taking part in those teams," Deegan said. "Next year we'll have U12 and the year after U14." Deirdre Killen from St Kevin's Camogie club said "it's great" that children are developing new skills when in winter "a lot of them would have been sitting at home" Deirdre Killen from St Kevin's Camogie club is also seeing growing demand. "We started in 2021 as camogie only, and are relatively new," she said. "We've put a lot of work into the juveniles and I think with girls â over the winter maybe a lot of them would have been sitting at home, so it's great that they are here developing new skills. "We hope to add hurling at some point as well." Oisin (right) also plays gaelic but enjoys hurling as well For some of the kids getting hurl on ball in Saintfield, their motivations for getting out of the house include everything from making friends, to dealing with school stress. According to Clara, who plays for Darragh Cross near Saintfield, the camp is "a break from SEAG" - the looming transfer test used as an entry point by many grammar schools. "It helps me unwind and gets me away from all the papers and the tests." This was a sentiment in some ways shared by Matthew, who isn't connected to a team. "Coming here means that when I go to secondary school I might know more people," he said. Connie from Carryduff said she likes to see her friends while playing camogie Connie from Carryduff agrees that friendships drive participation. "I like to see my friends and it keeps me fit." Others are seeking to try new things, improve skills or simply play. Jan said: "I thought I'd try a new sport." Ella (left) said she just likes "running around hitting a ball" Ella plays for St Kevin's and said: "I just like running around hitting a ball." Ethan from Kilclief said: "I was good before, but now I'm better." The goal of camps like this is to attract, develop and retain young players â Oisin from Saul explains it perfectly: "I play gaelic but I enjoy hurley as well." If forced to make a choice at this age he said: "I'd have to have a think about it." Headline: Alliance will engage 'without prejudice' on Irish unity - Long
Body: "We're not there to be advocates for change or advocates for the status quo", said Ms Long Alliance leader Naomi Long has said that her party will "engage respectfully" in any conversations about Northern Ireland's future. It comes after the tÃ¡naiste (Irish deputy prime minister) Simon Harris asked some political parties in Northern Ireland, including unionists, for feedback on Fine Gael's so-called "blueprint" on Irish unity. The Ulster Unionist leader, Jon Burrows, called the plans "political suicide". Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson called it a "crass attempt to outbid Fine Gael's rivals in Dublin". Long said Alliance would take part "without prejudice to how we might decide the constitutional question". Speaking on Sunday Politics , Long said: "We're not there to be advocates for change or advocates for the status quo, but we will engage constructively." She said Harris was also looking at how both parts of the island could work better together "even if there isn't unity", adding that Northern Ireland's financial challenges made that discussion necessary. Simon Harris said "no one political party owns the discussion about the future of this island" Among their proposals, Fine Gael has suggested appointing a junior minister in the Irish government for "north south relations". The party also published a document by an economist who works as an adviser to Harris, where it was suggested that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about â¬3bn (Â£2.5bn) to â¬25bn (Â£20.8) to the Irish exchequer. In a letter accompanying the proposals, he said: "No one political party owns the discussion about the future of this island, nor should any one party seek to determine its outcome. "That is why I believe this must be an inclusive conversation, informed by evidence, respectful of different constitutional perspectives and grounded firmly in the Good Friday Agreement and the principle of consent," he wrote. "I am writing to all major political parties across this island - I hope you will receive this report in the constructive and respectful spirit in which it is intended," he wrote in the letter, seen by BBC News NI. His proposals came days after the taoiseach (Irish prime minister), leader of Fianna FÃ¡il, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland . Robinson, DUP leader, said: "Simon Harris and the Irish Government can find time to write to unionists about breaking up the United Kingdom. "They should find time to answer the ICRIR's (Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery's) questions about the Irish Republic's role in Troubles' deaths." He said if Harris "wants to build trust with unionists" he "can start by answering" letters sent to Dublin by Sir Declan Morgan, the ICRIR's chief commissioner and give the Omagh [bomb] families a public inquiry in the republic". The SDLP leader, Claire Hanna, welcomed the letter and said: "A New Ireland must mean precisely that: an opportunity to build a new nation, not simply reverse partition". "Crucially, that preparation must also deliver a better Northern Ireland along the way, with stronger public services, greater economic opportunity and better living standards for communities," she added. Burrows, UUP leader, called Fine Gael's plans a "constitutional pet project" and said that his party "will not participate in any project designed to dismantle the United Kingdom". "We have no interest in a republican invitation to commit political suicide." He added that his party will work with everyone to promote prosperity: "We are willing partners in practical cooperation that benefits everyone. Simon Harris should focus on building trust and respecting our place in the union." In a response to Harris, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said his "courtship techniques are somewhat lacking". "My message to you is simple: you run your part of this island as your people wish, but butt out of the affairs and future of those pleased to be part of a larger and more prosperous United Kingdom, upon whose defence capacity you are glad to rely," Allister added. Headline: 'Portaferry's win was for Ciara' - Turpin
Body: Portaferry's win came two weeks after the passing of Ciara Mageean On a day when the Portaferry community came together to rally behind their hurlers, thoughts of the late Ciara Mageean were not far away. Before the St Patrick's men scored a 1-25 to 2-14 win over Dunloy to book their place in the Ulster Club SHC final on Saturday, 28 November, a minute's silence took place in honour of an icon of Irish sport who lost her battle with cancer two weeks ago, aged 34. Mageean, who played camogie for Portaferry as a youngster, also helped out with the club's senior hurlers in recent times. Finn Turpin, who scored six points from play in Portaferry's win on Sunday, spoke of what the late two-time Olympian meant to all within the Portaferry community and hopes their win can help put a smile on the faces of the town. "It's been a tough few weeks for the club, as a community and in town," Turpin told BBC Sport NI's Odhran Crumley after Sunday's win in Armagh. "That win was for her and hopefully her family can get a bit of joy out of that today because they did it for her. "Ciara, she was unbelievable. She was in with us the past few years, she sent us her expertise and what we could do. "It's unbelievable that we're back in an Ulster final and hopefully we can win it." Portaferry defeat Dunloy to reach Ulster final Portaferry manager Connor O'Prey echoed Turpin's sentiments, but rather than produce a one-off display to honour the Mageean family, he feels the ultimate tribute is by living up to the standards she set on the track and in life. "I think Daithi Sands summed it up really well , that we'll take our inspiration from how Ciara approached her journey to sport, and how then she approached her journey with her illness," he said. "We're a small community, we try and get behind each other as best we possibly can and no doubt Ciara's looking down on us a very proud Portaferry woman." Portaferry manager O'Prey was delighted with his side's work-rate Certainly, all in blue and gold will have been delighted by how their team booked a return to the final and a rematch against Slaughtneil, who have been their nemesis on the provincial stage. Portaferry battled for every ball, hunted in packs and brought an intensity Dunloy struggled with. When the Antrim champions began to get to grips with the challenge and narrow the gap to one with eight minutes to play, Portaferry got a slice of luck that has perhaps eluded them at this stage in the past as Tom McGrattan's shot dropped and evaded Ryan Elliott to roll into the net. There was no looking back from there and O'Prey is hopeful this level of performance can carry into the final as they seek the club's first provincial title since their maiden success in 2014. "It was a super performance from start to finish," O'Prey added. "The work-rate was top notch and everything we've been working on in training paid off. "They got a couple of soft goals. Yes, we got a soft goal towards the end to probably knock the stuffing out of them, but from start to finish, couldn't fault the work-rate from one to 15 and the subs who came on. "We'll take massive positives out of today. We know what Slaughtneil have to offer but this is a different Portaferry team. The belief, confidence and ability to get through games like today will stand to us."

Headline: Man injured in 'hate crime' stabbing
Body: The incident happened in the Cliftonpark Avenue area of Belfast A man has been taken to hospital after being stabbed in Belfast on Saturday morning. The incident happened in the Cliftonpark Avenue area between 07:30 and 07:45 GMT. Police understand the victim was out for a walk when three men confronted him. An altercation then ensued and the victim was stabbed in the chest. The attack is being treated as a hate crime by police. One suspect is described as wearing a tan, black and pink tracksuit. The second suspect was wearing a North Face tracksuit and the third suspect was described as significantly tall. The victim is being treated for injuries which are not life threatening. Police are appealing for anyone with information to contact them.

Headline: Traditional industries and AI: When old meets new
Body: Kukoon Rugs chief executive Paul Vallely says every department in his company uses AI "extensively" Carpet making may be one of the oldest skilled jobs in the world, but even this traditional industry has begun to adopt the most modern of technologies â Artificial Intelligence (AI). Kukoon Rugs is a family-owned firm that sells online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland. Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows the business to be more competitive, allowing him to scale up parts of the firm that he previously wouldn't have been able to. "I think every department uses it extensively, pretty much daily. That's from finance through to commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product." While acknowledging the history of his family's business in Newry, he believes technology like AI can only enhance it. "Rug making has been around for thousands of years, and has been around in this area for a long, long time. "The product itself maybe doesn't change too much, but every single bit of the process as to how we design and create the product, market it to the customer, and then get it to the customer, that's fundamentally changing. And that's through AI." Artificial Intelligence has often been accused of having a negative impact on creative industries , but Vallely says this isn't the case. "AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work." Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team". "I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more." Kukoon Rugs sell online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive. The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the industrial revolution in the 19th century. Nestled in the Sperrin Mountains just outside Limavady is Seating Matters which manufactures specialist clinical seating. Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street. For managing director Martin Tierney, AI has its strengths and weaknesses, but it is now an integrated part of his company's daily work. Seating Matters managing director Martin Tierney says AI has revolutionised many of the back office functions "AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says. While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions. "On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there." Tierney says he likens the power of AI to that of a calculator. "You know, way back in the 1800s, and everything's done on pen and paper. No one had a calculator, and they thought, what if a calculator comes along and replaces all the accountants? "Well, that didn't happen. It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again. "AI is doing that again, but doing it on steroids." He says implementing AI across his business has not only improved productivity it has also led to new jobs being created. "We have more team members now than we did before, and AI is allowing those people to be more productive, to do more intelligent work, and less of the boring work. "No one likes going upstairs and into a filing cabinet to pull out a drawer and flick through your paper. You know that's not a good use of anyone's time." Seating Matters' products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software. "You just chat to it, say: 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'" While staff at Seating Matters are encouraged to use AI to help solve problems and speed up some of the more mundane tasks, they do operate within guardrails. Tierney likens it to driving with the handbrake on. "We're not putting patient information or financial information on here. "Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone." There's more on this story on the BBC's The View . Headline: Residents return home as suspicious object is taken away
Body: Residents at the centre of an overnight security alert in Ballymena, County Antrim, have been allowed to return home. Police said they were called to the Moorfields Road area on Friday morning following reports of a suspicious object. A search was carried out and a cordon put in place near the main road between Ballymena and Moorfields village. Two houses were evacuated. Members of the public, including drivers, were advised to avoid the area. Ammunition Technical Officers (ATO) attended the scene and the object, along with a number of additional items, was removed for forensic examination on Saturday afternoon. Inspector McGillan said: "We would like to thank those who were evacuated during the public safety operation for their patience. "They are now able to return to their homes, with all roads reopened in the area. "We also want to reassure the local community that there is no ongoing risk to the public." Earlier, DUP councillor William McCaughey asked people "not to speculate" as to the reasons behind the security alert. He urged the public to give police "the space and time that they certainly need to finish off this investigation" and appealed to anyone with information to come forward. Headline: Eleanor Donaldson given supervision order and placed on sex offenders' register
Body: Eleanor Donaldson, pictured here in September 2024 The wife of former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson has been placed under a supervision order for three years. Appearing before Newry Crown Court, via video link, for the first time since 2025, a tearful Eleanor Donaldson was also told she would be placed on the sex offenders' register for five years. When Judge Paul Ramsey asked if she understood that she would be subjected to a supervision treatment order (STO), she nodded her head and said "yes". Eleanor Donaldson could not be given a prison sentence as she faced a 'trial of the facts' as it was determined she was medically unfit for a criminal trial. She was found to have done the acts in relation to five charges, including four of aiding and abetting her husband's offending. Last month Jeffrey Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims , including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions. His wife has also applied to appeal the verdict from her trial of the facts. The 60-year-old appeared on screen in the court for less than three minutes, dressed in black with two large cuts on her forehead. She kept her eyes closed and head tilted down throughout. While her husband was sentenced to 15 years in prison, Judge Paul Ramsey had four options available to him in dealing with Eleanor Donaldson under mental health legislation. They included a hospital order, a guardianship order, absolute discharge or a supervision treatment order (STO). It was on the advice of two medical experts that an STO was the "most appropriate" of those options. Neither the prosecution nor defence objected to this. Judge Ramsey explained to Donaldson the terms of her STO â including that she would be under the supervision of a social worker within the Craigavon Community Mental Health Team, with whom she would be required to keep in touch, attend appointments and submit to any required treatment. Before the judge addressed Donaldson at the conclusion of the 30-minute hearing, prosecution barrister Rosemary Walsh KC referred to victim impact statements, that spoke of anger and questions of why the offending happened. Walsh KC said "pain permeated" through the statements of the two victims in the case. A trial of the facts is an option that is open to prosecutors if a court determines that a person is unfit to stand trial and criminal proceedings cannot go ahead. It takes the place of a criminal trial and is used to determine whether an accused committed the acts alleged. It cannot result in a conviction, but if the court is not satisfied that the accused committed the acts alleged, then he/she will be acquitted. The procedure is allowed for in legislation by Article 49A of the Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986. The mechanism is not used often but one high-profile example was in the trial of former IRA leader Ivor Bell in 2019. Earlier this year, Stormont justice and health ministers launched a joint review of the legal framework on trials of the facts in the wake of the Donaldson trial. Various politicians expressed support for the review. In a statement provided by the Department of Justice at the time, a spokesperson said "the ministers of justice and health are aware of the public concern and interest in the legal and procedural framework on trials of the facts in Northern Ireland". Former senior judge, Sir John Gillen, will carry out the review .

Headline: Body found in Lough Erne formally identified as Carrie Mullane
Body: Carrie Mullane (Noonan) had been missing since she arrived in Enniskillen on 10 October A body recovered from Lough Erne in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, has been formally identified as murdered woman Carrie Mullane (Noonan), police have confirmed. The 39-year-old from Limerick went missing in Enniskillen on 10 October. A body was recovered from the lough on 9 November and a formal identification process took place. Michael Lynch, 35, of Trasna Park in Enniskillen, has been charged with her murder and preventing lawful burial. His mother Mary Lynch, of the same address, has been charged with withholding information from police. His nephew Kenneth Lynch, also of Trasna Park, was charged with withholding information and encouraging or assisting in the commission of an offence. Police said their "thoughts are with Carrie's family at this sad time, as they come to terms with their loss".

Headline: Man who transported Omagh bomb was an MI5 and Garda agent, inquiry told
Body: The 1998 Omagh bomb killed 29 people, including a woman pregnant with twins The detective who led the Omagh bombing investigation has told an inquiry that he believes the man who transported the bomb was an agent for both the UK security services agency MI5 and the gardaÃ­ (Irish police). Retired Ch Supt Norman Baxter gave evidence to the Omagh Bombing Inquiry on Friday. He said: "As I went through the investigation it became very apparent that an individual was a Garda agent. It became apparent that in one operation there was a high potential that he was jointly handled by the security services." Baxter said he also believed that intelligence services were aware of the bombers' activity before they carried out the Omagh bombing. Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the Real IRA bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles. Baxter said he "formed the view that Special Branch, the security service and GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters) knew prior to 15 August 1998 the identities of some if not all of the suspects involved in the Omagh bomb". "The amount of information they knew I can't assess but yes, they knew." Baxter told the hearing that there was "significant effort by the Garda to prevent their activities being uncovered". "The Irish government and particularly the Ministry of Justice, have failed to investigate the Garda operations in the period leading up to Omagh, he added saying he was "saddened" by the "absolute failure" of the police investigation. "It is very sad. I am very proud of my time in the police but this was a failure at leadership, a failure at government level. Baxter said that the Omagh bombers had "free rein" from the middle of 1997 and the authorities allowed that to continue "The Republic and United Kingdom, all the apparatus they had, all the technology, their source network, these people should have been stopped and there has to be a reason why that didn't happen." Baxter also alleged that the gardaÃ­ allowed bombs to be taken across the border into Northern Ireland and that "the government of Ireland had information that a bombing was imminent". He also told the inquiry about a test run of the bomb route was taken by two "known dissidents" the day before the bombing. Senior counsel to the inquiry Paul Greaney KC, who was reading from Baxter's report, outlined how the detective noted a vehicle bearing the registration number of Seamus McKenna's car was recorded entering the Thiepval military base in Lisburn in September 1997. It then re-emerged on the system on 12 August 1998 and was recorded crossing the border at Aughnacloy on 14 August, the day before the bombing. Another vehicle also travelled the route, it was linked to Liam Campbell, he continued. When asked about the report, Baxter added: "It might have been a test run in terms of timing how long it took from the origins of the bomb to the target site." Baxter said he concluded that the Omagh bombers had "free rein" from the middle of 1997 and the authorities allowed that to continue. "There were a number of opportunities in the past when this group could have been disrupted," he said. He said he felt guilt about having knowledge of the bombing that he was unable to share with the victims and families. "I sat for many meetings with various victims' groups and I listened to what they were saying about Garda collusion. "I listened to what they were saying about Garda knowledge, but Irish government cover ups, and everything in the north and I knew they were telling the truth but legally I couldn't tell them, and I have to pay great respect to the effort that has brought the victims to this place where there is a legal forum where the truth can be told without fear of prosecution. "It's such a tragedy that we are here when this could have been resolved." Later, Baxter said known members of the Provisional IRA were seen with the car the bomb was in at a GAA club in County Armagh the night before the bombing. The Provisional IRA were on a ceasefire when the attack happened. "Probably difficult for the families to hear this but that was the major missed opportunity that senior republican figures were with the bomb the night before and they did nothing." He said the bomb was in a maroon Vauxhall Cavalier at Cullaville GAA club where "senior members of the republican movement" saw the car. "There were members of the Provisional IRA present with the bomb the night before. "That is the only definitive point that I know that the bomb could have been stopped in Northern Ireland. "If one of those people had have called the security forces and said X and X, both are identified, have a bomb because they knew there was a bomb, there was a discussion about the bomb, and they could have stopped it. "They could have saved the lives in Omagh." He also said that he cannot rule out that there was a second informer involved in the bombing. Baxter said the investigation was resourced well. Michael Gallagher, whose son Aiden was killed in the 1998 Real IRA attack, helped to found the Omagh Support and Self-Help Group Michael Gallagher, whose son Aiden was killed in the 1998 Real IRA attack, said Baxter's evidence was "difficult to listen to, but hugely important to hear". "I always believed the MI5's job was to provide internal security in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and to hear that the intelligence was not being shared, that was a huge shock," he added. He said it was not an "easy thing to say publicly things that are not going to be liked by your former bosses". Gallagher added that it was "hugely important that I put a long fight in for the public inquiry, because otherwise Norman [Baxter] and others would have taken that information to their grave with them". "He's a hugely honourable person... he delivered that testimony in a way that nobody else could." Three days after the attack, the Real IRA released a statement claiming responsibility for the explosion. It apologised to "civilian" victims and said its targets had been commercial. No-one has been convicted of carrying out the murders by a criminal court. In 2009, Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all ordered to pay a total of Â£1.6m in damages to the relatives, but appeals against the ruling delayed the compensation process. A fifth man, Seamus McKenna, was found not liable in the civil action and later died in a roofing accident in 2013. Headline: Levelling the playing field for those with disabilities
Body: Ethan says his daughter Aoibheann's confidence has grown since she took up playing boccia Growing up Aoibheann struggled to find a sports club to join. Now, she plays boccia, a game designed for those with disabilities, and is beating several of her classmates. Dad Ethan said the "opportunity for Aoibheann to have something of her own to do, that's just for her" makes such a difference. The pair were taking part in a Junior Paralympic fun day aimed at showcasing several sports for those with a physical disability. It allows young people to try out different sports such as powerchair football, wheelchair tennis, wheelchair cycling, golf and boccia. Ethan says that out of the sports available boccia is "probably her favourite", adding it gives Aoibheann confidence. In boccia, the aim is for each team or individual to throw their ball closest to the white ball. It is similar to pÃ©tanque. "There isn't a lot of clubs and social gatherings that Aoibheann has an opportunity to take part in," he says. But boccia also allows her to play with her sisters, as they can use manual wheelchairs to take part in the game. "They all play together so it's a level playing field and it's just lovely to see them playing together where Aoibheann is fully involved in the game and it's not kind of segregated in anyway." Aoibheann says taking part in the Junior Paralympic fun day makes her happy: "I like meeting new people and doing the sports." Macie enjoyed trying out curling and boccia Macie has cerebral palsy and uses a walker and then a powerchair for whenever she gets tired. She had "a lot of fun" trying Boccia and curling, but says boccia was her favourite "just because I like throwing things". Her mum Laura says opportunities like these are so important, adding that since Macie goes to a mainstream school, she can "feel that wee bit of a difference", especially when it comes to sport. "It's so good to find somewhere to bring Macie to where she's included and she doesn't feel different. "You can tell by her wee face she absolutely loves it, and it's so good because every hour it changes to something different, so she gets to use the equipment. "The volunteers here are just lovely. They're so kind and make sure everybody gets involved and everybody feels comfortable." Gemma was at the fun day for the first time with her daughter. Naoise has Cerebral Palsy, left hemiplegia which affects the left side of her body - meaning "she just has to work a little bit harder whenever she's doing things with coordination". "It's really good to introduce Naoise to sports for all abilities and see what she can achieve," Gemma says. "We do try and do sports in school and try and do a little bit outside of school, so it's good for friendships and communication and fun most of all." After trying out tennis, archery, basketball and boccia, Naoise says: "I'm a sports girl." Her favourite was archery "because my mummy loves it". Thomas had a go at the powerchair football as well as wheelchair tennis Eight-year-old Thomas had a go at power-chair football. "It was a wee bit tricky," he says about pushing the ball with the powerchair. Dad Barry says it is very good to see Thomas, and his other children, getting to see try the different sports available. "It's brilliant...he can't do obviously all fully abled sports, so all this kind of craic is great." He says it has built his son's confidence. Ellie Kirk, who represents Ulster and Ireland, showed young children how to play wheelchair tennis Ellie Kirk represents Ireland and Ulster in wheelchair tennis competitions and says it's important to introduce young people to sports. "I think definitely when you're not as able bodied as well, it's really hard to get into sport." At the event the 17-year-old showed young children how to play wheelchair tennis. "I would never have been able to play tennis myself with my condition and to know that I am able to play tennis because of the equal playing field wheelchair tennis brings is really important. "I think when you find a sport that kind of levels out the playing field for everyone, it's really important and it's really good and it develops people's own confidence in themselves." She says it's important to have an outlet of sports for every child, no matter what their ability is. Niall Irwin is the regional development officer for Disability Sport NI Around 15 young people - along with their family members - attended the Junior Paralympic fun day at Antrim Forum this month, organised by Disability Sport NI. Niall Irwin, the regional development officer for Disability Sport NI, says it introduces people to different sports they might not have seen before. "It's really good for these kids, who maybe do have a physical disability, to do lots of different activities with their siblings." He adds, that since covid, participation in these kinds of sports has dropped. "We're just trying to get that up again, the participation levels. That's our job to try and get more people participating in sport at recreational and elite level. "So there is those pathways there, but it's just up to us to try and show that there is that possibility for people." Headline: Musical charts life of Derry nun on path to sainthood
Body: Lilly (left) and Ellen-Mary are two of the stars of the musical A musical about nun Clare Crockett, whose cause for sainthood is being considered by the Catholic Church, has been performed in her home city for the first time. A Famous Nun: Clare Crockett - A Life Brought to the Stage opened at St Columb's Hall in Londonderry on Friday. A second performance takes place on Saturday, on what would have been Sister Clare's 44th birthday. Sr Clare died in 2016 when an earthquake caused the collapse of the school in Ecuador where she was teaching music. "We're really looking forward to it and it's amazing that they've brought it to the town," her sister Shauna Gill, told BBC Radio Foyle . Written and composed by members of the Servant Sisters of the Home of the Mother, Sr Clare's religious order, the production was first performed last summer to a crowd of around 2,000 young people at a Marian Eucharistic event in Spain. Sr Rachel Maria, who helped bring the production to Derry, said it had been warmly received. "It was really well done, really beautiful, and it helped I think a lot of the young people really to have a think about their own personal relationship with the Lord.," she said. "We just thought it would be a beautiful thing to bring the musical here to Ireland, especially as this year marked the 10th anniversary of Sr Clare's death." Ellen-Mary took to the stage on Friday for the first time as Sr Clare The Derry performances are the first time A Famous Nun is being performed in English. It features a cast of women aged between 15 and 21 who have come from across the island of Ireland to perform. Sr Rachel, who knew the Derry nun in the years before her death, said it looks at Sr Clare's life before she became a nun. It also examines "how she encountered God and how she struggled to respond to her vocation", she added. Lilly plays the role of Sr Clare's conscience, guiding the audience through her thoughts and feelings "Sr Clare was very special, very talented," Sr Rachel said. "I have lots of memories of her just joking around, being funny, bringing joy to everyone around her. She was great craic, as they say." Following the Derry shows, the musical will be performed in the US. A mural of Sr Clare was painted in the Brandywell area of Derry to mark the 10th anniversary of her death Sr Crockett was born in Derry in 1982 and grew up in the city's Brandywell area. As a teenager she dreamed of becoming an actress. While on a chance trip to Priego in central Spain in 2000, she attended a Catholic pilgrimage and later said she felt called by God. That led her to join the Servant Sisters of the Home of the Mother. She entered the order at 18, going on to work with young people in Spain, the US and Ecuador. In April 2016, she was killed when an earthquake caused the collapse of a school where she was teaching music in Ecuador. Since her death, her story has attracted followers around the world. In 2025, the Catholic Church declared her a "Servant of God" , the first formal stage in the process that can lead to sainthood. Shauna Gill said her sister used to joke that she could be a "famous nun" Gill said the musical's cast for the St Columb's Hall shows were performing it "with such love". "They're just so excited to be doing it and they just love learning about Sr Clare and about her life." Her sister, she said, was finally "getting her name on the stage the way she always wanted". Gill said her sister had at times wanted to be "rich and famous" but had also wanted to be a nun. The musical opened on Friday with an audience of schoolchildren from across the north west Sr Clare, she said, would joke that maybe she could be a famous nun. "And sure that's her - not in the way we wanted but I'm sure she'd be very proud and happy," she said. Sr Clare is played by Ellen-Mary, while her conscience is portrayed by Lilly. Their performances explore Clareâs journey from a rebellious teenager, who found herself lost in a life of constant partying, to discovering her faith. Faye (left), Sophie (right) and teacher Zoe McFadden (centre) were among the audience to see the first show in Derry Among the audience were pupils Faye and Sophie from Scoil Mhuire Buncrana in County Donegal. "I knew a bit about Sr Clare beforehand, from what we had learned in Religion in school, but I definitely learned so much more after seeing the show and finding out about everything she went through," said Faye. Sophie said she loved learning about Sr Clare's life. She added: "I think her story shows that even if you take a wrong path, you can always find your way back, and I really enjoyed how they showed that on stage." Headline: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw me
Body: Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made her life "hell" at times As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates. At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it. Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years. As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable". "Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said. Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts". "I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down. Charlie didn't tell her parents about the severity of her condition for years The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness. Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions. Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years. The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times". But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years. It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits". If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery. But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age. Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety". "It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon." That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment. Charlie wants to raise awareness of the condition A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience. Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities. What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17. "I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said. "It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied. "It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus." McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case. Niall McGonigle was inspired to become a surgeon after his experience with a pectus deformity "There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said. "If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services. "But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead." McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding. Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions. She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister. "I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said. Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it. A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow. It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years. One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards. It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity. Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood. In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum". It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery". "The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically." Vacuum bell therapy is a non-surgical treatment that works best for younger people Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition. Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term. "If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future." Headline: Laughter and learning at BBC Children in Need-backed homework club
Body: Caitlin McAlinden teaches at Ledley Hall Boys and Girls Club In a community hall in east Belfast, chatter and laughter fills the air as children play pool, draw cartoons and finish schoolwork with friends. This is Ledley Hall Boys and Girls Club, which runs an after-school homework group with the help of BBC Children in Need. "It's a safe space for them," says Caitlin McAlinden. She is a special needs teacher but also gives each afternoon from Monday to Thursday to working as a part-time teacher at the homework club - and says it is of big benefit to the area. The centre has running since 1942, providing services and activities for the local community. For the past three years, with funding from BBC Children in Need , external , the centre has been able to help children up to the age of 15 with their homework, four days a week. About 45 children are registered, with between 10 and 30 attending each day. Children go to the club for a variety of reasons: their parents are still in work; they come for support with their homework; or just to spend time with their friends. The homework club is one of about 100 projects in Northern Ireland supported by BBC Children in Need "They benefit from it being in an informal environment, which works for a lot of young people who maybe don't like being in school a whole lot," says senior youth worker Michelle Fullerton. "It provides support for parents who either don't have the confidence to do homework or are at work. "They come home from work and the homework's already done and it's been supervised by someone who is a teacher." Ledley Hall received a three-year grant of about Â£34,000 in 2023, funding the salary of a part-time teacher and a classroom assistant to provide a homework club. It is one of about 100 projects in Northern Ireland that BBC Children in Need supports with Â£5.5m of funding, reaching more than 25,000 children and young people. This year's appeal on Friday aims to raise millions more pounds to help organisations like Ledley Hall carry on their work. Fullerton says the club would not be possible without the help of BBC Children in Need. "We charge 50p, and that's a nominal fee, but if parents were paying to have support for their kids after school to complete homework by someone who's a teacher it would cost a lot more," she says. She says educational statistics in the area are "really poor", adding: "This is our attempt to try and bring up the educational standards of the young people." Children benefit both academically and socially from the club, says Caitlin McAlinden The children who go to the homework club are pupils at nearby schools. "They know what the rules are about how we work in here and I think just having that safe space for them to come," she says. "They know that [we are here] if they need food, if they need support, if they need someone to talk to, if they just want somewhere to come and see their friends." The children benefit both academically and socially from the club, says McAlinden, and the need for groups like it is "huge" in areas such as east Belfast. "If we don't get our funding... then where do the kids go?" she asks. "They make friends from other schools, they get to maybe make friends with people in their school who they wouldn't usually talk to or anything like that." Holly Hamilton, Connor Phillips and Pudsey Bear will host this year's BBC Children in Need 2026 in Northern Ireland, filmed at St Teresa's Youth Centre in Belfast. You catch watch it on BBC One Northern Ireland and BBC iPlayer at 15:50 GMT on Sunday 15 November. The UK-wide show started at 19:00 GMT on Friday.

Headline: McDaid's Bakery announces £1.6m facility expansion
Body: U-Bake, known also as McDaid's Bakery, is undertaking the investment with support from Invest Northern Ireland's Agri-Food Investment Initiative (AFII) Londonderry-based bakery manufacturer U-Bake, known as McDaid's Bakery, is investing Â£1.6m in its Skeoge industrial estate facility, creating 15 new jobs and increasing production capacity. U-Bake is undertaking the investment with support from Invest Northern Ireland's Agri-Food Investment Initiative (AFII). The project will see the introduction of a new high-speed production line for high-volume products, robotic packing technology and increased freezing capacity. U-Bake is a fourth-generation family-owned business which manufactures fresh and frozen bakery products for food service, retail and wholesale customers across Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland and Scotland. The investment, which will receive about Â£210,000 in support from Invest NI, is expected to improve manufacturing productivity, reduce changeovers and downtime between production runs, and increase overall efficiency and output. Managing director John McDaid said growing demand, particularly in the Irish food-service sector, had highlighted the need to increase production capacity. "It is the first step in our long-term growth plans, enabling us to meet demand in Ireland while preparing to attract new customers across Britain and Europe." Headline: Man left 'traumatised' after racist attack
Body: The man says the attackers damaged one of his legs and also smashed the windshield of a friend's car A man who had his leg injured in a racially-motivated attack has described the ordeal as incredibly traumatic. The man, who wishes to remain anonymous, said that both he and a woman were chatting when they were both subjected to racial abuse before being attacked by a group of men, one of whom was armed with a baton. Police are treating three assaults and criminal damage in the Waterside area of Londonderry on Sunday night as racially-motivated hate crimes and believe they may be linked. Supt Sinead McIldowney said there was "no place in our city for this shameful type of behaviour". Speaking to BBC News NI, the man said he was now afraid to go out following the attack. "I got back from work as a carer and I was going to play video games down at my friend's place, so I was about to cross at the traffic lights. "My sister [his friend] was driving after coming back from work, so she parked by the side of Bond Street. As it had been a while since we had seen each other, we wanted to catch up and were having a laugh." He said the men approached them and asked where they were from and why they were laughing before shouting racial abuse and attacking his friend's car. "They just started hitting my sister's [friend's] car windscreen and, because she was a lady, I couldn't run on my own. I couldn't just leave her stuck there because I was scared they could probably open a door. They were already punching her through the window. "So, when she drove off, I was about to escape, but five of them blocked the entrance. You know, it's just a one-way entrance, so five of them just blocked it and surrounded me. They were trying to hit me, so I was trying to guard my head... The next thing I felt was this 'bam' on my knee with, like, a metal rod." He said the man tried to force him to the ground during the beating but he managed to escape and sought refuge in a friend's house before calling the police. "I feel traumatised, both physically and mentally drained," he said. "I can be going down the street tomorrow now and I see like three people gathered, I would be scared. "Even when I was at the hospital I couldn't sleep well because if I was sleeping and I just heard voices, I just keep thinking maybe they are coming for me again." The sister of the woman, who does not wish to be named in order to protect her identity, said her sister was punched in the back and that the attackers also struck her car, smashing the windscreen. She said her sister had been deeply traumatised by the ordeal. "My sister was punched and then they hit the windscreen, because she was already screaming, her mouth was open and when they hit the windscreen some of the glass particles went into her mouth." She said her sister managed to get back into her car and drive away but has been left very shaken. She said she could not understand why those responsible for the attack had targeted her siblings. "We are not troubling anyone and they were picked on because of their colour and it doesn't make any sense. "They just picked out random people going about their day. It's sickening." She added that her sister had been living and working in Derry since 2021, and described the city as home. The police said the incident occurred at about 21:00 GMT on Sunday when the woman stopped her vehicle near Dales Corner. Police said she was punched and the windscreen of her vehicle was smashed during the incident. At about 21:20, they said a man was reportedly confronted by a number of males as he walked along the Bond Street and Dales Corner area before being struck to the lower body with an iron bar. A third incident was then reported at about 21:30, when another man was allegedly assaulted inside licensed premises in the area after he managed to escape and get to safety. GaÃ«lle Gormley from the North West Migrants' Forum described the attacks as 'horrific' GaÃ«lle Gormley, from the North West Migrants' Forum, described the attacks as "disgraceful and horrific". Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme she said violence directed against anyone based on race, skin colour or ethnicity had "no place in this country and in this era". She said the attacks must have "felt like a horror movie" for the victim and perpetrators of racist violence should face harsher punishments. "The law must be changed and adapted," she said. "It must punish more severely any hate action and also online hate posts, targeting people of different skin colour, origins and ethnicity." Sinn FÃ©in councillor Christopher Jackson called the attacks "sickening". "Our minority ethnic communities make a valuable contribution to our city and they are welcomed by the vast majority of people of Derry and that needs to continue," Jackson said. "But we need those responsible for these sickening actions to be held accountable." Body: Around 400 letters were found discarded on at Mobouy Road - one of two discoveries in Derry last week Police have completed their inquiry into how hundreds of unopened letters came to be dumped on a country road near Londonderry. Mark H Durkan says the discovery of the letters is "absolutely shocking" Many of the letters discovered at Mobouy Road on 4 November were bundled together with elastic bands and included correspondence from health trusts and banks to addresses in the Derry area. A further bundle of mail â containing around 200 letters - was found by a woman who had stopped at Victoria Road to take a photograph of the sunset over the River Foyle on 5 November Speaking last week Durkan described the discovery of the letters as "absolutely shocking". Headline: Omagh inquiry told gardaí warned RUC of car bomb crossing border
Body: The explosion killed 29 people, including a woman pregnant with twins The Omagh Bombing Inquiry has heard that the gardaÃ­ (Irish police) warned the RUC that a car bomb was to cross the border the day before the atrocity. As the hearing resumed in Belfast on Monday, lead counsel for the inquiry Paul Greaney KC outlined the evidence to be heard over the week as he summarised the evidence to come from former chief superintendent Norman Baxter. It heard that in response to the warning, the RUC carried out a "proactive police operation" in Newry, which they believed might be the route to a target. The Omagh bomb crossed over from the Republic into Northern Ireland at Aughnacloy in County Tyrone. Greaney KC said that some of that evidence would "need further inquiries". Retired Chief Supt Norman Baxter, who was the senior investigating officer in charge of the investigation, is due to give evidence in the coming days. On Monday, the Inquiry was told how, on the 14 August 1998, during a police meeting, the regional head of special branch South interrupted with an "urgent" issue. The officer said that the GardaÃ­ "believed a car bomb was coming north the following day", which was the day the Omagh bomb exploded killing 29 people, including a woman pregnant with twins. The unnamed officer said he had no details of the vehicle and did not know where the target was. However, in the subsequent discussion between the deputy assistant chief constable and an Officer 1, Lisburn, Portadown and Banbridge were identified as targets. The inquiry heard that the evidence from Baxter will describe how "a proactive police operation" was set up in Newry to "protect the Banbridge corridor". Greaney KC pointed out that this was not linked to evidence about a warning call received by Finner Army Camp in County Donegal the day before the bombing. Previously, hard evidence said that the caller, using a public phone at a bar in Bundoran, said "Omagh Omagh Omagh". The hearing heard a statement given by the army officer who took the call. In it he said it was dismissed as a "prank call" and the content of the call wasn't escalated to An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na or the Northern Ireland security services. Greaney KC also pointed out that there was no evidence from the GardaÃ­ or the RUC of ever having received that warning. The inquiry's legal team said that this evidence would give rise to questions which "could not be answered" in this chapter of the inquiry. He said that the inquiry's legal team had written to the Irish Government for further information in relation to this and it hopes to return to the issue in a later stage. Sworn in to give evidence on Monday was the former Chief Constable Sir Ronnie Flanagan. He said the fact that the people responsible for the bombing have not been brought to justice is a "source of the most deep regret to me". Sir Ronnie was taken through his career in the police which included working for Special Branch and being trained by the FBI in America. He was Chief Constable of the RUC, then later the PSNI as the force was reformed. Sir Ronnie told the inquiry that he recognised that, as chief constable, he was "responsible for the police's actions and inactions" in the investigations into the bombing. He told the inquiry that in his line of his work, he was exposed on a firsthand basis to the death and devastation, but the aftermath of the Omagh bomb was "especially shocking". Sir Ronnie said that, while he didn't recall saying that he "would leave no stone unturned" in finding those responsible for the bombing, he believes the RUC and PSNI investigation into the bombing "kept faith" with that promise. He said he had a "direct and keen" involvement in the investigation but admitted that he was unaware of the winding down of the investigation 6 weeks after the bombing. Sir Ronnie added that he did not know of a further reduction in resources two months later. He also said that he was "unaware of the challenges" in the relationship between the RUC and An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na as any problems "hadn't been brought to his attention". Sir Ronnie said he shared a "warm relationship" with Patrick Byrne, the Garda Commissioner, and could have brought it up but it was never raised with him. He also said he had not heard of any of the issues with the operations of the police administration system - HOLMES - the use of which has been heavily criticised during the Inquiry. Sir Ronnie said he accepts that there were "grave shortcomings" with how the police used HOLMES in the Omagh Bombing Inquiry. Sir Ronnie rejected Baroness Nuala O'Loan's recollection of a meeting between them. It happened at Hillsborough Castle in 2001 ahead of the publication of a report by Baroness O'Loan in her role as Police Ombudsman which was highly critical of the RUC's investigations into the bombing. "The whole character of the meeting ascribed by the Baroness is not the character of the meeting as I recollect." During her evidence Baroness O'Loan said that Sir Ronnie had told her that the publication of the report "would destroy the peace process". "I never felt that for a second and would never have said that". When asked if he was "angry and upset" at the meeting, the former Chief Constable said: "I don't think so. Upset, disappointed, shocked even". He also apologised for his "crass" response to the Ombudsman's report in an interview after its publication. "I regretted it instantly. It was crass and insensitive and too many of my own police families have been afflicted by that curse and I was so ashamed if I had caused hurt to families similarly affected." Sir Ronnie Flanagan said that he there was "no reluctance" by him to cooperate with the police ombudsman report and the tension outlined by Baroness O'Loan was over access to "secret material". "I think the access afforded to the ombudsman's team was unprecedented and what was being requested here was the ability to actually remove secret material from Police HQ. I wasn't happy for the material to be removed". Headline: Harris asks politicians for feedback on Irish unity 'blueprint'
Body: Harris' party Fine Gael published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity last week The tÃ¡naiste (Irish deputy prime minister) has asked some political parties in Northern Ireland and the republic for feedback on his party's so-called "blueprint" on Irish unity. Simon Harris' party Fine Gael published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity last week. He has now asked some party leaders in Northern Ireland for their views, including unionist parties. It comes days after the taoiseach (Irish prime minister), leader of Fianna FÃ¡il, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his own thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland . Among their proposals, Fine Gael has suggested appointing a junior minister in the Irish government for "north south relations". The party also published a document by an economist who works as an adviser to Harris, where it was suggested that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about â¬3bn (Â£2.5bn) to â¬25bn (Â£20.8) to the Irish exchequer. Harris has asked for "views" on the plans as well as areas where there may be a need for "further consideration". In a letter accompanying the proposals, he said: "No one political party owns the discussion about the future of this island, nor should any one party seek to determine its outcome. "That is why I believe this must be an inclusive conversation, informed by evidence, respectful of different constitutional perspectives and grounded firmly in the Good Friday Agreement and the principle of consent," he wrote. The party leaders who have been sent the letter in Northern Ireland are: Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson, Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister and Alliance leader Naomi Long. The party leaders who were sent the letter in the republic are: the taoiseach, Sinn FÃ©in leader Mary Lou McDonald, AontÃº leader Peadar TÃ³ibÃ­n, Labour party leader Ivana Bacik, Social Democrat acting leader Cian O'Callaghan, Independent Ireland leader Michael Collins, Green Party leader Roderic O'Gorman and Richard Boyd-Barrett of People Before Profit. "There will be differing views and difficult conversations, but complexity cannot become an excuse for inaction," wrote Harris. "I would very much welcome your views on the proposals and the wider issues raised, including areas where we might identify common ground or where further consideration is required. "I am writing to all major political parties across this island - I hope you will receive this report in the constructive and respectful spirit in which it is intended," he wrote in the letter, seen by BBC News NI. The SDLP leader Claire Hanna welcomed the letter and said "a New Ireland must mean precisely that: an opportunity to build a new nation, not simply reverse partition". "Crucially, that preparation must also deliver a better Northern Ireland along the way, with stronger public services, greater economic opportunity and better living standards for communities," she added. The leader of the UUP, Jon Burrows, called Fine Gael's plans a "constitutional pet project" and said that his party "will not participate in any project designed to dismantle the United Kingdom". "We have no interest in a republican invitation to commit political suicide." He added that his party will work with everyone to promote prosperity: "We are willing partners in practical cooperation that benefits everyone. Simon Harris should focus on building trust and respecting our place in the Union." Headline: Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Body: Taoiseach MicheÃ¡l Martin said "our European security environment has been fundamentally reshaped by Russia's brutal war" Europe's security has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war in Ukraine, Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin has told 50 leaders who are in Dublin for a summit. The Republic of Ireland is chairing the EU presidency until the end of the year and its main showpiece events, the European Political Community (EPC) and informal meeting of the European Council, are taking place this week. The country has been preparing for the events for months, with gardaÃ­ (Irish police) carrying out the largest security and policing operation in the history of the state. Attendees include Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and heads of state across the EU. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) will support its Irish counterparts in policing the summit. Even though officers from abroad will not be involved in frontline policing, gardaÃ­ said they are being supported by the PSNI, police from Latvia and Portugal and other international law enforcement agencies. Parts of Dublin city centre are closed off and there has been widespread traffic disruption in city in recent days. The state has also been dealing with a number of bomb threats, which have included hoaxes, on schools and media organisations in recent days. MicheÃ¡l Martin welcomes Moldova's President Maia Sandu at the European Political Community summit On Thursday, about 50 international leaders gathered at the Convention Centre in Dublin for a meeting of the EPC. They included European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Nato chief Mark Rutte. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to attend as part of his efforts to form closer ties with Europe. Martin told those attending on Thursday that "our European security environment has been fundamentally reshaped by Russia's brutal war of aggression in Ukraine". "What is happening in Ukraine goes against all of our values and all of what we stand for." MicheÃ¡l Martin (R) welcomes Prince Albert II of Monaco at the ninth European Political Community (EPC) Summit in Dublin Addressing leaders at the EPC, Zelensky said Europe needs to "pay attention" when there is talk about security guarantees. He said: "Europe really needs to pay attention when the Americans and Russians talk about this, it's not just about security guarantees for Ukraine in fact it's more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia and we find this approach a bit strange." He said Russian President Vladimir Putin's wars are about "his attitude toward others not some kind of permanent confrontation with Europe that was impossible to avoid". Ukraine, AI and hybrid threats across Europe are expected to dominate key EU meetings in Dublin on Thursday and Friday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is in Dublin The EPC is an informal forum for European leaders to hold political and strategic discussions on issues of shared concern. It was set up in 2022 after Russian's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and meets twice a year. The theme of the summit in Dublin is "Europe â strong, secure, and connected". Leaders will discuss economic security, Ukraine, hybrid activity in Europe and democratic resilience. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms to describe non-military methods, for example cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. French President Emmanuel Macron speaks to the media It is believed there will be a "handful" of no-shows, including Turkey as it is hosting the COP31 climate summit. Earlier, Martin said that discussions for a European voice to represent the EU at US meetings with Russia on ending the war will "happen on the margins" of the summit. He said Europe is "united" and "doesn't believe in war", and is "appalled" by the "Russian invasion of Ukraine". "Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters. Martin added that he hopes there is progress amid talks with US envoy and Russia. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are flying to Dublin on Thursday to update Zelensky on talks with Putin. The two leaders met in Dublin on Wednesday. There will also be a meeting of a Friends of Ukraine group, co-hosted by the UK and Ukraine on the margins of the EU meeting, where Zelensky is expected to brief the leaders. It is understood that meeting is not part of the EU meetings happening this week. On Friday, a meeting of the informal European Council will take place, also in the Convention Centre. Headline: Ireland and Ukraine considering co-production of unmanned drones
Body: The taoiseach described Russia's actions in Ukraine as "barbarous" and "vile" Ireland's Taoiseach (prime minister) and the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have indicated that they may cooperate on the production of unmanned drones. The two leaders met in Dublin on Wednesday ahead of a meeting of European leaders on Thursday. Speaking at a press conference, Zelensky indicated a willingness to work with the Irish government in the co-production of drones. The taoiseach said work is ongoing between the two sides given Ukraine's expertise on drone technology and that the Irish are considering agreeing a memorandum with Ukraine on the issue. Martin said unmanned drones could benefit the Republic of Ireland in terms of maritime security. Headline: Aberdeen appoint Liechtenstein's Frick as head coach
Body: Mario Frick has been announced as the new head coach of Aberdeen, taking over from the sacked Stephen Robinson to become the club's fourth manager in 2026. Capped 125 times as a striker for Liechtenstein, the 52-year-old was last in charge at Luzern, leaving the Swiss club in the summer after five years. He follows Robinson, Peter Leven and Jimmy Thelin in leading the side in this calendar year and will take charge for the first time against Scottish Premiership bottom side Kilmarnock on Saturday. "Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team," said Pittodrie chief executive Adrian Bevington. "He was also exceptionally well regarded by the many people across the game we consulted during the process, and the board was unanimous in its belief that he is the right person to lead Aberdeen forward." Former Motherwell and St Mirren boss Robinson was dismissed on 9 November, with Aberdeen second bottom of the table and having lost four games in a row in all competitions. 'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign' Latest Aberdeen news, analysis and fan views Watch new Aberdeen boss Frick score against Scotland in September 2010 Frick, who also managed Vaduz in the Swiss Super League, will be assisted by Roman Matter and is the seventh permanent manager since Dave Cormack took control of the club in November 2019. As a player, his former clubs include FC Basel, FC Zurich, St. Gallen and Grasshopper, while his 16 international goals make him Liechtenstein's all-time top scorer. "Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play," added sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel. "He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment. "We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I'm convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact." Frick got Vaduz promoted in 2020 before helping Luzern avoid relegation following his move there in 2021. The next again year he guided them to a fourth-placed finish and European qualification, although they were knocked out of Conference League qualifying by Lee Johnson's Hibernian. Aberdeen say Frick "has built a strong reputation for transforming teams, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players during his coaching career". Hibs striker Thibault Klidje and current Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Muller both played under him.
