Headline: Final whistle a blessing as Scotland edge dull Test against Australia
Body: Tries: M Fagerson, Dempsey Con: Russell Pens: Russell Scotland edged a dull Nations Championship encounter against Australia at Murrayfield, a game that brought rugby fans crashing back down to earth after the brilliance of France's win against South Africa on Friday and the jaw-dropping wonder of Wales beating the All Blacks on Saturday. Matt Fagerson, an impressive juggernaut, and Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland, Harry Potter got one for Australia, all in the first half hour. We waited another 47 minutes before Finn Russell banged over a penalty to make it 15-5. Max Jorgensen's converted try with seconds remaining narrowed the gap. A little flurry at the end of a hugely disappointing, attritional Test. Apart from isolated moments, it was a game of turnovers, missed opportunities and a terrible absence of anything resembling class. Compliment the grunt, butâ¦ It was chaos. Every breakdown was a lottery, an ugly dogfight. The longer it went on, the more Australia became serial offenders. That game-clinching penalty from Russell was on the back of multiple Wallaby breakdown offences. There were some seriously creative and pacy players out there but we hardly saw them. Precious little fast ball, precious little buzz from two teams who are well capable of excitement. Neither attack sparked never mind fired. The final whistle came as something of a blessing. Nations Championship: Scotland hang on for scrappy win over Australia - reaction Scotland suffered a blow even before the first whistle when captain Sione Tuipulotu was ruled out with a knee injury. Tom Jordan replaced him in the midfield and Rory Darge took over the leadership role. Both are stand-up operators, but any Scotland team without Tuipulotu is a weaker outfit. Huge question marks hung over the pair before the start - Scotland having been blown away by the All Blacks last weekend as the Wallabies went down in flames at Twickenham. Depending on how it went - Scotland were warm favourites - this was going to be some sort of redemption for one and all sorts of retribution for the other. All of that was in the balance right until the end. Scotland now move above Wales into fourth in the northern hemisphere table, but their lack of a bonus point on Sunday could cost them. They'll take the win, though. In the scrappiest encounter, the home side drew first blood. They owned the ball in the early moments, wasted one opportunity to score off a lineout maul, but then struck at the second time of asking. Finn Russell started it all with a lovely grubber that had Carter Gordon in trouble. It eventually led to a scrum and men over for Scotland. An isolated Fagerson on the right touchline had been calling for it for what must have felt like an age to him. When it did come, he had the easiest job of sliding over. Russell missed the conversion, but he missed something - or somebody - else just after and it proved costly. One of the many things holding Scotland back is how easy they are to score against - and here was another case for the prosecution. Rob Valetini and Gordon helped put the Wallabies on the front foot but, when they swept to the left touchline, the whole thing might have come to a halt had Russell made his tackle on Potter. He didn't - and the wing ran on to finish with class. Scotland thought they'd scored just after but the ball was deemed out of play - a marginal call - when Kyle Steyn mid-air volleyed to Graham, who touched down. Jack Dempsey's try gave Scotland a lead that they would never cede Another injury befell the Scots midway through the opening half when Scott Cummings was replaced by Max Williamson. The Scots scored their second try soon after. Too much power in the phases and Dempsey drove over against the nation he once represented. Russell made it 12-5 and it stayed that way despite Billy Pollard being driven over from a lineout maul. The Wallabies were done for obstruction. The pre-match billing talked about a thrilling try-fest but it was low-key and error-strewn. You expected Scotland to bring their usual ambition but, if anything, they were conservative. The Wallabies tried to play more rugby, but their game was riddled with mistakes, too. It was chaos out there for large parts of it. Bodies everywhere. A million big hits. Just an awful absence of quality. Paris on Friday, this was not. Cardiff on Sunday, it was not either. Pollard got binned for going high on Blair Kinghorn early in the new half but Scotland could do nothing in those precious 10 minutes. They butchered a big opportunity from a close-range lineout - losing their own throw - then won it back and got turned over at the breakdown. Scotland played much of the second half in Aussie territory but only had those three Russell points to show for it. Just as well. Australia scored in the last seconds when Jorgensen ran in after a beautiful offload from Jeremy Williams. Ben Donaldson put over the conversion to make it 15-12. Too little, too late for the visitors. Just. Scotland survived. After two days of Nations Championship rugby that will live long in the memory, this one will have faded in the time it took fans to reach the car park. 'When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style'

Headline: Police watchdog issues workload warning as high-level case load soars
Body: Laura Paton has been Scotland's Police Investigations and Review Commissioner since April last year Scotland's policing commissioner has warned that high-level investigations, including deaths in custody, are taking longer due to a soaring case load. Laura Paton, the Police Investigations and Review Commissioner (Pirc), said the record level of demand was jeopardising her ability to help deliver justice on behalf of communities. Latest figures show the organisation is managing 191 investigations, including 49 deaths. This year Pirc has also had its highest ever number of simultaneous death investigations. Paton said the increase in demand was "beyond our control" and added there was a "limit to what we alone can achieve". Pirc's annual report covers the 12 months to 31 March, during which Pirc began 41 death investigations - a 128% increase from 18 in the 2024-25 period. This includes seven investigations into domestic abuse-related homicides and suicides. Senior police officer suspended over bullying claims Eleven officers convicted of crimes still on police payroll, chief confirms Police watchdog to probe 'unexplained' custody death The watchdog has carried out a strategic review to assess demand against resources while also setting a new future direction. But Paton said wider action was now needed as Pirc was experiencing a "sustained increase in demand". She added: "We will take all reasonable steps to work efficiently, prioritise serious investigations, and maintain the quality of those investigations, however there is a limit to what we alone can achieve. "In the absence of external intervention - such as a reduction in demand, additional funding or the delayed expansion of our statutory functions - a further deterioration in the timeliness of our investigations is inevitable." "This means that we will not be able to deliver the service that the public rightly expects; this will affect bereaved families and complainers, as well as confidence in police accountability and policing itself." The organisation also said it was expecting an increase in the public seeking assistance from Pirc as Police Scotland worked through a significant backlog of police complaints. Paton said this was of "considerable concern". She added: "Not only are members of the public waiting too long but the number of those who remain dissatisfied with the response and apply to Pirc for a review has increased. "We have also noted delays in Police Scotland's implementation of the recommendations arising from our reviews. "This concerning trend is being closely monitored." Police Scotland and the Scottish government have been approached for comment.

Headline: Why 'inspiring' Van Gaal influences Scotland head coach Pocognoli
Body: Sebastien Pocognoli played for Louis van Gaal at AZ Alkmaar Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli says he draws on the influence of legendary manager Louis van Gaal in his own coaching career. The Belgian played under the Dutchman during their time at AZ Alkmaar, a special period for Pocognoli during which he won the Eredivisie title in 2009. Van Gaal also previously took charge of the Netherlands, and now that he has moved into international football himself, the Scotland boss reflected on the 75-year-old's influence. "I take a lot from all of my gaffers, but probably he was the one with the most experience," Pocognoli told BBC Scotland. "I was very young and you know in that moment he had all the Barcelona young players between his hands, also Ajax players. "The way that he treats the young players in a direct way, honest way and hard way was for me really inspiring in my daily job now. "I was lucky to have a lot of good coaches but he was probably the most that impressed me day by day, and I felt progress under him. "That I think is the best thing for players as a feeling." Progress is exactly what every Scotland fan is yearning for. Under Steve Clarke, the amount of that very commodity plateaued. Years in the international wilderness were expelled with two European Championships and a World Cup appearance, but they were punctuated by disappointing results and dour tactics. Pocognoli's arrival signified not only a new era, but a new approach, formation, selection and outlook. It has been far from straightforward for the Belgian as he approaches 100 days in charge next week. Five games, two wins over North Macedonia, a draw in Slovenia and two humbling defeats mark his tenure so far. Within it, a fresh system and injection of different faces to offer a break from the norm, but also plenty signs that a transformation will not be an immediate reality. Scotland's failings in front of goal has remained, while it is clear the Scots are still getting to grips with a back three, albeit with enforced changes in personnel. "Everything in life takes time to build if you want to achieve something," said Pocognoli. Scotland to play with bravery and courage - Pocognoli You are Scotland boss Pocognoli - what would you do? Six goals to go - will McGinn catch Dalglish & Law? "So we know that in the performance world everything goes faster and quicker, but we have an objective and we know that we have to go through the up and down and the good moments. At the end I hope that all this experience can make us stronger. "I don't ask the players to be patient, it's just to believe in what we are doing." Pocognoli acknowledges he's not had much opportunity to immerse himself in Scottish culture after taking his first foray into international management. A wander around Glasgow is about all he's managed. And any further exploring will have to wait until after Monday's Nations League test in St Gallen. Finishing in the top two of their group seems a tall order for Scotland, who are requiring a win and snookers in Slovenia. It seems progression to the next Euros will instead roll on to the qualifying campaign next year. "We don't have the control of what will happen because Slovenia will decide," Pocognoli said. "But if we want to have a chance to go through to the group stage and to go to the play-offs we have to go with the bravery and try to play with courage and try to force something. "I don't believe that we are waiting for something then it will happen, so let's go through our quality and try to be aggressive and wait what happens in Slovenia." Headline: Shetland's first paramedic to retire after 38 years of island-hopping call outs
Body: Niall Bristow joined the ambulance service in the 1980s Before Niall Bristow joined the ambulance service in Shetland in 1988, the vehicles were driven by hospital porters and gardeners with no medical training. He initially trained as an ambulance technician, before becoming the isles' sole paramedic in 1992. Now there are 11 paramedics and six technicians serving the population of 23,000 on Shetland's 16 inhabited islands. And after a career which has even seen him feature in BBC TV shows like Shetland and Island Medics, Niall is retiring at the age of 61. Niall was part of a team of emergency workers in the 1990s There have been ambulances in Shetland since the mid-1970s. But before Niall joined the team, the service was run by men with manual jobs around the hospital. They drove patients to hospital but couldn't provide medical care. "A paramedic simply wasn't a thing", he said. Originally from Islay in the Inner Hebrides, Niall moved to Shetland at a young age. He worked for a bank for four years before joining the ambulance service. Niall said he was looking for a job that would keep him in Shetland, as he was in a "blossoming romance" and was keen to see how it developed. "I didn't quite know what I was getting myself in for," he admitted. Niall had no intention of pursuing a medical career but his girlfriend - now wife - showed him the job advert in a newspaper. Read more stories from the Northern Isles: Secondary school teacher to crofter - life on the UK's most remote island Forget the Mediterranean diet, I'm eating only food from Shetland for a month Britpop legends Ash take 'bit of a trek' to headline Shetland festival Niall said one of the big challenges of the job was Shetland's geography, as residents rely on a network of ferries to travel between islands. "A single job could take up to three or four hours," he said. Two large ambulances are stationed in Lerwick, Shetland's only town, and three smaller vehicles are based between the islands of Unst, Yell and Whalsay. Patients travelling from Unst - the most northerly inhabited place in the UK with a population of about 600 - to mainland Shetland have to take two short ferry trips. They are then transferred to a larger ambulance at the ferry terminal in Lerwick before the journey continues to the isles' Gilbert Bain Hospital. "These call-outs took up most of our day", Niall said. There was a white Christmas in Shetland in 1995 - but it caused widespread disruption One of the most memorable spells of his career was when heavy snow fell on Shetland in December 1995. It became known as the "Big Snaa" and left thousands of homes without power over Christmas and new year. Roads were impassable so Niall and his team were flown across the isles by the emergency helicopter. He said Shetland was brought to a standstill. "We were picking up pregnant women and taking them to hospital for scans," he recalled. Niall describes long call-outs because of Shetland's geography The size of Shetland meant that Niall frequently encountered a familiar face. "You were extremely likely to know someone on a call-out," he said. Niall also said he had lost count of the number of times people said they felt "reassured" because they knew him. The job also involved sharing tragic news with people he knew very well. "It was hard and there were many tears," he said But he said the positives of working in the community "far outweighed the tough challenges". Niall also praised his colleagues and family for helping him through the difficult times in his career. Niall celebrating retirement with his grandson Arthur Niall also highlighted some of the more surreal moments of being a paramedic, such as his appearance as an extra in the TV crime series Shetland . He said producers were intrigued by his team's "authentic uniforms", and it was an "exciting task" compared to his usual working days. Niall also featured in the BBC series Island Medics . After 38 years he said was "extremely proud" to be leaving the service in good hands. Niall told BBC Scotland News he was now looking forward to spending more time with his grandson, Arthur.

Headline: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
Body: Protesters marched down the Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres. Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament. The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe. The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit". Some demonstrators attended in eye-catching costume to draw attention to particular issues Innovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector". However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth". Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk. Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase. She was also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it was operational. Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need. "At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment. "The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed." AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves. At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW. But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world. The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies. The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild". Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all. "Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland." Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres Friends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres. She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland. "These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments. "There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well. "The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be." Headline: Fifteen taken to hospital after deliberate fire at Glasgow flats
Body: The fire service said four appliances were sent to the fire in Ibrox Police are treating a fire at a block of flats in Glasgow as deliberate. Four fire engines were sent to the four-storey building on Copland Road, in the Ibrox area, just after 17:00 on Friday after reports of a fire on the ground floor. Firefighters and paramedics initially said they were dealing with "multiple casualties" and police have now confirmed 15 people were taken to hospital as a precaution. The fire was extinguished and crews left the scene by 22:00. A number of windows remained open at the flats on Saturday The flats are next to Ibrox Subway station A section of Paisley Road West was closed while fire crews tackled the blaze. One image from the scene showed a firefighter up a ladder while at least two residents looked out from a first floor window. A Police Scotland spokesperson said the building was evacuated and added: "The fire is being treated as wilful and inquiries are ongoing."

Headline: I never thought I'd make it as an actor but now I'm up for a Bafta
Body: Scott Ellis Watson landed his first acting role in the hit film I Swear When Scott Ellis Watson dropped drama in school he could never have guessed he would one day be walking the red carpet as a nominee at the Scottish Baftas. The now 16-year-old thought acting was out of reach, and gave up the subject to focus on becoming a pilot, but after an acclaimed turn as the young John Davidson in the hit movie I Swear, he was rewarded with another prominent role in the movie adaptation of BBC drama Ghosts. Scott, from Bishopbriggs in East Dunbartonshire, tells BBC Scotland: "I just never thought that film acting was a career that I could have done, so I never really chased it. I didn't have that faith in myself." I never thought I'd make it as an actor but now I'm up for a Bafta I Swear tells the true story of John Davidson, a Galashiels boy who developed severe Tourette's Syndrome as a teenager and went on to become a vocal campaigner for his illness, winning an MBE in 2019 for his efforts. It was one of Scotland and the wider UK's most notable critical and commercial hits of 2025, and the accolades are still coming. After winning three awards at the national Baftas, it is also up for eight Scottish Baftas. In fact, all three nominees in the Best Actor category are from the film - including Scott. Describing himself as "flabbergasted" to be up for the honour, Scott has his kilt ready for the glamorous event in Glasgow on Sunday. The young actor said he felt a big responsibility to do justice to John Davidson's experience of being a teenager with Tourette's The role was Scott's first, but he initially sent his audition tape for a smaller part, a character called "Lad One". When the team received it just six weeks before filming was due to start, they asked him to come in and try out for young John. "I was like 'I've never done any acting before' and then I went in and got the role. Then I went on holiday for two weeks to Florida and I couldn't get a tan so I was wearing a cap and factor fifty, and I was sat in the shade." He spent his holiday on video calls with voice and movement coaches, and when he returned he had two weeks to "lock in", learn his lines, and how to imitate John's movements and tics. He and John worked "closely together" to get the portrayal right. He says he felt a huge sense of responsibility to John. Touchingly, afterwards John sent him a card, writing: "Thank you so much for being me so well in the film." "Everyone was working together, making sure we did it right. I think they called it a passion project - so rather than it being for cinemas it's for John and for awareness." Playing the part when he was just 13 years old also came with its own difficulties. Some of the words and phrases he had to shout out were embarrassing and inappropriate, particularly in one situation where he had to shout an explicit phrase to a female cast member around the same age. Scott made his acting debut in I Swear when he was just 13-years-old "I still had to shout at a girl my age, regardless of if I was acting or not it still felt uncomfortable. They said 'if you want to try something different then we can', and I was like 'no this is the way you want the story; I'll have to do it'." Instead, the team asked him to shout "chuck the stick" when rehearsing, and only used the real phrase when the cameras were rolling. Scott's next project gave him the chance to try something new. He starred in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House, which was released in October and debuted at number one in the UK and Ireland box office. His part, Jack Marsh, is a daring teenage ghost hunter whose body was taken over by a sleazy ghost after a sÃ©ance went awry. Scott says: "With I Swear, there was a lot of getting it right but with Ghosts there was a lot of creative freedom... I Swear is a serious drama with humour in it, whereas Ghosts is a comedy with a little bit of drama in it." More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland The 16-year-old plays the lead role in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House Scott has already landed his next role in All in the Same Boat - a comedy-drama based on the true story of the gay cruise ship stewards who worked alongside British troops aboard a requisitioned liner during the 1982 Falklands War. The film, which is set to get underway next year, will see Scott starring alongside the likes of Rupert Everett and Stephen Fry. With his career ahead of him, and an exciting night coming up at the Scottish Baftas, Scott has big ambitions but thinks I Swear might be a hard gig to beat: "It's touched so many people, and people still reach out to me to say how it has impacted them, and that's all I could ever ask for." Headline: Could street lights in Glasgow's dark lanes improve women's safety?
Body: Parts of some Glasgow lanes in the city centre are considered a safety risk On any given night, Glasgow's Sauchiehall Street is filled with a throng of people, from students going clubbing to people enjoying a pint. However, yards away from the pubs and clubs runs a dark, partially unlit lane where 167 crimes have occurred in the past five years, including four sexual assaults. Campaigners and locals say Sauchiehall Lane, and other dark and badly-lit alleys like it in the city centre, can be dangerous - especially for women. But efforts to improve the narrow side streets has stalled due to their piecemeal ownership - where dozens of separate landlords and businesses only have responsibility for very small parts of each lane. "Street lighting will not suddenly stop sexual violence, but it's basic safety and not something that we should be highlighting as a problem years after it's already been established as a problem," says Nicola Love, of Rape Crisis Scotland. Em Johnson believes parts of Sauchiehall Lane are dangerous Sauchiehall Lane is about half a mile long and it is owned by dozens of businesses or landlords. They only have responsibility for the area around their property. While some owners have made sure to have lighting, a walk through the lane at night shows parts in darkness. Two rapes were reported in the lane over the past two years, with the victims in both cases being women under 20. Em Johnson has lived in a flat overlooking part of Sauchiehall Lane since 2024. They contacted BBC Scotland News through Your Voice and said: "It's a very studenty area, there's a lot of places you'd go for a night out on Sauchiehall Street, and then you cut down the lane. "There's student housing around there, loads of international students, and you have young people who can be vulnerable, maybe having had a drink. "It is very dark at night - there are bits with some lights but other parts where there isn't. Sometimes I'll hear a scream and you're never sure what's happening, if it's just someone having a good time on a night out or if it's something serious." More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Other parts of the city centre have the same issue, such as West Regent Lane. Glasgow City Council has attempted to encourage lane owners to take further responsibility, but told BBC Scotland intervening any further faces "significant challenges" due to the piecemeal ownership. Christy Mearns, a councillor for the Anderston/City/Yorkhill ward, has been trying to make headway on the issue for years. "The council does not have the money to take on things that should be the responsibility of the owners themselves, but the problem is ownership of these lanes is very fragmented and disjointed," she says. "There does need to be more work done there, especially given a number of serious incidents there with young women. "These are important lanes for access, and security and safety issues arise as a result of that, so how can we facilitate private owners into doing more? But it is challenging, even just trying to get majority agreement among owners." The city council does take responsibility for some lighting within private lanes, but only "on a lamp, lantern and minor fault basis". "Something more significant, like rewiring, is out of scope for the council's remit," adds Mearns, who says this happened recently with West Regent Lane. "It would be costly and the council simply doesn't have the budget to take on that burden." Nicola Love, of Rape Crisis Scotland, says better public lighting is a basic requirement The city council previously stated in 2022 it was committed to " feminist town planning ". This is intended as a response to the way cities have been traditionally designed by men, ignoring things that would concern women in the process - such as a lack of lighting in public spaces. Love feels such a commitment requires actual action to be taken, not just words. "We know that women will purposely avoid badly lit and secluded areas because they do not feel safe, and that feels like such a step backwards. "There seems to be a tussle over who is responsible for it. Where it's a council, get to work. Where it's a private business, we should be thinking about ways that we can legally compel building owners to pull their weight. "I can't understand why building owners would rather pass the buck than work together to find a solution. It's such a simple ask from women and it shouldn't be so difficult to get this right for them." Mearns agrees with that, but feels it's impossible to "point the finger at any one person or agency". "Some owners may be absent or not occupying the properties in some cases. That also talks to another problem, which is the difficulty of having many absentee landlords. "There are very high value landlords in some of these spaces that clearly don't care very much." Parts of the lanes are lit, but piecemeal ownership means it is not consistent Issues with Glasgow's lanes are not new - in 2006 it was proposed to close some lanes at certain times using temporary barriers, to keep people on brightly lit main streets. Those plans came to nothing. A spokesperson for Glasgow City Council said the local authority is currently working with Police Scotland and the business community on ways to improve the situation. Police Scotland's Ch Supt Emma Croft said the force is striving "to deliver prevention and education, to enhance visibility and engagement and to improve support to women and girls within communities and to those who are sadly victims of crime." Some changes are in development. A recent council meeting saw an agreement that private lane toolkits - which help property owners work together on joint action regarding adjoining lanes - will "form the basis for a new framework for city centre lanes". Johnson hopes steps like that will take effect sooner rather than later. "I understand it's difficult to sort things like this. But sometimes it can feel like no-one cares about this." Headline: Ruins and restorations: New archive chronicles Scotland's castles
Body: The archive includes everything from already upgraded buildings to ruins like Caisteal Maol on the Isle of Skye The global fascination with Scotland's castles shows little sign of dimming. From Americans fulfilling a lifelong dream to TV star Alan Carr moving into his "turret era", interest in owning one has rarely been higher. For those of us with more modest budgets, the striking looks and stories behind these structures are an enduring attraction. Now a new archive hopes to provide a comprehensive, detailed and nationally-accessible picture of the condition of the nation's castles, their history and what their future might hold. Inside the Â£3.25m castle bought by Celebrity Traitors winner Alan Carr Alan Carr bought a Scottish castle. Could you? Richard Oram has just retired as professor of medieval and environmental history at Stirling University and is president of the Scottish Castles Association (SCA). He said Dorothy Walker, who previously chaired the group, pushed strongly for the creation of an archive and it is an idea he was happy to run with. Although there are other collections out there, he said none of them was "as ambitious or as comprehensive" as what they hope theirs can become. "It's not to be a sort of a closeted-away, academics-and-professionals-only type of thing," he explained. "This is intended to be nationally-accessible and community-supported. "It's something that can only really gain its maximum potential by working with other people around the country." The collection shows how properties like Aikwood Tower near Selkirk have developed Aikwood Tower is a grade A-listed traditional Peel Tower Barns Tower near Peebles is another property to have undergone some major changes The dusty pink tower dates back to the 15th Century Braemar Castle in Aberdeenshire was saved when the local community stepped in in 2007 In 2019, the community began a new Â£1.6m project to conserve Braemar Castle Kilmartin Castle north of Lochgilphead is another site to have been developed The site now operates as a luxury guesthouse It consists, primarily, of a series of unique images of the buildings which have been built up by a number of people over decades. "We're either charting the decline from a lived-in building into a ruin or the gradual climbing from being a ruin back into habitation or use," he said. "A lot of that kind of record doesn't survive in a place that most people can see it. "They either know the building as a pile of rubble or they know the building as a private house or something of that kind and they don't know how it got from one state into the other." Among the archive is the Alastair Maxwell-Irving collection of plans and drawings stretching right across the country from Dumfries and Galloway to the North Sea coast. Elsieshields Tower near Lockerbie is a 16th Century L-plan tower house "I think this is one of the really exciting things for the moment is there's this huge upsurge of interest in Scotland's castles," said Oram. "It's always been strong, it's always been a recognised part of Scotland's culture and heritage. "But there's now, once again, this fashion, particularly amongst North Americans, but not just North Americans, for acquiring and living in a romantic Scottish castle and a lot of restoration." Ballone Castle near Tarbert took about 10 years to restore for family living "Amongst the things that we're trying to do with the archive is also produce a body of evidence around what can feasibly be restored and what is actually beyond the point of return," explained Oram. He said that tied in with Historic Environment Scotland's discussions around "managed decline" and how to allow a building to deteriorate but still be visited if safe and record it appropriately for future generations. "The goal is something that gives us an up-to-the-minute, sound overview of the building as it is now with a good understanding of its historical development and the history behind that building," he explained. The archive captures sites like Findlater Castle in West Aberdeenshire He said that consisted of telling the story of the people who owned and developed it, but also how it had been adapted over time. "You've got places that are originally a 14th Century tower, for example, but they've been turned into really comfortable houses in the later 18th, 19th and 20th Centuries," he said. "So it's what's been compromised, what's been added, what of the original fabric remains." He said they hoped to "strip away a lot of the mythology" around some buildings and work with communities and organisations around the country to provide the best information possible. Midhope is another tower house near South Queensferry All of it will be available online and also, physically, at Stirling University - and Oram said it would tell the story of the castles as plainly and simply as possible. "It's to try and get away from some of the really starchy, confined, Secret Squirrel type of language that often descriptions of these buildings are wrapped up in," he said. A launch of the archive takes place at Dunbar Castle on Wednesday. "We're trying to really build interest and enthusiasm across the country," he said. "But I think the critically important thing for us is to really push and get a better understanding of our buildings, our national heritage. "It's something that we're hopeful will really be there to fire up the enthusiasm of the broader public and all the people that we know around the country that are absolutely passionate about castles." Headline: I'm a British Photography Award winner – I'm still worried about what comes next
Body: David Gilliver was nominated in the self portrait category for a photo called "What goes on inside your head?!" Award-winning photographer David Gilliver has built an international reputation from his playful miniature worlds, secured global commercial clients and collected some of the industry's most prestigious prizes. Despite being nominated in four categories at this year's British Photography Awards - winning one of them - the 47-year-old fears he may not be able to sustain a career behind the camera. He said if 2027 is like 2026, he may have to find a part-time job. His fears highlight the pressures facing even established artists, as consumers cut discretionary spending and art sales fall. Summer Vacation 2021 won the award during the Covid-19 lockdown Gilliver has been a mainstay at the British Photography Awards since the Covid-19 pandemic when his depiction of miniature swimmers on the pool-like lines of a medical mask impressed the judging panel. His latest nominations come after more than three decades behind the camera. His roots in professional photography go back to the late 1990s when he enrolled in a fine art photography degree at Glasgow's School of Art. It was during this time when he developed a passion for macro photography, a style using perspective to create amusing and striking images. His individual take on it involves miniature figurines, his "little people", positioned against true-to-size objects to create juxtaposed scenes. But after struggling to find sustained work, he "took the plunge" to find more stable employment and headed to the Channel Islands, where his sister lived. In 2001, he moved to Guernsey and found a role in the finance industry. "It was meant to last six months, but that turned into 14 years," he said. Though a more lucrative avenue at the time, the day job couldn't entirely overshadow his creative work. "My art practice [was] very much alive in the background," he said. "It was during my time on Guernsey that I became interested in light painting and night photography. "I started going out at night time and discovering the island under the cover of darkness, which no-one else seemed to be doing at the time, and documented Guernsey in a very unique manner." He began experimenting with light patterns while in Guernsey This was flipped on its head in 2012 when he herniated a disc in his spine while "swinging kettlebells around" at a fitness class. "It completely wrecked my lower back," he said. "I was in absolute agony. I could barely sit down." After years of surgery, physio appointments and several attempts to return to the office, he decided the pain was unbearable and he was forced into a life-changing decision â to drop the career and make photography pay while also raising a young daughter. "I just quite simply had to make it work," he said. A Mountain of Tea was nominated in the Macro category of this year's awards Over the next decade he hustled and honed his craft with a focus on the "little people" series and light photography in order to position himself in two niche areas of the art in a bid to make a living from it. In four of the last five years, he has won accolades at the British Photography Awards, being nominated in four categories at the 2026 ceremony. The competition now welcomes more than 40,000 entrants each year, with just 40 people receiving awards at the annual gala in central London's Royal Lancaster hotel. "When I was shortlisted for four this year, I was quite speechless actually, because normally it's just one or two images that you manage to sneak in," he said. Wine EMERGENCY!! was nominated in the food and drink category at the British Photography Awards 2026 A shoot with an international car company won the commercial award this year, but another highlight was being nominated in the food and drink category with an absurdist scene of miniature firefighters extracting juice from grapes to refill their wine bottle. "I had the cheek to enter that into the food and drink category alongside professional food photographers." This child-like playfulness has been part of why his style has been so successful, with Gilliver saying despite his years in the profession, his work is still only 10% technique and camera skills, and 90% creativity. "The strength of the work lies in the concepts and the silly ideas," he said. His unique style also often prompts others to ask "What goes on inside your head?", the title of his entry in this year's self-portrait category. It shows his little figurines playing, working and dancing around his head. David experimented with several self-portraits with himself and his "little people" But despite the awards, the industry is still tough in the current economic climate, Gilliver said. As people feel squeezed by inflation, he said he has to keep "extremely busy" to fill his schedule, doing everything from teaching workshops to writing books. "The problem with years like this year where it's a very nervous economy and people aren't spending as much, one of the first things people stop doing is buying art and that has been very evident," he said. "I mean, I'm probably over 60%, 70% down in terms of art sales, which is quite concerning. "My monthly workshops, they are probably at least 50% down as well." The awards have helped him to secure several commercial shoots with companies able to pay a larger sum than the average art buyer, but he isn't entirely sure what lies ahead. "Things feel like they're going well on paper, and there's not much further elbow room in terms of general improvement," he said. "I think that's where things are a little bit worrying." Despite this, he is determined to carry on. "I'm going to squeak by this year, I think, just." Another big commercial shoot is on the horizon and he hopes it could put 2027 on more stable footing. But unlike other artists who eventually quit to find a more stable profession behind a desk, Gilliver said his health leaves him with few alternatives. "If I don't make this work, I have nothing else to really fall back on," he said. Headline: Trouble at the top - the crisis of confidence in Scotland's NHS leaders
Body: The report detailed problems affecting Dr Gray's Hospital but it said management failings affected the whole region The verdict from Scotland's healthcare watchdog on NHS Grampian could hardly have been more damning. Major problems at Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, but deficiencies stretching across the whole region, a failure to learn from mistakes and "recurring patterns of harm". Thursday's report from Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) is more evidence that frontline NHS staff feel they are carrying the can for poor leadership by highly-paid, powerful people at the top of Scotland's health boards. Centre stage this time is chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight, who earns between Â£170,000 and Â£175,000 a year. She ordered this review, but does not escape blame. 'Dramatic action' needed after NHS Grampian leaders criticised in damning report - Swinney The report reveals she was forced into a humiliating apology earlier this year, for giving misleading information about a review into a patient's death during surgery. Not only did HIS find the investigation into the death was inadequate, it also found the chief executive then misled HIS by saying senior executives had not seen the review or signed it off. In fact, executive medical director Hugh Bishop had been sent the review, and had discussed it in a meeting, but claimed he had "no recollection" of this. Misinformation provided by Skaife-Knight to the watchdog caused "significant distress" to staff at lower levels, who felt the management had tried to shift the blame onto them. She apologised to both HIS and the affected staff, and took steps "intended to rebuild trust". Some of the people in senior positions at the time of the investigation. L-R: Laura Skaife-Knight, chief executive; Paul Bachoo, former acute medical director; Dr June Brown, former executive nurse director; Dr Adam Coldwells, former interim chief executive; Dr Hugh Farrow Bishop, former executive medical director HIS has described this as the most serious review it has ever had to undertake â and it details a pattern of management failure that goes beyond a single individual. Weak leadership across the whole of NHS Grampian led to failures in recruitment, in management, in governance. It highlights repeated failures to act on warnings about patient safety or to learn from mistakes. For now, the Health Secretary Angela Constance has said she is keeping faith in Skaife-Knight, saying "she has operated with candour" and "put her hands up when she made mistakes". Tell us about your experiences of health care with NHS Grampian Constance said almost half of the board had changed, a new chairperson was about to step in and she expected them to hold senior executives to account. With NHS Grampian already in special measures because of financial difficulties, further escalation is inevitable. The health secretary said she would update parliament next week on what further action the government will take. For now it is the north east of Scotland in the spotlight, but these are themes that will resonate with NHS staff right across the country. In July, emergency medicine consultants in Glasgow wrote to Health Improvement Scotland warning of a risk of "whole-system failure" and ongoing risks to patient safety. Health Secretary Angela Constance will update parliament next week on what further action the government will take The doctors said the situation in the emergency department at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital had deteriorated since an inspection in 2024. They, too, held health board executives responsible, noting staff had scored their confidence in leadership at 32/100 in a recent survey. They questioned the transparency of their chief executive, Prof Jann Gardner, claiming she encouraged them to engage with a 2025 independent review of culture and relationships, the results of which have never been published. NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde said it continued to address the issues raised and that a programme of improvement work was ongoing. Elsewhere, the chief executive of NHS Ayrshire and Arran also stepped down this year, after it suffered financial near-collapse No-one can doubt NHS bosses have a tough job but they are all paid generous six-figure salaries. Public perception around their performance will be a talking point for the government and MSPs as they move forward with plans announced in September to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two . There is a debate about whether this is the right move for patients, but there is also a question over whether huge structural changes can improve the accountability of NHS leadership or not.

Headline: Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King
Body: Andy Robertson is one of two centurions for Scotland men Andy Robertson says it gives him "goosebumps" any time he thinks about it. Friday at Hampden, North Macedonia the visitors, a 102nd cap to be won and, when it is, he'll be level in the pantheon with Sir Kenny Dalglish, the football man he loves more than any other. On Monday in St Gallen, Switzerland - all being well - Robertson will break the great man's record, a mark that has stood for 40 years. The Tottenham left-back is sitting in the boardroom at Queen's Park in the shadow of Hampden with a phone in his hand and eyes fixed on his 19-year-old self coming off the bench in Warsaw on 5 March, 2014. "Nervous, excited, living the dream, not knowing what road I was on," he smiles as he looks at the moment he takes his first touch in international football. "As I was going on, Gordon [Strachan, Scotland manager] said to me, 'remember why you're here, play like you play at Dundee United, don't play safe'. The first ball, when it came to me, I just drove forward about 30, 40 yards. "I had pretty much every emotion that day. My mum and dad were there. My brother. My aunt and uncle. My other uncle. There's a picture of me and my brother [Stephen] at the airport after the game. He had a big Poland hat on and a half-and-half scarf. He was well oiled by that point." Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia Robertson says he'd have laughed out loud had you told him then what lay ahead of him - two Premier Leagues, two League Cups, an FA Cup, a Champions League, a Super Cup, a Club World Cup, soon-to-be the most capped male Scottish players in history and, by a mile, the one with the most games as captain of the men's team. "I've never actually been confident," he says, which is a surprise admission given everything he's done. Maybe what he means is that he always had a quiet belief in his own ability but found that constantly questioning himself was who he was and who maybe who he still is. "I've always doubted myself and that's always got the best out of me. I've always tried to prove people wrong and prove myself wrong. The one thing I didn't do was look too far ahead. I always just lived in the here and now and that's served me well." In the room where he's talking there are a dozen normal chairs and away to the side, detached from the rest, is an elaborate seat. A high-backed, ornate, somewhat regal affair. It looks fit for a king and, given the history Robertson's about to make, maybe he should plonk himself in it. And that brings us back to the man whose record he's about to match and surpass. "There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," he says. "Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny. You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career "He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught. "Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain. "We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself." It's a lovely thing, that. Robertson, about to draw level with Dalglish, is only thinking about Dalglish. The depth of feeling comes tumbling out of him when he starts telling stories about what King Kenny means to his family and how he seemingly created a miracle by momentarily curing Robertson's beloved late grandfather's hearing. "I always remember my agent talking to me about the first time he met Liverpool," Robertson says of a time when he was still with Hull but about to move to Anfield. "He met the chief scout and sporting director and all of a sudden Kenny 'accidentally' walked into the room. It was 100% planned, I know it was planned. You can watch Tom English's interview with Andy Robertson on the BBC Scottish Football YouTube channel HERE , external "One of the things right at the top of the list for me was the fact [by joining Liverpool] I got to meet Kenny in person and I've actually got to have a relationship with him and his family, because his family are special. "My dad, in particular, has met people in football through me, but I've never seen him being starstruck by anyone apart from Kenny. "I always remember, we'd just beaten Barcelona 4-0 [in May, 2019] to qualify for my second Champions League final. My grandad was at the game and I managed to grab Kenny afterwards. I says, 'Kenny, would you mind coming in to see my grandad and my uncle? They would love to see you'. "Bear in mind his grandson's just qualified for another Champions League final and he basically barged me out of the way and shook Kenny's hand. "My grandad had hearing aids. He couldn't really hear much of us but he heard everything Kenny said, so it did open a lot of questions in the family as to how bad the ear problem was with my grandad. He's no longer with us but to see how happy he wasâ¦ Kenny was his hero." When Robertson moved to Liverpool for the hilariously small sum of Â£8m in 2017, his wife, Rachel, was expecting their first child. The Dalglishes, he says, helped so much that he could hardly ever repay them for their support and friendship. On the pitch and off, the transfer to Liverpool as a 23-year-old was the greatest move he could have possibly made. In reflective mood, on the cusp of Scottish football history, Robertson talks about his mother and father and his brother. "They're as proud of my brother as they are of me," he said. "The exact same, whatever achievements we have. But I think they're more proud of the men we've become. That was always most important for me. "Anyone who knows me, my family, my friends, I always want them to like the person first, the footballer second. Anyone that only wants to know me as the footballer, then I don't let them get too close but if they want to know me as the person first and foremost, then they're the people that are really in my close circle. "I've still got the same friends I went to nursery with at three years old. Three of my best friends." Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson Robertson hits 100 Scotland caps - but which other men make top 10? Robertson says he often thinks about the game in Scotland and whether young kids today are getting the kind of opportunities he got. "We talk about that - my story, John McGinn's story, Ryan Christie's story," Robertson said. "There'll be a hundred people going, 'I could have been that'. Football has a lot to do with ability and mentality, but also you need a little bit of luck as well. "It's about trying to protect the 15, 16, 17-year-olds just now and we all have a duty to help with that. We always want the young players to come in and I just love their energy, I love how excited they are. Findlay Curtis just bounces about all the time. "These are the kids that are going to bring the country forward. They're all sitting at the other end of the table playing games we don't even know about but it's great for us to sit back and go, 'OK, we're part of this squad, but when we leave, then hopefully Scotland will be in a good place." To Friday, then. A record-equaller but, to Robertson, this is no nostalgia trip. This is a game Scotland desperately want - and need - to win. He says they were a yard off it in all areas last time out against Slovenia. "Unacceptable," he recalled. "We didn't give our fans anything to shout about." He departs with fighting words about the desire within the squad to make amends. Out the door, down the corridor and onwards into history. Seconds later, he returns. "Forgot my washbag," he laughed. "Bet Kenny didn't have one of these!" Glasgow, Liverpool, Scotland - the ties that bind.

Headline: Scotland created Grand Theft Auto - is its video game industry still thriving?
Body: Grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled to launch on 19 November As the world waits for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in history, its origins can still be traced back to a group of young developers working in Dundee almost 30 years ago. The original GTA was built by Scottish studio DMA Design, laying the foundations for what would become one of the most successful video games franchises ever made. "It was entirely the work of a Scottish team, all novices, we had no games design degrees at that point," says Brian Baglow, who worked as a writer on the game. "The only people who believed in it were DMA Design. The publisher wanted to kill it," he says. DMA Design was officially renamed Rockstar North in 2002 Over the last three decades, the game has sold hundreds of millions of copies while DMA Design became Rockstar North, moving to Edinburgh, and employing more than 1,000 people. But while Rockstar is the superstar of Scotland's gaming industry, the story extends far beyond GTA. Chris van der Kuyl, who co-founded VIS Entertainment in the early 1990s, says Scotland's games industry is almost unrecognisable from the one he entered 30-odd years ago. "When we started out, people didn't think about Scotland at all," he says. "There were a few people dotted around, but the main people were DMA in Dundee." As the sector grew, more structured routes into games development began to emerge. Abertay University in Dundee launched the world's first computer games degree in 1997, helping establish a formal pathway into the industry which Van der Kuyl says created a flow of new talent which was crucial to the industry's growth. "Without a talent pipeline and new people coming into the industry, there would be no industry," he says. In 2005, van der Kuyl co-founded Dundee-based 4J Studios, which went on to have huge success adapting Minecraft for consoles such as Xbox and Playstation. He estimates that those console editions have sold about 70 million copies. "There's no way you'd ever be able to predict that level of success for anything," he says. 4J Studios developed seven distinct versions of Minecraft His company now employs 57 people, a fraction of the size of Rockstar North but still one of the biggest games firms in Scotland. Many of the other developers are small but still making a vital contribution to Scotland's reputation, van der Kuyl says. "You've got companies that are only two or three people doing quite interesting stuff as indie developers." he says. Scottish government figures show the number of games companies operating in Scotland was about 130 in 2024, up from just 15 in 2010. Over the same period, industry turnover grew from Â£38.1m to Â£339.7m. Van der Kuyl believes Scotland is now recognised internationally as one of the leading places to make games, comparing its reputation to established development hubs such as Sweden and the west coast of the United States. Glasgow-based Screen Burn is another of Scotland's most successful independent game studios, employing 27 staff. Formerly known as No Code, the studio earned a Bafta for Best British Game in 2020 with Observation, a sci-fi mystery that puts players in control of a space station's artificial intelligence. The studio has recently attracted attention for its latest release, Silent Hill: Townfall, a new instalment in one of the world's most popular horror game franchises. Rather than being handed an existing concept, the team pitched its own story, setting the game in a fictional Scottish town. Silent Hill: Townfall is set in the fictional village of St Amelia, inspired by St Monans in Fife Screen Burn co-founder Jon McKellan says the project gave the studio a rare opportunity to put its own mark on an established franchise. "This is our pitch, this was our story, we really put our stamp on it," he says. For McKellan, Screen Burn's success demonstrates the growing diversity of Scotland's games industry, which now includes both global giants and independent studios. But he says the dominance of Rockstar North can make it difficult for smaller companies to attract the same attention. McKellan describes Rockstar as "a massive, immovable object" within Scotland's games sector. "It's kind of like if you spend all your water on the one plant, you'll have one great tree and the rest of it will die out," he says. A scene from Silent Hill: Townfall in which a character faces a towering figure emerging through dense fog His own career reflects some of those challenges. After the Dundee studio where he landed his first job collapsed, McKellan says he had little choice but to leave Scotland to continue working in games. "There were no other opportunities in Scotland at the time, it was either Rockstar or move down south," he says. He spent five years in England before returning to Scotland to create his own studio. While Scotland's games industry has expanded significantly, McKellan says sustaining a studio remains a challenge. Unlike film and television, where work is often organised around individual productions, games companies often need to maintain teams through development cycles that can last several years, he says. "We have people on salary that work year in, year out, whereas film tends to be short bursts of work," McKellan says. McKellan says the biggest challenge is creating enough opportunities to sustain and grow studios in Scotland, with many graduates struggling to find work in the sector. He says Scotland already has the creative talent to compete internationally, but needs more opportunities to keep developers in the country. "We're maybe hiring one or two people a year, we can't absorb every graduate that's coming out." he says. For McKellan, Screen Burn's work on Silent Hill: Townfall shows what smaller Scottish studios can achieve when given that chance. "There's some really great talent in Scotland. If they're given the right opportunities, they can create a bit of a wave of cool content that people aren't expecting," he says. For Baglow, who worked on the original GTA and is now a leading voice in Scotland's games industry, the continued success of the franchise shows the strength of the sector. "The fact that not only has it achieved the success it has, but it's still being made here in Scotland, should be seen and championed as our biggest cultural export ever," he says. Baglow says the biggest challenge facing developers today is not making games, but finding players. With development tools becoming more widely available, more people and studios can create games than ever before, he says. While this has made development easier, it has also made competition for audiences increasingly intense. "The challenges facing developers is not making video games, it's now user acquisition, as in finding players," he says. Baglow says studios can find themselves needing a major commercial hit to survive. "That need for a breakout consumer hit, and if you don't get it, it kills your studio," he says. However, Baglow says that the expertise built within game studios - including user engagement, digital design and 3D visualisation - could be applied in other industries, ranging from healthcare and education to financial services. "Any sector that is struggling either to build engagement with a user, a consumer, a player, or needs to teach its staff and train its staff up, there's a role for video games in all of that," he says. For Baglow, Scotland's challenge is no longer proving it can create successful games, it is ensuring the industry has the investment and support needed to build on that success.

Headline: 'How am I meant to plan anything?' The frustration of a seven-month driving test backlog
Body: Megan Hart says long driving test waits have left her facing uncertainty as she prepares for the arrival of her new baby Megan Hart hoped learning to drive would make life easier before the arrival of her new baby. Instead, the 38-year-old has found herself caught in one of Scotland's longest driving test backlogs, with no guarantee she will be offered a practical test before her due date in April. "It's going to become impossible," she said. Megan lives in Arbroath where waiting times for tests reached almost seven months in October, making it the second-longest wait in the UK. Megan says passing her test would be hugely important to her family life She says passing her test is not just about convenience. Her eldest son has epilepsy and regularly attends medical appointments, while her partner often works away from home. Without a driving licence, she says getting her family where they need to be can be a struggle, especially with poor public transport links for families living outside Scotland's cities. "Transport here is awful, especially with the kids." What it's like being trapped in the driving test backlog? Megan first looked for a driving test in August and even bought a car so she could get extra practice, alongside her instructor-led lessons. As she was applying for a test at a remote test centre, she paid the test fee and was placed on the DVSA's "on hold" system, which is used to allocate test dates when none are immediately available to book. The uncertainty is also adding to the financial pressure, Megan says. She continues to pay for lessons despite having no indication of when she might be able to take her test - and worries about the prospect of having to wait months more if she does not pass first time. "I wouldn't even like to add up how much I've spent, to be honest," she said. The scale of the backlog in Arbroath has grown significantly in recent years. In October 2026, DVSA figures showed the median wait between booking and taking a practical driving test had reached 27.4 weeks, the second-longest in the UK behind Callander's 31.5 weeks. By contrast, learners in Inverness faced waits of just 3.9 weeks. The Arbroath figures have reduced slightly from the September peak of 29.9 weeks, which was close to the 30.7-week high recorded during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Waiting times have remained above 20 weeks for much of the past two years. Driving instructors say the official figures can understate the problem because they do not always account for the time learners spend waiting before they are even allocated a test date. Learning to drive is already expensive, even before the cost of talking extra lessons. The DVSA estimates most learners need about 45 hours of professional tuition before taking a test, costing more than Â£2,000 before test fees are added. Long waits can push costs even higher as learners continue paying for lessons to stay test-ready. For many learners, every additional week means more lesson fees, greater uncertainty and a longer wait for the opportunities that come with holding a driving licence. Among them is 17-year-old Ruby, also from Arbroath, who has been unable to secure a test date despite joining the waiting list in June. Ruby believes the delays are discouraging young people from learning to drive "A lot of my friends aren't wanting to do lessons because of how much it costs and how long the wait is," she said. Ruby said being unable to secure a test was delaying the freedom and flexibility she had hoped driving would bring. "I wouldn't have to rely on buses or my mum as much," she said. Driving instructor Matt says some learners are waiting far longer than official figures suggest Matt Smith, a driving instructor in Arbroath, said the delays were creating challenges for learners and instructors alike. "This is the worst I've seen the tests for a long time," he said. He said long waits force learners into difficult decisions about whether to continue paying for lessons, reduce the frequency of their tuition or stop altogether until a test becomes available. Matt said this affected him as an instructor as he wasn't able to take on new pupils while his bookings were full. "If I bring too many on I become bloated and then I can't accommodate all of the pupils I have," he said. "A pupil who learns very, very quick will have to spend more money continuing to do lessons which will stop skill-fade from happening to keep them test-ready." Matt said the published figures do not always reflect the true length of time learners wait for a test. "They advertise tests about 24 to 25 weeks away, but that doesn't include the 10 to 12 weeks that pupils are waiting to be given a test date," he said. He believes a shortage of examiners is at the heart of the problem. "The demand is great and that is not going to reduce, so the supply of examiners needs to increase," he said. "There are not enough examiners to match the demand of the pupils." A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was working to improve test capacity but Arbroath's waiting times could fluctuate because it operated as an outstation of Dundee, using a "book-to-hold" system rather than having permanent examiners based there. The DVSA said driving test waits remained high due to increased demand and changes in booking behaviour since the pandemic. It added that examiner numbers were now at their highest level in recent years and that recruitment was continuing, including in Dundee. According to the latest figures, driving test waiting times fell for the sixth consecutive month in October 2026. The DVSA said it was making progress in reducing waits nationally and remained committed to ensuring learners could access tests when they need them. "We know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," they said.

Headline: Dundee City Council faces £4.1m overspend this year
Body: Councillors will discuss the report at a meeting on Monday Dundee City Council is facing a projected overspend of more than Â£4m this year as the local authority attempts to save money. A new report , external has revealed that the council overspend in its general fund has risen by about Â£800,000 from last month's estimate. It means the council is expected to spend Â£4.1m more than it had budgeted for this year, with some savings failing to materialise and growing costs in other areas. The latest predictions come as the council faces having to find nearly Â£13m worth of savings next year. The council's latest financial report on its spending this year said councillors previously agreed Â£4.4m worth of savings by cutting 100 posts from budgets across various services. These savings were expected through a combination of voluntary retirements or redundancies and the non-filling of vacancies. However, Â£2.2m of those savings have yet to be achieved. Dundee bin collections and Christmas lights could face cuts Dundee councillors approve Â£21m Raac repair scheme While service reviews are ongoing, the report warns: "There remains a risk that some of these savings will not be delivered in full this financial year." To date, the council anticipates only Â£1.1m will be achieved, resulting in a shortfall of the same amount. The report also revealed that increasing demand and costs associated with third-party payments in the children's social work and early years services are putting financial pressure on the authority. Early years is projecting an overspend of Â£1.5m due to the "number of children and volume of hours of care that are currently being funded". Other areas of overspend at the authority include the council's corporate fleet with an overspend of Â£896,000 and unplanned repairs and maintenance works for council buildings. The report outlines a financial recovery plan to "ensure this position reduces", including only recruiting to vacant posts deemed essential and restricting overtime to essential areas only. Councillors will discuss the latest financial report on Monday. Story by local democracy reporter Liam Rutherford.
