Headline: Why is Scotland's housing shortage getting worse?
Body: It is three years since Scotland's largest cities declared "housing emergencies", followed months later by the nation as a whole . Since then, homelessness has hit record levels while the cost of renting or buying property has continued to rise. The solution to this crisis would appear straightforward - build more houses. But delivering this is more complicated, with responsibility falling to central and local government as well as to private housebuilders. Scottish ministers claim the country boasts the UK's highest rate of housebuilding , external but the pace is falling, and there are questions about whether the right homes are being built in the right places. So far, 13 Scottish councils have declared housing emergencies for a variety of reasons. They include rising pressure on homelessness services, high levels of people in temporary accommodation and a lack of affordable homes compared to lengthy waiting lists. Homelessness has increased to a record level , with Scottish government data showing , external more than 19,000 households in temporary accommodation paid for by councils - a 10% rise on the previous year. This includes 10,715 children living in temporary accommodation, such as a bedsit. A total of 35,000 households were assessed as being homeless or threatened with homelessness in 2025-26. As of March this year, there were more than 140,000 applications on council waiting lists for social housing. This figure does not include some large authorities like Glasgow which runs its social housing through housing associations, and has more than 6,000 live applications waiting. The overall social housing stock , external held by councils and housing associations has been rising since 2017 - the year after the Right to Buy scheme was abolished in Scotland - but has only recovered to its 2004 level. In March this year, there were 89,000 fewer social homes available than when the Scottish Parliament was reconvened in 1999 - despite a 9% rise in Scotland's population over the same period. While demand for social and affordable housing has been rising, the total number of homes actually being built has been falling. The housebuilding sector was only starting to recover from the 2008 financial crash when the Covid pandemic hit. In the 2025-26 financial year, a total of 17,640 new homes were completed according to Scottish government figures , external - the third year in a row where the figure had fallen. There is little prospect for an immediate improvement, as the number of new projects started over the last two years were the lowest since 2012-13. As to why this is happening, housebuilders point to a range of factors. The sector faces familiar problems with the cost of doing business, with construction materials particularly vulnerable to inflationary shocks like that which followed the war in Ukraine in 2022. Industry bodies also complain about a lack of suitable land , external earmarked for building, and say it takes too long for planning permission to be given to new developments. Red tape is also a concern. Homes For Scotland - which represents about 200 housebuilding firms - says the "regulatory burden being imposed by government" over recent years has added tens of thousands of pounds to the cost of a new-build home. They note that Chancellor John Healey promised in his UK budget not to make major changes to building regulations for the rest of the parliamentary term. Recent examples in Scotland include a levy to address unsafe cladding on tall buildings, new rules requiring "climate-friendly" heat sources and better energy efficiency. Scottish Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News that ministers were alive to the concerns of housebuilders, but that these standards helped reduce energy bills and improved housing for disabled people. The rate of new build homes being completed has slowed in recent years There is a notable disparity in rates of building in different parts of Scotland, with construction particularly concentrated in the area around Edinburgh. In 2025-26, 32% of the new homes completed in Scotland were in the Lothians. If you add in Fife, which is also a popular area for people commuting to the capital, then this corner of the country accounts for 39% of all new homes built, despite only having 23% of the population. Look to the west and the figures flip around; Glasgow and the surrounding councils have 32% of the population, but only 26% of the housebuilding. This is true even in relatively affluent areas with high rates of population growth, like East Renfrewshire - where just 87 new homes were completed last year. Glasgow has a homelessness problem so acute that the city council is spending almost Â£70m a year putting people up in hotel rooms. Along with Edinburgh, the city has been declared to be in a state of "systemic failure" by the Scottish Housing Regulator. Glasgow faces particular pressure with refugee households seeking support, with 44% of the 8,025 homelessness applications last year from people with refugee status or leave to remain - compared to 16% across Scotland as a whole. And yet there were fewer new home "starts" there last year than in East Lothian, a more rural area with one sixth the population, with city leaders in Glasgow blaming rising construction costs . Plans have just been announced for 6,500 new affordable homes to be built on brownfield sites - previously developed land which is currently unused - over the next six years. The council also says it has identified 59 sites across the city as potential locations for another 12,173 new homes, which could be built by 2032 if funding becomes available. It is also looking at repurposing disused shops for housing. Flats like these ones in Edinburgh were built as council homes but now are a mix of social and private housing There has been a historic shift in Scotland's population towards Edinburgh, with the capital's financial and service sector booming while areas in the west struggle to recover from the decline of traditional industries. Demand for homes around the capital has driven up property prices. Edinburgh, Midlothian and East Lothian all feature in the top four areas in Scotland , external with the highest house prices, all well above the national average , external . This makes it attractive to housebuilders seeking a return on investment - and it also means businesses in the construction trade and related supply chains are more likely to thrive there. Meanwhile those in the industry say there are fewer small-to-medium sized building firms in more rural areas to take projects forward. Higher prices in the east of Scotland have meant problems with affordability for some. A study for Shelter Scotland , external suggested that 62% of newly-formed households - people entering the housing market for the first time, such as those leaving the parental home - in this area were unable to afford the current market. For Scotland as a whole, the figure was 55%. That same study suggested an extra 15,693 affordable homes need to be built each year to end the housing emergency. The Scottish government does not have an overall housebuilding target, but it did set one in 2022 for affordable homes - to complete 110,000 of them by 2032 , external , with at least 70% available for social rent and 10% in island and rural communities. The latest figures show 36,500 completions towards this target. The Scottish Parliament Information Centre says that with just over five years left to go, this means on average 15,000 homes need to be delivered each year , external . In 2025-26, there were 6,832 completions as part of the Affordable Housing Supply Programme - down from a peak of 10,466 in 2022-23. So the rate of delivery needs to more than double, and then be sustained at record levels, if the target is to be met. Scotcast: Our housing shortage and the 'big city doughnuts' Martin Geissler is joined by Aimee Stanton and Phil Sim to crunch the numbers on how weâre getting on with housebuilding and discuss the current housing picture across the country. Ministers say they are committing Â£4.1bn over the next four years to support the delivery of "around 36,000 affordable homes". Builders have welcomed the longer-term certainty offered by this funding, but that would still only get half way to the 110,000 target with two years remaining. Modelling by the Fraser of Allander Institute , external think tank suggests it is more likely to take until late 2036. The Scottish government says it "remains focused" on achieving the 110,000 target, while acknowledging that it is "challenging". Somerville said it could be met through longer-term investment in publicly funded affordable housing schemes - through vehicles like the Scottish National Investment Bank - as well as support for private developers. The government is also setting up a new national agency next year - More Homes Scotland - which hopes to "remove barriers and accelerate housing delivery". Headline: 'I look after history in a fantastic place' - meet the UK's youngest lighthouse keeper
Body: At the age of 28, Jeri Cormack is the UK's youngest retained lighthouse keeper. She is one of 17 part-time keepers working for the Northern Lighthouse Board, tasked with looking after the network since its automation in the 1990s. Tackling often fierce weather, Jeri inspects and maintains three historic lighthouses at the edge of the British mainland - Noss Head, Dunnet Head and Duncansby Head.

Headline: Welsh Labour still committed to demands for more Senedd powers, says Skates
Body: Ken Skates took over as Welsh Labour leader after May's elections Ken Skates says Welsh Labour has not ditched calls for new powers for the Senedd, after telling conference on Saturday that the party had focused too much on the issue in the past. The Welsh Labour leader told the BBC it remained party policy that Labour wants Westminster to hand over control of policing and the Crown Estate. He would not be drawn on whether it would be wrong for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to refuse devolving those powers. Skates' comments followed a conference speech on Saturday where the party leader argued Labour had previously treated standing up for Wales as wanting more powers for the Welsh Parliament . A report into Welsh Labour's defeat in the Senedd elections in May criticised the "Red Welsh Way" political strategy of former First Minister Eluned Morgan , arguing demands for more powers had fallen flat with voters. The report was presented at the party's conference in Llandudno, which concluded on Sunday. Skates said Red Welsh Way was a "response to divided opinion in the party" and said Morgan had been in an "unwinnable situation" when she became first minister in 2025 . Asked by the BBC Politics Wales programme whether Labour was still calling for powers on the Crown Estate and policing, Skates said: "I've been really clear, you know, we need transfers of powers on the basis of what's best for Wales from Westminster to Cardiff Bay, but that's been the focus of all debate for far too long. "We haven't had a good debate, deep debate, about what powers need to be transferred onward from Cardiff Bay to places like Aberystwyth to Wrexham to Merthyr, to communities right across Wales." Pressed on the same question for a second time, he said: "Yes, yes, and there's been no change in policy on that." Former Welsh Labour leader Eluned Morgan lost her seat in May's Senedd election Asked if Burnham would be wrong to refuse the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate, he added: "This is a live debate that's taking place at the moment, and our party policy in Wales has not changed." Owned by the monarch, the Crown Estate possesses more than Â£603m of land in Wales, including 65% of the seabed surrounding the coastline. Both Labour and Plaid believe the estate should be devolved so money raised from windfarms and other projects can be spent exclusively in Wales - the UK government has previously argued it would make no commercial sense . Andy Burnham has signalled he was open to the devolution of policing , although no firm proposals have yet been made. All the latest political news from Wales and beyond, presented by Bethan Rhys Roberts. In his speech on Saturday, Skates said Morgan had "steadied the ship" when she became Welsh Labour leader, "in the most difficult of times and the worst set of conditions". He said Morgan "cleaned up the boy's mess". Asked whether Skates took responsibility for being part of the "boy's mess" because he was co-chair of the campaign to elect Vaughan Gething, who later had to resign, he said: "Oh no, it wasn't just that. "This was about the dysfunctional nature of the Senedd group. It was divided, and it was largely divided because of the boys. "She came in the most difficult of times, and she led with incredible passion." Ken Skates denied that the party had dropped the Red Welsh Way, or clear red water - both strategies used to distinguish Welsh Labour from UK Labour. He said Labour would be "fighting as one team with a distinct offer to people and that is that we are going to seek health and wealth for all. Other parties have their own priorities. "Our purpose is to make sure that people's lives improve and we'll be asking right across the parliamentary Labour party and councils in the trade union movement and of course in the Senedd, [is] what we're doing making people better off?" Earlier, on BBC Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement programme , Skates said the report by Prof Anand Menon's PF First was not a "charge sheet" but outlined "what went wrong over many, many years", and pointed to how Labour can recover. "What's clear from the report is that Eluned was in an unwinnable situation when she took over leadership. "We didn't lose because of Eluned, we lost in spite of Eluned's fierce, courageous leadership," he said. He said the Red Welsh Way was "in response to divided opinion in the party at the time". "We're a different party now. OK, we're smaller in number, but we are completely united in the Senedd. "That helps in terms of ensuring that everybody is fighting for the same purpose." Labour has nine MSs in the 96 member Welsh Parliament. It held half of the available seats prior to the Senedd election in May. Headline: 'We've waited 73 years to be here' - Wales fans ecstatic after win over New Zealand
Body: Saturday marked the first time Wales had beaten New Zealand in 73 years Welsh rugby fans were "fizzing off their heads" on Saturday night after ending 73 years of hurt against New Zealand in an epic Nations Championship encounter. The match at the Principality Stadium ended 35-28 to the hosts as the All Blacks' run of 34 successive victories against Wales - dating back to 1953 - came to a juddering halt in Cardiff. Wales fans were left stunned by a result that came just a week on from having to grind out a win against Japan. The Prince of Wales, who is patron of the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) also congratulated the team on the win, saying it was a "fantastic result". Three times Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time in history they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors. All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game. But the approach backfired spectacularly after a brilliant performance sparked astonishing scenes in Cardiff . A crowd of 55,152 could scarcely believe what had unfolded, and there were scenes of wild celebration with players in tears as Wales began taking in arguably the most famous win of their 145-year Test match history. Wales now holds The Raeburn Shield - a fan-created trophy that traces match-winners in men's rugby union back to the first international match in March 1871 Prince William shared a post on Instagram saying it was a "fantastic result by the Wales rugby team". "My congratulations to the players, coaches and everyone who played a part - you have given fans across Wales a day they will never forget". Celebrities and politicians were also quick to pay tribute to the team for their heroics on the field. Speaking on 5Live Breakfast on Sunday morning , First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "Yesterday, meant a heck of a lot to us. "We are a pretty sporting mad nation. Rugby is very important to us as a nation. "The fixture against New Zealand is a particularly important fixture. We are a smallish country but in the rugby world, we are the biggest powers. He continued that "73 years we have failed to beat them, we have come close". "I have watched Wales come close some 20 years or so ago but sport is wonderful and awful at the same time. It became this psychological block. "Well, no more. That is it, we can go forward now with a new generation knowing that we can beat New Zealand." He said the crowd on Saturday "wasn't the biggest, but no doubt that changes". "I full expect the game next week to be a sell out." Gavin and Stacey star Jones shared her sheer delight in an Instagram video, with the actor looked visibly stunned following the incredible win over New Zealand. "This has been decades in the making. Huge congratulations to you all," he wrote on Facebook. Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said he managed to watch the final part of the game after speaking at the Welsh Labour conference in Llandudno. "After 73 years we've finally beaten the All Blacks! Can barely believe what I've just witnessed," he said. Hannah went to the game with her 81-year-old dad John Jenkins was eight-years old the last time Wales beat New Zealand, and without a TV, he was not able to watch the game. Now 81, he has seen his team beat the All Blacks. John, who now lives in Shropshire but travels for every match, said he has been present at all of the big occasions in Welsh rugby, and Wales' win against New Zealand was the "most memorable". "I'm not a gambling man, and if I'd known how to place a bet, I would have bet on Wales because I had this gut feeling that we were going to win. "Everybody in the last 20 minutes was so anxious," he said. His daughter Hannah, 50, who also travels to every match despite living in Chichester, said "it felt like a party in the first half, we couldn't quite believe what was happening". John said: "For 10 minutes after the final whistle, Hannah was sobbing on my shoulder." Hannah said: "For me and dad to be able to go and watch it together, I keep thinking about turning and looking at his face after we scored the first try - we were just kind of incredulous." Wales fans ecstatic after win over New Zealand A couple celebrating their wedding day had to delay the speeches by 15 minutes as their guests had to see out the game. Photographer Rhian Jones, 32, from Ammanford, who captured the celebrations, said the "entirety of the wedding breakfast were on their phones". "The atmosphere was just so intense, people were screaming, it was incredible and everyone was on edge. "The bride actually said she felt such a pressure because she was so scared that they were going to lose on her wedding day and obviously it would have dampened the spirit, but of course we didn't," she said. "We celebrated the couple, celebrated the victory and it was incredible." She added none of the guests at the wedding in Carmarthen had seen that in their lifetime. "I tried to edit during the wedding breakfast but I didn't edit anything and I just sat on there with the saxophonist and videographer watching my phone which is very unprofessional, but what are you going to do when it's making history. "I can't wait to tell my children, and certainly they will be telling their children this in years to come." Kyle said his granddad got tired of waiting and fell asleep just before the full-time whistle Kyle Aston said his 102-year-old granddad had always been a huge rugby fan and was 29 when Wales last beat the All Blacks. "It would take the long painful wait of 73 years until victory was ours once again, but unfortunately he got tired of waiting and fell asleep just before the full-time whistle," he said. "Sharing that moment with my grandfather is something I'll never forget. "Fortunately we are able to watch things back theses days so at some point we will relive the biggest rugby win of our life time." Warren Atkins says "you would have struggled to move", when asked on how packed the pub was Warren Atkins from The Cottage pub on St Mary's Street in Cardiff said they were already packed but it was "next level" afterwards. "We were quite busy before the game but then during the end of the game and after the game it was a different kettle of fish. He added that the performance was a "promising start" for Wales, and was getting in more beer for next week's game. "I think we need to step it up a notch again next week seeing how busy it was this week. "We were expecting busy but you can never prepare yourself for what's to come." Darren Williams went to Caernarfon Rugby Club to watch the match Darren Williams lives abroad but comes home once a year to visit his family in Wales. He came to Caernarfon Rugby Club to watch the match and said the result was "excellent". "I hope they can continue like this and keep moving forward," he said. "The atmosphere was excellent and very enthusiastic." Daron Owens said everyone at the rugby club was "ecstatic" after the game Daron Owens said she was "really glad" to be at the rugby club to witness such a brilliant performance. "It was great to see everyone so proud. Everyone was cheering so loudly, it was a really positive place to be." One fan pitch side at Principality Stadium said they had waited "73 years to be at this game", adding that they were in "total shock but absolutely delighted". Headline: I took in three children with my husband, who was adopted, then found out at 40 that I was too
Body: Reform UK Member of the Senedd Catherine Cullen says her parents were a "fantastic influence" on her Twelve years ago, Catherine Cullen had already adopted two children with her husband - himself an adoptee - when she made a shocking discovery. "I was registering a child's birth and I wanted the long version of my birth certificate, which I had never had," she said. "I ordered it and when it came, it was adoption certificate, not a birth certificate." Cullen was 40 and had no clue her mum and dad, who had raised her in a "very Valleys upbringing" in Cwmbran, Torfaen, were not her birth parents. "My parents had obviously kept that to themselves for their own reasons," she says. "My reaction was very calm to begin, but it wasn't long before shock set in." Catherine Cullen speaks for Reform in Wales' parliament on issues affecting children and young people She said she "poured the energy" of the shock into discovering who her birth parents were and eventually located them using her own research. Cullen went on to adopt one more time, bringing the number of children she has with her husband to six, including her three birth children. Two are now adults, three are teenagers, and the youngest is nine. Now aged 52 and a Reform UK politician in the Welsh Parliament, Cullen said her family experience had given her a particular interest in the issue of adoption, which she said was "one of the most important things you can do for children". "My adoption was a really successful one and I felt we should give that back," she said. Before she entered politics, Cullen gave up teaching to stay at home with her children, which she described as "one of the most fulfilling experiences". Before that, she worked as a science teacher and, after her stint as a full-time parent, she completed a master's degree in additional learning needs. She told BBC Wales' Sunday Supplement in October that her interest in the area was partly shaped by family experience, with three of her children on the autistic spectrum. Cullen was among the Senedd members who met King Charles III at the ceremonial opening of the Welsh Parliament in October She said politics was a constant presence in the family home growing up. "My mother, being from Tredegar and Aneurin Bevan land, was always very political," she said. Cullen said her parents were a "fantastic influence", but despite growing up in what she called a Labour-supporting household on a council estate, her political views changed as an adult. "Friends said you need to look at manifestos because at that point I was not sure," she said. "I voted Conservative for a while and then I had been watching Nigel Farage and the late Ann Widdecombe in the background. "When Reform came on the scene, I knew that's where my political allegiances were going to lie." After being elected to represent the Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni constituency in Wales' parliament for the first time in May, she said her large family were "very proud" of her. She said she now hopes to use her role in the Senedd to boost support for people who have experienced adoption. "I would like to see adoptees having emotional support for a lot longer, and support in locating birth families if they require it," she said. She added that it was "up to the adoptee how they formulate a relationship with their birth parents". She also feels that children were "sometimes left in care for too long". "Adoption is a really important way of showing care, compassion and love and it gives a child a foundation from which they can thrive, learn and grow," she said. Cullen said she viewed adoption "through the lens of my children and the process I went through with them", and that more care was needed by parents going through it. "It's not up to scratch. There's a lot to do." Headline: 'One of the greatest wins' - Wales stun All Blacks to go from no-hopers to heroes
Body: Highlights: Wales beat New Zealand for first time in 73 years One of the greatest Wales wins of all time. That is how former captain Sam Warburton described the monumental result against New Zealand in Cardiff on Saturday. At the time of the kick-off, the All Blacks were effectively the top-ranked side in the world following South Africa's tension-filled loss to France on Friday night. So no-one gave Wales a glimmer of hope - even Warburton - with some bookmakers offering odds of 30-1 during the week. The question, not of when but can Wales beat the All Blacks again has beset them since 1953. That 73-year wait has been marred by cheating, national scandal and pure sporting drama. Little wonder then that few wanted to leave the Principality Stadium long after the final whistle had sparked unprecedented scenes of utter joy, tears and relief to the strains of Yma O Hyd. The outpouring of unbridled emotion was after a losing run - stretching across 34 matches - that has hung like a millstone around the necks of generations of Wales players. Like so many former stars, Warburton tasted success with the British & Irish Lions but lost all five meetings with New Zealand even as part of one of the most successful Wales teams of all time during the Warren Gatland era. Even the legendary team of the 1970s fell short with their country, although Sir Gareth Edwards was among the smallest Principality Stadium crowd for a Wales-New Zealand fixture to witness history. How many more will claim in years to come that they were there as well? Wales believed they could create history - Lake All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett Warburton said: "When you think what the fans and this team has been through, from the highs of a Grand Slam seven years ago, down to 12th in the world rankings and a record losing run of any tier-one nation, we've been down in the pits. "No-one gave Wales a chance; that's why this is one of the greatest Welsh wins of all time. "Yes, New Zealand had made changes but that was one of the most heroic defensive performances I have ever seen." Dan Biggar, sat alongside Warburton for host broadcaster ITV, put the result into wider perspective given the chaotic state of Welsh rugby right now. "That was probably the biggest shock in world rugby since Japan beat South Africa in the 2015 World Cup," he said. "There have been so many times over the last couple of years when we've left this stadium doubting we we would ever see a result like this. "This is not a day for analysis; it's just to celebrate being Welsh." Dafydd Jenkins equalled the world record for number of tackles in a Test match Most fans inside the stadium would not have been born the last time Wales beat New Zealand. Winston Churchill was prime minister and Queen Elizabeth II had not long had her coronation when Wales last beat the All Blacks in 1953. Respected rugby commentator Huw Llywelyn Davies attended the game as an eight-year-old with his father, who was writing for the weekly Welsh-language newspaper Baner ac Amserau Cymru. "I never thought I would see it happen again, not unless I lived to 100," said an emotional Davies, now 81, as he stepped away from the media seats inside the Principality Stadium. "With everything that has been going in Welsh rugby recently, I didn't think we would beat them this decade, but the way we matched them physically was incredible." Wales had only come close on a handful of occasions with one-point defeats in 1978, when New Zealand lock Andy Haden infamously dived out of a lineout to gain a match-winning penalty, and then in 2004. Wales even turned to four New Zealand coaches in Sir Graham Henry, Steve Hansen, Gatland and Wayne Pivac to help break the hoodoo, but none of the quartet could inspire a Test victory over the land of their birth. So there will be added satisfaction that it was a Welshman who masterminded the long-awaited win. Steve Tandy's unlikely heroes may not have the household names of teams gone by, nor the winning pedigree, but they had courage when it mattered. Three times they held up black shirts over the try-line during a second-half defensive effort that at times beggared belief. Initial statistics had second-row Dafydd Jenkins equalling Thierry Dusautoir's world record of 38 tackles in a single match - also set against New Zealand in 2007. Jac Morgan and man of the match James Botham also topped 30 tackles, while centre Eddie James and captain Dewi Lake were not far behind. It earned high praise from former New Zealand captain Sean Fitzpatrick. A winner in all six meetings with Wales, the ex-hooker has ties to that day seven decades ago when his father Brian made his New Zealand debut. Observers say he was unlucky not to be awarded a try after he was adjudged to have been tackled just short of the line. How different history might have been. "New Zealand played well in patches and terrible in others but this is all about Wales," said Fitzpatrick, now a board member of Welsh region Scarlets. "The way they started the game and took their tries showed the amazing belief they had. But the defensive effort was out of this world." Wales also found their teeth in attack, scoring five tries in their biggest ever tally against the All Blacks as these wounded dragons finally awoke. Time will tell if this historic result will breathe fire back into Welsh rugby beyond on momentous day in Cardiff. Will any of the 2026 team be honoured as Wales' 1953 match-winner Ken Jones was with a statue in his hometown of Blaenavon? Headline: Billie Piper to star in new horror set on 'outskirts of old Welsh iron town'
Body: Sketchbook will star Billie Piper alongside child actor Woody Norman, as a mother and son who are reunited after years apart in foster care Actor Billie Piper is set to star in a new supernatural horror filmed on the "outskirts of an old iron town" in Wales. Located "somewhere on the perimeter" of Merthyr Tydfil or Aberdare, Sketchbook will feature Piper, alongside child actor Woody Norman, as a mother and son who are reunited after years apart in foster care. It will be directed by Swansea-born filmmaker Jamie Jones, who hopes the film will tap into "important and real issues" while still providing the thrill of a horror. "I think a lot of people will relate to the issues, of growing up and social exclusion, going on beneath it all - but on the surface it's a really exciting horror film," he said. Jones, who received a BAFTA Cymru breakthrough award for his work on his feature debut Obey, said he wanted the film to be dark, fun, tense and exciting, but also have substance. "There needs to be something meaty you can chew on and there is that with this, in abundance." Director Jamie Jones, from Swansea, says filming in his home country is "only a good thing for Wales" The film starts in foster care and follows the son returning home to his mum, Piper - a single, working class mother "struggling to cope". "Because his mother wasn't coping, she needed a bit of support and a bit or a break from him," said Jones. "The sense of rejection he feels is then when the horror genre then starts to seep into the narrative. "This horror then starts to unfold is kind of like a metaphor for families that are in impossible situations." Jones said he drew upon "real social experiences to drive the narrative", including his own experiences with mental health, neurodiversity and systematic care. A sketchbook acts as a form of physical expression and a "safe place" for the son as he sketches out his emotions. "He draws ultimately as a way of expressing himself and to feel like he has some form of control," said Jones. "The way that the narrative unfolds, the two things crash together, so to speak. Which I think is a really fun journey for viewers to go on... it's a roller coaster ride." Uprising star Woody Norman will feature as Billie Piper's son It will be the latest film for Piper, who is known for roles in BBC's Doctor Who, Secret Diary of a Call Girl and the Netflix series Collateral. Jones said Piper's performance in the psychological drama Two for Joy inspired his decision for her to star as the mother. "I've always loved Billie Piper and I think she's had a fabulous life and career," he added. "She is the salt of the Earth, you know, she's very warm, she's very loyal, she's got all of these great qualities, but she's struggling. "When the odds are stacked against you, it's tough, you know. You've just got to try your best, and that's what her character does. "It just felt like the perfect role for Billie." Lots of details are yet to be ironed out, but filming is set to start in February. Despite being set in Wales, Jones is undecided if Piper and Norman will have to adopt a Welsh accent, as the characters nationality does not play a huge role in the film. "It's not necessarily about being Welsh, or about Wales, per say, but I want to set it in Wales because that's where I'm from. "I would like to do that as much as possible, if you're from somewhere, I think it's good to set things in a place you know and you know the texture, the nuances and the humour. "Which helps make it all entertaining. I wanted to get the visual language of the old iron towns in there... but I'm not going to locate it specifically." He said he sees a lot of the themes, including class divides, to be universally understood and the setting will help him give the film a grit he understands. "The setting is important, and where they are, and the world and community is important," said Jones. "But what's important is that they are working class or struggling. The more you talk about universal themes, the bigger your audience can be, and you can bring your audience in to a story that is also set in Wales. "The Welsh thing can sneak under the hood. "I think that's only a good thing for Wales." Headline: Chief executive of failing health board leaves for new job in England
Body: Carol Shillabeer joined as chief executive of Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board in May 2023 The boss of Wales' largest and most troubled health board is leaving her post for one in England. Carol Shillabeer became the chief executive of Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board - which has spent nine years in special measures - in May 2023. The health board covers all of north Wales, and has been under the highest level of oversight due to concerns about care quality, patient safety and leadership . Shillabeer will join Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust in north west England as their chief executive in the new year. The Welsh government said matters of personnel and employment were for the health board but it continued to hold it to account for its performance. When she took on the job Shillabeer said she knew she had taken on one of the toughest jobs in the NHS, if not the whole of Wales. She was appointed after the Welsh government put Betsi into "special measures" for the second time in its history. Eleven independent board members were forced to resign and, shortly after, Shillabeer was drafted in from the neighbouring Powys health board. Betsi Cadwaladr health board has been beset by problems since its inception in 2009 Her departure comes months after Healthcare Inspectorate Wales (HIW) visited the emergency department at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd, Denbighshire, in May, and said it needed "significant improvements". A follow-up in August found progress had been made but challenges remained and "enhanced oversight" of the department was still needed. At the time Shillabeer apologised "unreservedly" and said improving care was a priority. Earlier this year, the health board was given a "final chance" to improve . Since 2013 there have been a number of highly critical reports into the health board, with it being placed in special measures in 2015 for the first time. On many key NHS performance figures, Betsi Cadwaladr health board continues to be Wales' worst performer. Shillabeer said it had been "an enormous privilege" and she was "very proud of what colleagues across the organisation have achieved during an extremely demanding period". Dyfed Edwards, chair of the health board, congratulated Shillabeer and said she joined "at an exceptionally challenging point" and "provided committed and determined leadership over the past three and a half years. "Considerable work remains to be done and we are very clear that our improvement journey continues," he said. The health board said it would announce interim and longer-term leadership arrangements "in due course". Having previously called for her resignation , Conservative leader in Wales, Darren Millar, said Shillabeer had failed to address NHS failures in the region or improve performance. Headline: Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister's strategy
Body: Andy Burnham became prime minister in July The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat. On Saturday morning Andy Burnham addressed the first Welsh Labour conference since May's Senedd election . He suggested the previous Labour government did not do enough to pass powers down to communities, and said it was "hard" to accept the party was no longer in power after 27 years of running the Welsh government. He spoke before a review into what went wrong concluded that former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy of calling out Westminster played a role in the party losing power. The report by Prof Anand Menon, of PF Global, said Morgan's calls for constitutional change like the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate did not get through to voters. A source close to the former first minister said it was "ludicrous" to suggest that Morgan was focused on constitutional issues. Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party for focusing too much on powers for the Senedd . In a subdued speech, Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" where "everyone" was "signed up and on the same page". He spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election. Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils. "Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place. "We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places." He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom". Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction". "Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve. "We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" Addressing the event at Venue Cymru in Llandudno, Burnham said he loved "everything about Wales". He said his last visit to Wales - to Aberfan - left the "biggest mark" of his visits to the country. Referencing the fight for justice in the years after the disaster, Burnham said he wanted a "country where all people and all places are treated fairly and with dignity". He said his vision for the country is a "reindustrialised nation with revitalised high streets". Burnham said Labour should be "immensely proud" of the things it achieved in Wales - including free school meals, free prescriptions and the creation of Transport for Wales. The prime minister said he wanted to show how "being in the UK is good for Wales because of the partnership that we can develop together". He said he had put the full devolution of employment support on the table with the Welsh government. It was announced at the Budget that standing charges for gas will come to an end. Burnham confirmed that the charges will be scrapped in the new year. Menon's criticism of the Red Welsh Way was one of several findings in his review of what went wrong at the May election. It included that the party suffered a long-term decline in support to other left wing parties, laid bare as Labour took flak for dissatisfaction with public services at both UK and Welsh levels. It said "weaknesses in political communication" also left the party without "clear answers when voters wanted them". The review says Labour should set itself against Plaid Cymru's "constitutional project" , by seeking more powers based on what they would deliver rather than "debating powers in the abstract", prioritising the NHS, the economy and the cost of living. It said voters felt they had not delivered on all three issues. Eluned Morgan made history in May's Senedd election, becoming the first leader of a government in the UK to lose her seat while in office Morgan sought to differentiate herself from Sir Keir Starmer with a flagship speech in 2025, where she set out her approach called the Red Welsh Way. Morgan said she was willing to "call out" Westminster Labour, and demanded the devolution of the crown estate to the Senedd. Menon's report said the strategy "struggled to land on everyday policy, instead tied up in constitutional positioning and the relationship with Westminster". Naming Morgan, the report said her policy recalled Rhodri Morgan's "clear red water" approach but "was not its equivalent". "Demands such as transferring the Crown Estate and devolving policing did not speak to voters on the doorstep, who found themselves more concerned with the economy, cost of living and the NHS." The Labour campaign shifted from Red Welsh Way to "power in partnership" - attempting to send signals about the relationship with UK Labour in government. The report said that "still did not provide clear policy objectives". Labour has shared most of Plaid's constitutional demands, including the devolution of policing, the Crown Estate and rail devolution, with the exception of independence. Plaid beat Welsh Labour in the May election , and was now running the Welsh government. Menon's report said the result was "not necessarily" about Welsh identity, saying that "has been flat for a decade". But, it added: "Welsh Labour voters who switch to Plaid do score more strongly on their Welsh identity than those who stayed." It said voters "tend to judge whether a party stands up for Wales mainly on delivery: The NHS, the cost of living and the economy." A source close to Morgan said it was "ludicrous" to suggest she was focused on constitutional issues, adding that she had concentrated on the NHS and bringing quality jobs to Wales. The source claimed Welsh Labour had run a "terrible campaign" which was "lacklustre", and said the biggest issue was the unpopularity of Sir Keir. On Morgan's resignation as Welsh Labour leader , which came within minutes of her failure to retain her seat in the Senedd, the source accused the Welsh party of trying to "control" her, even "down to the words of her resignation speech". Former First Minister Mark Drakeford said of the suggestion that calls for more devolution to the Senedd did not cut through to voters: "It was less it seemed to me that it didn't cut through to voters, that it hadn't cut through to our colleagues in Westminster. "We needed evidence from our colleagues in London that that was still the case and unfortunately that evidence just wasn't there in a way that allowed us to convince the Welsh population of that." The review said that NHS and access to healthcare were the biggest concern for 79% of voters who left Labour for Plaid and 80% who left Labour for Reform. The report said only 8% of Labour to Plaid switchers named devolution or independence as a top issue. However, 49% wanted a stronger Senedd, while 26% wanted independence. It said 73% of adults preferred more power for regions, councils and local areas to more power for the Senedd. PF Global polled 1,387 adults from August to September 2026. Headline: Bride jilted at the altar gives marriage another go - on Friday 13th
Body: Kayley Stead was set to get married in 2022 but her fiancÃ© didn't turn up A bride who was jilted at the altar says "everything has fallen into place" as she prepares for her second wedding in four years. Kayley Stead became a social media sensation in 2022 when she decided to go ahead with the celebrations despite her fiancÃ© not turning up. But after reconnecting with an old university friend, she was able to find love again, and the pair are set to tie knot on Friday 13th. Referring to the mysterious superstition that the day is considered unlucky, Kayley, from Swansea, said she "loves a risk" and is feeling great about their big day. "It just feels right, and it feels completely different from the last time when I was planning it," she said. Kayley said she is feeling prepared to marry her fiancÃ© Richard Perrott who she met when they were on the same course in university a decade ago. "Luckily, I learned all the dos and don'ts last time and what to prep for," she told Radio Wales Breakfast . "But the nerves are definitely coming in, which I think is normal." She said "everything has fallen into place" this time around and she feels that, despite the emotional rollercoaster she went on a few years ago, it happened for a reason. Richard and Kayley are preparing to tie the knot after meeting at university "If I didn't, I wouldn't be here right now. I wouldn't be marrying the man that I was meant to marry and that I met 13 years ago. "It's just insane. The dress is magical." Despite the number 13 having unlucky connotations, it has a special meaning for Kayley, and is in some ways her lucky number. "Number 13 was my childhood home. We found out that we've known each other for 13 years this year, and it's also my nephew's birthday, so he's going to be turning three. "He thinks it's his big birthday party, if I'm honest." The guests at Kayley's previous wedding still made it a memorable occasion "He better be there, otherwise he's going to have a lot to answer for," she said. She said they were both very lucky to find each other and he had reassured her "a thousand times" that he will be there. "I know the love that he's got for me is in abundance." Kayley said it was "meant to be" and she is so glad she gets to "marry the man that I want to". Headline: Baker makes 'mega' 10ft custard slice for couple's wedding
Body: 'We made a giant custard slice for a wedding cake' A baker said she has been inundated with bookings after creating a special three metre (9.8ft) custard slice for a couple's special day. Fablas Ice Cream were booked to cater the wedding of Liz and James Harding - who say they are both "passionate about custard" - in Brecon, Powys. The couple said the idea came after they saw the custard slices on the company's social media, and thought they would ask if a "mega" one could be made. The company's managing director Lauren Evans said it was probably the "biggest thing we've ever created", with the slabs produced at the bakery in Cowbridge and then transported to the event, where it was assembled and decorated. The custard slice was custom made for Liz and James Harding's wedding day Lauren said they "jumped at the chance" to create the unique slice, which took months of planning. She described it as "nerve-wracking" as they had one chance to do it. "But we absolutely smashed it and it was a roaring success with all the guests" - although it was so popular there "wasn't even a slice left for the bride's mother". She said they used fresh cream, meaning they had a "very tight timescale". "We were very proud of it and we did learn some things along the way," she said. Head Baker Charlotte Thomas (left) said it was a "privilege" to create the slice The couple said they live close to the company's stores. "I didn't want a traditional wedding cake and saw on Instagram they'd started doing custard slice birthday cakes," said Liz. "So I wondered if they'd do me a mega one," she added. She said they were "over the moon" with the result and felt "honoured" to be the first to have the supersized slice. Liz said they were keen to have a wedding that was special to them, stressing it was important to "do whatever works for you". She also said she was pleased about the attention it received online. "If you're gonna be remembered for one thing, this isn't a bad thing." Liz and James Harding had the idea after seeing custard slices made online Lauren said they had received messages from as far afield as New Zealand and Australia, hearing the different "names people call them". She said her favourite was a "snot block" - a term in Australia - although she does not believe the name will catch on in the UK. Charlotte Thomas, head baker for Fablas, said it was a "privilege" to be part of the couple's day, saying she "really enjoyed the challenge" of creating it. Lauren said she had to give credit to Charlotte for executing it perfectly and making it one continuous custard slice. The giant custard slice proved popular at the wedding Lauren said they have "so many exciting projects to get our teeth into" and they had received many inquiries since posting the video. She hopes the wedding table custard slice becomes a "tradition" across Wales because of their work. "Never in our wildest dreams did we imagine making them as wedding table cakes," she said. Headline: 'You makes Barry proud' - Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page to enter I'm a Celeb jungle
Body: Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page is to take part in the 26th series of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page has confirmed she will appear on the upcoming reality TV series I'm a Celebrity, with her former co-star Ruth Jones urging her to "have a crackin' time". Page, who played Stacey Shipman in the BBC comedy, is joining this year's line-up of celebrities on the forthcoming show in Australia. The 49-year-old, from Swansea, said she had her sights on becoming the first Welsh Queen of the Jungle. "You makes Barry very proud, I'm not gonna lie," said Jones - assuming her former Gavin and Stacey character Nessa Jenkins - on Instagram. "They're gonna make you stick all manner of matter in your gob. And I'm not talking Gwen's omelettes... Just don't over do it, alrigh'? You knows what a weak constitution you has." Joanna Page, pictured with Ruth Jones (right), has her sights on becoming the first Welsh Queen of the I'm a Celeb jungle Speaking ahead of her trip down under, Page said she believed her co-stars will be "shocked" when she arrives in the jungle for the ITV reality show. "I also know they will find it funny. They know exactly what I am like and they will laugh." Page said being the first Welsh queen would be a "pretty good title to take home", but added she was just as excited to see how long she could last. "I'm going to see this to the end and I'm going to be strong. I am going to get the most out of this." Eleven celebrities will enter the Australian jungle camp on Monday As a mother-of-four, Page said she hoped her part in the show will help her "reconnect" with who she was before becoming a mum. "This is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. I'm very much an impulsive person and I just make a gut decision, so I said 'yes' straight away," said Page. She said she hoped to find "peace and time for my thoughts" away from the everyday worries about feeding the children and getting everyone ready for the school run. "I can be me, I can be Jo and not just mummy all the time. I think that will be nice." "I will never get to do anything like this again. I am telling myself, 'Come on Jo, let's take yourself off to Australia and give yourself an experience'. "It's exciting and it's going to be life-changing." Ruth Jones - aka Nessa - said she was "so excited" to see Joanna Page head to the Australian jungle Page will enter the jungle alongside footballer Wayne Rooney, TV personality Chloe Burrows and soap star Claire Sweeney. Rooney will follow in his wife Coleen's footsteps after she finished as runner-up on the 2024 series, and said he hoped "people will see me for who I am". He said he had "always wanted to do" the show, joking that because of his short-lived football managerial career, he had more time on his hands. "I like to have fun and I like to think I am actually a fun guy to be around. "I do like to mess around a bit and I do talk a lot. People will have their own opinions, but I hope they will see me as a genuine person." Page will be also joined by Paralympian and TV presenter Ade Adepitan - who will be the first contestant in a wheelchair to appear on the show â something he said his eight-year-old self would not believe. "Words like 'honour' and 'privilege' are the ones I feel, but I don't think they sum it up enough," he said. "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. "It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first. I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here! starts on Monday 16 November at 21:00 GMT on ITV. Headline: Wales must look to back up All Blacks win - Tandy
Body: Wales captain Dewi Lake is the only player to be involved in all 14 internationals under head coach Steve Tandy Wales head coach Steve Tandy has challenged his side to back up their wonderful win against New Zealand when they host Australia next weekend. After beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years with the 35-28 win at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales will play the final game of the Nations Championship - before the play-offs - against the Wallabies on Saturday evening (20:10 BST). Tandy says Wales will attempt to not dwell on what they achieved on Saturday against New Zealand as they aim for a third successive home win. "We have to keep going and we've got a massive game against Australia next weekend," said Tandy. "It's going to be a different kind of test for us after we have had back-to-back home wins. "We've gone up another notch or another couple of levels, so it's important we back that up. It's about making sure when we come in that we're ready to work." Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds Highlights: Wales beat New Zealand for first time in 73 years After defeat by England, Australia lost 15-12 against Scotland on Sunday, a result which leaves Wales fifth in the northern hemisphere table. Wales are behind Gregor Townsend's side on points difference, with Scotland finishing their campaign against Japan. Tandy's side have won three out of five games in the Nations Championship against Fiji, Japan and New Zealand with defeats in the summer against Argentina and South Africa. Captain Dewi Lake has highlighted what has changed for this campaign to enable Wales to defeat New Zealand and rise one place in the world rankings to ninth. "Our skills are better and I think we're a better team, which is credit to Steve and his coaches," said Lake. "I think the belief is also different and the mindset has shifted. "We've spoken about it a lot and it's probably easy sometimes to say we've changed our mindset and believe in ourselves. "It feels different. Everybody has come in with a voice and a belief and [we] are challenging each other to get better. Ultimately that's what grows a group quickly." Wales believed they could create history - Lake All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett Tandy believes Wales' young players need to be given the environment to express themselves. "There's a young group that needed care," Tandy said. "Those connection pieces we speak about a lot and it's something we pride ourselves on." He highlighted players like Eddie James, Dan Edwards and, among those gaining caps and growing in confidence. "It's trying to give them the freedom to play, because it's a tough place to play in Wales when things are not going right," the Wales head coach added. "They're young men and we want these players to go out there and play with freedom. "They need to have that and we believe in that support for them, because sometimes it may be a little bit of a burden. "We've got to make sure these boys have a safe space." Headline: Cardiff's Kronk? The gym where Welsh champions train
Body: The Phoenix gym has steadily grown its reputation as a centre of boxing excellence In the red corner, a two-time world champion staying sharp as he waits for his return. His opponents, a succession of boxers readying themselves for an undercard bout that could be a key step in their careers. And out the back, the fancy dress climax to a Halloween boxing camp for local kids that mixed the sweet science with arts and crafts. Welcome to Llanrumney Phoenix ABC, situated on the eastern edge of Cardiff as the suburbs rise up and away from the city centre of the Welsh capital. Barrett stops Gwynne for vacant lightweight title Adames beats Welshman Warburton by unanimous decision Cordina unlikely to fight Pacquiao on Joshua-Fury card It is both six kilometres and a million miles away from the bright lights of the Principality Stadium, the focus of the boxing world on 11 December when it stages the heavyweight showdown between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. But it is also the place where the steps towards it are made. Some are further along than others, such as Joe Cordina, whose image complete with world title straps is one of several champions that hang high above the main sparring ring, flanked by a plethora of punchbags. Or former featherweight champ Lee Selby, now a bareknuckle boxer but lending his experience to the sparring as Gavin Gwynne gets ready for his own battle with Zelfa Barrett, a bout that would ultimately end in a fifth-round stoppage for the Welshman. Then there are those of the next generation, priming themselves for a primetime audience with this week's BBC-broadcast show on the undercard of Lauren Price's title defence against Michaela Kotaskova at Cardiff's Utilita Arena, the exciting pair of Brandon Scott and Rhys Edwards included. The closeness of the fight night and the amount of fighters creates a tangible buzz between the buzzes of the timer that pings into life every three minutes. Words of advice and tips from their own fights won â and lost â are shared between rounds, between the jokes at each others' expense. Eleven pros throwing countless punches, all adding up to the sense this is one of the centres of the Welsh boxing world. Cardiff's Kronk, , external if you like. Gary Lockett turned to training after a middleweight career that saw him win the WBU title as well as challenge WBC and WBO champion Kelly Pavlik in 2008 "You've got every level here, from former world champions to guys who dream about that, British title level, prospects â but everyone is treated the same," says Brandon Scott, who has recently returned closer to home following a spell training in Sheffield. "I had a trial and trained with the boys and it felt I'd been here for years. I was asking Gary to please train me the next day." Gary is Gary Lockett, the former middleweight world title challenger, recently inducted into the British Boxing Hall of Fame and who has coached since hanging up his gloves in 2008. "I came here in 2018," says Lockett, who accepted an invite that year from the club's founder and proud local, Tony Richards, to set up camp in the gym that doubles as a community hub in one of the more deprived areas of the city. As well as running classes for aspiring young amateur boxers, it has won recognition for inclusion activities and the support it offers. "We obviously have our guys training for their fights, but we're also part of this community. That's important," Lockett says. "We're not Premier League footballers who are on a different planet to most people. "And we make sure there's no bad eggs here. We want them to be good people first and foremost, as well as good boxers. "My first aim is always to educate to be the right kind of person out of the ring." Live on BBC Two Wales and iPlayer from 21:00 GMT That is obvious. But it's also clear that it's what could be earned inside the ring that inspires the electricity in the air this October morning. The thought of a sell-out fight night in the city looms large, with Price's rising tide as a boxing star helping to lift Lockett's stable in terms of opportunities. "I like to think of Cardiff as a fight town, but we do struggle in Wales with the big promoters coming here," says Lockett, who also manages around 20 fighters, including the Enzo Maccarinelli-trained Willy Gilheaney and Josh Kelly who will also appear on the Price undercard. "It's very hard to build these guys on small-hall bills, so we need platforms like this. They know they need to take the opportunity, sell as many tickets as you can, because this could be your shop window and the chance to be signed by a big promoter." Brandon Scott - who is yet to be beaten in his nine pro fights - joined Gary Lockett's camp earlier this year Swansea's Scott has had the experience of that, earning an early-career deal with promoter Eddie Hearn's Matchroom. Injuries and some personal issues saw him take time away before â fittingly â arriving at the Phoenix under Lockett. "Everything is back to normal," says the 23-year-old, who next faces journeyman Mexican Erik Omar Lopez. "I had a lot at a young age and perhaps I needed a bit of time to mature, and now mentally and physically I'm in the right place. "I feel like I'm starting my career over again and, coming here, I've giving myself the best chance to go again." The boxer with a Spiderman tattoo and who calls himself the "baddest nerd on the planet" says he is "still a silly goose" but Lockett says he is learning more and more, including an "eye-opening" time training in Japan. His sparring session with Edwards is fascinating, several fighters taking a break from their own workouts to offer tips as the similarly styled featherweights enjoy the endurance test. Rhys Edwards is one of several Phoenix boxers who will feature on the Lauren Price undercard In fact, a smile never seems to be off the face of Edwards, whose fight with former world bantamweight title challenger Lee McGregor serves as the main support act to Price's headlining bout. "I'll probably sell 30 tickets before leaving the house," laughs the 26-year-old, one of 11 siblings from Penygraig who previously admitted to sleeping in the Llanrumney gym close to fights to avoid the chaos at home. Not afraid of social media - a TikTok of him dodging shots in a pillow fight hit more than 10m views a few years back - and admitting to feeling like a minor celebrity such is the extent of the support he gets from his valleys hometown, Edwards is aware of the serious business fast approaching as he puts in the work. Having recovered from a first professional defeat in December 2024 â losing on points to Peter McGrail after taking the Riyadh fight with four days' notice â he missed out on a chance of a British title in a draw with Gully Powar in Cardiff in April. "It's kind of make or break â anything less than a win will push me back a year or two," Edwards says. "A big win sets me up, so the stakes are high." As is the opportunity, something the Llanrumney gym is all too aware of as the hits come and the hard work continues. And all hope that it leads to something more down the road where the bright lights beckon and championship fights call. But it all begins in places like Llanrumney. Headline: What Wales need to stay in Nations League top tier
Body: Having been unbeaten in Craig Bellamy's first nine games, Wales have only won four of their past 16 matches It can be easy to get tangled up in the complexities of Nations League permutations and, although Wales still have a few uncertainties to iron out, the picture is becoming clearer for Craig Bellamy's side. Following their 3-1 defeat in Norway on Saturday, Wales will finish bottom of Group A4 even if they win their final game against reigning champions Portugal on Tuesday. But that does not mean they will definitely be relegated from the top tier. Instead, they will play one of the teams from League B in a relegation play-off in March. However, one thing is for sure, as a result of the Norway loss, Wales will not be among the top seeds for Euro 2028 qualifying. "We wanted to be in pot one. That was the drive," said head coach Bellamy after the defeat in Oslo. "Some people might say, 'what makes you think you should be in pot one?' But I do. "Maybe I'm naive. I see in big parts of that game we can be in pot one. Let's take the good bits from the game, definitely improve on certain moments of the game and just keep pushing." Only the two worst-performing sides are automatically relegated to League B. Turkey and Czech Republic lost on Sunday and finish bottom of their groups without any points in League A. Wales have three points courtesy of their win against Norway in Cardiff, so avoid being automatically relegated. Wales have conceded eight goals during this Nations League campaign The relegation play-offs will be held across two legs at the end of March, with the first leg between March 25-27, and the second between March 28-30. As a League A side, Wales will be seeded and therefore play at home in the second leg. The draw for the play-offs takes place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, on Friday, 20 November. The sides that finish in the top two of League A's four groups will also discover the quarter-final draw on the same day. Wales played their part in League A - Bellamy With one game left to play, it's not yet clear. Slovenia, Hungary, Kosovo and Bosnia-Herzegovina are currently all in second place in their groups. However, Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland could also be potential opponents. Wales have scored three goals in five games during this Nations League campaign All teams finishing third or higher in League A will be named as top seeds for Euro 2028 qualifying. By missing out, Wales could now be drawn alongside one of Europe's heavyweights in their group. Spain, France, Italy, Netherlands and Portugal are among the sides already guaranteed pot one seeding for the draw on 6 December in Belfast. England will also be a top seed, although Thomas Tuchel's men will be kept apart from Wales and the other Euro 2028 co-hosts in qualifying regardless. When it comes to reaching the Euros, the 12 group winners and eight best-ranked runners-up qualify directly. For any of the co-hosts who don't make it via that route, there are two automatic spots available. Those will be awarded to the best-ranked between the four nations who haven't qualified directly. If Wales still have not made it, there is still the back-up option of the play-offs. He crossed down the left wing early in the second half, yet it is one of his 25 tackles that is one of the moments to watch and rewatch. At 35-21, a try looked certain when Anton Lienert-Brown burst towards the line but James reached out, stopped the New Zealand centre a metre out and ensured there was no offload. The All Blacks would go over one more time but it was a moment to encapsulate Wales' defensive desire. "I honestly can't feel a thing," he said while still in his kit, almost an hour after the final whistle. "I haven't been able feel my feet for a long time now. Headline: Clayton slumps out of Grand Slam with heavy Cross defeat
Body: Greaves won the Women's World Matchplay for the third time in July Beau Greaves was eliminated from the Grand Slam of Darts at the group stage despite ending her campaign with a win over Niels Zonneveld in Wolverhampton. Greaves, 22, beat Dutchman Zonneveld 5-3 but it was not enough to keep her in the competition after Saturday's heavy defeat by Luke Littler . The three-time women's world champion fought back impressively from 3-1 down, winning three consecutive legs to take the lead in the best-of-five match. She missed two match darts in a tense final leg but 28-year-old Zonneveld could not capitalise, failing to take out 154 before Greaves finished with double eight to seal the victory. Zonneveld will face defending champion Littler next and will need to beat him 5-2 or better in order to progress instead of the world number one. Earlier in the day, Rob Cross started his campaign with a crushing 5-1 win to eliminate fifth seed Jonny Clayton, who suffered back-to-back defeats. Clayton claimed the first leg but Cross surged back to win five in a row and finished with an average of 114.32, including three 180s. Sixth seed Ross Smith was also knocked out despite edging a 5-4 thriller against German Gabriel Clemens. The pair were neck and neck at 4-4 before Smith won the deciding leg, but his defeat by Rusty-Jake Rodriguez on Saturday meant that he could not qualify. Northern Ireland's Josh Rock, who was eighth seed, is also out after defeat by Kevin Doets, while 15th seed Luke Woodhouse has been also eliminated. Headline: Defensive desire a Welsh hallmark - Roberts
Body: Jamie Roberts (centre) never managed to beat New Zealand in his 94-cap Wales career Former British and Irish Lions centre Jamie Roberts said Wales' heroic defensive effort against New Zealand in the 35-28 win showed what it meant to be Welsh. It was the first time since 1953 Wales celebrated beating the All Blacks, ending a run of 34 successive defeats in one of world rugby's historically most one-sided fixtures. On three separate occasions Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defence that denied the visitors. "That defensive set in the second half epitomised in a way what it is to be Welsh," Roberts, who won 94 caps for Wales, told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That resilience, that bravery, that kind of never-say-die attitude that made us all so proud." Lock Dafydd Jenkins topped the charts at 38, which matches the individual world record tally set by France captain Thierry Dusautoir in the 2007 World Cup quarter-final at the same Cardiff ground. Jenkins was followed by Jac Morgan (31), James Botham (30), centre Eddie James (25) and Dewi Lake (24). Wales had the top nine tacklers on the field, with replacement prop Gareth Thomas making 19 in just 26 minutes. "It's heroic and as the days go past we would just appreciate it a little bit more how special yesterday was," said Roberts. "I woke up this morning just thinking had it happened? "It was unbelievable and only sport can make you feel those emotions." Lock Adam Beard and hooker Dewi Lake were among seven Welsh players who made more than 20 tackles against New Zealand Roberts says he hopes the players understand the magnitude of the victory. "It's a generational win and I salute the 23 lads who put in that heroic performance," said Roberts. "I hope the lads appreciate what they've done for the country by putting a huge amount of pride in the jersey for a generational win. "It's a young squad that's finding their way, we're developing combinations as we look ahead to the World Cup next year." Roberts is also a Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) board member at a time when the game has been in disarray in Wales on and off the field. The WRU board is proposing to cut a professional side by 2028 while the governing has posted an Â£18m loss . The Wales men's national team slumped to a record 18 straight Test defeats in a winless run that lasted 16 months, which also saw the side slip to a lowest world ranking of 14th. "Therein lies the the kind of David v Goliath narrative," said Roberts. "You have to put this one in context of where Wales have been in the last couple of years. "They've been in a very difficult place and that's what makes the win all the more sweet. "It's a group of young men who have gone through a lot of challenges in the last couple of years and there lies the resilience, heart and effort. "A lot of those players have gone through such a difficult time, so to come out swinging like that and perform like that was sensational." "So many good and great Wales sides down the years have failed to beat the All Blacks at a time where they were higher ranked," said Roberts. "Trophy-winning teams have failed to do it and that's what makes this win all the more remarkable and special." Roberts says the pride was felt inside and outside of the Principality Stadium. "I've not felt emotions like that in a long time, certainly not since I've retired, seeing how much happiness there was around the place was unbelievable," said Roberts. "Not just the people at the stadium had a huge amount of awe in that performance, but it touched everyone watching around the world. "There was so much joy out around Cardiffc, and that would be reflected across the country and for Welsh people across the globe."
