Headline: Somali Olympic boxer Ali weeps as world title dream realised
Body: Ramla Ali was the first boxer from Somalia to compete at an Olympics Ramla Ali secured her first world title at the age of 36 after defeating Mikiah Kreps in a split-decision victory in Arlington, Texas. The win is a crowning moment for the Briton, who fled a war-torn Somalia as a child before going on to become an Olympian, activist, author and now the WBO and IBF super-bantamweight champion. With her biopic about her remarkable life just released, Ali fulfilled a dream long in the making and that seemed far away when she was swept aside by Yamileth Mercado in her first attempt two years ago. An emotional Ali fell to her knees in tears as she was confirmed the winner with scorecards that read 97-92, 96-93 and 98-91 in her favour, dedicating the victory to her late father. "When we were in the changing room, my coach said, because my dad passed away in May, 'Do this for him'," Ali said. "That's where those emotions came out at the end, because I did it for my dad." "I can't put into words what this means to me and what this means to all of Somalia," she added. "I've hopefully inspired so many young girls and boys out there to dream big and that's all I've ever wanted to do." As Ali wept, there was devastation for Kreps who was convinced she had done enough to win the contest. The previously undefeated American suffered a knockdown in the third round, walking onto a flush left hook from Ali. Kreps was unhappy with the knockdown call but replays showed the heavy shot caused the 30-year-old's glove to touch the canvas as she tried to steady herself. With a 10-8 round in the bag, Ali was unable to build on the moment, having to stand firm as Kreps came storming back and applying constant pressure. Kreps outlanded Ali with 115 punches to 78 and secured 91 power shots to Ali's 70 and one judge certainly was convinced of her as a clear winner with a wide 98-91 scorecard. With the fight threatening to slip away from her in the second half, Ali said every round was a mental battle to rise from her stool. "I remember going to the corner every round and I remember saying 'I'm so tired, I can't do this'. All my coach responded was 'think about your dad, do this for your dad'. I think that really pushed me. I really boxed out of my skin, I was so knackered. I did it for him," Ali said. "Every time I went to the corner, I kept saying, 'I'm so tired. I'm so tired,' because your work rate was just next level." Ali speaking in 2022 as her and Crystal Garcia Nova became the first women to box as professionals in Saudi Arabia With two world titles secured, Ali could set her sights on an intriguing unification bout with Skye Nicolson after the Australia kept hold of her WBC belt on the undercard. Nicolson is also signed to Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions and beat Japan's Miyo Yoshida by unanimous decision. But Ali will for now celebrate her victory as she delivered yet another high point in an incredible life that might have seen as impossible when her family escaped Somalia when she was just a baby. Ali settled in London as a refugee and was the first Somali boxer to represent the nation as an Olympian at Tokyo 2020 before becoming the first Muslim woman to win an English title as an amateur. Since turning pro in late 2020, Ali has been proclaiming her goal to become world champion but saw her credentials in that department derailed in 2023 when she was knocked out in her ninth fight. As a model often on magazine covers, as well as a dedicated activist for young women running her own non-for-profit organisation Sisters club, many questioned why, and if, Ali should continue boxing. Those doubters grew louder with the 2023 world title disappointment, but Ali was not to be denied. Caroline Dubois was in Texas to watch Alycia Baumgardner move up to her weight class In the main event, Alycia Baumgardner had her post-fight victory speech interrupted by Caroline Dubois. Baumgardner, 32, outclassed Elif Nur Turhan to become a two-weight world champion by claiming the IBF lightweight belt. The victory sets Baumgardner on a collision course with British WBO and WBC champion Dubois, who fights WBA belt holder Stephanie Han in February. After Baumgardner said she wanted to be undisputed at lightweight, Dubois asked her 'are we going to fight' from ringside. The back-and-forth continued with 25-year-old Dubois repeatedly urging Baumgardner to commit to their contest, while the American insisted she needed to beat Han first. Dubois is unbeaten in 15 fights, but a victory over Baumgardner - an undisputed champion at super-featherweight and unbeaten since 2018 - would be a potentially career-defining win. Headline: Managerial 'inconsistency' hurting Ghana - Hughton
Body: Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout. The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month. Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty. The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia. "When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa. "You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager." Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32. However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman. But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra. "What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton. "And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score." Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there". Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right) Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived. Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast. The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years. Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time. Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s. With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent. "Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old. "You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher. "Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system." Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation. "In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said. "They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming. "The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be. "I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure." Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive. They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa. Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers. Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements. Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position. "Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated. "You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out. "There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that." With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren. As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step. *Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years? Headline: Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
Body: There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country. In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career. Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction. On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria. Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue. But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force. Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification. The ministry has defended , external Agnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised. But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic. Those selected are trained for months before being inducted into regiments When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force. But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces. "Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme. These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen. The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed. This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations. Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches. The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend. "The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says. The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported , external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment. Many young men from small towns spend months preparing for the selection process to join the defence forces But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers. Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued , external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills. Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years. "It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says. "Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight." Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment. Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI , external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer. But the change could create fresh challenges within military units. Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits. Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion. Indian soldiers are deployed through the year at the country's borders with China and Pakistan There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget , external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment. By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness. "We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods. He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience. Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment. "The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks. Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says. "We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that." The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment. The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes. For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career. But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

Headline: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
Body: Protesters in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Friday demanding a new minimum wage Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage. Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend. The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (Â£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP. Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (Â£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis. On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in. A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted. Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out. He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest". Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara. Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time. The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories. "BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said. "Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law." But critics say workers are being sacrificed for factories to churn out products at competitive prices. Joly Talukder, the vice president of the Garment Workers Trade Union Centre, told BBC's Newshour that "workers have carried the costs for years" while factory owners and global retailers profit from their exploitation. "They are asking for a wage they can survive on. How can any person of conscience stand against such a basic human demand?" she said. On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers. The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November. Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

Headline: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
Body: FBI redacted examples of the 900 victim videos secretly recorded by North Korean hackers State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say. More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman. This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) from the company. US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim. Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet. Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call â except that the audio would appear to malfunction. A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims. Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities. The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user". "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday. "If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

Headline: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
Body: Moment teen rescued after six days in Australian bush A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive. William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria. Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search. He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life". Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up. The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy. "He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added. "He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive." Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again." Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive. "It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

Headline: At least 24 killed after bus collides with truck in north-east India
Body: The crash took place on a highway bordering Kaziranga National Park in the Golaghat district of Assam At least 24 people have died and 11 others injured after a bus collided with a truck in Assam, north-east India. The accident happened near Kaziranga National Park, a Unesco World Heritage site, and the injured have been admitted to Jorhat Medical College and Hospital. Several of the deceased are college students, according to Assam's rural development minister Atul Bora, but they have not yet been publicly identified. Bora added that witnesses reported one of the vehicles may have been speeding when the crash took place, but "the exact reason will be known after [an investigation]". Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma wrote in a post on X that "the scale of this loss has shaken all of us". He adds: "Our foremost priority now is to make sure the injured receive the best possible medical care without delay." Family members of one of the victims pictured at the accident site The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon. Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous for its one-horned rhinoceroses. Nagaon is an important agricultural and commercial centre in central Assam, about 120km (74.5 miles) west of Bokakhat by road. Lurinjyoti Gogoi, chief of a regional opposition party, said road safety has long been a major concern in the state. "The government must take it up seriously," he said. Road accidents are responsible for thousands of deaths in India every year. In 2023, 172,000 people lost their lives on Indian roads, or 474 a day â roughly one every three minutes. The count increased to 183,382 deaths in 2025. Experts say the crisis is rooted not just in infrastructure but in human behaviour, enforcement gaps and systemic neglect. Headline: Indonesia's vice-president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
Body: President Prabowo (left) said he was sorry to lose Gibran Rakabuming Raka (right), who has been mired in a growing controversy over his high school credentials Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government. Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid. His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto. Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president. "[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia". "He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said. Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office. Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials. Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated. "No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said. It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion. The Supreme Court ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran. Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school. On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi said. Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival. Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40. But tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared. Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country. In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati. Last week, authorities arrested several senior officials, including presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation to Prabowo - on suspicions of wiretapping the president. Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi. Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration. But neither man has confirmed the rift. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Jokowi said he still supported Prabowo's leadership. Jokowi also said Gibran's resignation was part of "political dynamics" and he had told his son "the position was temporary". All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation. Across the country, students and activists have staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption. Headline: New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
Body: The newly opened Periyar Arivulagam library is at the centre of the allegations An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI. The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city. The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books. The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations. Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state. The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references. It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread. The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; Â£26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay. Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month. Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam. He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs). One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages. It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics. Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books. The library was inaugurated by Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean DrÃ¨ze as its author. The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean DrÃ¨ze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House. DrÃ¨ze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission. BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business. A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts. The controversy has prompted writers, academics and publishers to question how the books were selected for public libraries. More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have signed a joint statement calling for an independent inquiry, the release of procurement records and an audit of library collections across Tamil Nadu. They have also called for the recovery of public money if the investigation finds that funds were misused. The group questioned how the disputed books could have passed through a selection process involving expert committees, price negotiations and several levels of review. The state government has ordered an internal audit of public library collections. Rajmohan said 523 books had already been removed from the historic Connemara Public Library in Chennai city after preliminary checks raised concerns about their authenticity and quality. Disputed books have also been removed from Periyar Arivulagam, while anti-corruption officials examine procurement records and inspect other libraries, he added. The controversy also sparked a political row in Tamil Nadu. Rajmohan accused the previous DMK government of ordering the disputed books and said the state would seek to recover public money if the investigation found wrongdoing. The DMK has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and has called for an investigation into the purchases.

Headline: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
Body: India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissent Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory." Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained . The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire. The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent. The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security". This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests. But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University. The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister "They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement." The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online. "It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations. "The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority." Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar. In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms. Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat. Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun. His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed". The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy "We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month. Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly. Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum. CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar. The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court. Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders. "We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer. Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect. "A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College. The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP. Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November "Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order." The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent. Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence". Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape. Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress. "Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added. They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views. Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India. CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents. Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc , an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities. CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation. When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling. "I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."
